en: Preface to the *Dazhuojie* (Excellently Elucidated) of the *Lotus Sūtra*:
All sūtras are rules for practice; however, the wondrous meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* alone provides earnest guidance.

It earnestly demonstrates the gates of skillful means (*upāya-dvāra*) through various parables and various manifestations of transformative power, endeavoring to cause those who have not yet believed to believe.

Those who have not yet understood are led to understanding; those who have not yet attained goodness are brought to goodness; and those already established in goodness are caused to increase it. Vertically, this extends through the three periods of time;

horizontally, it spans the ten directions. Everywhere it awakens people to veneration; in every place it inspires solemnity and obedience. Through the provisional, the real is revealed, and the true essence of that reality leaps forth in the very act of being expressed.
By means of the one, the three are suspended, and the ultimate destination of those three lies latent in the process of approaching it.

Outside the steps, I am eighty-five years of age; my physical vigor declines daily, and my resources are increasingly strained. Reflecting back, I have not yet repaid the Great Kindness, and time slips away like a galloping horse through a crevice.
I have urgently collected various treatises on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, among which the annotated commentary by the Master Zhiyi of Tiantai is the most detailed.

That Master elucidated the four teachings—*āgama*, *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*, and *bodhisattva* (the *zang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan* teachings). Within the *āgama* teaching, the Bodhisattva Vehicle is generally classified as...
I am not without lingering doubts regarding the *Xiao zhuang*. Furthermore, having examined the National Teacher Qingliang’s *Wujiao zhiguan*, I have extracted its complete system.

I have meticulously analyzed every sentence and section of the seven fascicles to provide appropriate exegesis. As soon as I had completed the transcription of these volumes, I entrusted them to the engravers.
It is as if reviving the spirit of the ancient worthies who held candles to roam at night;

it also enables one to read with speed, so that the mind and eyes may quickly find clarity, like the bright sun adorning the heavens, where all myriad phenomena receive its brilliance and are illuminated by its light.
This commentary on the sutra is clear and lucid, serving as a guide for oneself and others. May it bring merit to the Dharma-treasure, benefit to the human heart, and advantage to...

How could the world and future generations [benefit] from this? To be preoccupied with deliberating upon what constitutes the "wondrous Dharma" or what constitutes the "lotus flower" is to fail to perceive the fundamental root;
it is merely to seek branches and pluck leaves—what benefit could such things possibly provide?
In the second month of summer in the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, Xu Changzhi, having performed his ablutions,
inscribed this upon the first fascicle of the *Excellently Explicated Sutra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Law* (Miaofa Lianhua Jing Zhuojie),
originally translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Commentary by Xu Changzhi, the Wayman of Wuyuan, for the Zhou Family.

Chapter One: The Prologue (The term "xu" [prologue] means sequence, cause, or narration. Items of similar meaning and category are gathered into a single section; hence it is called a "pin" [chapter]).

(One further perfects the origin of the Dharma; since it is not a form, how could it admit of words? If you truly wish with a compassionate heart to seek its source, know that from the beginning there has never been two kinds of heavens. Thus have I heard.
[Thus it was said. Referring to the sūtra, Ānanda declared for himself: "I have heard this from the Buddha.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain.

[At one time. When the Buddha was assembled with the great assembly. "Buddha" means awakening; he awakens himself and awakens others. In the city of Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra, together with a thousand kings, established the city and resided among the five mountains.
"Dwelling" means residing here to preach the Dharma. Gṛdhrakūṭa means Vulture Peak.]
(Śākyamuni Buddha preached this sutra in three assemblies. The middle assembly was held within the Stūpa of Many Treasures, while the first and last assemblies were both held on this mountain.)
He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.

(Great refers to their dignified capacity, possessing the Great Way, the Great Function, and Great Wisdom. Bhikṣu means "mendicant," for they beg the Dharma from the Buddha and beg for food from others. Assembly is the Sanskrit term *saṃgha*, which here means "harmonious community. Arhat means "one who is unattached," "unborn," or "worthy of offerings.

Worthy of offerings means being worthy of receiving the offerings of humans and devas throughout the ten directions. Unborn means not giving rise to any deluded thoughts, karma, or conditions. Unattached means being free from all worldly passions.)
He was free from attachment to form;
all taints were exhausted, and he was no longer subject to afflictions. Having attained his own welfare, he had destroyed the fetters of existence and his mind had attained mastery.

(Regarding "outflows" [āsrava]: there are three outflows—the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance. All causes and effects within the three realms are termed "other," while the merit of wisdom and abandonment is termed "self. Regarding "mastery": it is the full possession of meditative concentration and wisdom.)
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya (Ājñāta is his name;
Kauṇḍinya is his clan; Kaśyapa is his surname, meaning "Drinker of Light"; Mahā means "Great").

Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—these three brothers, in a former life during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, together erected a sacrificial pillar. The elder brother served as the preceptor to King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples; each of the two younger brothers likewise had two hundred and fifty.
Because the Buddha performed ten kinds of supernatural transformations, the teachers and their disciples were all subdued and entered the monastic life under the Buddha.
Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

(Śāri means "due to his mother, Mṛgī"; putra means "son. Thus he is called Śāriputra. Among the disciples, Maugalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers, being able to travel by flight to the ten directions).
Mahākātyāyana (who was foremost among those who skillfully analyzed meanings and expounded the teachings of the Way). Aniruddha.

(He was named Ruci. In the past, during a time of famine, he offered millet rice to a pratyekabuddha. Consequently, for ninety-one kalpas, he experienced the bliss of his desires among gods and humans.)
Kapphiṇa and Gavāmpati (Kapphiṇa: Kaphiṇa is the name of a lunar mansion;

he was born because his parents prayed to the mansion Kaphiṇa. Gavāmpati: Upon hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, he immediately said, "The Buddha has passed away; I too shall pass away").
Revata. Pindola Bharadvaja. (Revata: a name for a constellation;
one who sits in meditation and enters samādhi with an undisturbed mind. Bharadvaja: "bha" means residual habit, referring to the habitual tendencies of a Brahmin.)
Bakkula and Mahākauṣṭhila (Kauṣṭhila means "Fine Appearance";
he was one hundred and sixty years old. Kauṣṭhila means "Great Thighs"; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra).
Nanda; Sunda-ra-nanda (Nanda means "well-joyful";
Sundara means "beautifully lovely," which is the name of his wife).

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (Pūrṇa is translated as "Fulfilling the Vow," which is his father's name; Maitrāyaṇī is translated as "Compassion," which is his mother's name; "putra" is a general term for a woman).
Subhūti (Subhūti means "Born of Emptiness" and is also named "Good Fortune"), Ānanda, and Rāhula.
(Ānanda, named "Joy," was of vast and extensive learning; Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, meaning "Covering and Obstructing," was a biological son of the Buddha).
Such were the great arhats, renowned and well-known to the masses.
(This assembly of many kinsmen and acquaintances is, in its entirety, the nature of the single Dharmakāya; it is the name of the single Dharmakāya).
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those still in training and those beyond training.
(To investigate the truth and sever delusions is called "Learning" (*śaikṣa*); to exhaustively realize the truth and eliminate all delusions is called "Beyond Learning" (*aśaikṣa*).
Mahāprajāpatī, the bhikṣuṇī, together with her retinue of six thousand people.
Pāṭī (also known as Mahāprajāpatī),
Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, and the bhikṣuṇīs, together with their retinues, were also present.
There were eighty thousand bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

*Anuttara* (An) is translated as "none" (*wu*); *samyak* (Nu) is translated as "above" (*shang*); *sambodhi* (San) is translated as "correct" (*zheng*); *mārga* (Miao) is translated as "equal" (*deng*); and *bodhi* (Puti) is translated as "awakening" (*jue*). Thus, it is the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Correct Awakening. "Non-retrogression" refers to non-retrogression in stage, non-retrogression in practice, and non-retrogression in mindfulness.

"Perfectly equal" means "one and the same. In this one and same Dharma-body, looking upward, one does not see the sanctity of the Buddhas; looking downward, one does not see the ordinariness of sentient beings. Looking around the four quarters, one does not see the differences among the myriad species; looking within oneself, one does not see the distinctions of the three periods of time.

Furthermore, Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) perfectly encompasses the ten directions and the three periods of time; there is nothing that is not awakened. This is called the Mahāyāna: it broadly contains the ten directions and the three periods of time, with nothing that is not carried upon it. It is precisely as the saying goes: "In the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly present;
upon awakening, all is empty, and the great chiliocosm vanishes."
They all attained dhāraṇīs and the eloquence of joyful exposition (dhāraṇī means "total retention").
They turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
(The meaning of "wheel-turning" is also the meaning of "crushing and grinding," as it subdues all Māras and non-Buddhists).
Having made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, he encountered the roots of manifold virtues in the presence of those Buddhas and was constantly praised by them.
(He opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; having known and seen his own Dharma, he is identical to all Buddhas, and is therefore praised by all Buddhas).
He cultivates his body with loving-kindness, skillfully enters the Buddha’s wisdom, and attains mastery over great insight.
His body pervades the Dharma-realm; his compassion is universal. With the threefold wisdom in a single mind, he is said to have attained thorough penetration.
Having reached the other shore, his fame is heard everywhere throughout immeasurable worlds.
(Perfect virtue is true; it accords with its name.
It is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, (relying upon the ten dharma realms to establish their protection and salvation).
Their names were Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Mañju means "wondrous virtue";
Śrī means "illumination that penetrates to the ultimate nature," which is termed "contemplation").
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta and the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
(Mahāsthāmaprāpta’s planting of his feet causes the world and the palaces of Māra to tremble; Sadāprarudita follows sentient beings through kalpas without abandoning them.)
The Bodhisattva Never-Relaxing (Aksayamati),
the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi (named so because his mind never rests and his hands can produce Buddhas),
and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
(Medicine can cure the two kinds of illness—of body and mind—of sentient beings.
Vīradatta Bodhisattva, Ratnacandra Bodhisattva, Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Pūrṇacandra Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva of Boundless Power; the Bodhisattva Who Transcends the Three Realms;

[the one who bestows the Dharma upon sentient beings is named] Brave Bestower (Vīradatta); [the one who clearly realizes the three truths is named] Jewel Moon (Ratnacandra); [the one whose three wondrous wisdoms eliminate darkness is named] Moonlight (Candraprabha); [whose three wisdoms are without deficiency like the full moon, and whose object and wisdom are merged in profound stillness, possessing great power and function].
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla (Bhadra means "well-guarded" or "noble-headed"; Maitreya is the clan name for "the Compassionate One").
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāstṛ, and eighty thousand such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas were all present together.
(Ratnakūṭa means "Jewel Heap"; Śāstṛ means "Teacher," who gathers the path of wisdom and causes others to enter the Right Path.)
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras (Śakra is also called "The Able One";
he is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven), was present.
Furthermore, there were the devaputra Candraka, the devaputra Samantagandha,
and the devaputra Ratnaprabha (these three devaputras were ministers of Śakra, like high-ranking officials).
The Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues and ten thousand devaputras—
(the Four Heavenly Kings are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals, residing on the four sides of Mount Sumeru).
The Devaputra Īśvara and the Devaputra Maheśvara, together with their retinues of thirty thousand devaputras;
and the Lord of the Sahā World, Brahmā Śikhin, Mahābrahmā Prabhāsa, and others, together with their retinues of twelve thousand devaputras.
(Brahmā is a Western [Indic] term; here it is translated as "Free from Desire. Śikhin is translated as "Topknot. Prabhāsa refers to the gods of the Second Dhyāna Heaven and so forth).
There are eight dragon kings: the Dragon King Nanda and the Dragon King Upananda.
(Nanda means "Joy"; Upananda means "Excellent. These two dragons constantly protect the kingdom.
Sāgara Dragon King and Vāsuki Dragon King.
The Nāga King Kāla (translated as "Salt Sea"), the Nāga King Śaṅkhapāla (translated as "Many Heads"),
the Nāga King Takṣaka, and the Nāga King Anavatapta.
The Naga King Karkoṭaka (translated as "Manifesting Poison"), the Naga King Takṣaka (translated as "Free from Affliction"),
the Naga King Manasvin, the Naga King Utpala, and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
(Na-si means "great body" and "great strength. Pra-bha is translated as "dark-colored lotus," referring to those who dwell supported by a pond).
There were four Kinnara kings: Dharmakinnara-rāja, Sudharmakinnara-rāja, Mahādharmakinnara-rāja, and Dharmadhara-kinnara-rāja, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
(Kinnaras are divine beings who resemble humans but have a single horn; thus they are called "non-humans. They are the deities of the Dharma-music of the Heavenly Lord.

There were four Gandharva kings: the Gandharva King of Music, the Gandharva King of Musical Sound, the Gandharva King of Beauty, and the Gandharva King of Beautiful Sound. Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
(Gandharvas—meaning "those who smell fragrance"—subsist on fragrances; they are the deities of the secular music of the Heavenly Emperor.
There are four asura kings: the asura king Bali, the asura king Kharaskandha, [the asura king Vemacitra, and the asura king Rāhu].
The asura king Vemacitrin and the asura king Rāhu each came accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
(Asura means "not upright"; Khaṇḍa means "broad-shouldered"; Citra means "pure mind"; and Rāhu means "obstructing-holder," for he is able to obstruct the sun and moon.)
There were four garuḍa kings: the garuḍa king Mahātejas, the garuḍa king Mahākāya, the garuḍa king Mahāpūrṇa, and the garuḍa king Manojña;
they were accompanied by their respective retinues of many hundreds of thousands.

(Garuḍa—translated as "Golden Winged"—possesses a wish-fulfilling jewel on its neck and takes dragons as food. It possesses great majesty and virtue because it overawes all dragons with its power; it is "Greatly Satisfied" because the dragons it devours always fully satisfy its own desires).
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of attendants—(Vaidehī means "she who contemplates";

she was the mother of King Ajātaśatru. Ajātaśatru means "the one whose enmity was not yet born. On the day he was born, a physiognomist divined that this child, once born, would harm his father; therefore, he was named "the one whose enmity was not yet born")— *Note: The provided text contains a partial definition of the names Vaidehī and Ajātaśatru, which has been integrated into the translation for clarity.*

Each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side. At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, honored, revered, and praised him.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Innumerable Meanings*, which is the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas.
Protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha.
(The Mahāyāna sūtras have seven greatnesses: greatness of dharma, greatness of mind, greatness of understanding, greatness of purity, greatness of adornment, and greatness of time.)
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings; his body and mind were unmoving.

(Samādhi means "regulated and upright concentration," or "right concentration," which is also called "right reception. Immeasurable Meanings refers to the mutual perfection of wisdom and concentration. To "enter" means to maintain control over body and mind.)

At that time, the heavens rained down māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly. The entire buddha-world shook in six ways.

*Maṇḍārava* means "pleasing to the mind"; it is a white flower. *Māñjūṣaka* means "soft and supple"; it is a red flower. As for the six kinds [of earth tremors]: shaking, rising, and surging—these three are movements of form; quaking, roaring, and crashing—these three are sounds.
At that time, the great assembly in the gathering— monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as the various minor kings and universal monarchs—
attained what they had never experienced before. With joy, they joined their palms and focused their minds with single-minded devotion.

Observing the Buddhas: (The dragons, ghosts, and others who are permitted to attend the Dharma assembly; because their vehicle-zeal is urgent while their precept-observance is lax. Due to the urgency of their vehicle-zeal, they are able to hear the Dharma; due to the laxity of their precept-observance, they fall into the realms of dragons and ghosts. *Māraga*: the great-bellied serpent deity.)

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception. (As for this white tuft:

when the Buddha was first born, it was five feet long; during his period of ascetic practice, it grew to fourteen feet; upon attaining Buddhahood, it reached fifteen feet. It is hollow both inside and out, pure within and without.)

Within this world, one sees that land in its entirety; thus, there is no interval between the forms and emptiness of the ten directions. At this Buddha’s site, one hears that Buddha preaching the Dharma; thus, there is no interval in the principle.

Within a single moment, one sees all bhikṣus practicing the myriad deeds, passing through infinite kalpas, attaining Buddhahood, delivering sentient beings, and entering Great Nirvāṇa, with people later erecting stupas for them; thus, there is no interval between the three periods of time, the past, and the present. For the essence of the wondrous Dharma is precisely the wondrous mind inherently possessed by humans.

This wondrous mind is vast without boundary and minute enough to enter a speck of dust; it has no beginning before and no end after. Because people are ignorant of this mind, our Buddha manifested this very wondrous mind perfectly within the light-mark between his eyebrows—namely, the lands of the ten directions.
The earth-circle manifests this wondrous mind.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above, within this world, one sees in their entirety the sentient beings of the six realms of existence in those lands.

(Avīci means "without interval. Nirmāṇarati refers to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where there is no obstruction. The six destinies are: devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, pretas, and animals. *Gati* means "destiny" or "course of rebirth.")
Furthermore, they see the Buddhas currently residing in those lands and hear the sutras and teachings spoken by those Buddhas (the teachings of those Buddhas and this Buddha are identical).

And he also saw those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who were practicing the path and had attained realization (the "practitioners" refers to those cultivating the practices of the truths, conditions, and perfections across the three vehicles;
the "attainers of the path" refers to those who have attained the path of seeing and the path of cultivation).
Furthermore, he saw various bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, practicing the bodhisattva path through various causes and conditions, various inclinations and understandings, and various characteristics.
(Whether it be that Buddha or this Buddha, after the Tripitaka, the intended meaning of what was taught is the same).
Furthermore, one sees various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa; furthermore, one sees, after the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, [the veneration of] the Buddha’s relics.

He erected a stūpa made of the seven treasures (when that Buddha entered nirvāṇa, a stūpa was erected; this is the same as for the Buddhas of this land. Nirvāṇa is called "Great Parinirvāṇa. "Great" refers to the *dharmakāya*; "extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to *vimukti*; and "crossing over" (*pāra*) refers to *prajñā*).
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests these signs of supernatural transformation.
For what cause and condition does such an auspicious omen exist? Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into samādhi;
this is an inconceivable and rare occurrence. Whom should I ask about this? Who is able to answer?"

(Maitreya, because the Buddha emitted light that perfectly manifested the ten directions and the three periods of time, gave rise to doubt. Not knowing that the ten directions and the three periods of time were fundamentally complete within himself, Maitreya was narrow-minded; thus, he posed his questions in successive layers.)
He further thought to himself: "This Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, has already personally approached and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
he must surely perceive this rare and wondrous sign. I shall now question him.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, all formed this same thought.
He reflected: "This is the mark of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal powers. Whom should I now ask? (The spirit is named Heavenly Mind;
the faculty of penetration is named Wisdom Nature).
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts, further observed the fourfold assembly: the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others in the assembly, with one mind, asked Mañjuśrī:

"By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared, emitting a great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, such that the adornments of those buddha-fields are all clearly seen? Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva...
Sāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
“Mañjuśrī, for what reason does the Guide emit from the white tuft between his eyebrows a great light that shines everywhere, raining down *māndārava* and *mañjūṣaka* flowers?”
The sandalwood-scented breeze gladdens the hearts of all; by this cause and condition, the earth is everywhere adorned and purified.
When this world shakes in six ways, the fourfold assembly is filled with joy, their bodies and minds feeling a sense of sublime ease.

An unprecedented experience occurred (the fragrance belongs to the flowers; the fragrance of the flowers is like sandalwood, hence it is called "sandalwood-scented wind"; the flowers gather upon the ground, and the ground thus becomes adorned and pure).
The light from between his eyebrows shines upon the eastern quarter,
so that eighteen thousand lands all become the color of gold. From the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
throughout all worlds, it illuminates the realms of birth and death where beings of the six destinies pass.
The karmic conditions of good and evil deeds, and the resulting retributions of beauty or ugliness—
all these are seen here; furthermore, one beholds the Buddhas, the Holy Lords and Lions,
who proclaim the sutras that are subtle and supreme, their voices pure, emitting gentle sounds.
He instructs countless billions of bodhisattvas with a Brahma-voice, profound and wondrous,
which delights the ear. In each world, he expounds the True Dharma through various causes and conditions, illuminating the Buddha-dharma with immeasurable parables.

Awakening sentient beings (The "Holy Lord" refers to the sovereign among all Bodhisattvas. His lion-like roar resounds like a thunderous bellow, a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to crush and subdue the armies of Māra, demonstrating his ten powers to the assembly).
If there are people who encounter suffering and weary of old age, illness, and death,

I preach for them the Nirvana that brings an end to all suffering. If there are people with merit who have made offerings to the Buddhas and aspire to the supreme Dharma, I preach for them the Pratyekabuddha path.
(Śrāvakas plant the seeds of merit over three lifetimes; Pratyekabuddhas plant the seeds of merit over a hundred kalpas.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices and seek supreme wisdom, for them he preaches the path of purity.

(They are called "sons of the Buddha" because they inherit the lineage of the Buddha through true compassion. They are said to have "various practices" because they cultivate the six perfections. They are said to possess "unsurpassed wisdom" because they seek the path of the Buddha. They are said to have a "pure path" because among the six perfections, they are free from the six defilements.)
Mañjuśrī, while I dwell here, I have seen and heard such things as these, numbering in the thousands of billions;
though they are so numerous, I shall now briefly describe what I saw in that land:
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, through various causes and conditions.

And they seek the Buddha-way [as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges (the *Gaṅgā*; fine and many; non-Buddhists call it the "River of Merit" and enter its waters to wash away sins; the Buddha also conforms to worldly custom and thus constantly refers to it).
There are those who practice giving— gold, silver, coral, pearls,
mani-jewels, conch shells, agate, diamonds, and various rare treasures; male and female slaves, vehicles,
and precious ornamental litters and carriages— joyfully bestowing these gifts and dedicating them toward the Buddha-way.
May I obtain this vehicle, supreme within the three realms and praised by all Buddhas.
Or perhaps there may be bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings, flower canopies,
and elegant decorations.
(Chopped off. This refers to carriages used by those of the rank of Great Officer and above.
Again I see Bodhisattvas giving their flesh, hands, feet, And even their wives and children to seek the Unsurpassed Way; Furthermore, I see Bodhisattvas giving Their heads, eyes, and bodies.
Delighting in giving, they seek the wisdom of a Buddha. Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings who,
having gone to the presence of the Buddha, inquired about the unsurpassed path,
and then abandoned their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and consorts to shave off their hair and beards.

And yet, one wears the Dharma robes (that which is questioned as most venerable is called the Unsurpassed Way; that which is discarded without contempt is called the Land of Bliss; "shaving off" means that both body and mind are detached).
Sometimes one sees a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in quietude and delighting in reciting the sūtras;
again, one sees a bodhisattva who, with courageous vigor, enters deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way; and again, one sees one who is free from desire.

Constantly dwelling in seclusion, he deeply cultivates meditative concentration and attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*)—[free from the desires of the desire realm and free from the desires of the two vehicles; while ordinary beings possess only the five powers, those of the two vehicles possess all six].
Again, I see Bodhisattvas in tranquil meditation with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses. Furthermore,
I see Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm,
able to question the Buddhas and, upon hearing [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
(Deep in wisdom, his insight exhausts the root of principle; firm in resolve, his vows are vast.

Furthermore, he sees a son of the Buddha, fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom, who expounds the Dharma for the multitude using immeasurable analogies, delighting in the preaching of the Dharma and transforming all bodhisattvas.
He destroys the hosts of Māra and beats the Dharma drum.

(Regarding "destroys the hosts of Māra": the contemplation of emptiness destroys the four Māras; the contemplation of the conventional destroys the eight Māras; the contemplation of the Middle Way likewise destroys the eight Māras. This [first] Māra can rob one of life; the remaining affliction-māra, the aggregate-māra, and the celestial lord-māra can rob one of the life-force of wisdom.
Regarding "beats the Dharma drum": it means one should turn the Wheel of Dharma, first using the truly wondrous Brahma-voice to awaken sentient beings.)
Again, I see Bodhisattvas sitting in silent, tranquil stillness; though devas and nāgas pay them homage, they do not feel joy.
Again, I see Bodhisattvas dwelling in the forests, emitting light to rescue those in the hells from suffering and lead them into the Buddha-way. Again, I see the Sons of the Buddha.
Never having slept, he practiced walking meditation in the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way;
furthermore, seeing those endowed with full precepts whose majestic deportment was flawless and pure as a precious jewel,
he sought the Buddha-way.

(There are ten [aspects] of ethical discipline: first, unimpaired; second, unbroken; third, unpierced; fourth, untorn; fifth, conforming to the Path; sixth, unattached; seventh, praised by the wise; eighth, sovereign; ninth, conforming to meditative concentration; tenth, complete).
Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha dwelling in the power of patience;
though arrogant people revile and beat them, they are able to endure it all in their quest for the path of the Buddha.
(Their inner minds remain tranquil, enduring the insults from without.)
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who have abandoned all frivolous laughter and foolish associates, and who draw near to the wise;

with single-mindedness they eliminate distraction and concentrate their mindfulness in mountain forests for hundreds of thousands of millions of years in order to seek the Buddha-way. Or one sees Bodhisattvas...
Delicacies and fine foods, hundreds of kinds of medicinal decoctions,
and renowned robes and superior garments worth ten million, or priceless garments, offered to the Buddha and the Sangha—
ten thousand myriad billions of such items, including sandalwood and precious caskets.
Various exquisite bedding, offered to the Buddha and the Sangha;
pure gardens with flourishing flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools—
offering such things as these to the Buddha and the Sangha, diverse and subtle, with joy that never tires.
Seeking the unsurpassed path, there may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescence through various instructions for countless sentient beings.
(Quiescence is the principle; that which is preached is the causal condition.)
Or one may see a bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena,
which is without dual characteristics and is like empty space (the nature of phenomena is empty; practice in accordance with this nature).
Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha whose minds are free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom;
Mañjuśrī, I also see bodhisattvas after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa making offerings to the śarīra relics; I also see sons of the Buddha.
He constructed countless stūpas and temples, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; adorning the realm with these sublime jeweled stūpas,
each five thousand yojanas in height and exactly two thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
with a thousand banners and streamers upon each individual stūpa and temple.
With pearl-encrusted canopies and jeweled bells chiming in harmony, gods, nāgas, spirits, humans,
and non-humans constantly provide offerings of incense, flowers,
and music to Mañjuśrī and the sons of the Buddhas, in order to honor the śarīra relics.
The stupas and temples are magnificently adorned; the realm of the land is naturally transformed,
exceptionally wondrous and beautiful like the king of celestial trees (the Pārijātaka tree), its flowers in full bloom.
The Buddha emits a single ray of light; I and the assembled multitude behold this realm with its various wonders and excellencies.
Through the spiritual power of all Buddhas, their wisdom is rare and marvelous as they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands; we behold this.
An unprecedented occurrence has occurred! O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly.
The fourfold community looks up to you with joy; they gaze upon you and upon me. For what reason, World-Honored One, have you emitted this radiance?
O Son of the Buddha, answer now, resolving our doubts and bringing us joy.
For what benefit does he emit this light? Is it because the Buddha wishes to proclaim the sublime Dharma attained while seated at the site of enlightenment?
Or is it to bestow predictions of future buddhahood and reveal the various Buddha-lands, adorned with all manner of jewels and purified, as well as to allow us to behold those Buddhas?

"This is no small matter—and it concerns me as well. I wish for you to question me, and I wish for you to receive your answer from me. Mañjuśrī then said, "I and you both dwell on the stage of training; we wish to fathom the Buddha’s intent, yet it is difficult to deliberate upon together."
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the devas are all gazing upon you, venerable one;
what is it that you intend to speak?
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and the other great beings, as well as the virtuous sons...

"O sons, as I reflect—'reflect' (wei) meaning to contemplate, and 'measure' (cun) meaning to deliberate; contemplating the present as it was in the past, and measuring the past as it is in the present."

Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, desires to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the great rain of Dharma, to blow the great conch shell of Dharma, to beat the great drum of Dharma, and to expound the great meaning of Dharma.
Sons of good family, in the past, I have witnessed this omen among the Buddhas of the past:
after emitting such light, they immediately proclaimed the Great Dharma. Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so; he desires to—
All sentient beings are able to hear and know this Dharma, which is difficult for all the worlds to believe; therefore, he manifests this auspicious omen (to cause sentient beings to hear and know:

"hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing; it gathers the immeasurable into one, transforms the teachings and principles of the Three Vehicles, shatters ignorance and the like, and reveals the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; hence it is called a Dharma difficult to believe).

(Manjusri replied: "In the past, amidst the assemblies of former Buddhas, I once saw the emission of light, which perfectly manifested throughout the assemblies of the worlds of the ten directions and unified the three periods of time as they preached the Lotus Sutra. Today, the Buddha has likewise emitted light that perfectly manifests;
from this I know that the Buddha is about to preach the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra.")
"O sons of good family, it has been immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past.

(Immeasurable and boundless refers to a vast numerical magnitude. Because the human mind is narrow and small, one does not spontaneously realize the nature inherently possessed within. The Buddha manifests great radiance to cause every person to suddenly awaken to their original nature; such is its greatness.)"
At that time, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

(Asaṃkhyeya means "immeasurable. One who is free from falsehood is named Tathāgata. One who is a true field of merit is named Arhat. One who knows the dharma-realm is named Samyaksaṃbuddha. One who possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna. One who does not regress is named Sugata. One who knows the realms of sentient beings and lands is named Lokavid.

One who has no equal is named Anuttara. One who tames the minds of others is named Puruṣadamyasārathi. One who serves as the eye for sentient beings is named Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām. One who knows the three categories of beings is named Buddha.)

He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life of Brahma-faring.
(This Mañjuśrī cites the ancient Buddhas; the seven virtues of the Sudden Teaching are identical to those of the present Buddha).
For those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate Nirvāṇa.

For those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. For all Bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Six Perfections.

Pāramitā. (Because they open the Buddha’s vocal teachings, they are called Śrāvakas. Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path—these four are all examined as true and not false; therefore, they are named the Four Truths. Nirvāṇa is the Nirvāṇa of True Emptiness. Pratyekabuddha refers to the Pratyekabuddha [or Solitary Realizer].

This passage shows Mañjuśrī citing ancient Buddhas to reveal the Middle Vehicle. As for the Six Pāramitās: giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—each also reaches the other shore. Mañjuśrī cites ancient Buddhas to reveal the Bodhisattva Vehicle of the Six Perfections.)
He caused them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and to perfect the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Next, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa; next, yet another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
In this manner, twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, titled Candrasūryapradīpa, and likewise shared the same clan name, Vairadeva. Maitreya,
You should know that the first Buddha and the last Buddha were both of the same name, Sūryacandrapradīpa, fully endowed with the ten titles;
the Dharma they preached was good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.

(The single characteristic, the characteristic of quiescence; that which is able to know and understand all various types of phenomena is called the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha.)

(First, citing one Buddha, he fully enumerates the teachings of the sudden and gradual vehicles, which are identical to those of the present Buddha. Next, citing twenty thousand Buddhas, these too are identical to the present Buddha. *Phalada*—this is translated as "Swift," and also as "Sharp-facultied.")

When that last Buddha was still a layman, he had eight princes: the first was named Meaningful, the second Good Meaning, the third Immeasurable Meaning, the fourth Jewel Meaning, the fifth Increasing Meaning, the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Meaning, the seventh Resonance Meaning, and the eighth Dharma Meaning.
These eight princes possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, each governing four continents.

When the princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal positions and likewise followed him into the homeless life.
They resolved upon the Mahāyāna path and constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). All became Dharma-preachers;
they had already planted various roots of goodness under the presence of ten million Buddhas.

In the past there were eight sons of the Buddha; now there is one son of the Buddha. The significance of these matters is the same: they have both resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna, which refers to the Four Great Vows; they have both practiced the Brahma-vihāras of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Twenty thousand Buddhas shared the same name, signifying that those of the Two Vehicles share the same virtues.

Since the virtues and natures of those of the Two Vehicles are identical, and since there are none among ordinary beings who are not likewise identical, it is called the "Final Buddha. The eight sons are the eight consciousnesses; therefore, they are all termed "mind" (*manas*).
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Ananta-artha*, a teaching for bodhisattvas and that which is protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Ananta-artha-vyūha-samādhi*, remaining with body and mind unmoving.
At that moment, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers.
Rohita flowers, mañjuṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjuṣaka flowers were scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
The entire buddha-world shook in six ways. At that time, within the assembly, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās].
The upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans,
as well as the minor kings, universal monarchs (cakravartin), and the rest of this great assembly, having attained what they had never experienced before,
rejoiced with palms joined and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion. At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The light of these marks shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as we see them now.

These Buddha-lands were exactly like this when the former Buddhas manifested the six portents within their own lands; they were entirely identical to what we see today. From this, we know that the six portents manifested by those former Buddhas in other lands were likewise identical to what we see now.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who desired to hear the Dharma.

When these bodhisattvas saw this light universally illuminating the Buddha-field, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested.
(Formerly, within the assembly of the Buddha, there was a doubt; this is the same as the doubt of Maitreya now).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Myōkō (Prabhāsa), who had eight hundred disciples.

In the past, when the Buddha arose from meditative concentration, he preached the sutra through the medium of Prabhāsvareśvara; now, when the Buddha arises from meditative concentration, he preaches the sutra through the medium of Śāriputra. In the past, the Buddha had eight sons who took Prabhāsvareśvara as their teacher; when the Tathāgata arose from concentration, he addressed Prabhāsvareśvara and entrusted [the teachings] to him.
Now, the Buddha’s son Rāhula likewise takes Śāriputra as his teacher; the Buddha’s arising from concentration and his entrustment are identical.

At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi and, through the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Dharma taught for bodhisattvas and protected by the Buddhas. For sixty intermediate kalpas, he did not rise from his seat.
Those in the assembly who were listening likewise remained seated in one place for sixty intermediate kalpas, their bodies and minds unmoving as they listened to the Buddha’s teaching.
It was said that it lasted for the duration of a meal. During this time, not a single person among the assembly—neither in body nor mind—experienced weariness or fatigue.

(In the past, when the former Buddhas preached the sutras, the duration was equal to an eon; whereas here, "a meal's time" refers to half a day. Because of their resolve to hear the Dharma and the Buddha’s majestic power, they sat through the entire period, forgetting its length.)
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas,
he spoke these words amidst the assembly of Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, and asuras: "Today, at midnight,
the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."

In the past, when the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra, he immediately entered parinirvāṇa; this is the same as for the present Buddha. "Brahmā" refers to the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), who is also the lord of the three realms. "Māra" is the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Śramaṇa" means "diligent in cessation"; it refers to one who diligently practices various virtues and brings all evils to rest.
"Brāhmaṇa" means "pure conduct," referring to those among the non-Buddhist paths who have left the household life.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa. The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prediction, addressing the bhikṣus:
"This bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a buddha, titled Viśuddhakāya, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

(Regarding "bestowal and prediction": "bestowal" refers to the transmission of the sacred word; "prediction" refers to the granting of a prophecy in accordance with one's mental aspiration. *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One. *Arhat* is translated as "Worthy of Offerings. *Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Perfectly All-Knowing.
These are three of the ten titles [of a Buddha], cited here in brief.)
After the Buddha had bestowed this prophecy, he entered *nirvāṇa* without remainder during the middle watch of the night.
Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (*Prabhāketu*) upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor *kalpas*.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Wonderful Light as their teacher; through his instruction and transformation, they were made firm in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. These princes made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas;
they have all already attained the Way of the Buddha. The last among them to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.
(Dīpaṃkara: because when the Prince was born, light like that of a lamp shone from all parts of his body).
Among the eight hundred disciples, there was one named Yaśaskāma. He was greedy for gain and offerings;
although he recited many sūtras, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned, and so he was called Yaśaskāma. This man also planted various [roots of merit]...

By reason of these roots of goodness, they shall encounter immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring them, respecting them, and praising them.
Maitreya, you should know this: who else could that Bodhisattva Wonderful Light have been at that time? It was none other than my own self. Who was the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame?
It was none other than you yourself. Seeing this present auspicious sign, it is no different from what occurred in the past; for this reason, consider it well.
He reflected: "Today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, amidst the great assembly, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

(Manjusri takes up what was previously said and reiterates it once more: "The Buddhas of antiquity were thus; the Buddhas of the present are thus; even the Buddhas of the ten directions are thus. All of them open the three and reveal the one—the single path without duality.")
I recall that in the past, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, there was a Buddha, the Honored One among Men, named Candrasūryapradīpa.

That World-Honored One expounded the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and countless billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. This was before the Buddha had left the household life.
The eight princes born to him, seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, likewise followed him to practice the holy life.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Immeasurable Meanings* (*Anantamukha-sūtra*), extensively analyzing it for the great assembly.
After the Buddha had finished preaching this sūtra, he remained upon his Dharma-seat.
Seated in the full-lotus posture in samādhi, This is called the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
The heavens rained down māndārava flowers, And celestial drums resounded spontaneously. Gods, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits Made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
All the buddha-fields Immediately shook with great trembling; The Buddha emitted a light from between his brows.

Manifesting various rare and wondrous events, this light shines toward the eastern direction, revealing to all sentient beings throughout eighteen thousand buddha-fields the places where they undergo birth, death, and the retribution of their karma.
There are those who see these buddha-fields adorned with various jewels, possessing the colors of lapis lazuli and crystal; such is the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
He also saw all the devas and humans, the hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to that Buddha.
Furthermore, he saw all the Tathāgatas, who had spontaneously attained the path of Buddhahood;
their bodies were like mountains of gold, upright, majestic, and most subtle, as if within pure lapis lazuli.

Within, there appears an image of pure gold (made of crystal, beryl, lapis lazuli, and blue-colored gems—gems produced from mountains in the Western Regions; through the Buddha-way and the way of skillful means, one practices with focused intent until one spontaneously accords with the principle).

(Attaining the Buddha-way is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Lapis lazuli is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). The golden image is the Manifestation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) appearing in response to beings. The East is the direction of movement).
The World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, Expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma.
In each and every Buddha-land, the śrāvaka assemblies are countless; Illumined by the Buddha’s light, All behold those great congregations.
There are some bhikṣus dwelling amidst the mountain forests, who with diligence uphold the pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl.
Furthermore, one sees bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and so forth, their number like the sands of the Ganges;
this is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light, and therein one also sees various bodhisattvas.
Deeply entering various meditative concentrations, their bodies and minds were tranquil and unmoving as they sought the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, he saw various bodhisattvas who, knowing the mark of the cessation of all phenomena, each preached the Dharma in their own lands while seeking the Buddha-way.
At that time, the fourfold assembly beheld the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
Manifesting great supernormal powers, their hearts were all filled with joy; each asked the others, "What is the cause and condition for this?
The Honored One, revered by gods and men, having just arisen from samādhi, praised the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light:
"You are the eye of the world, the one to whom all turn for refuge and faith."
"Able to uphold the treasury of Dharma as I have taught it—only you can realize and know this.
Having thus praised him, the World-Honored One caused Wondrous Light to rejoice, [saying]:
"The Eye of the World; the Bodhisattva is the eye for both the mundane and supramundane worlds, transforming and guiding thousands of people."
While preaching this Lotus Sūtra for a full sixty intermediate kalpas, he did not rise from his seat;
the sublime and wondrous Dharma he expounded was entirely received and upheld by the Dharma Master Wonderful Light (who,
like Śāriputra receiving the present Buddha’s entrustment, received and upheld the Dharma of the former Buddha).
When the Buddha had finished preaching this Lotus Sūtra and had caused the assembly to rejoice, he immediately on that very day addressed the multitude of devas and humans:
"I have already explained for you the meaning of the true reality of all dharmas;
tonight, at midnight, I shall enter nirvana."
(The Buddha’s proclamation of his passing away was the same as that of the present Buddha).
You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain free from negligence; for Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, appearing but once in ten million eons.
(As in the past, the Buddha entrusted [the Dharma] to the present Buddha).
The World-Honored One’s sons and others, Hearing that the Buddha was entering nirvana, Each harbored grief and distress:
"How swift is the Buddha's passing!"
(When the assembly heard that the Buddha was entering parinirvāṇa, they wept with grief, just as they do now for the present Buddha.
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforts the immeasurable multitude: "When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or fear."
(As the Buddha of the past consoled the assembly, so too does the Buddha of the present.
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has already attained thorough penetration into the outflow-free true reality (*anāsrava-dharmatā*).
He shall next become a Buddha, named Viśuddhakāya, and he too shall deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings.
On this night the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is spent.

His relics were distributed and immeasurable stūpas were erected. Monks and nuns, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, redoubled their diligent efforts to seek the unsurpassed path; such was the Dharma Master Wonderful Light.
They upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma for eighty minor kalpas, extensively proclaiming the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
These eight princes were converted and inspired by Prabhāpāla; they shall firmly abide in the unsurpassed Way and behold countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all those Buddhas, they will practice the Great Way in accordance with its truth.
They attained Buddhahood one after another, receiving their predictions in succession.
Finally, there was the God among Gods, named Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Teacher of all Sages, who delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.

(Note: "God among Gods" [Tianzhongtian] refers to four types of gods: first, the worldly god; second, the celestial-born god; third, the pure god; and fourth, the god of ultimate meaning. The present Buddha transcends these four types and is thus called the God among Gods.)
At that time, this Dharma Master Wonderful Light had a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit.
Seeking fame and profit without satiety, he frequented the households of the noble classes, abandoning what he had practiced and recited;
he fell into forgetfulness and his mastery was lost. For these reasons:
Known by the name Qiú-míng (Seeking Fame), he also performed various wholesome deeds;
he beheld innumerable Buddhas and made offerings to them all. Following and practicing the Great Way, he was fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*.
Now he beholds the Lion of the Śākyas, and hereafter he shall become a Buddha, named Maitreya.
Universally delivering all sentient beings, their number is immeasurable.
(The lion is a metaphor for the Great Lion’s Roar; the young lion is courageous and robust, while the host of beasts flees and crouches in submission.)
After that Buddha had passed into extinction, you were the one who was indolent; the Dharma Master Wonderful Light was none other than my own self.
When I saw the lamp-lighting Buddha, the original light and auspicious signs were just like this;
by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sutra, for the present signs are identical to the original auspicious signs.
This is the skillful means of all Buddhas; now the Buddha emits a radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true reality.
All you people should know this now: join your palms and wait with single-mindedness, for the Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain to satisfy those who seek the Way.
(First part clarifies the reason for speaking; it admonishes the assembly to give rise to longing and aspiration. Second part teaches the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
For all those seeking the three vehicles who harbor any doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate them for them, leaving none remaining.
(Maitreya raised successive doubts, and Mañjuśrī repeatedly provided resolutions; when matters were exhausted and principles fully realized, the exchange of questions and answers was perfected.

(Of the eighty thousand bodhisattvas, with Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara at their head: while the Mind-King remains entangled in saṃsāra, there are eighty thousand modes of affliction; when it transcends the world, these become eighty thousand gates of wondrous Dharma.

Although there are eighty thousand gates, they are governed by wisdom and compassion; therefore, Mañjuśrī is first, followed by Avalokiteśvara. Once wisdom and compassion are complete, one possesses great power; thus, Mahāsthāmaprāpta follows next. Possessing such great power, one can advance directly without retreat amidst circumstances that are either adverse or favorable.)

Therefore, it is followed by Constant Diligence (*Sadā-vīrya*). Through diligence, one’s practice and maintenance are uninterrupted; thus, it is followed by Unceasing (*Anikṣipta-dhura*). Being unceasing, one is able to produce the Jewel of the Dharma (*Dharma-ratna*); thus, it is followed by Treasure-Palmed (*Ratnapāṇi*).

Once the Jewel of the Dharma is complete, one can provide medicine according to the ailment; thus, it is followed by King of Medicine (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*). Bestowing jewels sustains the body, while bestowing medicine sustains the mind—how heroic this is! Therefore, it is followed by Brave Bestower (*Vīradatta*). By practicing generosity with such valor, one is able to transform the afflictions of stinginess and greed.

One suddenly attains purity and coolness; therefore, it is followed by Ratnacandra (Jewel Moon). The moon can dispel the darkness of delusion and produce great radiance; therefore, it is followed by Candraprabha (Moonlight). Once ignorance is destroyed, the light of wisdom is revealed alone; therefore, it is followed by Pūrṇacandra (Full Moon).

When wisdom is fulfilled, one is able to shoulder the Great Dharma; therefore, it is followed by Mahābala (Great Power). When power is sufficient, one can bear all things simultaneously; therefore, it is followed by Anantabala (Infinite Power). Having perfected both self-benefit and benefit for others, one is able to transcend the realm of dust and toil;

therefore, it is followed by Trailokyavikrāmin (Transcender of the Three Realms). Having transcended the realm of dust, one provides protection; therefore, it is followed by Bhadrapāla (Bhadrapāla). Protection involves earnest and diligent effort, like a mother guarding her child; therefore, it is followed by Maitreya.

When loving-kindness flourishes in the world, it constitutes a great treasury of the Dharma; therefore, it is followed by the *Ratnakūṭa* (The Heap of Jewels). When the Great Dharma is fully sufficient, one can act as a leader for the multitude to draw them out from the path of delusion; therefore, it is followed by the *Śāstṛ* (The Teacher).
Chapter Two: The Expedient Means (Upāya).

"Expedient means" refers to benefiting others according to their specific capacities. It is like a great city: those coming from the east enter through the eastern gate, and those coming from the west enter through the western gate.
"Breaking through empty space is the original reality; every single thing is the entire body. If you, as a person, further seek expedient means, it remains as dust upon a lotus leaf.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra:

(At that time refers to the moment when Mañjuśrī had finished answering the questions. Samādhi means "right reception," "right concentration," or "right mind. It is like a cloudless sky or still water, like the bright sun or refined gold; it is without the slightest flaw and encompasses all within its emptiness and tranquility.)
The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.

(This wisdom consists of the threefold wisdom within a single mind. It is called "profoundly deep" because it penetrates vertically to the very bottom of principle; it is called "immeasurable" because it extends horizontally to the limits of the Dharma-realm.)

(As for the mind of the Buddha, no one can know or perceive it. It is precisely because it is vast and lofty, expansive and pure, without the distinction between emptiness and form, and without the separation of past and present—that it is True Suchness and Perfect Enlightenment, the Pure Dharma Body, identical to the Great Ultimate and the Infinite Ultimate, and thus admits of no scrutiny or measurement.)
This gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; it is beyond the comprehension of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Because the Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, fully practicing the immeasurable Dharma of all those buddhas.
With courageous and diligent energy, his fame is universally renowned, and he has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas. Following...
That which is taught is appropriate; its underlying intention is difficult to comprehend.

(It is "appropriate" because it accords with principle and is ultimate; it is "accomplished" because it has reached the further shore; it is "according to what is suitable" because it accords with the capacities of beings; it is "difficult to comprehend" because it is not known by those on the seven stages of expedient means.)

(Their wisdom is profoundly deep. Because they have personally attended upon countless Buddhas, hearing the teachings directly and practicing their path themselves, they possess great antiquity, great vastness, great courageous diligence, and great accomplishment in virtue and the Way.)
Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables,
employing countless skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments.

Through countless skillful means—namely the seven kinds of skillful means—he preaches the ten wholesome acts of scattering for those who have detached from all attachments; he preaches the ten wholesome acts of purification for those who have detached from attachment to the three miserable realms; he preaches the Tripitaka for those who have detached from attachment to the desire realm; and he preaches the Bodhisattva Dharma for those who have detached from attachment to views and afflictions.
Free from attachment to *nirvāṇa*, he teaches the Buddha-dharma; free from attachment to the love of dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
(As for "attachment": when the mind enters various objects, it cannot be dissolved and unified into the single Dharma-body, nor can it clearly realize the vision and knowledge of Buddhahood.)
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the pāramitās of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, immeasurable and unimpeded. His powers, fearlessnesses, dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis penetrate deeply to the infinite; he has accomplished all unprecedented dharmas.

"Immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) of the Buddha-stage. "Unimpeded" refers to the four unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the Buddha-stage. "Powers" refers to the ten powers (*bala*). "Fearlessnesses" refers to the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*):

the fearlessness regarding the realization of all-knowledge, the fearlessness regarding the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path, and the fearlessness regarding the path leading to suffering. "Meditation" refers to the meditation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). "Concentration" refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. As for "liberation," it means to exhaust the source of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and to enter deeply into the boundless realms of samādhis and meditative concentrations, thereby accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to analyze and skillfully expound all dharmas in various ways, using words that are gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude.
Śāriputra, to speak in brief, there are immeasurable and boundless unprecedented Buddha-dharmas that the Buddha has fully accomplished.
Cease, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further.
(This Dharma is profound and tranquil; as it transcends the path of language, one ceases [discursive thought] to praise it.
Why is this? It is because the Buddha has realized a foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma, which is known only by a Buddha and a Buddha.
One is thus able to thoroughly exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

This true reality of all phenomena is the ultimate principle perfectly realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions; it is the innate enlightened nature possessed by sentient beings; and it is the states of worldly transmigration—suffering and joy, rising and sinking. In total, these do not transcend the ten dharmas. First, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Second, nature; third, essence; fourth, power; fifth, activity; sixth, cause; seventh, condition; eighth, fruit; ninth, retribution; tenth, the ultimate of the root and the branch (meaning that each and every one of the myriad phenomena before one possesses a fundamental basis).

That which is called all dharmas: such are their marks, such their nature, such their substance, such their power, such their activity, such their causes, such their conditions, such their fruits, such their retributions, and such their equality from beginning to end.

(Regarding the external associations: nature belongs to the internal essence as its substance; function is its power; creation is its activity; habituation is its cause; auxiliary causes are its conditions; the fruit of habituation is its result; the former is the root; the latter is the branch; and the point of ultimate convergence is its finality).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; Neither the gods nor the people of the world, Nor any class of sentient beings, can know the Buddha.
The Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses, And his liberations and samādhis—"
As for the Buddha and all his other dharmas, there is no one capable of measuring them. Originally, following countless Buddhas, he fully practiced all paths;
these most profound and subtle dharmas are difficult to see and difficult to comprehend even over immeasurable billions of kalpas.
Having practiced these various paths, he attained the fruit of enlightenment at the site of awakening.
I have fully known and seen such great fruits and rewards, The meanings of their various natures and characteristics.

(Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have practiced this path. This verse praises the Buddha’s personal approach to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas’ paths. It praises the profound and subtle nature of the path. It praises the unprecedented dharmas that are difficult to comprehend. It praises the underlying intent that is difficult to understand. Having practiced the path for immeasurable kalpas, this verse praises the perfection of the pāramitās;

this cites the perfection of the cause. Having attained realization at the site of enlightenment, this cites the perfection of the fruit. "Fully known and seen" praises the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision as vast, deep, and far-reaching.)
Only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know this matter; this Dharma cannot be shown, for its verbal expressions are quiescent.
Among all other classes of sentient beings, there is none who can understand it, except for the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and the assembly of the disciples of the Buddhas.
Those who have made offerings to all Buddhas, whose outflows are entirely exhausted, and who dwell in their final bodies—
such persons as these cannot withstand the power [of the Buddha's wisdom]. Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra,
and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s knowledge.
Even if the ten directions were filled with beings like Śāriputra, and the other disciples likewise filled the lands of the ten directions—

if they all together attempted to measure it, they still could not know the sharp wisdom of a Pratyekabuddha who has reached his final body of no-outflows, even if such beings likewise filled the worlds of the ten directions.

Their number is like that of bamboo groves; all these together with one mind, should they wish to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, would be unable to know even a small fraction of it.
Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds have made offerings to countless Buddhas, thoroughly comprehend all meanings and principles, and are moreover skilled in expounding the Dharma.
Suppose rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds were to fill the lands of the ten directions;
if they were to concentrate their minds with wondrous wisdom for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and together contemplate them all, they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even those non-regressing bodhisattvas, whose numbers are like the sands of the Ganges, if they were to concentrate their minds together to seek it out, [could not know it].
Furthermore, they cannot know it. Again, he addressed Śāriputra:
"The untainted, inconceivable, profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma— I have now fully attained it. Only I know its characteristics;
the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ."
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, one should give rise to the power of great faith.
After a long time, the World-Honored One will surely speak the truth, declaring to the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas:
"It was by my power of skillful means that I caused you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and to attain nirvāṇa."
He showed them the teachings of the Three Vehicles; because sentient beings were attached everywhere, he led them so that they might emerge [from suffering].
At that time, within the great assembly, there were various śrāvakas, arhats whose outflows were exhausted, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others.
One thousand two hundred people— including those who had resolved to become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— each had this thought:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise skillful means,
saying that the Dharma attained by the Buddha is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand, and that its intended meaning is difficult to discern?"

"This is something that no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can attain. The Buddha has taught the single meaning of liberation, and we too have attained this Dharma and reached nirvāṇa; yet now we do not know where this meaning leads."

(First, regarding the teaching on the single treasury of liberation for the three types of persons: they share the same liberation. Attaining this dharma leads to nirvana; all of these are skillful means. Since it is not yet known which among them is the ultimate reality, it is said that "one does not know where the meaning of this principle leads.")
At that time, Śāriputra, perceiving that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts and that he himself had not yet fully understood, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and by what condition do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas’ foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma that is difficult to understand?
Since the distant past, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha. Now, the fourfold assembly all..."
There is a doubt; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter.

For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma? At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, Only after a long time has he preached this Dharma.
(The three types of wisdom are perfectly luminous and can destroy the darkness of ignorance; therefore, he is called the "Sun of Wisdom.")

I have spontaneously declared that I have attained such powers, fearlessnesses, and samādhis, as well as inconceivable dharmas such as dhyāna, concentration, and liberation—dharmas obtained at the site of enlightenment. No one is able to pose a question;
my intent is difficult to fathom, and there is no one capable of questioning me. Thus, without being asked, I speak of this myself.
Praising the path he has traveled, his wisdom is most subtle and profound.
Those who have attained the state of the Buddhas, the out-flow-free arhats, and those seeking nirvana—all now fall into a net of doubt:
"Why does the Buddha speak thus? So too do those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, as well as the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as the gandharvas and others, gaze at one another with hesitation, looking up in reverence to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings:
"What is this matter? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for the sake of the assembly of śrāvakas.
The Buddha has declared me to be the foremost among all śrāvakas; yet now, regarding my own wisdom—
Shrouded in doubt, he could not discern whether this was the ultimate Dharma or the path to be traversed.

(Śāriputra, though foremost in wisdom, could not discern the Buddha’s two types of knowledge—expedient and ultimate—regarding the ultimate Dharma; he doubted the fruit, while doubting the path, he doubted the cause.)
The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth, with palms joined, gaze up and wait; may you utter the subtle and wondrous sound and speak for us according to reality.
(Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one is born into the Dharma-body; hence they are called "sons born from the Buddha’s mouth.")
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges; the bodhisattvas seeking buddhahood, numbering eighty thousand;
and furthermore, the wheel-turning sage-kings from ten billion lands, all joining their palms with reverent hearts, desire to hear the complete path.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were to be spoken, all those in the world—gods and humans alike—would be filled with wonder and doubt. Śāriputra spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will speak; I pray that you will speak. Why is this? Because in this assembly there are countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas..."

Only those sentient beings who have previously seen various Buddhas, whose faculties are sharp and keen, and whose wisdom is clear and lucid, are able to give rise to reverent faith upon hearing what the Buddha has taught.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Dharma King, Unsurpassed Honored One, please speak; pray do not hesitate. In this assembly, there are immeasurable multitudes who are capable of reverent faith.
The Buddha again restrained Śāriputra, saying: "If one were to speak of this matter, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—would [be terrified]."
One should be struck with alarm and doubt; monks of overweening pride are about to fall into a great abyss. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak further. My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. To those of overweening pride,"
