At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard this, spoke again to the Buddha with great earnestness: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak; we pray that you will speak!
Within this assembly, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings like us, who throughout successive lifetimes have already received transformation from the Buddha."
"These people will surely be able to revere and believe [this], remaining peaceful and secure for a long night, and receiving great benefit.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
O Unsurpassed One, Honored Among Two-Legged Beings, I pray you will proclaim the foremost Dharma. I am the eldest son of the Buddha;
please deign to explain it in detail. In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes who are able to revere and believe in this Dharma.
The Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed such as these, all of whom now stand with palms joined in single-minded devotion.
We twelve hundred, as well as the others who seek Buddhahood, wish to hear and receive the Buddha’s words;
for the sake of this assembly, we pray that you will deign to explain them in detail, so that upon hearing this Dharma,
they may give rise to great joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have earnestly requested three times, how could I not speak?
Listen attentively now and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in detail.
As these words were being spoken, five thousand members of the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—immediately rose from their seats.
They paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew. Why was this? Because these individuals had deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses, as well as overweening pride;
they claimed to have attained what they had not attained and claimed to have realized what they had not realized. Possessing such faults, they did not remain.

(When the obstacles of the five turbidities are many, it is called "heavy sin. When one clings to the small while obscuring the great, it is called "deep-rooted. To claim to have attained the three fruits when one has not yet attained them, or to claim to have realized the stage of no-more-learning when one has not yet realized it, is called "arrogance.")
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not stop him. Then the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves;
it consists purely of the solid core. Śāriputra, it is well that such people of overweening pride have departed."
"Listen well now; I shall speak for you. Śāriputra said, "So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals—just as the udumbara flower appears but once in a long time."

(The Udumbara flower—known as "spiritual and auspicious"—appears once every three thousand years. When it appears, a Cakravartin King emerges. In Jambudvīpa, there is a road for the Cakravartin Kings, one yojana wide; when no Cakravartin exists, it is submerged by the ocean waters.
When a Cakravartin appears, the ocean waters recede and the tracks of the golden wheel manifest, and this flower then grows).

This wondrous Dharma is not ordinary speech or written characters; it is the speech and characters that proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Furthermore, it is the speech and characters that admonish and instruct those who believe in the Buddha-dharma.

It is also the principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of one's own wondrous mind. As for "true reality," it transcends the path of words and thought, and the sphere of mental activity ceases. Sound and form cannot demonstrate it; yet, sound and form are merely borrowed as skillful means. Those of the Two Vehicles do not understand this, falsely claiming they have escaped birth-and-death and entered nirvana.

One does not know that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, nor that by severing afflictions one realizes bodhi; one does not know that afflictions are themselves bodhi. Since Śāriputra had not yet awakened to this, he again earnestly requested the teaching three times. The World-Honored One replied: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals.

This may be called "straightforward in speech and perfect in intent," for through such skillful means, it aids in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Would there be anyone who would not swiftly enter the Buddha-vehicle?
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
(This is an exhortation to believe, for fear that beings might give rise to slander.)
Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intentions are difficult to understand.
(The Buddha teaches through expedient means in accordance with the three types of capacities.)
Why is this? By means of countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, I have expounded all dharmas.
(This cites the present Buddha’s power of expedient means and explains the skillful means of all Buddhas; their subtle wisdom is identical.)
This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; only the Buddhas are able to know it. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.

(The Buddha, by means of non-discriminative wisdom, realizes the non-discriminative Dharma; this is the ultimate meaning. His nature is vast and extensive, hence it is called "Great. The Buddha’s ritual conduct is termed "activity. The various capacities of sentient beings invoking the Buddha serve as the cause, while the Buddha responding to those capacities through teaching serves as the condition.)
Śāriputra, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world? It is solely for the sake of one great causal matter.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that they may attain purity;
they appear in the world because they desire to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings; they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings...

Because he has awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he appears in the world; because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he appears in the world.

(The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the inherently endowed, fundamental, wondrously enlightened essence. Those who are deluded do not know it. The Buddhas appear in the world to reveal and instruct upon this wondrously enlightened essence; the patriarchs of successive generations have transmitted this wondrously enlightened essence.)
“Śāriputra, it is for this one great cause and condition that all Buddhas appear in the world.
The Buddha told Śāriputra, “The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas; whatever they do is always for this single purpose.”

"Only by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision do I instruct and awaken sentient beings. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely through the Single Buddha Vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise. Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable directions..."
He then uses various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression to expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;

all these teachings are for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Śāriputra, future Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise, by means of immeasurable and innumerable directions...

He employs various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression to expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; all these teachings are for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Śāriputra, in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-lands in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones...
World-Honored One, you bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings.
(The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of a great causal matter; this [Bodhisattva] likewise appears in the world to benefit sentient beings.)

The nature and Way of the Great Sages of the ten directions are not different; the nature and Way of the Great Sages of antiquity are not different; the nature and Way of the Great Sages of the future will not be different. The nature inherently possessed by every person is likewise without difference.

These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Śāriputra, these Buddhas merely teach and transform...
“Bodhisattvas, because they wish to show the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, because they wish to awaken sentient beings to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision— Śāriputra, I now do likewise.
Knowing that sentient beings have various desires and attachments in their deep minds, according to their respective natures, I employ various [means].”
He preaches the Dharma by means of causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, through the power of skillful means.

(The various desires of sentient beings refer to the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of the five vehicles: the past is called "faculties," the present is called "desires," and the future is called "dispositions. That which is deeply attached to in the mind is the faculty; "skillful means" refers to opening up the three [vehicles] according to what is appropriate.)
Śāriputra, all this is for the sake of attaining the single Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra, even in the worlds of the ten directions there is no second vehicle, much less a third. Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the evil world of the five turbidities, namely:
the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, and the turbidity of lifespan.

The *kalpa-kaṣāya* (degeneration of the eon) refers to a long duration, not a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). The *sattva-kaṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings) consists of three [factors]: views, pride, and karmic fruition. The arising of the three calamities constitutes the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (degeneration of afflictions). The intensification of various views constitutes the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (degeneration of views). The destruction of speech and the reduction of lifespan constitute the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (degeneration of life).

Thus it is, Śāriputra. In times of turmoil during the kalpa-turbidity, sentient beings are heavily defiled; they are stingy, greedy, and envious, and have brought to fruition various unwholesome roots.
Therefore, by the power of skillful means, the Buddhas distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
(When the Buddhas appear in the world, their true and fundamental intention is solely to reveal that every person inherently possesses perfect enlightened nature; there is no other expedient means.)

Śāriputra, if any of my disciples claim to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas, yet have neither heard nor known of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and the matter of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas, they are not disciples of the Buddha; they are not arhats;
they are not pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Śāriputra, those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who claim to have already attained arhatship...
“Han, this is their final body; they have attained ultimate nirvana and no longer aspire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You should know that such people are all those of overweening pride (adhimāna). Why is this?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible.”

(To say that it is impossible not to believe this Dharma is incorrect. This Dharma is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. It is also the knowledge and vision of worldly people; there is only the difference between [the absence of] self, person, sentient being, and life-span.)
Except after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present before them. Why is this?

Because after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, persons who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sūtras as these are difficult to find. Even if they were to encounter another Buddha, regarding these sūtras...
One will then attain definitive understanding.

(Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, this sutra still remains. By hearing this sutra, one immediately attains definitive understanding. Such a person is difficult to encounter; because his skillful means are inexhaustible, he is called a "remaining Buddha").
"This sutra is the very body of the Tathāgata in his former lives; it is the wisdom-life of all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, you all should with one mind believe, understand, receive, and uphold the Buddha’s words. The Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, speak no falsehoods.
There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [spoke in verse]:
He spoke in verse:
"There were monks and nuns harboring overweening pride, upāsakas with arrogance,
and upāsikās lacking faith— these fourfold assemblies numbered five thousand."
Not seeing their own faults, they have deficiencies and omissions in the precepts;
cherishing their own flaws, these people of small wisdom have already departed. They are the dregs among the assembly;
by the Buddha’s majestic power, such people of meager merit are removed, for they are incapable of receiving this Dharma.
(When there is a lapse in the discipline, it is called "deficient. When there is a lapse in that which is concomitant with meditative concentration and the Path, it is called "outflow").
This assembly has no branches or leaves; there are only those who are pure and genuine. Śāriputra, listen well:
the Dharma attained by all Buddhas is taught for the sake of sentient beings through the power of immeasurable skillful means.
The thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, The various paths they travel, Their diverse desires and natures,
And their past deeds, both good and evil— Having fully known all these, The Buddha, through the power of skillful means,
Using various causes, analogies, and speech, Causes them all to rejoice; At times he speaks the Sūtras.
Gāthās and Itivṛttakas, Jātakas and Adbhutadharmas, as well as the explanations of Nidānas, Avadānas, and Geyas, and the Upadeśa Sūtras. (The mental inclinations of sentient beings are manifold;

therefore, the Dharma is taught according to what is appropriate. These various approaches to the Dharma are called "diverse. Regarding the *itivṛttaka*: it recounts events from former worlds. Regarding the *jātaka*: it recounts events from former births. Regarding the *adbhutadharma*: [it recounts] the Buddha’s...)

He manifests various supernormal powers, which sentient beings find marvelous and unprecedented. As for "causes and conditions," these refer to all matters concerning the dependent origination of the Buddha’s teachings. As for "similes," they are like using a finger as a metaphor for the moon.

Those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings, Who are greedily attached to birth and death, And who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, Have not practiced the profound and wondrous path— Afflicted and distracted by manifold sufferings, For their sake I preach nirvana;

I say this is a skillful means To cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. I have never said to you: *Note: This passage is from the Lotus Sutra (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), Chapter 2, "Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya).*
When I was about to attain the Buddha-way, I did not yet speak [of it], because the time for speaking had not yet arrived.
Now that the time has come, I shall definitively expound the Mahāyāna.
These ninefold teachings of mine were spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; since entering the Mahāyāna is the fundamental goal, I have therefore preached this sūtra.
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, Whose natures are gentle and who possess sharp faculties;
Having practiced the profound and wondrous Way under immeasurable Buddhas, For the sake of these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra.
I grant this prediction to such people: In a future age, they shall attain the Buddha-way, For with a deep mind they have mindfulness of the Buddha.
Because they have practiced the pure precepts, these individuals shall attain Buddhahood upon hearing this teaching. Great joy pervades their entire bodies;
the Buddha, knowing their mental dispositions and conduct, therefore expounds the Mahāyāna for them.
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, if they hear the Dharma I teach—even if it be but a single verse—they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
It is merely by using provisional names that he guides sentient beings, speaking of the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, when the Buddhas appear in the world, this alone is the one true reality.
The other two are not the truth; He never uses the Lesser Vehicle To deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; According to the Dharma he has realized, Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, He delivers sentient beings by this means.
Having personally realized the Unsurpassed Way, The Mahāyāna is the Dharma of equality.
If I were to convert even a single person by means of the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed;
such a thing is not permissible. If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them, nor does he harbor greed or envy.
Having severed all evils within the dharmas, the Buddha, throughout the ten directions—
And alone I am without fear; with my body adorned by marks, its radiance illuminating the world, I am honored by immeasurable multitudes.
For them, I preach the Seal of the True Reality (the bodily marks are brilliant and distinct;

the light and color are dignified and majestic; thus I am honored by the multitude. In Mahāyāna sūtras there is but one Dharma-seal; if there were seals such as impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa, these would belong to the Hīnayāna).
Śāriputra, you should know: I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
(This vow was not merely a personal pledge for enlightenment; it was also a wish that all living beings might enter together into the Buddha-wisdom.)
As I have vowed in the past, it is now fulfilled; I transform all sentient beings,
causing them all to enter the Buddha-way (so that sentient beings may realize the Buddha-wisdom, verifying that my vow was not in vain).
If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way; yet those without wisdom are confused and deluded, refusing to accept the teaching.
I know these beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness and are firmly attached to the five desires;
because of their foolish craving, they give rise to affliction through the causes and conditions of various sensual pleasures.
They fall into the three evil realms and transmigrate within the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons.
(The five desires are form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Delusion is ignorance; craving is greed. From delusion arises craving, and thus there is suffering and affliction.)
The subtle form of the conceived embryo constantly grows from lifetime to lifetime.
Those of meager virtue and little merit, oppressed by manifold sufferings, enter the dense forest of false views.
Relying on such views as "existence" or "non-existence," they are fully possessed of the sixty-two [views] and are deeply attached to illusory dharmas.

Firmly clinging to what cannot be relinquished, Arrogant and self-conceited, with a crooked and insincere mind, For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, They shall not hear the name of the Buddha, Nor shall they hear the True Dharma;
Such people are difficult to deliver. Therefore, Śāriputra, I have taught these skillful means for their sake.
I preach the path that exhausts all suffering and point toward Nirvana; yet though I speak of Nirvana, it is not true extinction.
All dharmas, from their very origin, have always been characterized by quiescence.
When the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in future ages. I possess the power of skillful means.
The World-Honored Ones of all ages have revealed the Dharma of the three vehicles, yet they all preach the path of the One Vehicle.
Now, this great assembly should eliminate all doubt and confusion; the words of the Buddhas do not differ, for there is only the One Vehicle and no second.
Throughout countless kalpas in the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who entered parinirvāṇa.
There are hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis, their number beyond measure;
such are the various causes, conditions, and parables of these World-Honored Ones, through the power of countless skillful means, they expound the characteristics of all dharmas.
These World-Honored Ones all preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle, transforming immeasurable sentient beings.

Causing them to enter the Buddha-way; furthermore, the various Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all beings in the world—gods, humans, and the rest—employ further diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth.
If there are classes of sentient beings who encounter the Buddhas of the past, [they too shall be led to this].
If they hear the Dharma and practice giving, or maintain the precepts, practice patience, exert diligence,
cultivate meditation and wisdom— those who thus cultivate various forms of merit and insight—
all such persons have already attained the Buddha-way. After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, if there are beings with virtuous and gentle hearts, such as these sentient beings...

All have already attained the path of Buddhahood. After those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, one shall make offerings to their relics by erecting ten billion kinds of stupas, adorned with gold, silver, and crystal;
with musaragalva, agate, and rose-colored pearls, as well as lapis lazuli beads—pure, vast, and magnificently decorated, adorning all these stupas.
Some may erect stone temples, or those made of sandalwood and aloeswood; or of *karkandhu* wood and other timbers, bricks, tiles, clay, and earth.
Or, in the midst of a wilderness, they may pile up earth to form a temple for the Buddha;
even children playing may gather sand to make a stupa for the Buddha—all such persons as these [attain merit].

Have all already attained the Buddha-way. If a person, for the sake of the Buddha, Erects various images, carving and sculpting them with manifold features, They have all already attained the Buddha-way.
Whether made of the seven treasures, brass, bronze, red or white copper, White wax, lead, or tin, Or iron, wood, or clay—
Or those who, with glue, lacquer, and cloth, Adorned and fashioned images of the Buddha— All such people as these have already attained the path to Buddhahood.

Those who painted images of the Buddha, With marks adorned by a hundred blessings, whether doing it themselves or employing others— They have all already attained the path to Buddhahood. Even children playing in their games...
Whether using grass, wood, or a brush, or even with their own fingernails, those who have thus inscribed images of the Buddha—
such persons gradually accumulate merit, become fully endowed with the heart of great compassion,
and have all already attained the path of Buddhahood; they merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
If a person, with a reverent mind, makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to stupas and temples, to precious images, or to painted images;
or if they cause others to perform music— beating drums, blowing horns, chanting,
or playing flutes, pipes, lutes, *konghou*, *pipa*, gongs, and cymbals— such various and wondrous sounds as these.
They offered all they possessed as an act of worship, or with a heart of joy sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues—even a single small sound—and all have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
(In the liturgical chant, "bai" refers to chanting praises; it also refers to blowing the great conch.)
If a person with a distracted mind offers even a single flower as an offering to a painted image,
they will gradually see countless Buddhas. Or if someone prostrates, or merely joins their palms,
or even raises a single hand, or slightly bows their head— by making such an offering to the image, [they shall attain the same merit].
Gradually seeing immeasurable Buddhas, one spontaneously attains the unsurpassed path;

widely delivering countless multitudes, one enters nirvana without remainder, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted (the bonds of cause and fruit being exhausted is called "without remainder"; as the fuel of the faculties is exhausted, the fire is extinguished).
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and recites "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
(Namo; pronounced *namo*; this translates as "taking refuge in life" or "reverently following.")
Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, whether they were still in the world or had entered parinirvāṇa—whosoever heard this Dharma has already attained the path of Buddhahood.
As for the World-Honored Ones of the future, their number is immeasurable;
these Tathāgatas likewise preach the Dharma through skillful means. All such Tathāgatas [act in this way].
By means of immeasurable skillful expedients, I deliver and liberate all sentient beings.
If there are those who hear this Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha. This is the fundamental vow of all Buddhas:
"The Buddha-way that I have practiced, I desire that all sentient beings may likewise attain this same path."
Though the Buddhas of future ages May preach hundreds of thousands of billions Of countless Dharma-gates, In reality, they are but the One Vehicle.
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, Know that dharmas are eternally without self-nature, And that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions;
Therefore, they preach the One Vehicle. This Dharma abides in its own station.
The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding; having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher, through skillful means, speaks thus for those honored by gods and humans:

"The Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions, their number like the sands of the Ganges, appear in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, and they likewise preach this Dharma."
Knowing the supreme tranquility, through the power of skillful means, though he displays various paths, they are in reality the Buddha-vehicle.
He knows the various conducts of sentient beings, what their deep minds intend,
the karma practiced in the past, their desires, natures, and the strength of their diligence, as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
By means of various causes and conditions, through parables and also through words, I preach according to what is appropriate and by skillful means;
now I do likewise, for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, proclaiming the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates.
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings.
I teach all dharmas through skillful means, causing all to attain joy. Śāriputra,
you should know that with my Buddha-eye I behold the sentient beings of the six realms, who are impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom,
entering the perilous path of birth and death, where their succession of suffering is never severed.
In this perilous path, life is easily severed; though life is short, it continues on—this is the turbidity of life.
Deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail, one covers oneself with craving and greed, becoming blind and unable to see.
(The long-haired oxen of the southwestern tribes protect their tails with their own bodies; because people cherish their tails, they kill them).
One does not seek a Buddha of Great Power, nor the Dharma that severs suffering.
(An eon in which no Buddha appears is called "turbid"; if there were a Buddha in such an eon, though it be turbid, one could destroy it).

Deeply immersed in various false views, they seek to abandon suffering through suffering (for view is itself sensation, and sensation is itself suffering; by practicing these causes of suffering, it is difficult to abandon the fruit of suffering).

For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion (compassion for sentient beings of the five turbidities; employing skillful means, he leads them toward the Buddha-wisdom).
When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I contemplated the tree and walked back and forth;
During those twenty-one days, I pondered such matters as these: "The wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme, Yet sentient beings have dull faculties;
Attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance— To such types of beings [this teaching would be difficult]."
"How may they be delivered? At that time, the various Brahma kings, as well as Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
the Four World-Protecting Kings, and Maheśvara, together with the remaining hosts of devas and their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions,
paid homage with palms joined in reverence and requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
I then reflected to myself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha-vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith, they would fall into the three evil realms.
It would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all, but to quickly enter parinirvāṇa. Thus I recalled the Buddhas of the past.
Through the power of the skillful means I have practiced, the path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles.
While I was reflecting in this way, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared before me, consoling me with Brahma-sounds:
"Excellent, Śākyamuni! You are the foremost guide; you have attained this unsurpassed Dharma."
Following all Buddhas, he employs the power of skillful means (Śākyamuni is his clan name;
"Śākya" means "able to manifest. He bestows the One and leads [beings] to the three, introducing them into the Buddha-wisdom).
We, too, have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma; for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and teach the three vehicles.

Because those with little wisdom delight in inferior teachings and do not believe they can become Buddhas themselves, we employ skillful means to distinguish and teach various fruits. Although we speak of the three vehicles, [it is ultimately the One Vehicle].

It is solely for the sake of instructing the bodhisattvas that Śāriputra, you should know, I heard the holy lion’s deep, pure, subtle, and wondrous voice proclaiming "Namo to all Buddhas. Furthermore, I formed this thought:
"I have appeared in this world of turbid evil; as all the Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice in accordance with them."
Having reflected upon this matter, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī. "The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, [the Buddha] preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus" (Vārāṇasī is the name of a river;

that is, the Deer Park. First, for Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he preached the Four Truths; next, for Aśvajit and Bhadrika, he preached rebirth in heaven; third, for Kāśyapa and Kauṣṭhila, he led them to the fruit of sainthood—these are the five bhikṣus).
This is called turning the wheel of Dharma; Thereupon arises the sound of Nirvāṇa, As well as the distinct names of Arhat, Dharma, and Saṃgha.
(Turning the transformative Dharma within the Buddha’s mind so that it enters the minds of others is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. Since Nirvāṇa is termed "arising," it is called a "sound.")
Since kalpas long ago, I have praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvana, saying that the suffering of birth and death is forever ended;

Śāriputra, you should know this. I see my sons among the Buddhas—those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way—in their countless thousands, tens of thousands, and millions, all with hearts of profound reverence.
They have all come to where the Buddha is; they have previously heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means.
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha-wisdom;
now is precisely the time for it. Śāriputra, you should know that there are people of dull faculties and small wisdom.
Those who are attached to signs and arrogant cannot believe in this Dharma. Now, I rejoice and am fearless among these bodhisattvas;
I have directly set aside expedient means and preached only the unsurpassed path.
When the bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed. As for the twelve hundred arhats—
All shall likewise become Buddhas, Just like the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
In the ritual manner of preaching the Dharma (this ritual serves as a skillful means to guide sentient beings).
I now do likewise, preaching the Dharma free from conceptual discrimination. The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is rare and distant;
it is difficult to encounter them. Even if they appear in the world, it is further difficult to hear this Dharma.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, hearing this Dharma is likewise difficult. So too is it difficult for one to be able to listen to this Dharma.
Such a person is likewise rare, like the udumbara flower; throughout an entire kalpa, they are cherished by all, for such a one is seldom seen even among gods and humans.
To hear the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word, is to have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is most rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower. You all should have no doubt:
I am the King of All Dharmas. I announce to the great assembly that I teach and transform bodhisattvas solely through the vehicle of the One Vehicle; I have no śrāvaka disciples. You, Śāriputra...
Śrāvakas and bodhisattvas should know that this is the sublime Dharma, the secret essence of all Buddhas.
In the evil world of the five turbidities, beings take pleasure only in various desires; such sentient beings will ultimately not seek the Buddha-way.
In future ages, when wicked people hear the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, [they will reject it].

Those who are deluded and do not believe or accept [the teaching], who destroy the Dharma and fall into evil paths—[but] for those who possess shame and remorse, whose will is pure, and who seek the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus; by means of billions of skillful expedients.
They preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; those who have not practiced it cannot understand this.
Now that you all already know these matters of the skillful means employed by the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, you should no longer harbor any doubts.
With hearts filled with great joy, you should know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.
*The Outstanding Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle One;
*The Outstanding Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Two.
Originally translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Commentary by Xu Changzhi (Jin Zhou) of Wuyuan, the Wayman Without Reliance. Chapter Three:
The Parable (The term "parable" [pìyù] refers to using categories for comparison; it is called a "parable" because it opens up understanding so that one may awaken).

"The principle is lucid and refined; the self-characteristic is empty. Meeting thus, one naturally does not perceive laxity or indolence. In every particle of dust, the five desires are present; in every particle of dust, there is wondrousness. Within the Dharma-realm, how could there ever be difference or sameness?
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and was filled with gladness.
(Internal understanding within the mind is called *prīti*. The joyful movement of physical form is called *udāra*).
He immediately rose and joined his palms, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance.
(Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without any other thought signifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision).
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy at having attained what I have never experienced before.
Why is this? In the past, I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha as this: that various bodhisattvas were seen receiving the prediction of their future buddhahood."
Yet we were not included in this matter; we are deeply grieved, for we have lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision. (As for "grieving":

hearing that the great were praised and the small disparaged, one feels internal doubt while externally feeling contempt. Regarding "losing the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision": it means losing the vision of the Buddha-eye and losing the knowledge of the Buddha-wisdom.)
“World-Honored One, I often dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking. I constantly reflect:
‘We have entered the same Dharma-nature; why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna? This is our own fault.’”
"It is not the World-Honored One's fault.

(To say 'this is my own error' means: because I was deluded regarding the provisional [means], what concern is this for the principle and the teaching? Because I was confused regarding the real [truth], what concern is this for the Buddha’s partiality? To recount past errors is to cite one's own transgressions and take them upon oneself)."
Why is this? If we had waited for the explanation of the causes by which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna.
However, we did not understand the skillful means employed in the teachings given according to what was appropriate;
upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, we accepted it immediately as we encountered it, contemplated it, and realized its realization. World-Honored One, from the past until now—
Throughout the day and throughout the night, he constantly reproached himself:

"Those who do not understand skillful means do not realize that the Three Vehicles are provisional expedients; they instead immediately accept them as ultimate and thereby attain only the limited fruits of the Lesser Vehicle."
Now, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never before heard, all my doubts and regrets have been severed;

my body and mind are at ease, and I have attained a sense of swift peace and security. Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth, and transformed by birth from the Dharma.
They have attained a share of the Buddha-dharma. At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before. My heart harbors great joy, And the net of doubt has been entirely removed.
From of old I have received the Buddha’s teaching, And have not lost the Mahāyāna."
The Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous; it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
Having attained the exhaustion of outflows, I too have heard it and my grief and distress are removed.
Whether I am dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter, sighing deeply and reproaching myself.
How can we deceive ourselves, saying: "We too are sons of the Buddha;
having entered together into the outflow-free Dharma, we shall be unable in the future to proclaim the Unsurpassed Way"? [The thirty-two marks of a golden body:

from the wheels on the soles of the feet, up to the hands, the pores, the two shoulders, the two armpits, the body like that of a lion, the complete set of teeth, the moisture in the throat, the profound and far-reaching Brahma-voice, the white tuft between the eyes, and so forth.]
The Ten Powers and all the liberations are together within this single Dharma; yet they do not attain these eighty minor marks (from the crown of the head down to the eyebrows,
ears, body bones, fingers and ankles, facial complexion, hands and feet, and a serene and pleasant demeanor, walking like a king of elephants and moving according to the Dharma like a king of swans).
The eighteen unique qualities (the eighteen *āveṇika-dharmas*:
no error in body, speech, or thought, up to wisdom; knowledge of the past, future, and present, etc.)—such merits as these I have all lost.
When I am walking alone in meditation, [I am filled with remorse].

Seeing the Buddha amidst the great assembly, his fame filling the ten directions, and bringing vast benefit to sentient beings, I reflected that I had lost this advantage. I thought to myself, "I have been deceiving myself.
Day and night, I constantly contemplated this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I had lost it or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the various bodhisattvas; thus, day and night, I have contemplated such matters.
Now, hearing the Buddha’s voice, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate—an outflow-free teaching, inconceivable, which leads all beings to the site of enlightenment.
(Former doubts now questioned:
"I was formerly attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins; the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached Nirvana."
(Within saṃsāra there is nirvāṇa; this is the intent of the Mahāyāna. If there were no nirvāṇa within saṃsāra, that would be the intent of the Hīnayāna).
Having completely eliminated all false views, I attained realization of the dharma of emptiness; at that time, my mind thought to itself that I had reached extinction.

Wrong views are the attachment of ordinary worldlings; entering the dharma-nature is the attachment of the two vehicles. "Brahmin" refers to a *brāhmaṇa*; this exists only in the five regions of India.
Only now do I realize for myself that this was not true parinirvāṇa.
When I attain Buddhahood and am endowed with the thirty-two marks, and when gods, yakṣas, nāgas, and other spirits pay me homage— at that time,
and in the midst of the great assembly, may it be said that I have forever reached extinction without remainder.
When it was said, "I shall become a Buddha," and they heard such a sound of the Dharma, all their doubts and regrets were completely removed.
Yet, when first hearing what the Buddha had spoken, great alarm and doubt arose in their hearts:
"Could this not be a Māra who has become a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind? Then the Buddha, through various causes and conditions, spoke with skillful words and parables.
His mind is as peaceful as the ocean; having heard this, my net of doubts is severed.
The Buddha has spoken of the immeasurable Buddhas who attained parinirvāṇa in past ages, who all dwelt securely within skillful means and likewise taught this Dharma.
The Buddhas of the present and future are also immeasurable in number, and they too, by means of various skillful means, [teach this same Dharma].

The preaching of such a Dharma as this—just as the World-Honored One has done from birth, through renunciation, the attainment of the Way, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma—is likewise taught through skillful means. The World-Honored One speaks the true path;
Pāpīyas could never do such a thing. Therefore, I know for certain that this is not Māra acting as a Buddha.
Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra.
But hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice—profound, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous—as he eloquently expounded the pure Dharma, my heart was filled with great joy;
my doubts and regrets were exhausted, and dwelling in true wisdom, I am certain that I shall become a Buddha.
Venerated by humans and devas, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and transforms all bodhisattvas.

(Praise this wondrous sutra extensively; it is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. One should give rise to reverence and respect, one should uphold it with all one's heart, and one should contemplate it deeply to achieve great awakening.)
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare before this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others:
in the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly instructed and transformed you in the presence of twenty thousand koṭis of buddhas."

"You, too, have followed me and received instruction throughout the long night. Because I have guided you through skillful means, you have been born into my Dharma. (Regarding "having received instruction throughout the long night":

although one was already greatly transformed in the past, ignorance had not yet been destroyed; regarding "being guided by skillful means to be born into my Dharma": though there was great transformation in the past, it is now that great understanding has arisen.)
Śāriputra, in the past I instructed you to resolve upon the path to Buddhahood, yet you have now forgotten it all and instead claim that you have already attained parinirvāṇa.
(To have "forgotten it all" means to have abandoned the Great Vehicle and practiced the Small Vehicle.)
Now, desiring to cause you to recollect the path practiced according to your original vow, I shall preach this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of the śrāvakas;
it is titled the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teaching of the bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas' mindful attention.

(Recalling his original vow: "This attainment of liberation shall not be in vain. First, I shall bestow provisional teachings to establish intermediate minor virtues; later, I shall reveal the ultimate truth, thereby fulfilling my original vow and great aspiration.")
Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed,
you shall make offerings to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; you shall uphold the True Dharma and fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas,

and you shall attain Buddhahood, known as Puṣpārāma (Flower Light), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, [Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, and Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām].
The Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. The land is named Vimalā.
That realm is level and even, pure and magnificently adorned, peaceful, secure, prosperous, and joyful. Gods and humans are numerous and flourishing.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with eight intersecting roads marked by golden cords on their sides. Alongside these are rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which are always...
Puṣpaphala. The Tathāgata Puṣpārāma also taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.
Śāriputra, although the time when that Buddha appeared was not an evil age, he preached the Dharma of the three vehicles because of his original vow.

(Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas. When a brahmin begged for his eyes, Śāriputra spat upon them and trampled them; he then became angry and regressed to the state of an ordinary person. He made a vow that on the day he attained Buddhahood, he would open the gates of the Three Vehicles. This is why it is called his "original vow. Śāriputra is the same as Śāradvatīputra.)
That eon was named Great Jewel Adornment. Why was it called Great Jewel Adornment?
Because within that land, bodhisattvas were regarded as great jewels. Those bodhisattvas were immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable;
they could not be reached by calculation or analogy, and no one could know them except through the power of a Buddha’s wisdom. When they wished to travel, precious flowers would receive them.
It is so. These bodhisattvas have not merely first resolved their minds; they have all long planted the roots of virtue.

Under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, they have purely cultivated the Brahma-faring. They are constantly praised by all buddhas, always cultivate the wisdom of the buddhas, and possess great supernormal powers.
They skillfully know the gateways of all dharmas; they are upright and without guile, and their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast. As...

Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas will fill that land. The lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma will be twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained buddhahood; the people of that land will have a lifespan of eight small kalpas.
After twelve small kalpas have passed, the Tathāgata Puṣpārāma will bestow upon the bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and he will address all [the bodhisattvas].
"Monk, this Bodhisattva Sthiramati shall next become a Buddha, named Puṣpadantapadavikrāmin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The Buddha-field of that one shall likewise be such as this.
Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Puṣparāja, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma..."
He remained in the world for another thirty-two intermediate kalpas. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Because he employs the wisdom of the Middle Way to eliminate the two pervasive defilements, his land is named 'Free from Defilement' (Vimalā). Because he employs the wisdom of equanimity to sever the delusions of self and person, his realm is level and upright. Since delusions are severed and defilements removed, it is fitting that the ground be like lapis lazuli."
Śāriputra, in a future age, shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, named Huaguang (Flower Radiance).
He shall deliver immeasurable multitudes and make offerings to countless Buddhas.
Having fulfilled the bodhisattva practices and merits such as the ten powers, he shall realize the unsurpassed path after the passing of immeasurable kalpas.
The eon is named Great Jewel Adornment; the world is named Free from Defilement.

It is pure and without blemish, with a ground of lapis lazuli, its paths demarcated by golden cords. There are trees of various colors made of the seven jewels, always bearing flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The bodhisattvas of that land are always firm and steadfast in their resolve and mindfulness.
They have fully perfected all the *pāramitās* of supernormal powers;
having well studied the bodhisattva path under countless Buddhas, such great beings were transformed by the Buddha Puṣyarṇa when he was a prince.
Having abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory, they reached their final birth.
Having left the household life to attain the Buddha-way, the Buddha Flower-Light will remain in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas.
The people of that land shall have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
When the True Dharma has completely vanished, the Semblance Dharma shall remain for thirty-two [eons].
His relics will be widely distributed, and gods and humans will all make offerings to them. Such were the deeds performed by the Buddha Flower-Light;
all his matters were exactly like this. That Most Honored One among two-legged beings, supreme and without peer—that was indeed your own body.
At that time, the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— as well as devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, should all rejoice within themselves.

The great assembly of gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, seeing Śāriputra receive the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, were filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an act of worship to the Buddha. Śakra-devānām-indra...

The Brahma King and others, together with countless sons of gods, also made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *mandārava* flowers, *mahā-mandārava* flowers, and so forth.
The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in the void, revolving of their own accord.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music were performed simultaneously in the void, and rain fell.
A multitude of celestial flowers appeared, and he spoke these words:

"The upper robe"—that is, the great robe—turns of its own accord. When Śāriputra received his prediction, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) turned spontaneously; thus, cause and effect, the primary and secondary, self and others—all were transformed.
In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he once again turns the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
(The wheel of the three sublime dharmas of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings).
Formerly at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Four Truths, explaining in detail the arising and ceasing of all phenomena—the five aggregates;
now once again you turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma.
This Dharma is most profound and subtle; few are able to believe it.
Since time immemorial, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One’s teachings, yet never before have we heard such a profound and wondrous supreme Dharma.
We all rejoice in this Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One, O Śāriputra of great wisdom.
Now that we have received this noble prediction, we too shall likewise become Buddhas in all worlds, most honored and unsurpassed. The Buddha-way is inconceivable;
you teach the skillful means according to what is appropriate. Whatever meritorious deeds I possess, whether in this life or in lives past—
And having seen the merits of the Buddha, he dedicates them all toward the path of Buddhahood (it is also like this, as was the case when Śāriputra received his prediction upon his realization).
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret. In the presence of the Buddha..."
They shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their own minds formerly dwelt on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
The Buddha constantly taught and transformed them, saying: "My Dharma can bring one away from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

These individuals, both those still in training and those beyond training, each considered themselves to have already abandoned the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as views of existence and non-existence (*bhava-vibhava-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth. They said:
They had attained nirvāṇa, yet now, having heard before the World-Honored One what they had never heard before, they all fell into doubt and confusion.

(Previously it was said that the three were ultimate; now it is further said that the one is the reality. Since the former were three and the latter is one, they could not distinguish between their identity and difference; therefore, it is said that they all fell into doubt and confusion.)
“Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
(The first three [questions] and the last one constitute the causes and conditions).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: “Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ various causes and conditions?”
Are all these parables, expressions, and skillful means for teaching the Dharma intended for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
All that has been taught is for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.
(Whether emanated bodhisattvas or those who are provisional or real, all enter the Buddha-way).
However, Śāriputra, I shall now further clarify this meaning by means of a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.

(This serves to welcome and console him. Since his previous reproaches were so severe, he might have feared self-immolation out of shame and resentment; now, by permitting the use of analogies, he is enabled to understand well.)
Śāriputra, suppose there is a great elder in a kingdom,
city, or village— this elder being the Tathāgata, the Lord of one transformation—
who is advanced in years, possesses immeasurable wealth, and has many fields, houses, as well as servants and attendants.

To be advanced in years means to be extensively proficient in both the present and the past, which is analogous to the Buddha’s wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*). To be decrepit and matured in faculties and will is analogous to the Buddha’s abandonment-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Possessing immeasurable wealth serves as a general analogy for his myriad virtues.
That house is vast and expansive, yet it has only a single gate.
(The "single gate" refers to the gate of the Buddha-way. The Buddha-way is a single principle; since principle is that which is elucidated by the teaching, it is called a "gate").
Many people— hundreds, two hundred, or even five hundred— dwell therein (as an analogy for sentient beings in the five realms of existence).
The hall and pavilion are dilapidated; the walls and partitions have collapsed; the bases of the pillars are rotten;

the beams and rafters are leaning precariously. (The hall and pavilion are a metaphor for the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The walls and partitions are a metaphor for earth, water, fire, and wind. The tree roots, beams, and rafters are a metaphor for life-force, vitality, and the mental consciousness. Their decay, collapse, and precarious state are a metaphor for the impermanence of the three realms, which undergoes ceaseless change and transformation.)
Simultaneously on all sides, flames suddenly burst forth, incinerating the house and its contents.

(The eight sufferings pervade the four elements and the four modes of birth; hence it is said they are "on all sides. Since all are equally impermanent, it is said they arise "simultaneously. "Suddenly" serves as a metaphor for what was originally non-existent now coming into being: originally there was no such suffering, yet through ignorance it exists.)
The sons of the elder, whether ten, twenty, or even thirty in number, were within this house (which is like the differing dispositions and desires of sentient beings).
The elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides (which is an analogy for the sentient beings of the six realms).

The four sides are an analogy for the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. One gives rise to the inversion of purity regarding the body; the inversion of pleasure regarding feelings; the inversion of permanence regarding the mind; and the inversion of self regarding phenomena.
Because these four inversions arise, there is birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from what is loved, enmity with what is hated, and the pervasive suffering of the five aggregates.
He was immediately seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself: "Although I am able to emerge safely from this burning gate, [I feel] great compassion arise for sentient beings;

I am alarmed because I contemplate their regression from the Great Vehicle, and I am terrified because I worry about their giving rise to evil. To be unendangered by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings is called 'peace' (an); to be unmoved by the four inversions is called 'secure' (yin)."
Yet those sons, within the burning house, were attached to their play and delights; they were neither aware nor conscious of it, neither startled nor terrified.
As the fire approached and pressed against their bodies, causing them acute pain, their minds felt no revulsion or distress, and they had no intention of seeking escape.

Attachment to views is called "sport"; attachment to craving is called "play. "Not wearying" means not being weary of the suffering of impermanence and not being concerned with the accumulation of afflictions. "Having no intention to seek deliverance" means not practicing the Path in order to seek nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: "My hands and body possess great strength;
I shall carry him out of the house using my lap, or perhaps using a small table."

Knowledge and vision are like a basket; the fearlessnesses are like a small table; the ten powers are like a desk. The Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, sets these three dharmas in motion.
He further reflected: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small. My children are young and lack discernment;
they are attached to their playthings and might fall down or be consumed by the fire."

(One gate; that is, the Single Buddha Vehicle. It is subtle and difficult to know, and is therefore called "narrow and small. Those with weak roots of goodness in the Mahāyāna are called "infants. Sentient beings have dull faculties and are unable to hear the Great Way, as it is difficult to cross.)
"I shall speak to you of things to be feared: this house is already burning; you should quickly exit at once, lest you be harmed and consumed by the fire.
Having formed this thought, he told his sons everything according to what he had contemplated: "All of you, come out quickly!"
Although the father felt compassion for them and sought to entice and instruct them with kind words, the sons were attached to their play and refused to believe or accept his advice.
They felt neither alarm nor fear, having no intention at all of escaping; furthermore, they did not even know what the fire was or what the house was.
What constitutes these losses?

Those who do not feel alarm or fear will not give rise to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) nor the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). They fail to recognize the eight kinds of suffering and the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), which can burn away their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), just as one who does not know fire or does not recognize a house fails to understand the causes for the loss of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
They merely run back and forth in play, looking only at their father.

(Running from light toward darkness is like moving east and west; the rapid coming and going between birth and death is like a gallop; the arising of views and attachments therein is like playing; because they do not follow the Great Teaching, it is said they "merely look at their father.")
At that time, the elder had this thought: "This house has already been consumed by a great fire.
If I and my sons do not emerge at once, we will surely be burned to death. I must now devise a skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity."

In the preceding passage, it was stated that one safely emerged through the gate of being burned; now it says that if one does not emerge in time, one will surely be consumed by fire. It should be understood that the one who previously emerged is the Dharma-body emerging; as for the present statement that "if one does not emerge in time," and so forth:

This is precisely the response-body (nirmāṇakāya). It manifests as having an illness in common with sentient beings; if sentient beings possess goodness, it appears at the opportune moment to receive them through transformation, thereby establishing skillful means and the provisional teachings of the three vehicles.
The father knew the former inclinations of his sons—that each had their own preferences for various rare treasures and extraordinary objects to which they were surely attached.

(He knew their former inclinations because they had previously practiced the Lesser Vehicle; he knew their inclinations because their desires and natures differed, such that each had their own preferences. Because they had practiced the Lesser, he met them with the Lesser; because they were not the same, he opened the One into Three.)
And he addressed them, saying: "These toys that you find delightful are rare and difficult to obtain. If you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later.
Such various things as these—goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts—are now outside the gate; you may play with them."

(The goat cart represents the Śrāvaka vehicle; the deer cart, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and the ox cart, the Bodhisattva vehicle. Those now outside the gate have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts and have emerged beyond the triple world.)
"You should all come out quickly from this burning house. Whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you.

At that time, the sons, hearing of the precious playthings described by their father, had their wishes fulfilled; their hearts became bold and vigorous, and they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to be the first to flee from the burning house.

"This is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned. 'Those who have just made their vow' refers to those for whom the faculties and the teaching correspond; this is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). 'The mind is courageous and sharp' refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). 'Mutually pushing and displacing' means pushing forward the principle of the Four Noble Truths and displacing and subduing delusions and views; they vyingly hasten toward the True Path, swiftly perceiving the principle.

'Contending to emerge' means emerging from the suffering of the triple world (*tridhātu*), attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and exhausting all afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*)—only then do they emerge from the burning house."
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely;
they were sitting on the open ground at the crossroads, free from all obstructions, their minds composed and filled with joy and exultation.

(When the son leaves the burning house, his mind becomes immediately tranquil. The "four crossroads" refers to the Four Noble Truths. When the afflictions of the three realms are exhausted, it is called the "open space. Abiding in the fruit without further progress is called "sitting. Because the delusions of views and thoughts are extinguished and the principle of the True Truth is revealed, there is no obstruction.)
At that time, the sons each said to their father, "Father, we pray that you will grant us at once those playthings you previously promised:
the goat-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts."
(The Mahāyāna capacity is awakened; they resolve to seek the Buddha-way).
Śāriputra, at that time, the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage.
These carriages were tall and wide, adorned with various jewels, surrounded by railings, with bells suspended on all four sides. Furthermore, canopies were spread and set above them. Moreover...
It was adorned with various rare and precious jewels, crisscrossed with jeweled cords, and hung with floral garlands. A luxurious couch was spread upon it, and a crimson pillow was placed thereon.

It was drawn by white oxen whose coats were pure and clean, whose forms were beautiful, who possessed great strength, whose gait was level and steady, and who moved as swiftly as the wind; furthermore, many attendants followed and guarded it.

"‘And so forth’ refers to the equality of all dharmas. Each [vehicle] reveals the reality of the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, and the immeasurable dharmas according to its own original practice. The height and breadth of the chariot are like the profound and far-reaching knowledge and vision of the Tathāgata; its adornment with various jewels represents the cultivation of the myriad practices. The surrounding railings symbolize the dhāraṇīs that encompass all virtues.

The bells suspended on all four sides are like the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence. The canopy represents the universal covering of all beings through compassion; its embellishment with miscellaneous jewels is the great kindness of the Tathāgata. The interlacing jeweled cords symbolize the Four Great Vows.

The hanging flower garlands represent the delighting and moving of sentient beings. The layered, soft cushions signify the pliancy of all meditative absorptions. That it is drawn by white oxen is a metaphor for untainted *prajñā*, whose essence is endowed with the myriad virtues."

The sinews are like the five faculties; strength signifies the power of subduing; walking with even steps is like the equal balance of meditative concentration and wisdom; and being as swift as the wind refers to reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Why is this? This great elder possesses immeasurable wealth; his various treasuries are all overflowing.
He then thinks: "My riches are infinite; it would not be right to give inferior, small chariots to my sons."
"These young children here are all my sons; my love for them is without partiality. I possess such great chariots made of the seven treasures, in immeasurable numbers.
I ought to give them each with an impartial mind; it is not fitting to treat them differently."

(Regarding "immeasurable numbers": this is like the present sutra’s revelation and clarification, wherein both the teaching and the practice all demonstrate the true reality (*dharmatā*). Regarding "each being non-differentiated": this means that without departing from one's original habitual tendencies, the true reality is revealed.)
Why is this? Because with these goods of mine, I could provide for an entire kingdom and yet still not run out; how much less so for my own children.
(This illustrates that by means of the Great Perfect Cause, one realizes knowledge and vision; even without conditions, one still delivers others.)
At that time, the sons each mounted a great vehicle; they experienced what they had never known before, exceeding their original expectations.

(This is like the Bodhisattvas hearing the Dharma, whereby the net of doubts is entirely removed; those of the three vehicles now obtain great vehicles, excelling at transformation and surpassing their original expectations.)
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Would this elder be guilty of falsehood for giving his sons these precious great chariots?
Śāriputra replied, 'No, World-Honored One. This elder merely enabled his sons to escape the calamity of fire and preserve their lives;
it is not a falsehood. Why is that? Because if they have preserved their lives, that in itself is sufficient.'"
They have already obtained objects of enjoyment (the fivefold Dharma-body of the Hīnayāna; entering the life of wisdom in emptiness is what constitutes having obtained these objects of enjoyment).
How much more so, then, those who employ skillful means to rescue others from that burning house.
(The teaching of the small vehicle is contained within the great; yet now one has obtained the great).
World-Honored One, even if that elder had not given so much as the smallest single chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood.

(This describes the householder’s original intention: whether [the sons] were small or large, they all possessed the fundamental aspiration; as for the small ones, it was not ultimate, so there was no need to give further).
Why is this? It is because the householder previously formed this thought: "By means of skillful expedients, I shall cause my sons to emerge. For this reason, there is no falsehood.
How much more so, since the householder himself knew that his wealth and resources were immeasurable, and he desired to benefit them all?
"Son, I shall give you equal great carts. The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said.

(The two instances of "excellent" describe how his avoidance of calamity was not in vain; for while the Buddha had promised three [vehicles] but granted only one, he himself declared it to be difficult [to attain]. Thus, by stating that Śāriputra’s words were not false, the Buddha inspires confidence.)
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this. He is the father of all the world.

Having forever exhausted, without remainder, all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the obscurations of ignorance, he has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, the powers, the fearlessnesses, great supernormal power, and the power of wisdom; he is endowed with the perfection of skillful means and the power of wisdom.
Pāramitā (The one of supernormal powers refers to one who has deeply cultivated meditative concentration, attained supernatural faculties, and is fully endowed with skillful means).
Possessing great loving-kindness and great compassion, they are never weary or indolent; they constantly seek out virtuous deeds to benefit all beings and are born within the triple world.

This dilapidated and ancient house of fire; for the sake of delivering sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, from grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and from the darkness of ignorance and the fires of the three poisons.
(The three poisons—namely greed, hatred, and delusion—are called "poisons" because they can destroy supramundane wholesome states of mind.
He teaches and transforms them so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He sees that all sentient beings are being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress, and furthermore, for the sake of the five desires and material gain, they undergo various [sufferings].

It is suffering. Furthermore, because of greed, attachment, and pursuit, one experiences manifold sufferings in the present life, and subsequently undergoes the sufferings of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Even if one is born in the heavens or among humans, there are the sufferings of poverty and affliction, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of encountering the hated and disliked—such various kinds of suffering as these.
(To clarify: the fire of the eight sufferings arises from the four inversions; combined with the fire previously seen, it rises from all four sides).

Sentient beings are submerged within it, frolicking and playing with joy, neither perceiving nor understanding, neither startled nor terrified, nor even giving rise to weariness or seeking liberation.
Within this burning house of the triple world, they run hither and thither; though they encounter great suffering, [they remain unaware].
One does not regard this as a calamity.

(Because one does not contemplate suffering and its origin, aversion does not arise; because one does not contemplate the path and its cessation, one does not seek liberation. Thus, one does not regard it as a calamity, meaning there is no intention to seek deliverance.)
Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha thought: "I am the father of sentient beings;
I should uproot their suffering and distress, and grant them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, so that they may sport therein."
(Exerting the power of great compassion. Delighting in the power of great kindness.

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further reflects: "If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernatural faculties and the power of my wisdom, setting aside skillful means, and were to praise for all sentient beings the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, powers, and fearlessnesses, sentient beings would not [attain liberation]."
By means of this, they are able to attain deliverance. Why is this? These sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress;
they are being scorched by the burning house of the triple world. How, then, could they understand the wisdom of the Buddha?
Śāriputra, it is like that elder who, although his body and hands possess great strength, does not employ it, but instead acts with earnest diligence.
Through skillful means, he strives to rescue his children from the perils of the burning house, and only then does he provide each with a precious great carriage.
The Tathāgata is likewise: although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them; rather, he relies solely on wisdom and skillful means.

Within this burning house of the three realms, he rescues sentient beings by preaching the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle—and speaks these words:
"Do not take pleasure in dwelling within this burning house of the three realms. Do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects.
If you become attached through craving, you will be consumed by fire. Depart quickly from the three realms; you shall then attain [nirvāṇa]."
The Three Vehicles: the Vehicle of the Śrāvaka, the Vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, and the Vehicle of the Buddha.

(The Śrāvaka takes the Four Noble Truths as his vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha takes the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as his vehicle; the Bodhisattva takes the Six Perfections as his vehicle. They transport one out of the Triple World and return to Nirvāṇa. To have left the Triple World is to be outside the gate.)
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. You should simply cultivate yourselves with diligent vigor.
By such skillful means, the Tathāgata entices and encourages sentient beings, further saying: "You should know that these three vehicles of the Dharma are all praised by the sages.
They are sovereign and unbound, requiring no further seeking or reliance. By mounting these three vehicles," [you shall attain liberation].
