By means of the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and so forth, he enjoys himself and thereby attains immeasurable peace and happiness.

Attaining the knowledge of non-arising constitutes mastery; attaining the knowledge of exhaustion constitutes freedom from fetters. "My births have been exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence" is called being without dependence. "What was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life has been established" is called being without seeking.

The faculties are the five faculties; the powers are the five powers; awakening is the seven factors of enlightenment; and the path is the eightfold noble path. Because one abides in the emptiness of true suchness and nirvana, it is said that there is peace, security, and happiness.
Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess an internal nature of wisdom, who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and with faith accept it,
applying themselves with earnest diligence and desiring to quickly escape the triple world to seek their own nirvāṇa— this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
It is like those sons who, seeking the goat carts, emerged from the burning house.

(This refers to the Buddha bestowing the teachings of the Three Vehicles. "Faith and acceptance" is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Diligence" is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Vigor" is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). They strive to escape the burning house but cannot transform others, like sheep that do not look back at the herd behind them).

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith, apply themselves with diligent vigor, seek spontaneous wisdom, delight in solitary seclusion, and deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. They are like those sons.
Seeking the deer cart, he emerges from the burning house.

(The Pratyekabuddha deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena; he is a practitioner of the Dharma who hears little from others but deduces much meaning for himself. Thus, he takes the deer cart rather than relying on humans, yet he still possesses the compassion of looking back.)
If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and diligently practice with vigor,

seeking all-knowledge, Buddha-knowledge, self-arisen knowledge, teacherless knowledge, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses, for the sake of compassionate mindfulness and peace and happiness.
Benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, bringing peace to devas and humans, and delivering all—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas. They are like those children who, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house.

(The Bodhisattva is called the "Omniscient One," which is precisely the Buddha-wisdom. In view of this cultivation of causes, it embodies the Mahāyāna principle of carrying both [self and others]. The Bodhisattva’s compassion in transforming sentient beings is like an ox’s patient endurance in drawing a load.)

Śāriputra, just as that elder, seeing his sons safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestows great chariots equally upon all his sons; so too is the Tathāgata, who is the father of all sentient beings.
If he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings [entering] through the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching...
They emerge from the perilous path of the three realms, which is filled with suffering and fear, and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa. At that time, the Tathāgata thinks to himself:
"I possess immeasurable and boundless power of wisdom, the fearlessnesses, and the various treasuries of the Buddha-dharma; yet these sentient beings..."
All are my children; I bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one shall attain parinirvāṇa alone, but rather all are led to parinirvāṇa through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
To those sentient beings who have escaped the triple world, I grant the requisites for delight—dhyāna, samādhi, and liberation—which are shared by all Buddhas.
These are of a single characteristic and a single flavor, praised by the sages, and capable of producing purity.

It is the wondrous, supreme bliss. (The "one mark" is the true mark; it is the Dharma-body. The "one kind" is the knowledge of all modes; it is Prajñā. It can produce pure and wondrous bliss. This bliss is the absence of suffering, which is called liberation. Its three virtues are lofty, vast, and adorned; this is called Mahā.)

Śāriputra, it is just as that elder first used three vehicles to entice his children and later gave them only great vehicles, adorned with precious objects and foremost in security; yet that elder was not guilty of falsehood.
(To lure them with the three carts, one eliminates the five turbidities. Once the five turbidities are eliminated, the great goodness is naturally preserved; therefore, one gives only the great cart.

The Tathāgata is also like this. He is without falsehood. Initially, he speaks of the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently, he delivers and liberates them using only the Great Vehicle. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom and...
It is the treasury of all dharmas, capable of bestowing the Dharma of the Mahāyāna upon all sentient beings; yet they are not able to receive it in its entirety.
Śāriputra, for this reason, you should know that by the power of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas, within the single Buddha-vehicle—
He explains them by distinguishing three [vehicles]. Desiring to restate this meaning, the Buddha spoke these verses:

(To clarify that the Tathāgata’s original intent in appearing in the world was to preach the Great Vehicle, yet because those of small wisdom take pleasure in and are attached to the triple world, he used skillful means to entice and lead them back to the Mahāyāna, thereby fulfilling their original aspiration.)

They do not know what constitutes fire; they do not know the three poisons and the four inversions. They do not know what constitutes the house; they do not know the four great elements and the five aggregates. They do not know what it means to lose [the way]; they do not know that losing one's footing leads to a fall into the three miserable realms.

The elder takes the Dharma-realm as his home; the sons take the five aggregates as their dwelling. The Dharma-realm is eternally peaceful, while the five aggregates are eternally precarious. These are all provisional names; one need only realize one's own mind, and there will be no dharma that cannot be attained.
For example, suppose there is an elder who has a large house; this house is ancient and moreover suddenly fallen into decay (the three realms are "ancient" because they have no beginning;
they are "old" because they were not created recently; they are "suddenly fallen into decay" because they are impermanent and base).

The hall and chambers are high and perilous (the head is the palace, the belly is the hall, and the back is the chamber; the continuous succession of moments is impermanent, hence "high and perilous").
The bases of the pillars are crushed and decayed; the beams and rafters are slanting;
the foundations and steps have collapsed, and the walls are crumbling and split apart; the plaster has fallen away, and the thatched roof is falling in disarray;
the rafters and eaves are misaligned and detached; the surrounding enclosures are bent and crooked, and they are filled everywhere with various impurities.

(The surrounding walls represent the six consciousnesses. The winding passages represent the six sense organs. Since the six sense objects thoroughly defile the six sense organs, it is said that "filth and impurity fill every place.
Five hundred people dwell within it; there are owls, nightjars, eagles, vultures, crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons.
(Using eight birds as metaphors for the eight types of conceit:
Vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; centipedes and millipedes (these are metaphors for the latent tendencies of anger).
Lizards, centipedes, weasels, wildcats, mice, and various other evil insects scurry about in all directions;
in places foul with excrement and urine, impurities overflow,
and dung beetles and other such creatures swarm upon them.
(This parable illustrates the latent tendency of delusion, which is none other than ignorance.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals chew and trample upon it; they gnaw at the corpses until bones and flesh are strewn in disarray.
Because of this, packs of dogs come vying with one another to seize and tear at them.
Hunger-stricken and emaciated, they are terrified and seek food everywhere (this is a metaphor for the latent tendency of greed; like jackals and foxes, they howl at night as strange beasts).
They fight and claw at one another, snarling and barking.
(This simile refers to the latent tendency of doubt. "Snarling" refers to the baring of fangs and the uttering of evil sounds.
That house was so terrifying and its manifestations were such that everywhere there were *chimei* and *wangliang* spirits.
(These collectively illustrate the five dull afflictions and the five sharp afflictions.
Yakṣas and malevolent spirits devour human flesh;
venomous insects and various evil birds and beasts breed, give birth, and each protects its own offspring.
The yakṣas vied with one another to come and scramble for their food;
having eaten their fill, their evil intent grew even more fierce. The sound of their quarreling was truly terrifying—this is a metaphor for false views.
The kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouch upon earthen mounds; sometimes they leave the ground by a foot or two, wandering back and forth, indulging in unrestrained play.
(This is a metaphor for the clinging to precepts and observances.)
They seize the two hind legs of the dogs and strike them until they lose their voices;
placing their feet upon the dogs' necks, they terrify them for their own amusement.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell therein and emit great, evil cries.
Crying out and seeking food (this is a metaphor for the view of a self),
there are further ghosts whose throats are like needles.
(This simile illustrates the grasping at views.
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose heads are like those of oxen; some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted, and they are cruel and ferocious in their violence.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they cry out and run about (this is a metaphor for extreme views).
Yakṣas, pretas, and various evil birds and beasts, frantic with hunger, rush in all four directions.
Peering through the windows and lattice screens— such are these various perils,
countless and terrifying (concluding the section on those of sharp and dull faculties).
This dilapidated and ancient house belongs to a single person, who has recently gone out.
Before long, [he thought]:

"The three realms are places where the Buddha transforms beings; therefore, they are said to belong to a single person. Because the sons departed and lacked understanding, the fire was set, which is a metaphor for the arising of the five turbidities."
Later, in his residence, a fire suddenly broke out; on all four sides, its flames simultaneously blazed fiercely.
The rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars split apart with a crashing roar, collapsing and falling down;
the walls crumbled and collapsed, along with the various spirits and ghosts.
Raising their voices in a great cry, the eagles, vultures, and other birds, along with the kumbhāṇḍas and others,
were so terrified and panicked that they could not escape on their own.
The fierce beasts and venomous insects hid in their burrows and holes, and the piśāca spirits likewise took refuge therein.
Because their merit is meager, they are oppressed by fire;
they slaughter one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh.
Jackals and other such creatures, as well as various great and evil beasts that have already died, all come vying with one another to devour them, amidst stinking smoke and blazing flames.
All four directions are filled [with these beings]:

in the Desire Realm, the four inversions and eight sufferings are like fierce flames; in the Form Realm, the four inversions and eight sufferings are like foul-smelling smoke; and there are *piśācas*, the spirits who devour essence.
Centipedes, millipedes, and various kinds of venomous snakes, scorched by the fire, scramble to flee their burrows;
*kumbhāṇḍa* spirits seize and devour them as they emerge.
Furthermore, there are various hungry ghosts whose heads are ablaze with fire, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat.

They run about in panic and distress (lacking the provisions of the outflows-free state; thus they are tormented by hunger and thirst. Being still within saṃsāra, they run about in panic. *Kumbhāṇḍas* are said to mean "the fearsome").
That house was thus: most terrifying, with manifold poisons, harms, fires, and calamities.
At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate and heard someone say:
(The householder—that is, the elder—stands up. The Tathāgata abides in the stage of the Dharma-body; when he hears the words of others, it is as if he hears the words of the Buddha.
"You sons, because you previously played about, you have entered this house;
being young and ignorant, you were joyfully attached to your play."

The rational nature is fundamentally pure and is not a phenomenon of the triple world; this is called "emergence. Because of ignorance, there is birth and death; this is called "entry. When great goodness has not yet taken root, it is called "infancy. Being shrouded by ignorance, it is called "ignorance."
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house; he thought it right to provide rescue so that no harm by fire should occur.

He exhorted his sons, describing their many calamities and hardships, the evil spirits and venomous insects, and how the fires of disaster spread, with all manner of sufferings following one after another.
In an unceasing succession, there are venomous snakes, vipers,
and various yakṣas and kumbhāṇḍa spirits; jackals, foxes, dogs, vultures, eagles, owls, hawks,
and centipedes and their like— all tormented by hunger and thirst, extremely terrifying.

This is a place of suffering and hardship; how much more so when there is a great fire (because one lacks concentration and wisdom, one suffers from hunger and thirst; because one has fallen into the realm of desire, one is burned by the great fire).
The sons were ignorant; though they heard their father’s instruction, they remained as before attached to their pleasures (lacking great ambition and yet not practicing even the minor [virtues]).
They played and sported without ceasing. At that time, the elder had this thought:
"These sons of mine are like this; they only increase my grief and distress.
Now, in this house, there is not a single thing to be enjoyed, yet these sons remain immersed in their play."
Not accepting my teaching, they will be harmed by fire; thereupon, he reflects and devises various skillful means (employing the bestowal of the teachings of the Three Vehicles).
He addressed his sons, saying: "I have various kinds of precious playthings and excellent chariots made of wondrous jewels (the 'wondrous jewels' being the skillful means)."
"Carriages drawn by rams, carriages drawn by deer, and carriages drawn by great oxen are now outside the gate.
Come forth, all of you! For your sake, I have prepared these carriages for you to play with as you please. When the sons heard this, they said:
Thus these chariots immediately rushed forward in competition,
galloping out until they reached an open space (galloping refers to the realization of the Truths; the open space refers to the stage of No-more-learning).
Freed from all suffering and hardship, the elder sees his sons emerge from the burning house and stand at the crossroads.
Seated upon the lion throne, he exclaims to himself in celebration:
"I am now happy! These children were so difficult to bring forth and raise."
Foolish and ignorant, they entered a perilous house filled with many venomous insects,
goblins, and fearsome spirits, where fierce flames of a great fire rose up from all four sides;
yet these children, greedy for pleasure and delighting in play, have now been rescued by me.
Causing them to escape from calamity; for this reason, all people, I am now joyful.

(Because they have become receptive vessels through transformation, there is celebration and joy. Because they are the great conditions for teaching, it is called "birth. Because they are slightly matured, it is called "nurturing. Because raising and sustaining them is not easy, it is "extremely difficult. Because their great elements are subtle, they are "foolish and small. Because they give rise to the five turbidities, it is called a "house").
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where their father was and said to him:
"We pray that you will grant us the three kinds of precious chariots as previously promised;
when we have come forth, you shall give us the three vehicles."
"According to your wish, now is precisely the time; please grant it to me.
(Previously he stood, which expressed a sense of alarm; now he sits calmly, seeing his son escape danger and attain fearlessness.)
The elder was immensely wealthy, possessing numerous storehouses filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli,
tridacna shell, and agate (symbolizing the complete equipment for preaching the Dharma).
With various precious substances, they constructed great chariots,
adorned and decorated with railings all around, with bells suspended on all four sides,
interlaced with golden cords and draped above with nets of pearls and tassels of golden flowers.
Hanging down everywhere, adorned with various colorful silks, it encircles [the structure] on all sides.

(The previous passage spoke of "hanging various flower tassels," which merely indicates that those who see them rejoice; the present passage states "hanging down everywhere," clarifying that the manifold capacities of sentient beings are universally transformed.)
With soft silks and cotton wool, he makes cushions and rugs;
with the finest, exquisite fine woolen cloth, worth hundreds of billions, fresh white and pure, he covers them above.
There is a great white ox, fat, strong, and powerful, its form and body beautiful.
Yoked with precious chariots and accompanied by many attendants who served as his guard, he bestowed these exquisite vehicles equally upon all his sons.
At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for delight; they mounted these precious chariots and traveled through the four quarters.
Sporting and joyful, free and unimpeded, he tells Śāriputra:
"I am also like this—the most honored among the assembly of sages, the father of the world.
(The Tathāgata possesses seven kinds of skillful means; "most honored among the worthy and holy" refers to this. As for the nine kinds, they refer to the nine realms.)
All sentient beings are my children; deeply attached to worldly pleasures, they lack the heart of wisdom.
There is no peace in the three realms, which are like a burning house filled with manifold sufferings—truly terrifying, and ever subject to birth and old age.
The fires of birth, death, grief, and affliction—such as these—are blazing without ceasing;
yet the Tathāgata has already departed from this burning house of the triple world.
He dwells in tranquil seclusion, at peace in the forests and wilds. Now, this triple world is all my own.
The sentient beings therein are all my children; yet now this place is full of many afflictions and hardships.
Although I alone am able to provide protection and rescue, though I instruct and admonish them, they do not believe or accept me regarding their various attachments to sensual desires.
Because their attachments are deep, by these skillful means he preaches the three vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings,
so that they may know the suffering of the triple world and be instructed and taught the supramundane path.
If these sons and others have a resolute mind, [he guides them accordingly].

They were endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (*traividya*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Among them were those who had attained the state of a *pratyekabuddha* and non-retrogressive *bodhisattvas*.

(As for the three types of clear knowledge: knowing past suffering through the knowledge of former existences; knowing future suffering through the divine eye; and severing the suffering of afflictions through the exhaustion of outflows.)
“Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to speak of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path to Buddhahood. This vehicle is subtle and wondrous.”
Supremely pure, unsurpassed among all worlds, and pleasing to the Buddhas;
worthy of being praised, honored, and prostrated to by all sentient beings;
possessing immeasurable billions of powers and liberations.
Through meditative concentration, wisdom, and the other dharmas of the Buddha,
they obtain such a vehicle that these sons may, throughout days, nights, and kalpas,
constantly sport together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, riding upon this precious vehicle.

Until reaching the site of enlightenment (attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision like the sun; ignorance is like the night. "Until reaching the site of enlightenment" refers to the stage of wondrous awakening).
For this reason, if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle.

Except for the Buddha’s skillful means (wherein he spoke of the One Vehicle as being without the three causes and conditions; for if one seeks with thorough scrutiny throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is only the One and not three).
I address Śāriputra: You all, my followers, are truly my children, and I am your father.
For kalpas upon kalpas, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings;
I have rescued you all and caused you to emerge from the triple world. Although I have previously spoken thus...
"You have attained extinction," you say, "merely by exhausting birth and death; yet in truth, there is no extinction.
What you should now do is cultivate only the wisdom of the Buddhas.
If there are bodhisattvas among this assembly who can listen with a single-minded focus to the true Dharma of all Buddhas—
Although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means, all those beings they transform are bodhisattvas.
For the sake of those people of limited wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire,
he teaches the Truth of Suffering, so that the hearts of these sentient beings may find joy.
An unprecedented attainment! The Buddha has taught the Truth of Suffering;

it is real and without deviation. (Regarding the Truth of Suffering: it does not transcend the cycle of birth and death within the six realms. That sentient beings feel joy [upon hearing this] accords with their habitual tendencies. "Real and without deviation" means that actual suffering cannot be made into pleasure. The first clarifies the capacity [of the audience]; the second clarifies the response [of the Buddha]).
If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering,
and who are so deeply attached to the causes of suffering that they cannot relinquish them even for a moment— for their sake, I employ skillful means to speak the Way:
"The cause of all sufferings has greed as its root."
(This clarifies the Truth of Origination).
If one extinguishes craving and has no further basis for dependence, the total cessation of all suffering is called the Third Truth.
(This clarifies the truth of cessation.
For the sake of the truth of cessation, one practices the path.
(This clarifies the truth of the path; the path consists of [cessation-related] concentration and wisdom.)
To be free from all bonds of suffering is called attaining liberation.
From what does such a person attain liberation? Merely by being free from delusion is it called liberation.

(The accumulation [of karma] is that which binds; suffering is that which is bound. To be free from suffering and its accumulation, so that there is nothing upon which to rely, is called attaining liberation.)
In truth, they have not attained all-encompassing liberation; the Buddha says that such people have not yet truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Because these people have not yet attained the Unsurpassed Way, it is not my intention to let them reach final extinction. I am the Dharma King.
Having attained mastery over the Dharma and brought peace and security to sentient beings, he thus appears in the world.

(All liberation is the Truth of Cessation; the Unsurpassed Way is the Truth of the Path. The Buddha originally intended to grant all liberation to beings and lead them to realize the Unsurpassed Way and enter Great Nirvana, yet sentient beings were unable to bear it. Now that their obstacles have been removed, he returns to teach this.

As the King of Dharma, the Buddha has attained mastery over both provisional and ultimate teachings; by opening the three provisional gates and revealing the one ultimate reality, he acts in accordance with his original intent.)
"You, Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world" (the Dharma-seal is the seal of true reality).
Wherever you travel, do not proclaim this recklessly. If there are those who hear it, they should rejoice and receive it upon their heads; know that such persons are *avaivartika*.
If there are those who believe and accept this Dharma of the sutra, these persons have already [in past lives]...
Those who have seen past buddhas, And have reverently made offerings to them, And have likewise heard this Dharma—
If there are those capable of Believing what you have spoken,
Then they shall see me, And they shall also see you, As well as the community of bhikṣus And all the bodhisattvas.
This Lotus Sutra is preached for those of profound wisdom;
those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be confused and fail to comprehend it.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power, O Śāriputra.
Even these [bodhisattvas] enter this sūtra through faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas?
Because they trust the Buddha’s words, those other śrāvakas follow this sūtra, as it is beyond the scope of their own wisdom.

(Explaining the Tathāgata’s benefits throughout the three periods of time: observing the goodness of the past, he teaches for its sake; observing the goodness of the future, he teaches for its sake. As for the present Buddha, he dwells eternally on Vulture Peak. *Avivarti* means "non-retrogression.")
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant and indolent, nor to those who harbor views of a self.
Do not preach it to ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires and cannot comprehend it upon hearing it. Nor should you preach it to those who lack faith.
To slander this sutra is to sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world— namely,
the nature of the revealing cause, the nature of the true cause, and the nature of the causal conditions.
Or again, those who frown with their brows knit and harbor doubts—
listen now as I describe the retribution for the sins of such persons: whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa,
whoever slanders a sūtra such as this, or sees one reading or reciting it.
Those who despise, loathe, and harbor resentment toward one who upholds this sutra—listen now further to the retribution for such a person's sin:
at the end of their life, they shall enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they shall be born once more.
Thus passing from one state to another for incalculable kalpas,
upon emerging from hell they shall fall among the animals— whether as dogs or jackals— with bodies emaciated, dark-hued, and afflicted by scabies;
tormented by those who touch them, they are further treated thus by humans.
Hated and despised by all, they are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst;
their flesh and bones wither away while alive, suffering bitter agony, and when dead,
they are pelted with tiles and stones, [their bodies] hunched and hairless.
Because they sever the seed of the Buddhas, they undergo this retribution for their sins:
they may be reborn as a camel or among donkeys, constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to whips and lashes;
they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else, because they have slandered this sutra.
Having incurred such offenses, one may become a jackal that enters villages with a body covered in scabs and sores, missing an eye,
and being beaten and pelted by children, undergoing various pains and sometimes meeting death.
Having died here, they again receive the body of a python;
its form is vast, five hundred yojanas in length, deaf and witless, with no feet.
It crawls on its belly, being gnawed and eaten by small insects, suffering pain day and night.
There shall be no rest for those who slander this sutra; such is the transgression they incur.
If they should obtain human form, their faculties will be dull and darkened;
they will be short, deformed, crippled, blind, deaf, or hunchbacked. Whatever they may say, people will not believe or accept it.
Their breath is constantly foul; they are possessed by malevolent spirits. Poor, lowly, and base, they are driven about by others.
Suffering from many ailments and emaciated, they have no one to rely upon;
though they seek the company of others, people pay them no heed. Even if they should happen to obtain something, [they cannot keep it].
Soon after, one forgets them; or, if one practices the way of medicine, though treating illness according to the prescriptions, it causes other diseases to increase, or even leads to death;
or, if one has an illness oneself, there is no one to provide relief or treatment, and even if one takes excellent medicine, the condition only worsens.
If others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, robbery, or theft— if such persons as these suffer calamities through their transgressions—
then such sinners will always be born in places of difficulty (the "places of difficulty" refers to the eight difficulties:

the difficulty of seeing a Buddha, the difficulty of hearing the Dharma, the difficulty of being deaf or mute, the difficulty of hell, the difficulty of the hungry ghosts, the difficulty of animals, the difficulty of not seeing a Buddha or hearing the Dharma, which is the difficulty of the Northern Continent, and furthermore, the long-lived heavens).
Mad, deaf, and mentally deranged, they shall never hear the Dharma.
For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they will be born deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete.
Constantly dwelling in hell as if wandering through a garden, Residing in other evil realms as if in one’s own home, Camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—these are the places where they roam;
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses. If they should happen to obtain human birth,
Deaf, blind, mute, and dumb; impoverished and subject to all manner of decline;
adorned with dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, and abscesses—using such diseases as their clothing, their bodies are perpetually foul-smelling, filthy, and impure.
Deeply attached to the view of self, they increase their anger and hatred;
their lust blazes so fiercely that they do not distinguish between humans and beasts. Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
Śāriputra, listen: as for those who slander this sutra, if one were to describe their transgressions—
Exhausting kalpas without end—by these causes and conditions—I therefore tell you:
among those who lack wisdom, do not preach this sutra.

(While it is the slander of the sutra that produces the offense, the sutra itself is not the cause of the offense; for both sin and merit arise from the mind. According to the Buddha’s original intent, this was solely to generate merit; those who are deluded merely bring blame upon themselves.)
If there are those of sharp faculties, whose wisdom is clear and lucid, who have heard much and possess strong memory,
seeking the path of the Buddha— for such persons as these, one may indeed preach it.
If there are people who have previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas and have planted various roots of goodness.
To one whose profound resolve is firm—such a person as this—one may then preach [the Dharma] (those of sharp faculties are present;
those who have planted roots of goodness are from the past).
If there is a person who is diligent, constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness,
and does not begrudge their own body or life— then for such a one you may preach. If there is a person who is respectful, free from divergent thoughts,
and has distanced themselves from all the foolish and ignorant, dwelling alone in the mountains or marshes— such a person as this...
Then one may explain it to them:
"Cultivating loving-kindness is to have compassion for those below; showing respect is to honor those above.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one sees someone who has abandoned evil associates...
One may preach this to such a person who associates with virtuous friends;
or if one sees a son of the Buddha whose precepts are pure, like a clear and bright pearl,
seeking the Mahāyāna sūtras— to such a person, one may preach this.
(To abandon evil and seek the good is external seeking; to maintain the precepts like a precious jewel is internal protection).
If a person is free from anger, upright and gentle, always compassionate toward all and respectful toward all Buddhas—only for such a person may you preach this.
Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind and through various causes,
conditions, parables, and modes of expression, preach the Dharma without impediment—
to such persons as these you may speak; if there should be any bhikṣus...
For one who seeks the Dharma in all four directions for the sake of omniscience,
who receives it upon the crown of the head with palms joined, and who delights solely in upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras—
refusing to accept even a single verse from any other scripture— it is to such a person that you may speak this.
Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too does one who seeks this sutra;
having obtained it, they receive it upon their heads. Such a person no longer aspires to seek other sutras, nor do they ever think of the scriptures of the non-Buddhists. Such a person—
One may then explain it to them as follows:

"Venerating the Buddha is for one's own practice; preaching the Dharma is for transforming others. Seeking the Dharma is the beginning of requesting instruction; single-minded cultivation is the culmination of relying upon it."

I tell you, Śāriputra: those who seek the Buddha-way and whose characteristics I have thus described would not be exhausted even after the end of an eon. To such persons as these, you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, so that they may believe and understand it.
(This is a summary of the characteristics of those who practice the ten wholesome deeds).
Chapter Four: Faith and Understanding (*Śraddhā-adhimukti*).

To stop at the ground of ultimate goodness without even a hair’s breadth of doubt is called faith (*śraddhā*); to enter the Treasury of Great Radiance (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) without even a hair’s breadth of delusion is called understanding (*adhimukti*).

"Every person is a Buddha—there is no need for doubt; If you do not believe this, you are merely deceiving yourself. If one day you can truly subdue yourself, What concern would sentient beings have regarding non-attainment of Bodhi?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma:
that the World-Honored One had conferred upon Śāriputra the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind and leaped for joy with exultation.

(Subhūti alone is called "Life of Wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*), while the other three are called "Great" (*mahā*). Generally speaking, all are both "great" and "wise. Furthermore, because the Buddha charged them to transmit the teaching in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and they were thus commissioned by those who possess wisdom, he refers to them as "Lives of Wisdom. They gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind.)
Therefore, to demonstrate our faith, we rose from our seats, adjusted our robes, bared our right shoulders, knelt with our right knees on the ground, and with single-minded devotion joined our palms.

Bowing with reverence and gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, we addressed the Buddha, saying: "We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha, yet our years are all advanced and our bodies decayed."
Pūrṇa thought to himself, "I have already attained nirvāṇa; I am incapable of anything further and shall no longer strive for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had been preaching the Dharma for a long duration, I was seated there, my body weary and exhausted.

They merely contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; yet regarding the bodhisattva dharmas—wandering in spiritual powers, purifying buddha-fields, and maturing sentient beings—their hearts find no joy.

(He has already attained *nirvāṇa*. Because he does not give rise to the Great Resolve, it is said that "he is incapable [of further striving]. Since the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is fully established, there is nothing more to rely upon or seek; thus it is said that "he no longer advances to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is called the three gates of liberation.

The selflessness of all phenomena is called the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). The fact that the distinct characteristics of male and female cannot be apprehended is called the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). That all phenomena are without signs and entirely devoid of volitional activity is called the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*)).
For what reason? World-Honored One, you have caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana.
Furthermore, we are now already advanced in years; regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation toward the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattvas—

Not a single thought of attachment or delight arose in us. Now, before the Buddha, we have heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas; our hearts are filled with profound joy at having attained what we never had before.
We did not expect that today we would suddenly hear such a rare Dharma, and we deeply rejoice at this great and virtuous gain.
(Hearing this rare Dharma, they obtain the benefit of awakening.
Immeasurable treasures are obtained without being sought. World-Honored One, we now wish to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.
It is as if there were a person who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another land for a long time—perhaps ten...

Twenty. Up to the age of fifty (because ignorance is dense and heavy, and the mind of understanding lacks power, they are called "infants"). To regress from the Great Vehicle is "abandonment"; to conceal oneself is "fleeing"; to head toward birth and death is "departing. The Dharma-realm of Nirvana is the Buddha’s own country; birth and death and the five desires are other countries.
To fall back and not return is called "dwelling for a long time."
As he grew older, moreover, he became impoverished; he traveled through the four quarters in search of food and clothing, and as he wandered on gradually, he happened upon his native land.

(When the permeation of roots of goodness has grown great, yet one remains within the triple world unable to find the method for transcendence, one is impoverished; scorched by the fires of the eight sufferings, one is distressed. To encounter one's original country means to clearly abandon false seeking and pursue the correct.)
His father had previously departed in search of his son but could not find him; he settled in a certain city where his family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures.

(The realm of true reality is the "family"; being endowed with the ten thousand virtues is "wealth"; the merit of the five perfections is called "riches," and Prajñā-wisdom is called "treasures"; that which guides all dharmas is called "immeasurable").
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like—all their granaries and treasuries were completely full and overflowing.

(The granaries are likened to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for concentration gives birth to the one hundred and eight samādhis; the treasuries are likened to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), for they can give rise to the wisdom of the eighteen emptinesses. To provide for oneself is "fullness"; to transform what is external is "overflowing.")
He has many servants, ministers, secretaries, and attendants; his horses, people, and carriages are numerous, and his cattle and sheep are beyond counting.
His income and profit from these enterprises extend throughout other lands.
(An elephant carries the Perfect Teaching Mahāyāna; a horse carries the Separate Teaching Mahāyāna; and an ox carries the Mahāyāna of both the Treasury and the Penetrating Teachings.
There were also a great many merchants and traders. At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities.

(Lacking the merits of the Mahāyāna, he is called a "poor son. Since his retreat from the Great Vehicle, he has encountered all manner of sufferings and developed a deep sense of weariness and aversion, desiring to seek liberation.)

He eventually arrived at the city where his father resided. For over fifty years since their separation, the father had constantly thought of his son, yet he had never mentioned this matter to anyone;

he merely brooded over it, harboring regret in his heart. He thought to himself that, being old and infirm, he possessed great wealth—gold, silver, and precious gems—and his storehouses were overflowing, yet he had no offspring. He feared that if he were to pass away at any moment...
He has passed away; his wealth and possessions have been lost, and there is no one to whom they may be entrusted. For this reason, he remembers his son with deep longing.

(This refers to the śrāvaka who was originally a child of the Mahāyāna; "harboring regret" means he regrets not having diligently instructed [and governed] him in the past, which caused him to run away.)
He further thought to himself: "If I were to obtain a son, I could entrust my wealth and possessions to him; I would then be at ease and joyful, free from further anxiety.

(The presence of a capacity for deliverance is called "obtaining a son"; bestowing upon him the prediction of Buddhahood is called "entrusting the Dharma-wealth"; as this accords with his original aspiration, he speaks again of joy.)

World-Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son wandered about seeking work and happened upon his father’s house (because he grew weary of suffering and delighted in joy, seeking the flavor of principle and gradually accumulating practice, he eventually perfected supramundane roots of goodness; by means of these roots of goodness, he was able to strike the resonance of the Buddha’s compassion; therefore it is said that he "happened upon his father’s house").
Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet.
He was surrounded by a respectful retinue of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders, his body adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold.
Officials, citizens, and servants stood at his left and right, holding white whisks in their hands.

"The pearl necklaces" refer to the four necklaces of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇī-samādhi*. "Worth ten million" refers to the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*), which adorn the Dharma-body. The "white fly-whisk" represents the function of provisional and ultimate wisdom: the right whisk is the wisdom of emptiness, which brushes away the dust of the four abidings;

the left whisk is the wisdom of the provisional, which brushes away the dust of the sands of *saṃsāra*. These two constitute the skillful means of the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that they stand in attendance.
It was covered with jeweled canopies and hung with various flower banners; fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground and various famous flowers were scattered about.
Precious objects were displayed in rows, and there was the coming and going of taking and giving. With such various adornments, its majestic power was exceptionally sublime.

"To cover it with a jeweled canopy" refers to true compassion. "Flowers" are the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); "banners" are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); "scented water" is the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Scattering various named flowers" refers to morality, concentration, and wisdom. "Arranging precious objects" refers to arranging the true merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

"Bringing out, putting away, taking, and giving": practicing for oneself is "taking," while transforming others is "giving. "Majestic power and virtue are especially sublime" means that the radiance is boundless.
When the impoverished son saw his father possessed of such great power and majesty, he was immediately seized with terror and regretted having come there. He thought to himself in secret:
"This must be a king, or one equal to a king; this is no place for me to obtain wealth through hired labor."

"Great wisdom is called great power; great spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) are called great majesty. Those who are 'terrified' are those of inferior capacity and weak faculties who are cowed by the Great Way. Those who 'regret having come here' are those who harbor the intention to retreat from the Great Vehicle. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is like a king, and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is like a king and his peers;
this is the fruit-retribution of the Mahāyāna, not something obtained through hired labor. Those of inferior capacity cannot receive the Great Transformation."
"It would be better to go to a poor district where there is room to exert one's strength and where food and clothing are easily obtained.
If I remain here for long, I may be coerced and forced into labor. Having thought this, he ran away quickly.
(Rejecting the great for the base and taking up the small; the state of one whose faith is shallow and whose doubts are deep).
At that time, the wealthy elder, sitting upon the lion throne, recognized his son at sight and was filled with great joy, immediately thinking to himself:
"I have wealth and treasuries that must now be entrusted. I have constantly thought of this son, yet had no means to see him;
that he has suddenly come of his own accord is most agreeable to my wishes. Though I am advanced in years, I still cherish him deeply."

"In the past, I saw sentient beings decline from the Great Vehicle and take up the Small; I wished to provide them with the capacity [for enlightenment], yet they lacked it. This was what I constantly contemplated, a source of pain for my great compassion. When there was no way to see them, I desired to rescue and deliver them, but they lacked the capacity. Now that they have suddenly come of their own accord, the capacity for liberation has been awakened."
"This is most agreeable to my wishes.
He immediately dispatched his attendants to pursue and bring [the child] back. At that time, the messengers ran swiftly to seize him.

(The phrase "dispatched his attendants" means that principle is the primary and instruction is secondary; this refers to dispatching the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas to preach the Mahāyāna. "Running swiftly to seize him" signifies revealing the Mahāyāna so that it may reach those with the capacity and lead them quickly toward Bodhi.)
The impoverished son was startled and alarmed; he cried out in grievance, "I have committed no offense against you. Why do you seize me?

(Having suddenly heard the Great Teaching, he is startled because it contradicts his own mind; he is alarmed because he does not recognize it. Originally he did not seek the Great [Vehicle], yet the Great has transformed him; hence it is said, "Why do you seize me?")

The messengers held him more tightly; they forcibly dragged him back (since there was no internal mechanism within, yet he was externally constrained by the Great Transformation—this is what is meant by "forcibly dragging him back").

At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "Though I am innocent, I have been imprisoned; this must surely mean death. He became even more terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate upon the ground.

(Lacking great skillful means, they will inevitably and forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; hence it is said they "will surely die. Because those of small intelligence do not understand the Great Teaching, it is said they "faint away.")
The father saw his son from afar and said to the messengers, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come.
(Since he lacks the great capacity, if his superior form were revealed and the Mahāyāna Dharma preached, it might damage his roots of goodness; therefore, he says, "Do not force him.")
Sprinkle cold water on his face to cause him to regain consciousness; do not speak with him further. (Regarding "face":

it refers to turning one's back to birth and death and facing toward Nirvana. Regarding "regaining consciousness": it means opening the Lesser Vehicle teachings to suit those of lesser capacity, enabling them to leave behind their distress and awaken to the Four Noble Truths. Regarding "do not speak with him further": it means one must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna.)
Why is this? The father knows that his son’s disposition is base and inferior, and he knows for himself that his own noble and exalted status is difficult for his son to accept.
Having recognized him clearly as his own son, he employs skillful means and does not tell others, "This is my son."

Those of the Hīnayāna loathe suffering and aspire to emptiness; they fear the great Dharma. Because it is known with certainty that [the son] had previously resolved upon the Great Mind under twenty billion Buddhas, it is said, "I know for certain that he is my son. Regarding the phrase "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth: within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, these are words spoken according to the intentions of others.
[This was done] as a skillful means to protect him).
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please. The impoverished son was filled with joy, having attained what he had never experienced before.
Rising from the ground, he went to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.

(Because he was not coerced by the Great Teaching, he is said to be "joyful"; because he has escaped the three miserable realms, he is said to "rise from the ground"; because a small amount of wholesome merit has arisen, he is said to "arise"; and because he seeks the Dharma of the Path within the Four Noble Truths, he is said to "seek food and clothing.")
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means. He secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
"You should go to him and speak gently to the impoverished son, saying: 'There is work here; we will give you double wages.'"

Regarding "this place of action": the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation are the places where one acts to sever the afflictions of views and mental defilements. Regarding "I will give you double the price": the Five Precepts and the Ten Wholesome Paths merely enable one to escape the three miserable realms; however, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can enable one to transcend the Triple World.

This constitutes the first multiple. Furthermore, the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress afflictions; whereas practicing the Four Noble Truths now can sever afflictions and lead to nirvana—this constitutes the second multiple.
If the impoverished son consents, bring him here and employ him. If he asks what he is to do, you may tell him:
"I will hire you to remove the filth; we two shall also work together with you."

(If one grants this, it is granted that there are those who seek to eliminate the afflictions of views and thoughts and realize nirvana, regardless of purifying buddha-lands or maturing sentient beings; therefore, it is said, "I hire you to remove dung," meaning we work together for mutual benefit.)
Then the two messengers immediately sought out the impoverished son; having found him, they fully recounted the aforementioned matters.
At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages and then proceeded to clear away the filth. When his father saw his son, he felt pity for him and marveled at him.

(Taking the price for the path that extinguishes [suffering], he removes the filth of suffering and its origin. That the father pities and finds it strange is because he finds it strange that [the son] does not seek the Buddha-way; what is lost is great, while what is gained is meager.)
Furthermore, on another day, he saw from within a window the body of his son from afar— emaciated and haggard,
covered in filth and dust, defiled and impure.

The meagerness of the power of cultivating causes is its weakness; the paucity of the power of cultivating merit is its emaciation; the four abidings are its dung and soil; and ignorance is its dust and grime.
He immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft upper garments, and ornaments of adornment, and put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes.
Dust covered his body, and he held a refuse-basket in his right hand, appearing as though he were filled with dread.

(The followers of the Two Vehicles are not fit to see these marks and signs of excellence; therefore, he removes them. His body being covered in dust signifies the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and outflowing (*āsrava*). His left hand symbolizes the Real, while his right hand symbolizes the Expedient).
He spoke to the laborers, saying, "Work diligently; do not be indolent. By this expedient means, he was able to draw near to his son.
Later, he further addressed him, saying, "Ho there, man! You shall work here constantly; do not go elsewhere. I shall increase your wages.
Whatever you require—bowls, vessels, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and the like—do not hesitate or feel uncertain. I also have old and worn-out servants [to assist you]."
If people have needs, they shall be provided for.

(This causes them to relinquish distractions and enter stillness; hence it says, "Ho! Man, do not go elsewhere," meaning one must certainly remain free from other conditions. "I shall increase your wages" means that within the contemplation of *yathābhūta* (as-it-is), one can give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.
Whatever may be required, all that pertains to the Right Path can be obtained by seeking it within the contemplation of *yathābhūta*).
"Be at ease; I am like a father to you. Do not harbor any anxiety. Why is this? I am old and advanced in years, while you are young and vigorous.
When you work, you never show deceit or indolence, nor do you harbor anger or complaints.
I have seen no such evils in you as are found in other laborers. From this day forward, you shall be like a son born of my own body."

Because they have attained the power of faith, they do not deceive. Because they have attained the power of diligence, they are not indolent. Because they have attained the power of mindfulness, they do not harbor anger. Because they have attained the power of concentration, they do not resent others. Because they have attained the power of wisdom, they do not utter complaints. As for "other laborers," this refers distantly to those such as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Immediately, the elder gave him another name and called him his son. At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer;
for this reason, for twenty years, he was constantly made to clear away dung.

Because he did not abandon the small [vehicle], the great capacity was not awakened. For these twenty years, he was constantly made to remove dung. These "twenty years" represent: one unimpeded path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the abandonment of the views; nine unimpeded paths and nine liberations for the abandonment of the [subsequent] afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*).
After this period has passed, they come to trust one another in their hearts and minds, and there is no difficulty in their coming and going;

yet, as for where they dwell, they still remain in their original place (because, upon hearing the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, they claim it is not within the scope of their own wisdom and are unwilling to turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great; therefore, it is said they remain in their original place).
World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill; knowing he would soon die, he said to the impoverished son:
"I now possess much gold, silver, and rare treasures, and my storehouses are overflowing. You must know all that is therein—how much there is, and what should be taken or given away."
(You should speak thus for the sake of the bodhisattvas; therefore it says, "You all know this.
My mind is such as this; you should embody this intention. Why is this? Now, I and you are no different.
"You should apply yourself with diligence so that nothing is lost" (this means:
when teaching the Prajñāpāramitā, do not let it be lost).
At that time, the impoverished son immediately accepted the instructions and took charge of all the goods: the gold, silver, rare treasures, and all the storehouses.
Yet he had no intention of seeking even a single meal. Nevertheless, his dwelling remained as it was in its original place;
his inferior mind had not yet been relinquished (though he aspired to the Great [Vehicle], he had not yet abandoned his inferior mind).

After a short time had passed, the father perceived that his son’s mind was gradually becoming open and expansive, that he had achieved his great aspiration, and that he now looked down upon his former thoughts.

(Regarding the seven kinds of skillful means—the immeasurable gradual and sudden methods arising from a single Dharma—once he heard this teaching, he reflected that the two vehicles should likewise enter into the One. While contemplating in this way, his mind gradually became open and expansive, and the Great Resolve immediately arose.)
As he was about to pass away, he summoned his son, as well as his kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, until they had all assembled.

Those who had received his transformation under twenty trillion Buddhas were designated as his "sons," while the Dharma-body of the ten directions was his "kinsmen"—all those whom the Tathāgata had together transformed and enlightened. First, he preached the Four Noble Truths and the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination; subsequently, he preached the Vaipulya (Universal) teachings.

Regarding the twelve divisions of the scriptures, he next expounded the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; this [sūtra] universally gathers all scriptures, harmonizing and integrating both gradual and sudden teachings so that they converge into this canon. Therefore, it is named "The Assembly of the King."
He then made this proclamation: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, born of me.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, he fled and wandered about in hardship and distress."
(The fugitive has turned his back on the Mahāyāna and given rise to ignorance; he is destitute and solitary.
For over fifty years, his original surname was so-and-so, and my name was so-and-so. Formerly, while in my native city, I harbored anxiety and searched for him everywhere.
Suddenly, having encountered him here, I have found him. He is truly my son, and I am truly his father.

(He has indeed followed me in receiving instruction and following me in gaining understanding. I have indeed previously taught the Great Dharma to him at the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas; he then fled back into the cycle of birth and death, fully experiencing the six realms of existence—hence it is said that more than fifty years have passed).
"Now, all the wealth and property that I possess are yours; the expenditures and revenues of the past are known to you.

(The phrase "all Mahāyāna, the ten thousand practices and ten thousand virtues" refers to "all that is possessed"; "the expenditures and revenues of the past are known to you" points to the instruction received from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the past.)
"World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, hearing these words from his father, was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.
He thought to himself: 'Originally I had no intention of seeking anything; yet now this treasure store has come to me of its own accord.'"

(Reflecting that we ourselves had no heart’s desire to hope for the Buddha-way, yet now suddenly hear that we have received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, it is said: "sought not, yet obtained.
World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata; we are all like the sons of the Buddha. The Tathāgata has always spoken of us as his sons.
World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we undergo various afflictions within saṃsāra.
Deluded and ignorant, they take pleasure in and are attached to inferior teachings.

(Regarding the three types of suffering: they arise from the three types of sensation. From painful sensation arises the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); from pleasant sensation arises the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and from neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation arises the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).)
"Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate and sweep away the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
By applying ourselves with diligent effort therein, we have attained nirvana. Having obtained this 'daily wage,' our hearts are filled with great joy;
we consider ourselves sufficient and say to ourselves: 'Because of our diligent effort within the Buddha-dharma, that which was to be attained has been widely secured.'"

"Much indeed. Yet the World-Honored One, knowing beforehand that our minds were attached to base desires and that we delighted in inferior teachings, simply left us be and did not distinguish for us that you all possess a share of the Tathāgata’s treasure-house of knowledge and vision.
Through the power of skillful means, the World-Honored One has spoken of the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
(While employing the expedient means of the three vehicles, he speaks of the true reality of the Mahāyāna.
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day’s wages for nirvāṇa, regarding this as a great gain; thus, we have no aspiration or pursuit toward this Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we have been instructed and expounded [in it] for the sake of the bodhisattvas. And yet—
We ourselves have had no aspiration for this. Why is that? Because the Buddha knew our hearts delighted in the lesser Dharma;
thus, through the power of skillful means, he taught us according to our capacity. Yet we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.

(The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, taught the Dharma of true reality together with those of the Two Vehicles. We did not recognize it; this is why we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.)
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no stinginess regarding the Buddha’s wisdom. Why is this?
Because although we have from the past truly been sons of the Buddha, we have merely delighted in the Lesser Dharma. Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma],...
The Buddha then preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for me. Within this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle;

yet previously, in the presence of bodhisattvas, he disparaged the śrāvakas who delight in inferior teachings. Nevertheless, the Buddha has in truth taught and transformed beings through the Mahāyāna.
(Since the principle is one, we know that the former three were not real. Now that we have abandoned the false and grasped the true, we certainly know this was not out of stinginess.
Therefore, we say that originally we had no mind to seek anything; now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously.
All that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been obtained.

"Because of this thorough understanding, one knows for oneself that we are truly the sons of the Buddha. We inherently possess the vast *dharmatā* and are endowed with perfect merit, no different from the various Bodhisattvas.

It is only because of our own delusion, through false conceptualization and attachment, that we wander in the cycle of rebirth—just like a destitute son who, having lost his way in his own hometown, flees to another land; though his father has not yet dared to recognize him. The 'fifty years' refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Within a single thought-moment arising in these five aggregates, fifty kinds of evil are present.

'Racing about in the four directions' refers to transmigrating through the four modes of birth. Relying on such worldly wisdom, one hopes to sever afflictions; this is what is meant by 'using the heterodox to manifest the orthodox,' as in the case of Kāśyapa and others, who all entered the Buddha-vehicle from among the non-Buddhists."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching; With joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before.
The Buddha has declared that the śrāvakas Shall themselves become Buddhas."
This unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained without seeking; it is like a young child,
immature and ignorant, who leaves his father and flees,
wandering through various lands in a distant country for more than fifty years, while his father grieves and longs for him.
He searched in all four directions; having become weary from his search, he stopped at a certain city and built a house there. He amused himself with the five desires;
his family was immensely wealthy, possessing much gold and silver, mother-of-pearl and agate, pearls and lapis lazuli.
Elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; litters, carriages, and vehicles; vast estates, servants, and numerous people;
income and profit from their coming and going extend throughout other lands;
there is nowhere they do not exist—traders and merchants numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis.
Surrounded by those who pay him homage, he is always cherished by kings;
ministers and noble clans all revere him together. Because of his various connections, many people come and go;
thus wealthy and powerful, he possesses great majesty.
But as my years grow old and advanced, my anxiety for my son increases all the more.
Day and night I think only that the time of my death is approaching; yet my foolish son has abandoned me for over fifty years.
What shall become of the treasures and goods in my storehouses? At that time, the impoverished son—
Seeking food and clothing, he traveled from village to village and from kingdom to kingdom;
sometimes he obtained something, and sometimes he obtained nothing.
Starving and emaciated, with sores and scabs breaking out on his body, he gradually made his way until he reached the city where his father lived.
Passing from one place of hire to another, he eventually arrived at his father’s house.
At that time, the elder was within the gateway, seated upon a great lion throne under a magnificent jeweled canopy,
surrounded by his retinue and guarded by attendants, some of whom were engaged in accounting.
With gold, silver, and precious treasures, He manages the coming and going of his wealth and property,
Recording it all in ledgers and documents. When the impoverished son sees his father— Magnificent, noble, and majestic— He thinks,
"This must be a king or someone like a king," And in his alarm and bewilderment, he wonders, "Why have I come here?"
He then thought to himself: "If I remain here for long, I may be coerced and forced to work. Having reflected thus, he fled away.
He inquired after a poor neighborhood, intending to go there to seek employment. At that time, the elder—
From his lion throne, he saw his son from afar; silently recognizing him, he immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him.
The impoverished son cried out in alarm, falling to the ground in confusion and distress, thinking: "This man is seizing me; I shall surely be put to death."
"What use have you for food and clothing that has brought you to this state?
The elder, knowing his son to be foolish and narrow-minded, did not believe his words;
nor did he believe him to be his father, so he employed a skillful means and sent others instead—men who were one-eyed, short, and deformed.
"To those who lack majesty and virtue, you may say: 'We shall employ you to remove all filth and excrement, and we will pay you double wages.
(Since the Great Transformation has ceased, he thus uses skillful means to preach the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle in order to attract and guide them.)"
Hearing this, the impoverished son followed along with joy; he removed the filth and dirt,
purifying all the rooms and chambers (purifying the six sense faculties and the five aggregates).
The elder constantly saw his son from the window; thinking that his son was foolish and inferior,
delighting in base deeds, the elder thereupon put on tattered,
soiled clothes, took up a dung-removal tool, went to where his son was, and approached him through skillful means.
He would command him to work diligently, saying: "I shall increase your wages;
you shall have oil for anointing your feet, food and drink in abundance, and bedding that is thick and warm.
Thus, through such harsh words, you must work diligently. Furthermore, with gentle words, he would say: "You are like my own son."

"Speech" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness. "Diligent practice" refers to the four right efforts. "Thick and warm bedding" refers to the four kinds of dhyāna, which are cultivated through contemplation, refinement, and repeated practice.
The elder, possessing wisdom, gradually allowed him to enter and exit;
for twenty years he managed the household affairs, showing him the gold, silver, pearls, crystal,
and various goods as they were brought in and out, making him know them all, yet he still remained outside the gate.
Dwelling in a grass hut, he thought to himself of his poverty:
"I have no such things" (because he had not yet abandoned his inferior mind, he remained in the grass hut).
The father, knowing his son's mind, gradually caused it to expand, wishing to bestow wealth upon him.
He immediately gathered his kinsmen, the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders;
before this great assembly, he declared: "This is my son.
He left me to travel elsewhere fifty years ago, and it has now been twenty years since I saw him return."
Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; having wandered everywhere in search of him, I have finally come here.
Whatever I possess—my house and my people—I entrust entirely to him, for him to use as he pleases. My son, remember your former poverty!
With inferior aspirations, I have now, in the presence of my father, obtained great treasures as well as houses and all manner of wealth;
I am filled with immense joy at having attained what was never before experienced. The Buddha is likewise: he knows that I delight in the small.
Never did [the Buddha] say, "You shall become Buddhas," yet he said that we have attained all the outflows-free states and achieved the Lesser Vehicle.
The Buddha’s disciples, the Śrāvakas, were commanded by the Buddha to preach the Supreme Path; those who practice this—
When I attain Buddhahood, I shall follow the Buddha’s teaching and, as a great bodhisattva,
use various causes and conditions, diverse parables,
and manifold expressions to expound the unsurpassed path. All you sons of the Buddhas shall hear the Dharma from me.
Contemplating day and night and practicing with diligent effort, at that time all the Buddhas bestowed upon him this prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
the secret treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas is intended solely for Bodhisattvas."
I expound the reality of things without making it "mine," speaking these essential truths just as that impoverished son,
upon approaching his father, knew of all the goods yet felt no desire to take them.
Though we speak of the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma, [the sentient beings] likewise feel no longing for it.
Those who lack aspiration are likewise so; we consider our own internal extinction to be sufficient, believing that by understanding only this matter there is nothing further to be done.
(The supreme path is precisely the wisdom of emptiness, *prajñā*. Because the afflictions of views and thoughts within the triple world are exhausted, it is called "internal extinction.")
If we were to hear of purifying buddha-fields and teaching and transforming sentient beings, we would have no joy whatsoever.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without arising and without ceasing, and are neither great nor small.
Regarding the untainted and unconditioned, they reflect in this way:

"We have not experienced joy for a long night; regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, we were without craving, without attachment, and no longer possessed of aspiration, considering our own [attainment] in the Dharma to be ultimate."
Throughout the long night, we have cultivated the Dharma of emptiness; we have attained liberation from the afflictions and sufferings of the triple world.
Abiding in our final bodies within the *nirvāṇa* with remainder, we have been taught by the Buddha;
that we have attained the Way is not in vain, and thus we have truly achieved it.
To repay the Buddha’s kindness, although we have preached the Bodhisattva Dharma for the sake of these sons of the Buddhas so that they might seek the path of the Buddha,
we ourselves have never had any aspiration or delight in this Dharma. Thus, the Guide has abandoned us, having perceived our state of mind.
At first, he did not urge them forward, but spoke of the actual benefits; just as a wealthy elder,
knowing his son’s inferior disposition, used the power of skillful means to gently subdue his mind before finally entrusting him with all his wealth, so too did the Buddha.
A rare event has appeared: knowing those who delight in the small, he tames their minds through the power of skillful means and then teaches them great wisdom.
Today we have attained what we never had before; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have gained it ourselves.
Just as that impoverished son obtained immeasurable treasure, so too, O World-Honored One, have we now attained the Way and its fruit;
regarding the outflow-free Dharma, we have obtained the eye of purity.
Throughout the long night, we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and it is only from this day forward [that we truly realize their fruit].
Having attained its fruit and reward, within the Dharma of the Dharma King, having long cultivated pure conduct, we have now attained the outflow-free, unsurpassed great fruit.
Today we are truly śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear.
We are now true Arhats; among all the worlds—gods, humans, Māras, and Brahmās—we are universally worthy of receiving offerings.
World-Honored One of great kindness, by means of this rare occurrence, you have compassionately taught and transformed us.
Benefiting us for immeasurable billions of kalpas—who could ever repay such kindness?
Even by providing for our hands and feet, prostrating with head and crown, and offering every form of worship, one cannot repay it;
nor even by bearing [the Buddha] upon the crown of one's head or carrying him on both shoulders.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one should serve with a devoted heart and respect,
offering exquisite meals, immeasurable precious robes, various bedding and furniture,
diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood, and all manner of rare jewels, thereby erecting stupas and temples.
Spreading jeweled robes upon the ground— through such acts as these,
even if performed as offerings for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— one still could not repay the Buddhas’ rare,
immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable power of great spiritual transformations.
Untainted and unconditioned, the King of all dharmas, Able to endure such matters for those who are base and inferior—
For ordinary people who grasp at signs, the Buddhas preach according to what is appropriate;
The Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over the Dharma, Knowing all sentient beings.
According to their various desires and inclinations, as well as their capacities,
he teaches the Dharma through immeasurable analogies; he knows the roots of goodness of sentient beings from past lives,
as well as those who have reached maturity and those who have not.
Having discerned and known [this], regarding the path of the One Vehicle, he taught according to what was appropriate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
*The Exquisite Commentary on the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*The Exquisite Commentary on the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
with annotations by the Wayfarer Xu Changzhi of Wuyuan (Wu-yuan) and Qin Zhou.
Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

The Way taught is one; the nature of all people is one. However, because people’s aspirations differ, their comprehension differs, and their diligence in cultivation differs, there are consequently differences in the fruits realized—namely, the Small, Middle, and Great Vehicles.
