Thus, after Kāśyapa and the other four disciples attained faith and understanding, the Buddha used the analogy that while they are all moistened by the same rain and grow from the same soil, the various plants and trees each develop differently.

(The true countenance of green bamboos and yellow flowers—/ The spring breeze originally has no dual heart. / If one can directly know the essential point,/ Then beneath the leaves and upon the branches, all are the Dharma-sound.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the great disciples: "Excellent, excellent! Kāśyapa, you have well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits.
It is exactly as you have said. Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable and boundless [qualities]."
"Immeasurable are these merits; even if you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you could not exhaust them.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never in vain."

(Although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real. Outside of the provisional and the real, there are no other teachings. Therefore, the Dharma King is cited and his words of sincerity and truthfulness are used to encourage faith.)
Regarding all phenomena, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means (all phenomena refer here to the seven stages of skillful means).
All the teachings he proclaims reach the ground of omniscience.
(The "ground" refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*). Its nature is vast and expansive, hence it is called "all-encompassing. It is quiescent yet eternally illuminating, hence it is called "wisdom.
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena, and he also knows the profound mental activities of all sentient beings, penetrating them without obstruction.
(He is able to illuminate skillful means; he is able to identify medicines; he is able to recognize illnesses. Each has its respective destination, namely the precepts, wholesome deeds, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, he exhaustively investigates and clearly understands them, demonstrating to all sentient beings the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"The clear comprehension of all phenomena is true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). What is seen by the Buddha-eye is called 'clear' (*vi-√mṛś*); what is known by true wisdom is called 'comprehended' (*pra-√vid*). All medicines and all illnesses are illuminated by true wisdom.

Kāśyapa, it is like this: for example, in a trichiliocosm, there are mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands, where various kinds of plants, trees, groves, and medicinal herbs grow, each with its own distinct species and different names and forms.

The great trichiliocosm is likened to sentient beings; the mountains, rivers, and streams are likened to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Administering medicine to cure illness is like using the Dharma to subdue evil and remedy delusion. Because the seeds of cause and effect within the five vehicles and seven stages of expedient means are not uniform, they are said to be of different "species" (*jāti*).
Dense clouds spread everywhere, completely covering the three thousandfold world system.
(Because he permeates the ten dharma realms with the fragrance of compassion and teaches the Dharma through his response body, it is said they "spread everywhere.")

At one time, they rained down equally, their moisture universally soaking all things: the herbs, trees, and forests, as well as the various medicinal plants—those with small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves;
those with medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, and medium leaves; and those with large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves.

The rain of Dharma moistens all universally; whatever habitual causes sentient beings possess, their seeds immediately sprout. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves are as follows: faith is the root, precepts are the stem, meditative concentration is the branch, and wisdom is the leaf. The great root is the bodhisattva’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

The various trees, whether large or small, according to their superior, middling, or inferior natures, each receive what is appropriate; though rained upon by a single cloud, they grow in accordance with their respective species, blossoming with flowers and bearing fruit.
(To accord with their spiritual dispositions is to employ skillful means according to their capacities; this refers to the seven types of causes and effects of habitual retribution.
Although they all grow from the same earth and are moistened by the same rain, the various plants and trees each have their own distinctions.

(Short grasses are likened to humans and devas; medium grasses to those of the Two Vehicles; superior grasses to Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching; small trees to Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching; and large trees to Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching. All possess the same Buddha-nature; all belong to the Mahāyāna.)
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so: appearing in the world like the rising of a great cloud,
he pervades the entire world with a great voice— devas, humans, and asuras— just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm.

(The great clouds arise: this illustrates the Tathāgata’s great compassion that covers and nurtures all beings. The great sound: this refers to the Buddha’s mouth. "Heavenly beings and humans," etc.: these refer to the three wholesome paths, which correspond to the root-natures of the three vehicles.)

In the midst of the great assembly, he uttered these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān."
(Recite the Ten Epithets.

Those who have not yet crossed over, I shall cause to cross over; those who have not yet attained liberation, I shall cause to attain liberation; those who have not yet found peace, I shall cause to find peace; those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, I shall cause to attain *nirvāṇa*.
(The Four Great Vows also relate to the Four Noble Truths, for they enable one to transcend birth and death and reach peace and happiness.
One knows, as it truly is, this world and the worlds hereafter.
(Through the knowledge of past lives, one reaches the past; through the divine eye, one reaches the future; through the exhaustion of outflows, one reaches the present).
I am the all-knowing one, fully endowed with these three knowledges.
The All-Seeing One (endowed with the five eyes),
the Knower of the Path, the Opener of the Path, and the Proclaimer of the Path.
(These three karmas are accompanied by wisdom.
You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to hear the Dharma. Thereupon, the Tathāgata contemplated this assembly.
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the presence of diligence or indolence—
(whereas the preceding analogies illustrated the differences among plants and trees, this now clarifies that there are sharp and dull faculties)—
he preaches the Dharma according to what each can bear, in various and immeasurable ways, causing all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.

(To act according to what each is capable of is precisely to accord with their individual aptitudes, free from the error of addition or subtraction. To joyfully obtain wholesome benefit means that each receives the nourishment of the Dharma and gains its profit.)
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life and be reborn in favorable realms hereafter, experiencing happiness through the Path.
They shall also hear the Dharma; having heard it, they will be freed from all obstacles and, within the midst of all dharmas, act according to their own capacity and power.
Gradually one attains entry into the Way.

(The Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all; even those in the three miserable realms receive its broad moisture and grow. As it is said regarding Prajñā, one is freed from all obstacles, which brings peace and security in this present life.)
Just as that great cloud rains upon all— upon the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal herbs—
and each receives its full measure of moisture according to its own nature, thereby attaining growth; so too does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma with a single characteristic and a single flavor,
namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, ultimately leading to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

(Regarding "one characteristic": the minds of sentient beings share the same characteristic of True Suchness; this is the "One Ground. Regarding "one flavor": the Dharma of the One Vehicle equally explains a single principle; this is the "One Rain.

In the past, the single reality-characteristic was expediently opened into seven characteristics, and within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, it was differentiated and taught as seven teachings. Ultimately, they all return to one characteristic and one flavor. Liberation, detachment, and cessation—these three characteristics are collectively the single reality-characteristic; therefore, it is said that they ultimately culminate in the knowledge of all modes.)

If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and having upheld, read, recited, or practiced it according to the teaching, they do not themselves realize or know the merit they have thereby obtained.

(Their upholding and exposition differ; their practice is likewise distinct. For humans and devas, there is the interpretation of precepts and wholesome deeds; for the Three Vehicles, there is the interpretation of the Truths, the Bases of Mindfulness, and the Factors of Enlightenment. Since these interpretations differ, they constitute distinctions.)
Why is this? Only the Tathāgata knows the seeds, characteristics, and essential natures of these sentient beings (the three paths are the seeds of the three virtues).

What is it that one recollects? What is it that one contemplates? What is it that one cultivates? How does one recollect? How does one contemplate? How does one cultivate? By means of what dharma does one recollect?
By means of what dharma does one contemplate? By means of what dharma does one cultivate?
(This refers to the three wisdoms apprehending their objects through hearing the Dharma).
By what dharma does one obtain what dharma?
(The causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits; this is differentiation. Sentient beings and all Buddhas are of one suchness and without duality; this is non-differentiation).
Sentient beings dwell in various stages; only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.

(The seven expedients consist of dwelling in seven positions, hence they are called "various. The Tathāgata speaks according to the intentions of others, expounding through skillful means so that all may reach the stage of omniscience.)
Just as those grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and various medicinal herbs do not themselves know their superior, middling, or inferior natures,
the Tathāgata knows this to be a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor— namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation,
the ultimate nirvāṇa of the eternally quiescent characteristic, which ultimately returns to emptiness.

(The Mahāyāna ultimately returns to emptiness; thus there is no differentiation. None of these are the "with remainder" or "without remainder" states of the two vehicles; rather, this is ultimate nirvāṇa.)

The Buddha, having known this, observes the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and protects them. For this reason, he does not immediately teach them the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
"O Kāśyapa, you are truly rare; you are able to understand that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and you are able to believe and accept it."

(He is able to know how to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; this describes his ability to lead others to realize the three vehicles. He is able to believe and accept it; this describes his ability to lead others to realize the one vehicle). Why is this so?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world.

(To say that cause and effect do not perish is "existence. There are twenty-five kings of samādhi who destroy these twenty-five existences; thus, he is called the Dharma King who destroys existence. These twenty-five existences are the three realms: the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of formlessness.)
According to the desires of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways.

The Tathāgata’s honored wisdom is profound and far-reaching; for a long time he has kept this essential point in silence, not being intent on preaching it hastily (because the great capacity [of the listeners] had not yet been aroused, he did not preach it hastily).
Those with wisdom, upon hearing it, will be able to believe and understand;

those without wisdom will harbor doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss. Therefore, Kāśyapa, teach according to their capacity through various causes and conditions, so that they may attain right view.
(The Mahāyāna is the correct view).
Kāśyapa, you should know: it is like a great cloud that arises in the world and covers everything;
the cloud of wisdom contains moisture, and its lightning flashes brilliantly.
The sound of thunder resounds afar, causing all beings to rejoice; the sunlight is eclipsed and the earth becomes cool.
Dark clouds hang low and spread out as if they could be grasped. (The cloud is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because it follows the movement of wisdom, it is called the "Wisdom Cloud. Because it can possess the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is said to "contain moisture. Its body emits great light like a flash of lightning, and its mouth thunders with the four types of eloquence like the sound of thunder. Upon hearing the Dharma...)

With joyful speech and serene delight, the ninety-five kinds of heterodox radiance do not appear; this is called "obscuration. Having removed the ninety-eight kinds of afflictions caused by the heat of views and thoughts, one is like the coolness upon the earth. With the appearance of dense, gathering clouds, the response-body descends into the world and is able to perfect the three realms of existence;
therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] "assumes" [this form].
That rain falls equally upon all, descending simultaneously from the four directions; it flows and pours in immeasurable quantities, saturating the entire land.

In the mountains, rivers, steep valleys, and remote recesses, there grow herbs, trees, medicinal plants, and various species of flora—both great and small—as well as the sprouts and crops of the hundred grains.
Sugarcane and grapes, moistened by the rain, are all made abundant;
even parched lands are universally saturated. Medicinal herbs and trees flourish together.
From that cloud issues water of a single flavor, yet the grasses, trees, and forests receive its moisture according to their respective capacities.

(The "hundred grains" refers to the five grains; they are likened to the Five Vehicles, which can produce a hundred virtues. Sugarcane and grapes are likened to meditative concentration and wisdom. The thorough moistening of dry land is likened to causing those who have not yet had faith to believe).
All the various trees— superior, middling, and inferior— each grow according to its size;
their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits,
and radiant colors all attain a fresh luster wherever the single rain reaches, according to their respective natures and forms.
The capacities of their natures may be great or small, yet that which moistens them is one and the same;
thus they each flourish. The Buddha is likewise: appearing in the world, he is like a great cloud that universally covers all.
Having appeared in the world, he acts for the sake of all sentient beings.
Expounding in detail the reality of all phenomena, the Great Sage, the World-Honored One,

To bring peace and security to sentient beings, he appears in the world;

Thus creating the causes and conditions, I contemplate all things as universally equal, without distinction between self and other, and free from thoughts of love or hatred.

As he does for one person, so it is for many; he constantly expounds the Dharma without ever engaging in other matters.

He then spoke these verses again:
"The Hero of the World, peerless and unequaled, Adorned by a hundred merits, Has attained unsurpassed wisdom."
We pray that you will speak for the sake of the world, to deliver us and all classes of sentient beings;
may you analyze and reveal this so that we may attain such wisdom.
If we are to attain Buddhahood, then so shall all sentient beings; O World-Honored One, you know the thoughts within the deep hearts of beings.
He also knows the path they travel, And he knows the power of their wisdom, Their inclinations, their cultivation of merit, And the karmic deeds performed in past lives;
Having fully known all this, the World-Honored One Shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, five hundred million worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.
In the spaces between those lands, even the dark and obscure places where the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not reach, were all filled with great light.
The sentient beings therein were able to see one another and all exclaimed, "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here? Furthermore, throughout those realms...
The palaces of the various devas, up to the Brahma palaces, shook in six ways; a great light shone everywhere, filling the world and surpassing all the radiance of the devas.

When Sarvārthasiddha was dwelling in the womb, the three thousandfold world-system was filled with a brilliant, vast light; even those places not reached by the sun or moon were all made luminous. The sentient beings therein were each able to see one another. When he first attained the Way, it was likewise:
in the morning he taught the gods of the Form Realm, at midday the gods of the Desire Realm, and in the afternoon the ghosts and spirits—thus preaching the Dharma during these three periods.
At that time, within five hundred million worlds in the eastern direction, the palaces of the Brahmā heavens were illuminated by a radiance twice as bright as their usual light.
Each of the Brahmā kings thought to himself: "The radiance of these palaces today is unlike anything seen before.
By what cause and condition has this sign appeared? Thereupon, the Brahmā kings each went to meet one another.
They deliberated on this matter together. At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Savior of All, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"In all our palaces, there is a radiance such as has never been seen before. What is the cause and condition for this?

We should each seek it together. Is it because a being of great virtue has been born, or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world, that this great light shines everywhere throughout the ten directions?"
At that time, the Brahma Kings from five million billion lands, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and traveled collectively toward the west to investigate the cause of these signs. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Gandharvas, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him.

Upon seeing the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, the Brahma kings immediately prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered celestial flowers over him.
The flowers they scattered were like Mount Sumeru; they offered them as well to the Buddha’s enlightenment.
The Bodhi tree was ten *yojanas* high. Having made offerings of flowers, each [Brahmā] presented his palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you will graciously accept and dwell in the palaces we have offered.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahmā kings, with one mind and in a single voice, praised him in verse:
The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter; Possessing immeasurable merit, he is able to rescue and protect all.
Great Teacher of gods and humans, Out of compassion for the sentient beings of the world in the ten directions, All universally receive his benefit and aid. From where we have come—
From five hundred million kotis of lands, we have renounced the bliss of profound meditative concentration in order to make offerings to the Buddha.
By virtue of our merits from previous lives, our palaces were most exquisitely adorned; we now offer them to the World-Honored One—may you graciously accept them out of compassion.
(Bowing with the head and face is the action of body; speaking these words and reciting verses of praise is the action of speech; single-mindedness is the action of mind.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha in verse, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and open the path to Nirvana. Then the Brahma kings, with one mind and in unison, said:
He spoke in verse:
"O Hero among Men, Honored One among the Two-legged, I pray that you expound the Dharma; With the power of great compassion, deliver sentient beings from suffering."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
Furthermore, monks, in five million billion lands to the southeast, the Great Brahmā Kings each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never seen before.
Overjoyed and leaping for joy, they conceived a sense of wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter. At that time, those...
Within the assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Mahākāruṇika, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"What is the cause and condition By which such a sign has appeared? The radiance of our palaces is such as we have never known before;
Is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, Or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world?"
"Never before have we seen such a sign; we should now seek it with one mind. Let us travel through thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands to follow this light and investigate it together.
It is most likely that a Buddha has appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
At that time, five million koṭis of Brahma kings, together with their palaces, each took a robe-satchel and filled it with various...
Together with the celestial flowers, they proceeded toward the northwest to investigate the cause of these signs.
There they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment, beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others surrounded him with reverent devotion.

When they saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered celestial flowers over him;
the flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us. We pray that you will graciously accept the palaces we have presented.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma Kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
To the Holy King, the Sovereign among Gods, With the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, Who has compassion for all sentient beings— To you we now pay homage.
The World-Honored One is most rare; Only once in a very long time does he appear.
For one hundred and eighty kalpas, Time passed in vain without a Buddha, And the three evil realms were filled.
The hosts of devas have diminished; now a Buddha has appeared in the world. He acts as the eye for sentient beings and the refuge for the world;
he protects all and is the father of sentient beings, one who brings compassion and benefit.
Through the auspicious merit of our past lives, we have now encountered the World-Honored One.

(The Buddha is the Sage of the Ultimate Fruit who reigns as sovereign over the ten realms and is praised by all devas; thus he is called the "King among Gods. The *kalaviṅka*—translated here as the "Bird of Wondrous Sound"—emits a subtle and exquisite cry even while still within its shell;
the Tathāgata’s voice is identical to this, hence it is called the "Kalaviṅka Voice. Sentient beings have lost their right view, and the Buddha points the way for them; thus he is called the "Eye").
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:

"We pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will turn the Wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings. Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses:
The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, Revealing the characteristics of all phenomena;
He delivers suffering beings, causing them to attain great joy. When sentient beings hear this Dharma, They attain the Path or are born in heaven;
Those in the evil realms decrease, And those who practice patience and goodness increase.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
Furthermore, monks, in five million billion lands to the south, the Great Brahma Kings each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never seen before.
Overjoyed and leaping for joy, they conceived a sense of rare wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter, asking: "By what cause..."
"Friends, our palaces possess such radiance as this. Now, within that assembly, there is a Great Brahmā King named Subhadharma, who speaks these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:"
Our various palaces are filled with a light of such majestic brilliance; this cannot be without cause or condition, so we must seek its reason.
Having never seen such a sign for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world?
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the north to investigate the cause of these signs. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.

The *garuḍas*, humans, non-humans, and others surrounded him with reverence. When they saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and scattered celestial flowers over him;
the flowers so scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Bodhi tree of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, each presented his own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you graciously accept the palaces we have offered.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to behold; he who has shattered all afflictions appears only once in more than one hundred and thirty kalpas.
To all sentient beings who were parched with hunger and thirst, he now fills them with the rain of Dharma—something never seen before.
This possessor of immeasurable wisdom is like the udumbara flower.
"Today we have encountered this opportunity; our various palaces have been adorned by the light [of your presence].
Out of great compassion, World-Honored One, we pray that you will graciously accept them.
Then, having praised the Buddha with these verses, the Brahma Kings each spoke thus: "We pray that the World-Honored One will turn the [Wheel of Dharma]."
The Wheel of Dharma. May all the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas in all the worlds obtain peace and security and attain liberation.
Then the Brahmā kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
I pray only that the Honored One among Gods and Humans May turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
Beat the great drum of the Dharma and blow the great conch of the Dharma, And let the great rain of Dharma fall everywhere.
To deliver immeasurable sentient beings, we all join in this request: Please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent. It was likewise in the southwest, and so on down to the nadir.

At that time, in five million billion lands above, all the Great Brahma Kings beheld their own respective palaces, which were brilliantly illuminated with a majestic radiance such as had never been seen before; they leaped for joy and felt a sense of wonder.
They immediately went to one another’s abodes and deliberated together on this matter: "By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance?
At that time, among that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
Now, by what cause and condition have our various palaces become so adorned with majestic power and radiant light,
never seen before? By what such wondrous sign— unheard of or seen in the past—
is it that a Great Virtuous One has been born, or that a Buddha has appeared in the world?
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces,
each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively to the lower direction to investigate the cause of these signs.

There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.

The *garuḍas*, humans, non-humans, and others surrounded him with reverence. Upon seeing the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were like Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made these offerings, each presented their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words: "May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we pray that you will graciously accept and dwell within the palaces we have offered. Then, in the presence of the Buddha, all those Brahma Kings—
With one mind and in unison, they spoke in verse:
"How excellent it is to behold the Buddhas, The Holy Honored Ones who save the world! They are able to exert effort within the prison of the three realms To deliver all sentient beings.
O Universal Wisdom, Honored One among gods and humans, You take pity upon the multitude of living beings."
You are able to open the gate of the ambrosia and extensively deliver all beings. In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, time passed in vain as there was no Buddha;

when the World-Honored One had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness, the three evil realms increased, the asuras flourished, and the hosts of devas gradually diminished.
Upon death, many fall into evil realms, For they have not heard the Dharma from the Buddha.
Their physical strength, wisdom, and other virtues All diminish accordingly. Due to the causes and conditions of their sinful karma, They lose both happiness and the perception of happiness;
Abiding in the dharma of false views, They do not recognize virtuous conduct or propriety.
Those who do not receive the Buddha’s transformation fall perpetually into the evil realms. The Buddha is the eye of the world;

appearing only after a vast expanse of time, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he manifests in the world and attains supreme perfect enlightenment. We, along with all other multitudes, rejoice most profoundly.
Rejoicing at this unprecedented marvel, we offer these palaces of ours, adorned by the grace of your light, now to the World-Honored One; may you deign to accept them out of compassion.
May the merit from this be shared universally with all, so that we and all sentient beings together may attain the Way of the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, having praised the Buddha in verse, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, and delivering and liberating many.
Then the Brahma Kings spoke in verse:
The World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma, Beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma,
And delivers suffering beings by revealing the path to Nirvana. I pray that you will accept my invitation, And out of compassion,
expound with your great and subtle voice The Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, having accepted the invitation of the Brahma Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes,
immediately turned the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects through three revolutions.

(Below this, first the Wheel of the Half-Syllables is turned. Regarding the "three turnings": these are the turning of demonstration, the turning of exhortation, and the turning of realization. The turning of demonstration refers to: "This is suffering," up to "this is the path. The turning of exhortation refers to: "Suffering should be known; origination should be abandoned; cessation should be realized; the path should be cultivated.

The turning of realization refers to: "Suffering has been known by me; it need not be known again," up to "the path has been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again. Demonstration means showing its characteristics; exhortation means urging one to practice; realization means citing one's own realization as proof for that [other].

Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull, three turnings are made for them. For the pratyekabuddhas, who are next, two turnings are made. For the bodhisattvas, whose faculties are sharp, one turning is made.)
That which cannot be turned by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world—(that which cannot be turned means that śramaṇas do not even understand it, much less turn it;
though pratyekabuddhas have awakened to it, they cannot speak of it; though brāhmaṇas have heard its name, they do not understand its principle;

the same applies to the Māra kings and Brahmā kings)—turning this Dharma and causing it to enter the minds of others so that they may attain awakening, thereby shattering the sixty-two views, is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. This Dharma of the Four Truths has three turnings, constituting twelve wheels.
That is to say: "This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

(For the Śrāvaka, this was the first turning of the Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing. Regarding "this is suffering": all conditioned mental activities are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence—namely, the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering, which consist of birth-and-death within the six destinies of the triple world.

Regarding "the origin": it means that which gathers and brings about [suffering]. This refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-kleśa*). These afflictions coexist with karma and are able to engender birth-and-death. With the gathering [of afflictions] as the cause, suffering is the result. Since every result must have a cause, it is said: "This is the origin of suffering."

This is the cause and effect of the mundane world. Regarding "cessation" (*nirodha*): cessation takes the meaning of extinguishing non-existence. When afflictions and karma are completely exhausted, one is no longer burdened by birth and death; therefore, it is called the "extinction of suffering. The foundation of the Truth of Cessation consists of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.

If the fetters of the "son" (the individual) are exhausted, it is called *nirvāṇa with remainder*. If the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*. Regarding the "Path" (*mārga*): this refers to the primary path and its auxiliaries. These two support one another and are able to lead one to reach *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is named the "Path. Because the Path can extinguish suffering, it is the "Path to the Extinction of Suffering.

Briefly stated, these are morality, concentration, and wisdom; extensively stated, they are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The Path is the cause and extinction is the fruit; this is the cause and effect of the supramundane.

And he extensively explained the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming.
With birth as condition, there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. (This is the Bodhisattva’s turning of the Wheel of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

They revolve such that the fruit becomes the cause; they mutually rely upon one another as conditions. Regarding "ignorance" (*avidyā*): its essence is delusion. Its nature is confusion and darkness, lacking clear understanding;

it is precisely the affliction (*kleśa*). Regarding "formations" (*saṃskāra*): in past lives, one performs various karmas. Because karma is created through affliction, it is said that "with ignorance as condition, there are formations. Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it has the meaning of discernment. The sense organs entering their objects are called "entrances" (*āyatana*). Through the sense organs confronting their objects...)

That which has not yet been fully understood is called *sparśa* (contact). As for *vedanā* (feeling), it is the act of experiencing; because experiencing gives rise to craving, it is said that "conditioned by feeling is craving" (*vedanā-pratyayā tṛṣṇā*). Because attachment arises from craving, it is said that "conditioned by craving is grasping" (*tṛṣṇā-pratyayo 'dhyavasāna*).

As for *bhava* (existence), once one is attached to various objects, one initiates wholesome and unwholesome karma, which accumulates and draws forth rebirth within the three realms of existence; therefore, it is said that "conditioned by grasping is existence" (*upādāna-pratyayo bhavaḥ*). As for *jāti* (birth), it refers to taking birth within the six destinies.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.

With the cessation of craving, grasping ceases. With the cessation of grasping, existence ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
(Suffering and its origin are precisely ignorance; the path and cessation are the cessation of ignorance. Since ignorance is the root, when ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease.)

When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* of people attained liberation from all outflows (*āsrava*) through the non-appropriation of all phenomena.

They all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and were endowed with the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). During the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma, [there were] ten million...
Billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
likewise attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by way of not grasping at any phenomena (*dharma*). From that time forward, the assembly of śrāvakas became immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable.

"One who does not grasp at any phenomena" means one who does not grasp at various views; this is the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). "One who has attained liberation" means one who is freed from the two bonds of cause and effect; this is the attainment of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). "One with profound and wondrous concentration" refers precisely to the attainment of liberation.
At that time, the sixteen princes all left home as youths to become śrāmaṇeras. Their faculties were keen and sharp, their wisdom clear and lucid;
they had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

(Śrāmaṇera means "one who rests in kindness," as he rests from evil and practices kindness. As for the "faculties," they are the six faculties. Because the six faculties are pure, they are clear and sharp.)
They all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of great virtuous śrāvakas have all already achieved [their goals].
World-Honored One, you should also preach for us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having heard it, we shall all together practice and study it. World-Honored One, our aspiration is the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, that which is within the profound depths of our hearts."
[The Buddha] reflected: "The Buddha himself has realized and known [this];
he clearly perceives that their obstacles have been removed and the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been awakened;
therefore, he requests [the teaching]. At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eighty trillion people saw the sixteen princes emerge.
The family members also requested to leave the household life, and the king immediately granted them permission. At that time, that Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇeras’ invitation;

after twenty thousand kalpas had passed, he preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the True Dharma)—the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas—amidst the fourfold assembly.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras [attained] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
Because of [the pursuit of] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they all together receive, uphold, recite, and master it.
(Prajñā is the practice; supernatural powers are the matter.
While this sutra was being preached, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras all believed and accepted it. Among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who...
Those who possessed faith and understanding were few, while the other sentient beings, numbering in the thousands of millions, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.

The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting. Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered the room and was dwelling in silent meditation, each...

He ascended the Dharma-seat and, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly (it was because the Buddha had entered meditative absorption that he was able to speak).
Each one [of these] delivered six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
they instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(To resolve upon Bodhicitta is to speak of "crossing over," which refers to the seven stages of expedient means; it is the meaning of reaching the other shore.
After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi and proceeded to the Dharma-seat.
Sitting with serene composure, he addressed the great assembly: "These sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras are truly rare.
Their faculties are keen and sharp; their wisdom is clear and lucid. They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of buddhas.

In the presence of those buddhas, they have constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, and revealed it to sentient beings, leading them to enter therein. You..."
All of you should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them. Why is this?

If any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas can believe in the sūtra teachings spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas, and accept and uphold them without disparaging them, such persons shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the wisdom of the Tathāgata, O Buddha.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has transformed six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;

in every lifetime they have been born, they have been together with these bodhisattvas, and having heard the Dharma from them, they have all attained faith and understanding. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered the four [buddhas]."

The myriad billions of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are not yet exhausted. (The Great Sage is skillful; relying upon the four *siddhāntas*, he speaks thus: sometimes, for those who weary of the long duration of the Buddha-way, he speaks of it as short; for those who conceive a sense of ease regarding the Buddha-way, he speaks of it as long—this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.

Sometimes, for the purpose of generating past roots of goodness, he speaks of it as long or short—this is the *puruṣa-siddhānta*. Sometimes, according to what the world desires, he speaks of it as long or short—this is the *loka-siddhānta*. Or, for those who, upon hearing the discourse on long or short, immediately attain entry into the principle.)
This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established truth). *Siddha* means "all-pervading"; *siddhānta* is a Sanskrit term, translated into Chinese as "bestowal" (*śī*).
"O monks, I now tell you: those disciples of that Buddha, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, have all now attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They currently reside in lands throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma. There are immeasurable hundreds..."
They have hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinue. Those two śrāmaṇeras will become buddhas in the eastern direction:
the first is named Akṣobhya, who resides in the Land of Joy; the second is named Sumerukūṭa. In the southeastern direction there are two buddhas:
the first is named Siṃhaghoṣa, and the second is named Siṃhadarśana. In the southern direction there are two buddhas: the first is named Gaganastha, and the second is named Nityoparata.
In the southwest are two Buddhas: the first is named Śakradevendra-lakṣaṇa, and the second is named Brahma-lakṣaṇa. In the west are two Buddhas:
the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātupratibhaya-saṃtrāsanakarī. In the northwest are two Buddhas:
the first is named Tamālapatracaṃdanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merudhvaja. In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Meghasvara...
In the second [direction] is the Buddha named Cloud Sovereign King; in the northeast is the Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears.
The sixteenth is I, Śākyamuni Buddha, who has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
*Sahā* (also transcribed as *Sokha*; here translated as "Endurance") refers to the trichiliocosm, which constitutes the transformation realm of a single Buddha. *Amitābha* means "Immeasurable Life."
"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us individually taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, so that by hearing the Dharma from us, they [set their minds] upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
(The words following this mean that after the great elements [have been transformed], they do not regress in the interim, but abide in the unsurpassed path).
These sentient beings—those who at present abide on the stage of the śrāvaka—I constantly teach and transform toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These people should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma. Why is this?
Why? Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

(This means that after the seeds [of enlightenment] were sown, they subsequently regressed toward the Lesser Vehicle and remained in the stage of a śrāvaka. Although the Buddha taught them through the Mahāyāna so that they might gradually enter the Buddha-way, they simply did not believe in the Buddha’s wisdom; therefore, they regressed from the Great Vehicle and turned toward the Lesser.)

At that time, those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed [by me], are none other than you, monks, and the śrāvaka disciples who will exist in future ages after my parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who do not hear this sutra;
they will neither know nor realize the conduct of bodhisattvas, and they will give rise to [attachment] toward the merits they themselves have attained.
They conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvāṇa. Yet, I shall become a buddha in another land under a different name.
Although these people have conceived the thought of extinction and entered into nirvāṇa, they shall seek the wisdom of a buddha in that land and there hear this sutra;
they shall attain extinction solely by means of the Buddha-vehicle, for there is no other vehicle, except for the skillful means taught by the Tathāgatas.
The Dharma.
(At that time, it is the season for sowing seeds. Those who attain Buddhahood in other lands shall ultimately hear this from here. "Other lands" refers to the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder.)
"O bhikṣus, when the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm,
they have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, and have deeply entered into meditative concentration."

When the time for *nirvāṇa* arrives—that is, when the Buddhas appear in the world and their work of transforming beings through the Way is about to be completed—just as Kāśyapa Buddha and the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa appeared in a pure land, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and immediately entered *nirvāṇa*;

so too Śākyamuni appears in a defiled land, preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and then proclaims his imminent extinction. Those who are pure of mind immediately obtain the benefit of the Tripiṭaka teachings and are freed from the five turbidities and the eight sufferings. Those whose faith and understanding are firm place their hearts in mutual trust regarding the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) teachings.
Those who have thoroughly realized the emptiness of dharmas, upon hearing the preaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, attain realization within the dharma of emptiness.
He then assembled the bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas and preached this sūtra for them: "In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction;
it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction. Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, has deeply entered the nature of sentient beings.
Knowing that they delight in inferior teachings and are deeply attached to the five desires, he has preached [these] for their sake."
Regarding nirvana: if such a person hears of it, they will immediately believe and accept it.

(The Tathāgata bestows the three vehicles as skillful means and provisional wisdom. Because sentient beings have inferior desires and dispositions, are attached to the five sensory objects, and are defiled by the five turbidities, he speaks of the nirvana of the three vehicles to cause them to break their defilements and escape calamity; later, he speaks of the One Vehicle.)
It is like a perilous and evil road five hundred *yojanas* long, desolate and devoid of people—a place of terror.

(The two types of birth and death—segmental and transformative—constitute the peril of the fruit. The afflictions of views and thoughts, the dust-like [afflictions], and ignorance constitute the peril of the cause. Because of these causes and fruits, it is called an "evil road.")

If there is a great multitude who wish to traverse this path to reach the place of rare treasures—(the two vehicles sever views and afflictions to exit the triple world, hence it is said they "wish to traverse this path"; they further sever the dust-like and sand-like ignorance to seek the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, hence it is said they "wish to reach the place of rare treasures").
There was a guide, wise and discerning, who well understood the characteristics of the dangers and the passability of the perilous path.

(The guide is the sixteenth prince. "Wise" refers to the purity of the eyes and ears; "discerning" refers to the purity of the mind—this is the purity of the six sense faculties. "Wisdom" refers to the threefold wisdom within a single mind; "clarity" refers to the full possession of the five eyes.)
He intended to lead the multitude across this perilous difficulty. However, the people he was leading grew weary and retreated midway.

(The "multitude" refers to those who seek the Great Vehicle but take the Small; "midway" means from the initial aspiration until reaching Buddhahood—between these two pillars—they give rise to the thought of retreating, and thus it is called "midway").
They addressed the Guide, saying: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear.

To retreat from the Great [Vehicle] would mean great extinction; to take up the Small [Vehicle] would mean rebirth as small beings. This cycle of birth and extinction weighs upon our Dharma-body. Our roots of goodness are feeble and we are shrouded by ignorance; thus we speak of being 'utterly exhausted. To dread birth and death is what we call 'fear.'"
They were unable to proceed further; the road ahead was still long, and they now wished to turn back.
The guide, possessing many skillful means, thought to himself: "These people are to be pitied. Why do they wish to turn back, abandoning such great treasures? Having had this thought, he...

By the power of skillful means, within a perilous path extending three hundred *yojanas*, he conjures a city (this specifically employs the teaching of skillful means to transform those of the Two Vehicles;

having severed the afflictions of views and thought, they emerge from the suffering of the triple world and provisionally realize the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness; hence it is said that he conjures a city).
He addressed the multitude, saying: "Do not be afraid; do not turn back. You may stay within this great city and do as you please.
If you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security. If you are able to proceed further to the place of treasures, you may go there as well."

(This refers to the encouragement to realize the three turnings: "Do not turn back" is the turning of encouragement; "you may act as you wish while staying here" is the turning of demonstration; "entering the city in safety" is the turning of realization).
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming, "We have now escaped this evil path;

we have swiftly attained peace and security. Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already reached their destination and the thought that they were secure.

(Having given rise to the thought that they have already crossed over—just as one who has attained the knowledge of exhaustion—and the thought of security—just as one who has attained the knowledge of non-arising).
At that time, the Guide, knowing that this multitude of people had already found rest and were no longer weary, immediately caused the conjured city to vanish.
He spoke to the multitude, saying, "Come, all of you; the place of treasure is near. That great city you saw earlier was merely a creation of mine, fashioned for the purpose of providing rest."

(The jeweled destination and the conjured city both represent the two levels of principle—the Great and the Small. By refuting the provisional principles of the Two Vehicles, they reveal the single true principle of the jeweled destination.)

"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise. Now he acts as your great guide, knowing that the various paths of birth and death, the afflictions, and the evil realms are perilous, difficult, and long-lasting—places that must be abandoned and crossed.

If sentient beings were to hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha, nor would they wish to draw near him; they would instead think: 'The path of the Buddha is long and distant; it will take a long time...'"
One must undergo diligent hardship before it can be accomplished. The Buddha knows that such a mind is timid, weak, and inferior;
thus, by the power of skillful means, he gathers these pitiable ones together, knowing them to possess limited capacities.
Within this Middle Way, for the sake of bringing about cessation, two types of nirvāṇa are taught. If sentient beings abide in these two stages, the Tathāgata then says to them:
"What you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you abide is near to the Buddha-wisdom.
You should examine and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not ultimate; it is merely a skillful means of the Tathāgata."
By the power of this, within the Single Buddha Vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three. Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjures a great city;
once he knows they have rested, he tells them: "The place of treasure is near; this city is not real, it was created by me.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The conjured city is unreal; the treasure land is not real. To manifest that both are non-existent, the preceding chapter permitted the three and the one, leading one to suppose that while the three are provisional, the one is real. How could it be known that the one is likewise not real? If the one were real, why would it be said that [the reward] is bestowed equally?

If [the treasure] were bestowed equally, who would receive it and who would not? It is simply because those of the three vehicles stagnate in the Lesser Vehicle and do not advance that the Buddha provisionally uses the metaphor of the conjured city. Upon exiting the city, he merely says, "The place of treasure is near," but does not specify its location;

this is because both the "three" and the "one" have vanished, pointing back to one's own mind. The "place of treasure" is the treasury, which is most convenient for practical use and requires no external seeking; hence it is said to be "near."
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas;
yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
The various devas, nāga kings, and hosts of asuras constantly rained down celestial flowers to make offerings to that Buddha, while the devas beat their celestial drums.
They performed various kinds of music, and fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers while raining down fresh and beautiful ones.
After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the Way of the Buddha.
The hearts of all the devas and the people of the world were filled with exultation. The sixteen sons of that Buddha, together with their retinues, [all followed him].
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions, they all proceeded together to the Buddha’s presence.
Prostrating their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma: “O Holy Lion, let the rain of Dharma fall to satisfy us and all beings!
A World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; appearing but once in the course of an eternity, you do so for the sake of awakening all living beings.”
All the worlds in the eastern direction were shaken;
five hundred trillion Brahma palaces radiated a brilliance such as had never been seen before.
Upon seeing these signs, the various Brahmās came one after another to the place where the Buddha was, scattering flowers as an offering and presenting their palaces.
They requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses. Knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted their request by remaining silent.

From the three directions and the four intermediate points, as well as from above and below, they likewise scattered flowers and offered palaces, requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma. "The World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult to encounter."
May you, through your original compassion, widely open the gate of ambrosia;
O World-Honored One of immeasurable wisdom, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. Accepting the request of those sentient beings, proclaim for them the various teachings:
The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, From ignorance to old age and death— All arise from birth as their condition.
Thus you all should know these many faults and afflictions.
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion nayutas attained the end of all suffering and all became arhats.
During the second preaching of the Dharma, a multitude as numerous as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers did not grasp at any dharmas.
They also attained arhatship; from that time onward they realized the Way, their number being immeasurable.
Even if one were to calculate for ten thousand virtuous kalpas, one could not reach their limit.

(Note: Ten myriads make a hundred million [億]; ten hundred million make a billion [兆]; ten billion make a ten billion [京]; ten ten billion make a hundred billion [秭]; ten hundred billion make a trillion [姟]. "Not receiving any dharmas" means being able to subdue and sever the afflictions of views and thought. "Great Pervasive Penetration" refers to the West in the East.)
In the south, they likewise saw the Buddha in the north; such is the greatness of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Seeing the Buddha wherever they were, it is said that their wisdom was supreme.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life as śrāmaṇeras and together requested that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma:
"We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the path of Buddhahood."
May I obtain, like the World-Honored One, the foremost purity of the eye of wisdom. May the Buddha,
knowing the mind of this youth and his practices in past lives, through immeasurable causes and conditions and various similes,
explain the six pāramitās and the matters of supernormal powers, analyzing the true Dharma.
The path practiced by the Bodhisattvas—this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached.
After that Buddha had spoken the sūtra in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a quiet chamber.
Seated with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*, those śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had not yet emerged from his meditation.
For immeasurable billions of beings, they preached the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom; each sat upon the Dharma-seat and expounded this Mahāyāna sūtra.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation through the Dharma;
the number of sentient beings saved by each of these śrāmaṇeras reached six hundred trillion.
After that Buddha has passed into extinction, these multitudes, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who have heard the Dharma,
shall always be born together with their Teacher in various Buddha-lands. These sixteen śrāmaṇeras, having fully practiced the path of the Buddha,
now currently exist throughout the ten directions, each having attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, those who heard the Dharma were each in the presence of various Buddhas.

Among them, those for whom I dwelt while gradually teaching the Buddha-way through the vehicle of the śrāvakas—I was included among the sixteen [disciples]—and because I had previously spoken this for you, I have used skillful means to lead you toward the wisdom of the Buddha; such is the fundamental cause and condition.

(The assembly of today has escaped this peril through the activation of a karmic opportunity, owing to causes and conditions from the distant past. As for the sixteen princes, they are the eight consciousnesses. The consciousnesses are fundamentally eight; each possesses both the phenomenal and the principle aspects, which, when expanded, become sixteen).
Now I preach the Lotus Sutra, Causing you to enter the Buddha-way. Be careful not to harbor fear or alarm;
It is like a perilous and evil road, Remote and desolate, with many venomous beasts, And furthermore, lacking water and grass— A place where people are struck with dread.

(Where there is no water or grass, it is a metaphor for not cultivating the path of a bodhisattva; the clarity and stillness of the water represent meditative concentration, while the variety of the grass represents wisdom.
Countless tens of millions of beings Wish to cross this perilous road, But the way is vast and far, extending for five hundred yojanas.
At that time, there was a guide Who possessed powerful memory and wisdom.
With a mind of clear understanding and resolve, he rescued the multitude from their perilous hardships.
When all the people were exhausted, they said to the Guide: "We are now utterly weary; we wish to turn back from here.
The Guide thought to himself: "These folk are truly pitiable; how can they wish to turn back?"
Having lost a great precious treasure, he immediately sought expedient means; constantly employing his supernormal powers,
he manifested a great city wall, adorning it with various houses and dwellings,
surrounded by gardens, groves, channels, and bathing pools, with multi-storied towers and high gateways, all filled with men and women.

(The various houses are like the contemplation of emptiness. The gardens and groves are the dhāraṇīs of the two vehicles, which are untainted dharmas. The nine successive concentrations are the channels and streams; the eight liberations are the bathing pools. The double gates are the three gates of emptiness.
The multi-storied pavilion is the wisdom of non-arising. The men and women are concentration and wisdom.)
Having thus performed this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying, "Do not fear!
You all may enter this city, each according to your pleasure. Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were filled with great joy;
they all conceived the thought of security and believed they had already attained deliverance. The Guide, knowing that they were rested, [proceeded further].
He gathered the assembly and addressed them, saying: "You all should press forward; this is merely a conjured city.
Seeing that you were utterly exhausted and wished to turn back midway, I used the power of skillful means to temporarily manifest this city.
Now, with diligent vigor, you shall together reach the place of treasure."

I am likewise thus, the teacher of all beings; seeing those who seek the Way faltering midway and unable to cross over birth and death due to the perilous paths of affliction, I employ the power of skillful means to speak of nirvana as a place of rest, saying to you: "Your suffering has been extinguished."
Having accomplished all that was to be done and knowing that they have reached nirvana, they have all attained arhatship.
Thereupon, he assembles the great multitude and for them preaches the true Dharma. By the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, he distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles;
yet there is only the single Buddha vehicle, and it is taught as two because it is a place of rest.
Now I shall speak the truth for you: that which you have attained is not extinction. To become a Buddha of all-knowledge, you must exert great diligence;
when you realize all-knowledge, endowed with the ten powers and other Buddha-qualities and the thirty-two marks, that is true extinction—the guide of all Buddhas.
For the sake of cessation, he speaks of nirvāṇa; having known this cessation, he leads them into the Buddha-wisdom.
(The reason for speaking of two [nirvāṇas] is because of the aforementioned "cessation"; thus, he speaks of two types of nirvāṇa.)

(Verse on the Twenty-five Existences) (The four continents and the four evil destinies, The six heavens of desire and the Brahma heavens, The four dhyānas and the four formless realms, The realm of non-conception and the *anāgāmin*.
*Myōhō Renge Kyō Chokuge* (Exquisite Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), Scroll Three.
*An Outstanding Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Four.
Originally translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Annotated by Xu Changzhi and Jìn Zhōu, Wayfarers Without Dependence from Wuyuan.

Chapter Eight: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon the Five Hundred Disciples (Whether one attains Buddhahood or not is merely a matter of discerning the depth or shallowness of flowers in the sky. Whether one receives a prophecy or not is merely a matter of comparing the length or shortness of a rabbit’s horns. Reaching this stage, I am the one who ties the jewel to the garment;
I am the one who is intoxicated with wine. What poverty or suffering remains to be cast off? What wealth or nobility remains to be attained?)

(A single luminous, pure, and awakened mind— Inherently possessed by every person, yet they seek it elsewhere. Only after receiving a prediction [of Buddhahood] do they become Buddhas; This is nothing more than exchanging gold for gold.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means according to what was appropriate, and further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples. Furthermore...

Having heard the account of his past-life causes and conditions, and further hearing that the Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign supernormal faculties, he attained what he had never experienced before.
His heart was purified and filled with exultation; he immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away, and he thought to himself: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary."

What he has done is most rare: in accordance with the world and its various dispositions, he employs skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma, drawing sentient beings out from their attachments everywhere. We are unable to proclaim the Buddha’s merits in words;
only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our deep-seated original vows. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "You all..."
"Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? (He is called "son" because he received his name from his parents.

(There are two meanings to "see": first, seeing the traces; second, seeing the merit. The multitude only sees the traces as those of a śrāvaka and cannot know that his original nature is that of a bodhisattva; hence the question, "Do you see him or not? [and] "Will he quickly attain Buddhahood?")
I have always praised him as the foremost among men in the exposition of the Dharma (marking his traces as the first in preaching the Dharma,
for he manifested supreme traces through the wondrous essence of the Dharmakāya).
I also constantly extol their various merits—
highlighting their fundamental ground of merit and wisdom, their myriad practices, and their Dharma-gates (or, as some say, "various")—

and I encourage them to diligently protect and uphold [the teachings], assisting in the proclamation of my Dharma, and being able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly while providing complete explanations.
The Buddha’s True Dharma greatly benefits those who practice the same Brahma-faring (fellow practitioners).

Those who assist in proclaiming my Dharma—namely, those who assist in proclaiming the teachings of both the *Hīnayāna* (Half) and *Mahāyāna* (Full) within the [Buddha’s] provisional traces—are as follows: when the trace was at the Deer Park, for those of inferior capacity who were *śrāvakas*, he protected and assisted in proclaiming the Tripiṭaka teachings of both the Half and Full [vehicles].

When the trace was in the Vaipulya [sūtras], manifesting the acceptance of rebukes and censures, he protected and assisted in proclaiming the teachings that clarify the Full [vehicle] in contrast to the Half. When the trace was in the Prajñā[pāramitā], he protected and assisted in proclaiming the teachings that carry the Half while clarifying the Full. When the trace reached the realization of awakening in the Lotus Sūtra...
This refers to upholding and assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma that abandons the partial and clarifies the complete [teachings].
No one except the Tathāgata is able to exhaust his eloquence in debate. You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to uphold and assist in the proclamation of my Dharma;
he has also, in the past, upheld and assisted [the teachings] in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas.
He proclaimed the True Dharma of the Buddha and was the foremost among those who expounded that Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the teaching of emptiness spoken by all Buddhas, he clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated it, attaining the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and was always able to preach the Dharma with meticulous discernment and purity.
Free from doubt, he was fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva. Throughout his entire lifespan, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya).
To the people of that Buddha’s world, he was universally regarded as truly being a śrāvaka. Thus, Pūrṇa employed this skillful means.
He benefits immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Furthermore, he transforms immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* persons, causing them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of purifying his buddha-field, he constantly performs the work of a Buddha, teaching and transforming sentient beings.

(Purṇa, it is not merely that you have assisted me in proclaiming the teachings of the Half and the Full; rather, in the presence of Buddhas of long ago, you likewise assisted in proclaiming the teachings of the Half and the Full, causing others to give rise to faith, and you protected, upheld, and assisted in their proclamation.

Furthermore, being clearly proficient in the Dharma of Emptiness, you were prepared to assist in proclaiming the Dharma that brings clarity to the Half and the Full. Through the four types of unimpeded knowledge—that is, the four unimpeded analytical powers—you enabled each person to attain understanding. Your eloquence was unobstructed, such that all who heard you fully comprehended your speech.)

All of these are true; each provides benefit according to those who can be saved. The establishment of the three bodhisattvas is precisely to assist in proclaiming the Dharma that sets aside the partial and clarifies the complete—the four teachings of the Tripitaka, the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect.
"O bhikṣus, Pūrṇa was foremost among those who preached the Dharma under the seven Buddhas; now, among those who preach the Dharma under me, he is likewise foremost.
In the Bhadrakalpa, he shall also be foremost among those who preach the Dharma under all future Buddhas.
He has always protected, upheld, and assisted in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma, and he shall do so in the future as well."
He shall assist in proclaiming the Dharma of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, establishing them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For the sake of a Buddha-land, he shall always be diligent and energetic in teaching and transforming sentient beings, gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva. After the passage of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall here...
The earth attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and was named Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, and Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām.
"Buddha, World-Honored One! That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field.
Its ground is composed of the seven treasures and is level as the palm of a hand, with no mountains, hills, valleys, ravines, or gullies. There are pavilions and towers made of the seven treasures."
It is filled to the brim. The palaces of the devas stand close to the void, where humans and devas meet and are able to see one another.
(Regarding the ground being as level as the palm of a hand: beneath the ocean floor there is a stone called "the Palm. This stone is not uneven by even so much as a single mote of dust.)
There are no evil realms of existence, nor are there women. All sentient beings are born by transformation;
