they are free from sexual desire, possess great supernormal powers, emit light from their bodies, travel through the air with ease, and are firm in their resolve, diligence, and wisdom.
All were of a golden hue, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. The sentient beings of that land constantly subsisted on two kinds of food:
first, the food of joy in the Dharma; second, the food of the bliss of dhyāna.

(Dharma-food means hearing the Dharma. Regarding "the food of joy in the Dharma": while the actual hearing belongs to dharma-food, the state of rejoicing after having heard it constitutes the food of joy. As for "meditation-food," this refers to sustaining oneself through the methods of meditation without requiring material food; the Dharma itself is joy.)

There were immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas who had attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the four kinds of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
They were well able to teach and transform all classes of sentient beings; their number was such that it could not be known even by calculation or reckoning.
All of them were endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). Such was his buddha-field.
Thus, he was accomplished with such immeasurable merits and adornments. The eon was named Jewel Radiance (*Ratnaprabhāsa*), and the land was named Well-Purified (*Suvimala*).
That Buddha’s lifespan lasted for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and the Dharma remained for a very long time.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven precious substances were erected, filling the entire land. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Listen attentively, O bhikṣus, to the path traversed by the sons of the Buddha. Because they have skillfully studied expedient means, it is inconceivable.
Knowing that the multitudes delight in inferior teachings and fear great wisdom, the bodhisattvas therefore manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through innumerable expedient means.

Transforming all classes of sentient beings, they claim for themselves to be śrāvakas. Though far removed from the Buddha-way, they deliver immeasurable multitudes, causing them all to attain accomplishment.
Although they have small desires and are indolent, they shall gradually cause them to become Buddhas; inwardly they conceal their bodhisattva practice, while outwardly they manifest as śrāvakas.
Having few desires and weary of birth and death, they truly purify their own Buddha-lands;
yet they manifest the presence of the three poisons and display the marks of false views to the multitude. My disciples act in this way, using skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
If I were to fully describe all the various manifestations and transformations they perform, sentient beings who heard of them would [be bewildered].
The mind harbors doubt: "How is it that this Pūrṇa, who in the past diligently practiced the path under billions of Buddhas,
proclaimed and protected the teachings of all those Buddhas, and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed wisdom,
manifested as the foremost disciple among them— renowned and possessed of wisdom?"
He speaks with fearlessness, able to bring joy to the multitude; never experiencing weariness, he assists in the Buddha’s work.
Having attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, he discerns the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of all beings.
He constantly proclaims the pure Dharma, expounding and elucidating such meanings as these.
He teaches the multitudes of billions, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma; meanwhile, he purifies his own Buddha-field.
In the future, he will also make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the True Dharma while also purifying his own Buddha-field.
Always employing various skillful means, he preaches the Dharma without fear.
He delivered countless multitudes and accomplished all-encompassing wisdom; He made offerings to all Tathāgatas and upheld the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
Thereafter he attained Buddhahood, named Dharmaprabhāsa (Dharma-Light);
His land was called Supariśuddha (Exceedingly Pure), Composed of the seven precious jewels; The kalpa was named Ratnaprabhāsa (Jewel-Light).
The assembly of bodhisattvas is vast, their number reaching immeasurable billions;
all have crossed over to the other shore, endowed with great supernormal powers and majestic virtue. They fill his buddha-field.

The śrāvakas are also innumerable, possessing the three types of clear knowledge and the eight liberations, having attained the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom. With such as these, he constitutes the Saṃgha.
All sentient beings in that land have completely severed lustful desire; they are born solely through transformation, their bodies adorned with the marks of excellence.
They feed on the joy of the Dharma and the rapture of dhyāna, having no further thought of other food.
There are no women there, nor are there any evil realms. Thus spoke the Bhikṣu Pūrṇa.

When merits are all fully perfected, one shall attain such a pure land; with such immeasurable matters as these, where the assembly of sages and saints is exceedingly vast, I have now merely spoken in brief.
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery over their minds thought to themselves: "We have attained this with joy."
"How marvelous! If the World-Honored One were to grant a prediction of enlightenment to each of us, just as he has for the other great disciples, would that not be most joyful?
(These twelve hundred people have all already attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; they are no longer afflicted by the outflows of views and thought, and thus their minds are at ease.)"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"These twelve hundred arhats, I shall now, in their very presence, grant the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in successive order.
Among this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand koṭis."
The Buddha then attained Buddhahood, being named Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance).
He was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān.
His five hundred arhats were Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, and Kā... [Kāśyapa].
Rādha, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakkula, Cunda, Śāgata, and others—
all shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all shall have the same name:
Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance).

*Kālodāyin* means "Black Light. *Udāyin* refers to the light produced at sunrise. *Cūḍapanthaka*—also called *Cūḍa*, meaning "Born by the Side of the Great Road"—was born as follows: His mother followed her husband to another country and became pregnant after a long time.

As she was about to give birth, she thought of returning home; while traveling halfway there, she gave birth. This happened twice, resulting in two sons. They were distinguished by their seniority: the elder was Cūḍapanthaka, and the younger was Śāṇavāsika, also called Pāṇḍuka, which means "Born by the Side of the Small Road."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The twelve hundred who all desired to receive a prediction were like those who, having partaken of a royal feast, long for the king’s decree. Those who share the name Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance) have likewise attained illumination through the Four Noble Truths.

Since the three vehicles equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths and each attains realization therein, one knows that the Four Noble Truths are the primary foundation of the three vehicles. Cunda was the first to be predicted because he was the first to understand the Four Noble Truths. Although the Buddha granted predictions to twelve hundred, he specifically mentions five hundred because these five hundred were present in the assembly, while the others..."

In the previous section, Kāśyapa and others preached the Buddha-dharma by employing the parable of the impoverished son: just as precious wealth within a treasury was originally one’s own property, yet because one could not immediately recognize it, the elder exhausted himself with skillful means to entice and lead him;

only after twenty years did he finally realize that he should claim his share. In this present passage, the jewel beneath the garment is used as a metaphor: it was never something external, but could be used at will.
The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall behold immeasurable buddhas; after an incalculable number of kalpas, he will attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
He will constantly emit great radiance, be endowed with all supernatural powers, and his fame will pervade the ten directions. Honored by all, he will constantly preach the unsurpassed path.
Therefore he is named Samantaprabha; his buddha-field is pure.
All the bodhisattvas are courageous and together ascend sublime pavilions, traveling through the lands of the ten directions.
With unsurpassed offerings, they present them to all the Buddhas; having performed such worship, their hearts are filled with great joy.
In a brief moment he returned to his own land; such was his supernormal power. The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas, and the True Dharma remained for twice that duration;
the Semblance Dharma remained for twice that again. When the Dharma was extinguished, the devas and humans were filled with grief.
Those five hundred bhikṣus will successively attain Buddhahood, all sharing the same name: Samantaprabha.
I shall bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them in succession: after my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha.

The world they shall transform will be just like mine today; their lands will be as adorned and pure, and they will possess the same supernormal powers, assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma.
The number of kalpas for their lifespan is exactly as described above.
Kāśyapa, you already know that these five hundred masters of self-mastery, as well as the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas, shall likewise be so.
As for those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim it to them.
At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions in the presence of the Buddha, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, and prostrated themselves, touching their heads to his feet. They repented and reproached themselves, saying:
"World-Honored One, we have constantly held this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate nirvana. Now we realize that we were like those lacking wisdom. Thus they spoke.
Why is this? We ought to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet we have instead become content with our own meager wisdom.
World-Honored One, it is like a man who went to the house of a close friend and lay down after drinking wine. At that time, the friend had business to attend to at the official court.
He tied a priceless jewel inside the man's garment and departed. (Tying the jewel is a metaphor for the Prince’s establishment of a karmic connection.

"A certain person" refers to those with the capacity of the Two Vehicles. "The house" represents the teaching of the Mahāyāna. The one who was drunk and lying down refers to how, at that time, the great capacity [for enlightenment] briefly emerged and ignorance was temporarily subdued;

having heard the sutra, there was a subtle understanding within the mind, like arriving at the home of a close friend. Yet, because ignorance had not yet been fully dispelled, it was like being drunk and lying down.)
That person lies drunk and does not perceive anything at all.

(This refers to the intermediate state of indolence and regression, wherein one does not receive the Great Dharma. "Lying drunk and not perceiving" means that the mind of ignorance is heavy, and thus one subsequently fails to remember.)
Having risen, he travels abroad to another country. For the sake of food and clothing, he seeks them with diligent effort, undergoing great hardship.
If he obtains even a small amount, he considers it sufficient.
(He was led from the top of this [mountain] and joined with the small [one], thereby receiving the transformation of the Three Vehicles).
Later, a close friend encountered him by chance and spoke these words: "Excellent, O man! Why do you toil for the sake of food and clothing?"

It was even so. In the past, wishing to enable you to obtain the pleasures of the five desires and enjoy them at will, on a certain day, month, and year, I tied a priceless jewel within the lining of your garment. It remains there even now, yet you were unaware of it;
instead, you toiled in hardship and distress to seek your livelihood—this was truly foolish of you.
(This shows the jewel; it is a metaphor for the causes and conditions of past lives.
You may now trade this treasure for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes, so that you will never lack anything.

(This exhortation to trade is like attaining the prediction of Buddhahood. Although the jewel is of great value, it must be traded for before it can be used. The internal realization of the cause of penetration—whereby one realization leads to all realizations—is traded so as to become manifest practice; whereby one practice leads to all practices.)
The Buddha is also like this. When he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience;

yet we soon forgot it, neither knowing nor perceiving it. Having attained the path of an arhat, we considered ourselves to have reached final nirvana, and thus our livelihood became difficult and fraught with hardship.
Having attained but a little, you were content with that. Yet your aspiration for omniscience remains undiminished. Now, the World-Honored One awakens us by speaking these words:
"O bhikṣus, what you have attained is not ultimate cessation. For a long time I have caused you to plant roots of goodness for Buddhahood;
however, through skillful means, I manifested the appearance of nirvāṇa, while you believed you had truly attained final extinction."
“World-Honored One, I now know for certain that I am truly a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because of these causes and conditions, I am filled with great joy and have attained what I never had before.
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Having heard this unsurpassed sound of the prophecy of peace, we experience a joy never known before.
We pay homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom. Now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, we repent of all our transgressions;
having obtained but a small portion of nirvana from the jewel of the immeasurable Buddhas, we were like ignorant and foolish men.
He then considers himself satisfied; it is like a poor man who goes to the house of a kinsman.

That house is exceedingly wealthy, and having prepared all kinds of delicacies, [the kinsman] secretly ties a priceless jewel inside the man's inner garment and departs. At that time, the man is lying down and does not perceive it.
This person, having already set out on a journey to another land, seeks food and clothing to sustain his life;
his livelihood is exceedingly difficult, and he is satisfied with what little he obtains.
He does not desire anything better, nor does he realize that within his inner garment there is a priceless jewel.

(The "delicacies" represent the skillful means first heard from the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; the "tying of the jewel" represents the prince’s subsequent teaching of the Dharma and his formation of the great causal conditions).
A close friend of his gave him a jewel; later, seeing this poor man, he sternly rebuked him and showed him the jewel he had tied upon him.
When the poor man saw this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy;
possessing abundant wealth and treasures, he indulged himself in the five desires. We, too, are just like this.
Throughout the long night, the World-Honored One has constantly looked upon us with compassion and taught us, causing us to plant the unsurpassed aspiration.
Because we were ignorant, we failed to perceive or understand;
having obtained a mere portion of nirvana, we considered ourselves sufficient and sought nothing more. Now the Buddha awakens us, saying that this is not true extinction.
Only upon attaining the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom Is one then said to have attained true extinction.
Now, having heard from the Buddha the account of the adornment of my prediction, As well as the successive transmission of the prophecy, My body and mind are filled with universal joy.

[The One Great Treasury of Teachings does not exceed the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings. Since the Tripitaka constitutes the Small Vehicle, half belongs to the Small and the full belongs to the Great. To assist in proclaiming both the partial and the full, the Small is subsumed within the Great. By contrasting the partial to clarify the full, the Great is further extolled in relation to the Small.]

[This] also [indicates that] the partial illumination and fullness [of the Lesser Vehicle] are subsumed within the Great; the partial illumination and fullness are discarded as one abandons the small and proceeds toward the great. This Great Master [Vasubandhu] judges the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata to be solely those addressed to Ānanda, Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Kauṇḍinya, and others.

He assisted the Buddha’s four teachings and proclaimed their complete principles. However, the Bodhisattva Vehicle within the Tripitaka is not the Lesser Vehicle; it was Master Qingliang (Zhiyan) who categorized them into the five teachings: Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect.

Chapter Nine: Bestowing Prophecies upon Those in Training and Those Beyond Training (Those in training and those beyond training are able, in a single thought-moment, to turn the light back and return to their original nature. Boundless evil karma is not merely extinguished all at once; boundless merit is fully realized simultaneously. What more need be said of "those in training" and "those beyond training")?

"Long-standing habits that have not yet been eliminated must be extinguished; to say 'habits are eliminated' or 'learning has ceased' is all empty talk. Every person has water and thus contains the moon, but I say that when there are no clouds, it is simply the sky.
At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought: "If we were to receive a prediction [of our future enlightenment], would it not be most delightful?
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and together addressed the Buddha.
They said, "World-Honored One, we too should have a share in this. The Tathāgata alone is our refuge.
Furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras; Ānanda has always been the attendant, upholding the treasury of the Dharma;
and Rāhula is the son of the Buddha. If the Buddha would grant us [the prediction of] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
"Regarding the prediction of my attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: my vows are now fulfilled, and the expectations of the assembly are likewise satisfied.
At that time, two thousand disciples—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and approached the Buddha.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One. Just as Ānanda and Rāhula had wished, they stood to one side.

At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Śāntarājasaṃgheśvarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara."
O Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, you shall make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas and uphold the treasury of the Dharma;
thereafter, you will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and transform twenty trillion *koṭis* of Bodhisattvas,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, enabling them to achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The name of the land is Constantly Erected Supreme Banner; its soil is pure, with lapis lazuli as its ground. The kalpa is named Pervasive Wondrous Sound.

The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, such that even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, it could not be known. The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twice that duration.
The lifespan [of this Buddha] and the duration of the Semblance Dharma shall each be twice that of the True Dharma.

Ānanda, this Buddha, King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Ocean Wisdom, is praised together by immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who extol his merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
I now declare within this Sangha: Ānanda, who upholds the Dharma, shall make offerings to all Buddhas and thereafter attain Perfect Enlightenment.
He shall be named Samudrareṇu-jñāna-viśvavaśitā-vaśavartin Buddha.
His land shall be pure, named Constantly Erected Supreme Banner, where he will teach and transform all Bodhisattvas.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges; the Buddha possesses great majestic power, his fame fills the ten directions, and his lifespan is immeasurable.

Out of compassion for sentient beings, the True Dharma shall last twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall last twice that again—lasting as long as the sands of the Ganges—for the sake of countless sentient beings.
Within this Buddha-dharma, the causes and conditions for planting the seeds of the Buddha-way [are thus established].
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds within the assembly all had this thought:
"We have not even heard of the great bodhisattvas receiving such a prediction; by what cause and condition do these śrāvakas receive such [a prediction]?"
[The Buddha] decided. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family, Ānanda and I simultaneously gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha Gaganarāja.
Ānanda always delighted in much hearing (*bahuśruta*), whereas I always exerted myself with diligent vigor (*vīrya*). For this reason, I have already attained [it]."
He shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Ānanda shall protect and uphold my Dharma, and likewise protect the Dharma-treasury of all future Buddhas.
He shall teach and bring to maturity the assembly of bodhisattvas; such was his original vow, and thus he has received this prediction.
Having heard this prediction before the Buddha’s very presence, as well as the adornments of his buddha-field and the fulfillment of his aspirations, Ānanda rejoiced.
His heart was filled with great joy; he attained what he had never experienced before.

Immediately, he recollected the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas of the past, attaining unimpeded mastery over them just as he had now heard them. He also recognized his own original vows.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous; he causes me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, just as I have heard them today.
I now have no further doubts; I shall abide securely in the Buddha-way, serving as an attendant and upholding the Dharma of all Buddhas.

At that time, the Buddha said to Rāhula: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Padmottara (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flowers), Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
You shall make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten worlds."
The Tathāgata has always been the eldest son of all Buddhas, just as he is now.

The adornments of the land, the lifespan in kalpas, the disciples he transforms, and the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma of this Buddha Flower of Seven Jewels are no different from those of the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Mountain and Ocean Wisdom and Supernatural Powers; he likewise served as the eldest son of that Buddha. After this...
"In the future, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha..."
The Dharma-hearer who is my son, throughout future ages, shall behold immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son;
single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way, Rāhula’s secret conduct is known only by me.
Though he now appears as my eldest son, this is shown for the sake of all sentient beings.
With immeasurable billions of merits beyond counting, they dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma to seek the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the two thousand disciples— both those in training and those beyond training— were gentle in mind, tranquil, and pure.

They contemplated the Buddha with their minds. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see these two thousand people, both those in training and those beyond training? "Yes, indeed, I see them," [Ānanda replied].
"Ānanda, all these people shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds;
they shall revere, honor, and respectfully uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Finally, at the same time, they shall each attain Buddhahood in lands throughout the ten directions."

The Buddhas were all identical in name, titled Ratnaketu (Jewel-Mark). They were Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpannas, Sugatas, Lokavidas, Anuttaras, Puruṣadamyasārathis, Śāstāras of devas and humans, Buddhas, and Bhagavans. Their lifespans lasted for one kalpa;
their lands were equally adorned; and their śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma were all exactly the same. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Venerable One, wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke these verses:
"These two thousand śrāvakas who now stand before me— to all of them I grant the prediction that they shall in the future attain Buddhahood.
The Buddhas whom they shall honor are as numerous as the atoms described above."
They shall uphold the treasury of his Dharma and later attain perfect enlightenment. Each, in the lands of the ten directions, shall possess an identical name;
simultaneously seated at the site of awakening, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom and all be named Ratnalakṣaṇa (Precious Mark).
Their lands, their disciples, their True Dharma, and their Semblance Dharma shall likewise be equal.
All are equal and without distinction; by means of their various supernatural powers, they deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Their fame is universally pervasive as they gradually enter nirvana.

At that time, two thousand disciples—both those still in training and those beyond training—hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and spoke these verses:
The World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom: Having heard the sound of the prophecy, my heart was filled with joy, as if drenched by the sight of ambrosia.

(Ānanda was the Buddha’s younger brother; Rāhula was the Buddha’s son. Those who receive prophecies later are closer [to the Buddha] than those who are more distant. Regarding the prophecies of these two, their kalpas, lands, adornments, lifespans, and retinues all emerge from the Bodhisattva’s [merit].)

"Superior" clarifies that his causal conditions were profound. Ānanda and the Buddha developed the aspiration for enlightenment at the same time; he did not seek swift realization but made a firm vow regarding the Dharma. Rāhula, before the Buddha, manifested himself as the eldest son while secretly practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Not wishing to remain stagnant as a minor *śrāvaka*, it was fitting that he be recorded as ranking above the *bodhisattvas*. (Rāhula is the same as Rāhula.)

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Dharma-Master (This chapter elucidates six kinds of dharma-masters: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; fifth, transcribing; sixth, making offerings. These are all models for humanity.)

(When people only fear that their faith is not sincere—once faith is sincere, the mind is itself the Buddha. It is like applying five colors upon white paper; there is no need for a hundred kinds of strenuous toil.
At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see within this great assembly the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras..."
Naras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
those seeking the vehicle of śrāvakas, those seeking the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas, and those seeking the path of the Buddha.
(Wishing to entrust the wondrous Dharma to Bhaiṣajyarāja so that he might receive it and proclaim it to the eighty thousand [bodhisattvas], ensuring its universal circulation.
All such persons as these— who, in the presence of the Buddha, hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
or who rejoice in it for even a single thought-moment— I shall all bestow upon them the prediction that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

(If there were those present before the Buddha who attained wondrous awakening according to their capacities—such as the five hundred and two thousand who possessed extensive learning and profound understanding—those now being singled out are rather the eight classes of beings, the fourfold assembly, and the followers of the three vehicles;

thus it says, "such as these. "All of them were before the Buddha" clarifies the time and occasion, namely that they encountered the Buddha while he was seated. "A single phrase or a single verse" indicates the extremely small amount of Dharma heard. "Even for a single thought-moment" indicates the shortest possible duration.

"Rejoicing" means that although they themselves had not yet practiced, they merely rejoiced in the Dharma. That "they all receive a prediction of attaining Bodhi" clarifies that they shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.)

The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there is anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment, I likewise grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Moreover, if there is another person who receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or copies the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
Even for a single verse, one should regard this scripture as a Buddha and offer various kinds of worship:
flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silken canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music; even to the point of joining the palms in reverent salutation.
(Explaining the characteristics of the inferior teachers of the present age; that is, the five kinds of Dharma-preachers and the ten kinds of offerings.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas in the presence of those buddhas.
Having fulfilled his great vows, out of compassion for sentient beings, he was born into this human world.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone should ask which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in future ages, you should point to these people and say that they will do so in future ages.

They shall certainly attain Buddhahood. Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, upholds, recites, explains, copies, or makes various offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, and necklaces.
With powdered incense, ointment, and burning incense; with silk canopies, banners, and streamers; with robes and musical instruments;
and with palms joined in reverent salutation—this person is one whom all the world should look upon with veneration and honor. One should worship them as if worshipping a Tathāgata.
You should know that such a person is a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and takes pity on all beings.
Born here, they vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

(The phrase "those who have made offerings" clarifies that their causes in past lives were profound; "out of compassion for sentient beings, they are born among humans" clarifies that their merit in the present life is great; "if anyone should ask... and so forth clarifies that their retribution in future lives is weighty.)
How much more so for those who are able to receive and uphold it in its entirety and offer various kinds of worship.

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons, having set aside their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for sentient beings, be born in this evil world after my parinirvāṇa to widely expound this sutra.
If there are good sons or good daughters who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person.
(Regarding those of inferior capacity who are nevertheless permitted to propagate the Dharma to assist the True Teaching):
It should be known that such persons are messengers of the Tathāgata, dispatched by the Tathāgata, and they perform the work of the Tathāgata.

(The sutras are spoken by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of suchness; they expound the principle of suchness. Today, the practitioner who upholds these teachings of suchness and proclaims the principle of suchness is an envoy of the Tathāgata. One who performs the work of the Tathāgata does so because the Tathāgata, through the wisdom of suchness, illuminates the principle of suchness as his task.)
How much more so when one preaches it extensively for others amidst the great assembly.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before the Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, his transgression would still be light.
However, if a person, with even a single evil word, disparages those—whether householders or renunciants—who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra, their transgression is exceedingly grave.

(For a beginner practitioner who recites the sutras, if one adds slander and disparagement, it can cause their studies to fail; therefore, the transgression incurred is great. Since the Buddha regards enemies and kin with equality and is not obstructed by such things, it is said that the offense is light.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that whoever reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha.
(The Buddha has taught this sūtra adorned with concentration and wisdom; therefore, those who read and recite this sūtra are able to cultivate the concentration and wisdom of the Buddha.)
Thus, one shall be carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.

(To bear on the back is "carrying"; to bear on the shoulder is "shouldering. If a person reads and recites this sutra, they will be able to attain the essence of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which is neither provisional nor real, and they will also be able to attain the function of the Buddha’s two wisdoms, both provisional and real.)
In whatever direction they may go, one should face them and pay homage.

With a single-minded focus, join the palms and respectfully make offerings, honoring and praising them with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and delicacies, while performing various musical performances—offering these supreme human offerings.
One should also hold celestial jewels and scatter them [over them], as if in the heavens.

"O Jewel-Heap, you should offer this to him. Why is that? Because if such a person joyfully preaches the Dharma and one hears it for even a brief moment, one will immediately attain ultimate, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

(Regarding "in whichever direction one turns": the preceding section clarified taking the Dharma as one's teacher; this section clarifies being capable of being a teacher for others. Whatever one pursues is entirely in accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); all such persons are worthy of reverence, compliance, and offerings.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The vastness expounded by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is precisely the vastness of one's own self-nature (*svabhāva*). The principles and meanings expounded by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are precisely the principles and meanings of one's own self-nature. That the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* encompasses the beginning and the end is precisely that one's own self-nature encompasses the beginning and the end.

That the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* penetrates both the sacred and the profane is precisely that one's own self-nature penetrates both the sacred and the profane. When a person does not awaken to their own self-nature, within the state of the perfect fusion of self-nature, they give rise to the views of self and others, giving rise to the sixty [kinds of delusion]."
From the two views up to the myriad differences, they revolve in saṃsāra without end.

If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom, one should always diligently make offerings to and uphold those who possess the Lotus Sūtra. Those who wish to quickly attain the wisdom of all modes—
One should uphold this sutra and make offerings to those who uphold it.
If there are those capable of upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, know them to be envoys of the Buddha.
Those who can uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* out of compassion for all sentient beings shall leave behind the pure lands.
Out of compassion for the masses, such a person as this is born here;
one should know that they can, at will, manifest birth in this evil world to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma.
One should honor these teachers of the Dharma with celestial flowers and incense, celestial precious garments, and heaps of exquisite celestial jewels.
In the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra should join their palms in reverent salutation as if making offerings to the World-Honored One.

With the finest delicacies, various sweets, and diverse garments, they should make offerings to these sons of the Buddha, hoping to hear it for even a brief moment. If one is able to do so in a future age...
To those who receive and uphold this sutra, I shall dispatch them among human beings to perform the work of the Tathāgata.

Even if, for the duration of an eon, they harbor unwholesome thoughts and, with a frowning countenance, revile the Buddha, they would incur immeasurable and grave offenses; yet, there are those who read, recite, and uphold this Lotus Sutra.
If one should utter harsh words for even a moment, their sin would exceed that of the former.
Suppose there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, throughout an entire eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses;
by virtue of such praise of the Buddha, they would attain immeasurable merit—far surpassing those who merely extol the holders of this sutra.

The merit of this exceeds that [of the former], even if for eighty billion eons one were to provide offerings of the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures to those who uphold this sutra.
Having made such offerings, if one should then hear it for even a moment, one ought to rejoice within oneself: "I have now attained a great benefit."
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the foremost.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Of all the sūtras I have preached, they are immeasurable thousands..."

Ten billion [teachings] have been taught, are being taught now, and will be taught; yet among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.

(The term "already" refers to the various gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* onwards. "Now" refers to [the teaching] at the same seat, which explains the *Anantārthika Sūtra*. "Will be" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The various gradual and sudden teachings such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* are all accompanied by expedient means.)

It is easy to gain faith in [the teachings of] the *Benevolent King* (Renwang jing). Now, regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, if one discusses the Dharma, all distinctions are harmonized and integrated into a single unity; if one discusses the persons, both master and disciple, as well as their original and manifested forms, are equally of long-standing antiquity; therefore, it is difficult to believe and understand.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.

(To conceal and not speak of it is "secret"; to encompass all dharmas is "essential"; to contain the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) is a "treasury. Regarding the prohibition against reckless distribution: it may be bestowed upon those of profound wisdom, for those without wisdom will not believe.)
It is protected by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Since ancient times, it has never been explicitly taught.

(That it has never been explicitly taught means that within the Tripiṭaka, it is not stated that those of the Two Vehicles become Buddhas, nor is the fundamental reality (*honjaku*) of teacher and disciple clarified. Although the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras speak of the treasury of true reality (*shinjissō*), they have not yet revealed the trace to manifest the fundamental; therefore, it is called "secret.
The "trace" refers to the outward manifestation.)
Furthermore, regarding this sutra, even while the Tathāgata is currently present in the world, there are still many who harbor resentment and envy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?

O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that after the Tathāgata has passed away, those who are able to write it down, uphold it, read it, recite it, make offerings to it, and explain it to others, will be covered by the Tathāgata’s own robe.
Moreover, they will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions. Such persons...
By the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness, you should know that such a person dwells together with the Tathāgata;
it is as if the Tathāgata were to stroke their head with his own hand.

"If it was thus even during the Buddha's lifetime, how much more so will it be in the future? The principle is that those who are difficult to transform [will find it hard to believe]. This Dharma resides in the person; therefore, the person is noble and precious. 'Clothed by the Tathāgata' means that one who can uphold and expound this sutra is practicing and learning the Great Patience (mahākṣānti);

this constitutes being 'clothed. 'Protected by the Buddha's mindfulness' means to revere the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and give rise to true wisdom (bhūtaprajñā). The Fourfold Faith is the power of faith; the Four Great Vows are the power of aspiration; and Great Wisdom is the power of roots of goodness."

Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this may be—whether it be where it is preached, read, recited, written, or where the scroll of the sūtra resides—one should erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, making it as high, broad, and magnificently adorned as possible. It is unnecessary to place relics therein. Why is this?
Because within it already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata. This stūpa should be honored with all kinds of flowers, incense, and necklaces.
With silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and with music, songs, and hymns, they shall offer worship, pay respect, honor, and praise.
If there are those who see this stūpa, prostrate before it, and make offerings, you should know that all such persons are drawing near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Wherever this Dharma resides, that place is noble. Indeed, at the places where the Buddha was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa, one should erect stūpas; it is not necessary to enshrine physical relics there, for the sūtra scrolls themselves constitute the relic of the Dharma-body."
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both householders and those who have left the home life, who practice the bodhisattva path;
yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this Lotus Sūtra, you should know that these people have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will then be able to skillfully practice the path of a bodhisattva.

(If one has not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path—having followed the three previous teachings and being unable to deliver others with skill—if they hear this sutra, they immediately enter the Perfect Teaching; this is called "skillful delivery" and constitutes "skillful practice.")
If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way and either see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it,
believe, understand, accept, and uphold it— know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

(One should know that those who will certainly attain the fruit of near-enlightenment are called "those in the proximate state" within the practice of peaceful conduct. This fruit of enlightenment has as its essence the locus of knowledge and vision through the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs for it on a high plateau.
Seeing only dry earth, he knows the water is still far off. Yet, exerting effort without ceasing, he sees moist soil and eventually reaches mud;
his mind becomes certain that the water must be near.

(First, regarding the gate of contemplation; second, regarding the gate of teaching. As for the gate of contemplation: the minds of sentient beings are possessed of all afflictions, which is called "high ground. Initially, one enters emptiness from the conventional; seeing only emptiness and not that which is not empty, one cuts off the delusions of the four abodes, like digging into dry soil.

Next, one emerges from emptiness into the conventional; first knowing it is not conventional, and now knowing it is not empty. By means of these two contemplations, one enters the Middle Way and is able to subdue ignorance, giving rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as if obtaining clear water).

The Bodhisattva is also like this. If one has not yet heard, understood, or been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it should be known that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If, however, one manages to hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it, one will certainly know that they have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
(Within the Lotus Sūtra, to obtain hearing, contemplation, and cultivation is precisely the perfect observation of the three wisdoms; only then can one approach the fruit.

(In the initial, middle, and final teachings of all Buddhas, there is none that does not point back to attaining Buddhahood within one’s own mind. If one can truly believe this without doubt, although one has not yet realized it, one already surpasses the Three Vehicles; Buddhahood is not far off. It is like seeing moist soil and knowing that water must be near.)
It surpasses that high plateau. Why is this?
Because all the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all bodhisattvas belongs to this sutra.
This sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true reality. This treasury of the Lotus Sutra is profound, firm, and far-reaching.
No one can reach it. Now, the Buddha teaches and transforms beings, bringing bodhisattvas to fulfillment and revealing [this truth] to them.

(All "bodhisattvas" clarifies that within the various teachings there are provisional causes. "Tripiṭaka-enlightenment" [Sambodhi] clarifies that all bodhisattvas attain provisional fruits. "Opening the gate of expedient means" means establishing the provisional for the sake of the real; this is entirely expedient means. To know this as the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely what "opening" means.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If there are śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sūtra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those possessed of overweening pride.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are good men or good women who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, desire to act for the sake of the four...

Regarding those who preach this Lotus Sutra, how should they preach it? Such sons of good family and daughters of good family must enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat; only then should they extensively preach this sutra for the fourfold assembly.

(The chamber, the robe, and the seat—these three are called the "Three Guidelines" [triyāna]. To cultivate objectless compassion is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber; to cultivate the patience of cessation is to don the Tathāgata’s robe; to cultivate emptiness within the center is to sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat. "Guideline" [yāna] means a track or path.)
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena.

(Compassion covers all beings; its benefits and advantages are returned to oneself. It is as vast as a house. Pity extracts all suffering; love bestows all happiness—namely, the constant bliss of humans, devas, and nirvana.

The Tathāgata’s robe is that which screens off external evils and one's own impurities, serving as a garment for each. The Tathāgata’s seat is that which settles the mind in emptiness; only then can one settle others and settle oneself, and this is called the seat).
Abiding therein, one should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively preach this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of all bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
(The five kinds of Dharma-preachers should use these three methods as their own standard of conduct and use them to transform others and benefit people.)
Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands I dispatch emanated persons to assemble for them a congregation to hear the Dharma;

I also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to their preaching of the Dharma. These emanated persons, having heard the Dharma, believe and accept it, following it in accordance and not opposing it.
If the preacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I then extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
The devas, gandharvas, asuras, and others listen to his preaching of the Dharma. Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause the preacher to behold my body.
If he should forget or lose any passages or readings of this sutra, I will preach it for him again so that it may be complete.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra.
This sutra is difficult to hear, and those who can hear it with faith and acceptance are likewise rare. It is like a person parched with thirst who needs water;
though they dig in a high plateau, they still see only dry earth, knowing that the water is yet far off, until gradually they see moist soil and mud.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that those people who do not hear the Lotus Sūtra can be known with certainty to be far removed from the Buddha’s wisdom. But if they hear this profound sūtra—
the king of all sūtras— and having heard it, contemplate it with earnest attention, they will realize the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.
One should know that such persons as these are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.
If a person preaches this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
amidst the assembly, they shall have no fear, and they shall extensively analyze and explain it, taking great compassion as their chamber.
The gentle robe of patience, with the emptiness of all phenomena as one’s seat—dwelling therein, one preaches the Dharma.
When preaching this sutra, if someone should revile one with foul language or strike with knives, staves, tiles, or stones, one should endure it by recollecting the Buddha.
Throughout my thousands of millions of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, he shall preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings (this generally clarifies the Tathāgata’s intent to benefit others through five matters). If,
after my parinirvāṇa, there should be those who can preach this sutra, I shall dispatch emanations of the fourfold assembly.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as pure men and women, shall make offerings to the Dharma Master.
Guiding all sentient beings, he shall gather them together to listen to the Dharma.
If anyone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, he shall dispatch emanated beings to provide protection for them.

If there is a person preaching the Dharma, Alone in a secluded place, In silence where no human voice is heard, reading and reciting this sutra, At that time I shall manifest for them A body of pure radiance.
If they should forget any passages or lines, I shall explain them so that they may master them. If a person possesses such virtues as these,
Whether preaching for the fourfold assembly, Or reciting sutras in secluded places, They shall all behold my body.
If a person dwells in a quiet, solitary place, I shall dispatch the celestial kings and dragon kings, Yakṣas, spirits, and ghosts, To serve as the assembly listening to the Dharma.
Such a person will delight in preaching the Dharma, Discerning it without any obstruction.
Because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, they are able to bring joy to the great assembly.

If one draws near to a Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the path of a Bodhisattva; by following and studying under such a teacher, one shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.

The three cycles of the Dharma are complete; the records of the fourfold assembly are perfected. Since the discourse on the Dharmakāya is exhaustive and the mind of the original vow is fulfilled, it moves the Stupa of the Past Buddha Prabhūtaratna, thereby bringing the present Śākyamuni Tathāgata to assemble his transformation bodies to open the stupa.
Thus, past and present are unified in a single thought-moment: the buddha-lands of the ten directions are none other than my own mind.
“The Dharmakāya is all-pervasive; do not seek it elsewhere. To seek it is clearly a mistaken thought. Remember the words of the ancients: ‘One who rides the ox need not go further to seek the ox.
At that time, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures before the Buddha. It was five hundred yojanas high and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air, adorned with various precious objects and five thousand railings.
There were shields and thousands of millions of niches and chambers, adorned with countless banners and streamers.
Precious necklaces hung down, and billions of precious bells were suspended above them. From all four sides issued the fragrance of *tamarapa* sandalwood, pervading the entire world.
Those various banners and canopies were made of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearl, and ruby.
It is constructed, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.

The railings are the dhāraṇīs; the thousands of millions of niches are the chambers of immeasurable compassion, and are also the immeasurable abodes of emptiness. The banners and streamers are the supreme signs of supernatural powers (abhijñā). The hanging jeweled necklaces represent the merits of the forty stages (bhūmi).

The billions of precious bells represent the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges. The fragrance emanating from the four sides represents the wind of the Path of the Four Truths. Its height reaching as far as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings represents the thorough mastery of the principles of the Four Truths.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down mandārava flowers as an offering to the jeweled stūpa.
All other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth did likewise.
Tens of millions of billions of beings made offerings to the jeweled stupa with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music;
they honored, revered, and praised it with deep respect. At that time, from within the jeweled stupa, a great voice issued forth, exclaiming: "Excellent! Excellent!"

The World-Honored One Śākyamuni, with his great wisdom of equality, has preached for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the Dharma that instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas. It is so, it is so;
World-Honored One Śākyamuni, all that you have spoken is true.

(This praise of Śākyamuni by Prabhūtaratna precisely confirms that the previous revelation of the provisional to manifest the real was not in vain. "Great Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of all Buddhas.)
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw a great jeweled stūpa abiding in mid-air and heard the sounds issuing from within the stūpa;
they all attained the joy of the Dharma and, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna. Knowing the doubts in the minds of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this precious stūpa emerged from the earth, and why does such a sound issue forth from within it? At that time, the Buddha told Mahāpratibhāna:

Bodhisattva, within this jeweled stūpa lies the entire body of a Tathāgata. In the distant past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddhā. In that place, there was a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna.
When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a great vow: "If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, during the ten..."
In any land where the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is being preached, my stūpas shall emerge before them for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as witnesses and exclaiming, "Excellent!

After that Buddha attained enlightenment, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body..."

"One should erect a great stūpa. By the power of that Buddha’s supernatural faculties and vows, wherever in the worlds of the ten directions there may be anyone preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, that precious stūpa shall emerge before them.
With his entire body within the stūpa, he will exclaim, 'Excellent, excellent! Mahāpratibhāna, now this stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has heard the preaching of the Dharma."
Because of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they emerged from the earth and praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we wish to behold this body of the Buddha."

The preceding passage employed provisional language and metaphors, with each instance specifically pointing to the self-mind of the practitioner. Fearing that this might still not be believed, the appearance of the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna is invoked as proof. The Buddha within the stūpa is none other than the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). Its height of five hundred *yojanas* signifies its vertical transcendence of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).

Its length and breadth of two hundred and fifty *yojanas* signify its horizontal pervasion throughout the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). Its dwelling "in mid-air" means it does not rely on heaven above nor adhere to earth below; it abides by way of the Middle Way of the *dharmatā*.

That there is a complete body within the jeweled stūpa signifies that sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata. Because the *dharmatā* is pure and gives birth to all the jewels of the Dharma, he is named Prabhūtaratna ("Abundant Jewels").
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna: "This Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a profound and solemn vow:

'If my jeweled stupa emerges before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and if there are those who wish to show my body to the fourfold assembly, then all the emanated bodies of that Buddha who are preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions shall return.'"
Only after they have gathered in one place shall my body appear.

Mahāpratibhāna, those emanations of mine, the Buddhas who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions, should now assemble. Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"We also wish to see the Buddhas who are the emanations of the World-Honored One, so that we may pay them homage and make offerings.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his brows. Immediately, they saw the Buddhas in lands to the east as numerous as the sands of five million billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers.
In all those lands, the ground was made of crystal, and they were adorned with jeweled trees and precious garments.
It is magnificent. Countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas fill its midst. Precious canopies are spread everywhere, and precious nets are draped above.

The Buddhas of that land preach all dharmas with great and wondrous voices. Furthermore, one sees immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
[This extends to] the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—[all illuminated by] the white tuft between the eyebrows.
The places illuminated by this light were likewise transformed in this manner. At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their respective assemblies of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Good sons, we must now proceed to the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha, and there offer worship to the precious stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
Thereupon, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity, with its ground made of lapis lazuli.
Adorned with jewel-trees, with golden cords demarcating the eight paths, it was devoid of villages, hamlets, camps, cities, towns, great oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, or marshes.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn everywhere across the ground.

A canopy of jeweled nets was spread over them, and various jeweled bells were suspended from it. Having moved all the devas and humans and placed them in other lands, he left only the assembly of this gathering.
At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great bodhisattva as his attendant and arrived at the Sahā world, each reaching beneath a jeweled tree.
Each of these jeweled trees was five hundred yojanas high, with branches and leaves...

Flowers and fruits were arranged in successive tiers as adornments. Beneath each of the various jewel trees stood a lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels. At that time, the Buddhas each sat cross-legged upon these thrones.
In this manner, they multiplied and filled the entire trichiliocosm; yet, even then, the emanated bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha in a single direction were not yet exhausted.

At that time, because Śākyamuni Buddha wished to accommodate all the Buddhas who had manifested as his emanations, he further transformed two hundred *nayuta* of *koṭi* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure.
It was pure, without hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras. Furthermore, he moved the devas and humans to other lands.
The land of his transformation was also made of lapis lazuli and adorned with jewel trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits beautifully arrayed in succession. Beneath each tree there was a precious lion throne, five [yojanas]... high.

It spans many yojanas and is adorned with various kinds of jewels. Furthermore, it is devoid of great oceans, rivers, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, Mount Sumeru, and so forth.
The various kings of mountains together constitute a single Buddha-field. The ground of jewels is level and even; canopies of interlaced jewels cover it everywhere.
Various banners and parasols are suspended, great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn across the entire ground.
(“Linda” means stone; “Sumeru” means Wondrous High).

Śākyamuni Buddha, for the sake of the Buddhas who were to sit there in the future, further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The asuras, moreover, moved the various devas and humans and placed them in other lands. The countries thus transformed also had ground made of lapis lazuli and were adorned with precious trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits being arranged in successive layers of adornment.
Beneath each tree there was a precious lion throne, five yojanas in height, likewise adorned with great jewels.
Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, nor Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa mountains,
the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, Sumeru, or any such peaks.
(Regarding the Iron Ring Mountains: those that encircle the four continents are distinguished by their greater and smaller sizes. Mount Sumeru resides in the center of the four continents.
All these kings of mountains together constitute a single Buddha-land. The ground of jewels is level and even; canopies of interlaced jewels cover it everywhere.
Banners and parasols are suspended, great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn across the earth. At that time, in the east...

The various Buddhas in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* Ganges-sand-like lands—each being an emanation of Śākyamuni Buddha—were each preaching the Dharma and gathering here one after another.
In this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions all gathered and sat in the eight directions. At that time, in each direction there were four million billion *nayuta*...

The Buddhas, Tathāgatas of other lands, filled that space. At that time, each of those Buddhas sat beneath a jeweled tree upon a lion throne and dispatched their attendants to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Each attendant brought a handful of precious flowers and addressed them, saying: "Good son, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to [visit] Śākyamuni Buddha."
[He] said: "I inquire after [the Buddha's] health, asking if he has little illness and little affliction, and if his strength and well-being are secure.
Likewise, I ask if the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas are all at peace. Having scattered these precious flowers as an offering to the Buddha, he spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha [named so-and-so] desires to open this jeweled stūpa. The dispatching of messengers by the various Buddhas was likewise for each. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha—
He saw that the emanated Buddhas had all assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones.
Hearing that all the Buddhas had granted their consent to open the precious stupa together, they immediately rose from their seats and remained suspended in mid-air.

The entire assembly of the fourfold community stood up with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the seven-jeweled [stupa] with his right finger.
The door of the stūpa emitted a great sound, like the lifting of bolts and keys to open the gates of a great city.

(Opening the stūpa signifies opening [the enclosure]; appearing [before] the Buddha signifies revealing reality. This also serves as a verification of what preceded and further prepares for what follows.)
Immediately, the entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa, seated upon a lion throne;
his entire body remained intact and undispersed, as if he had entered into meditative concentration. Furthermore, they heard him speak these words:
"Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha! You have well expounded this Lotus Sutra. It is for the sake of hearing this sutra that I have come here. At that time, the four...
The assembly, seeing that in the past, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago, the Buddhas who had entered parinirvāṇa had spoken such words, marveled at this unprecedented event.
They scattered clusters of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and upon Śākyamuni.
At that time, from within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha, saying: "Śākyamuni..."
“Śākyamuni Buddha, you may take this seat. Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stūpa and sat upon half of that seat, assuming the full lotus posture.
(The ancient Buddha’s stūpa appeared; he manifested extinction yet did not truly pass away. Śākyamuni entered the stūpa; he manifested birth yet did not truly arise.
At that time, the great assembly saw two Tathāgatas within the seven-jeweled stūpa, seated cross-legged upon lion thrones.
Each had this thought: "The Buddhas sit high and far away; we pray that the Tathāgatas, by their supernatural powers, will cause us [to see them]."
All together dwelling in the void, Śākyamuni Buddha immediately used his supernatural powers to receive the great assembly, so that they were all in the void.
With a great voice, he universally addressed the fourfold assembly: "Who among you is able, in this Sahā world-system..."
"I shall extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Now is precisely the time. Before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who shall uphold it. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though long since entered parinirvāṇa, still comes for the sake of the Dharma from within the jeweled stupa.
Why do you people not diligently seek the Dharma?
Since this Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has been for immeasurable kalpas, he has heard the Dharma everywhere.
Because they are difficult to encounter, by virtue of that Buddha’s original vow, wherever I go after my parinirvāṇa,
you shall always be there to hear the Dharma. Furthermore, immeasurable Buddhas who are my emanations,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will come desiring to hear the Dharma.
And seeing that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna had entered parinirvāṇa, each of them relinquished their wondrous lands and their assemblies of disciples—
along with devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, and all matters of worship—
in order to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time; thus they have come here to sit together with the Buddhas.
By means of supernormal powers, he moved immeasurable multitudes, causing the lands to be purified.
Each of the Buddhas proceeded to the foot of a precious tree, which was adorned like a pure lotus pond; beneath those precious trees were various lion thrones.
The Buddha sat upon it, adorned with radiant light, like a great torch burning in the midst of the night’s darkness.
From his body issued a sublime fragrance that pervaded the lands of the ten directions;
all sentient beings who were perfumed by it could not contain their joy, which was like a mighty wind.
Blowing upon a small tree branch, by this skillful means he caused the Dharma to endure for a long time.
He addressed the great assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, I shall personally utter a vow."
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa,
he utters a lion’s roar by virtue of his great vow. You sons of the Buddha,
you should understand this intention regarding Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata, myself, and all the emanated Buddhas who have gathered here.
Whoever is able to protect the Dharma should make a great vow so that it may endure for a long time.
Whoever is able to protect the Dharma of this sutra thereby makes an offering to me and to Prabhūtaratna;
this Buddha Prabhūtaratna resides within the jeweled stupa.
Constantly wandering through the ten directions for the sake of this sutra,
they also make offerings to all the emanated Buddhas who come from various worlds, adorning and illuminating them.
If one preaches this sutra, it is as if one were seeing me, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
And all the emanation buddhas, O good sons, each should reflect with careful attention that this is a difficult task;
you should resolve to make a great vow. Although other sūtras exist in numbers like the sands of the Ganges, even though such things are taught, they are not yet considered difficult.
If one were to take Mount Sumeru and hurl it to other directions, even casting it into countless Buddha-fields, it would not yet be difficult;

if, with a single toe, one were to shake the great trichiliocosm and hurl it far away to another land, it would still not be difficult; yet if one were to stand upon the Summit of Existence (Bhavāgra)...
To expound for the multitude Countless other sutras Is not yet considered difficult;
But if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, In this degenerate age, One can preach this sutra, That indeed would be difficult.
Suppose there were someone Who grasped empty space with their hand—
To travel about [in this manner] is not yet difficult; but after my parinirvāṇa, if one were to write it down oneself or cause others to write it, that would indeed be difficult.
It would be as if one were to place the great earth upon the tip of a toenail and ascend to the Brahma-heaven.
It is not yet difficult to do this; rather, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to read this sutra even briefly amidst the evil age—this indeed is difficult.
Even if one were to carry dry grass on one's back and enter into the conflagration at the end of an eon without being burned, that would not yet be difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for the sake of even a single person,
that would be difficult; yet if one upholds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma—
the twelve divisions of the scriptures— and expounds them for others, causing all who hear them...
To attain the six supernormal powers—though one may be able to do so—is not yet difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sutra and inquire into its meaning and intent—that indeed is difficult.
If a person preaches the Dharma, causing thousands of millions of beings...
If immeasurable and innumerable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
were to attain arhatship and be endowed with the six supernormal powers— though such a benefit is great—
it would not yet be difficult; but after my parinirvāṇa, if one can receive and uphold a sūtra such as this, that will be truly difficult.

For whom, then, are these [eighty-four thousand teachings and twelve divisions of scripture] intended? All of them encompass both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna. If they were limited to the Hīnayāna, they would merely cause the listeners to attain the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Lesser Vehicle and establish themselves at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This [reference to the Peak of Existence] serves as a metaphor for those who do not attain penetration.
Therefore, one knows that even a brief reading or a brief exposition of the Perfect Sūtra is truly no easy matter.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands, from the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras; yet among them, this sutra is the foremost.
If there are those who can uphold it, they uphold the body of the Buddha, O sons of good family.
After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?
Now, before the Buddha, you shall each speak your own vow: "This sutra is difficult to uphold;
if one can uphold it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and all the Buddhas likewise."
Such a person is praised by all Buddhas; this is indeed valor, this is indeed diligence, and this is called upholding the precepts.
One who practices the dhūtas will swiftly attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, and shall be able to do so in future ages.
One who reads and upholds this sutra is a true son of the Buddha;
dwelling on the ground of pure goodness after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they are able to explain its meaning.
Such a person is the eye of gods, humans, and the world, capable of expounding it for even a brief moment in an age of fear.
All devas and humans should offer worship to him.
(This clarifies that one who can uphold this sutra accomplishes the supreme practice. Chapter Twelve: Devadatta.
(This chapter is called "The Capacity to Hear the Sūtra. It is the essential method for cultivating the Way and the swiftest path to attaining Buddhahood.

"The essence of space is fundamentally devoid of clouds and mists; Even if clouds and mists appear, one’s perception is mistaken. If one realizes that space is originally without substance, The Immortal speaks of the lotus flower all day long.
