At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly of devas and humans: "In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas..."
He sought the Lotus Sūtra without weariness or fatigue. Throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king, vowing to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed.
Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, he diligently practiced generosity.

His heart was free from stinginess; he did not begrudge elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, slaves, servants, attendants, head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, or feet, nor did he spare his own life.
At that time, the lifespan of the people was immeasurable, yet for the sake of the Dharma, [he gave it all].
He renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to the crown prince. He beat the drum to proclaim a decree, seeking the Dharma in all four directions:
"Who can explain the Mahāyāna for me? I shall provide for them with service and attendance for the rest of my life. At that time, a rishi came and addressed the king, saying:
"I possess a Mahāyāna teaching called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you.

Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately followed the seer, providing all that was required. He gathered fruits, drew water, collected firewood, and prepared food;
he even used his own body as a bed and seat, never wearying in body or mind. Thus he served him for a thousand years.
For the sake of the Dharma, he served him with diligent effort, ensuring that nothing was lacking. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall a past kalpa when, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, though I was a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.
I struck a bell to announce to the four quarters: "Who possesses the Great Dharma?
If you can explain it to me, I shall become your slave. At that time, there was a rishi named Asita.
The Seer Asita (known as "Peerless") came and addressed the Great King: "I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world.
If you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you. When the King heard the words of the Seer, he [listened].
With a heart filled with great joy, he followed the seer, providing whatever was required—gathering firewood and fruits—and respectfully offering them at the proper times.
Because his mind was set upon the sublime Dharma, his body and mind were free from weariness;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently sought the Great Dharma.
Nor did he seek it for himself, nor for the pleasures of the five senses;
therefore, as a great king, he diligently sought and attained this Dharma, and subsequently achieved Buddhahood. For this reason, I now speak it for you.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "The king at that time was none other than myself. The rishi at that time is now Devadatta."

It is because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that I have been able to fulfill the six *pāramitās* and the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

There are three types of spiritual friends: first, the protector; second, the fellow practitioner; and third, the instructor. Regarding the "protector": one's own body and mind are considered internal, while the body and mind of others are considered external. Regarding the "fellow practitioner": oneself and others mutually encourage and inspire one another.

Because people differ while their practice remains the same. As for "instruction" (*śāsana*): proclaiming the words of the Sage is called "teaching" (*śāstra*), and instructing me is called "bestowing" (*śāsana*).

The thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the purple-golden hue, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four means of integration, the eighteen unique qualities, and the supernatural powers of the Way—all these, as well as the attainment of perfect enlightenment and the universal salvation of sentient beings, were made possible solely because of the spiritual friend Devadatta.
He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, after an incalculable number of eons have passed..."

In a future kalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The world shall be named Devamārga.
At that time, the Buddha Devendra shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon the path of the Pratyekabuddhas;
and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path, attained the forbearance of non-arising, and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

(Devadatta was the Buddha’s evil friend throughout many lifetimes; yet the Buddha said, "It is because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend that I have fulfilled the six pāramitās. This is an instance of treating adversity as favorable. Although he belonged to the class of nāgas, he cultivated the bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, the nāga is a different species; she was not a man; at eight years of age she was not of venerable seniority; and for a mere instant she did not practice for long. That she attained Buddhahood by offering a pearl in a single thought clarifies the understanding of the Buddha-nature.)
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.
A stupa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire bodily relics; it was sixty yojanas high and forty yojanas in length and breadth.
All the devas and human beings offered various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, unguents, robes, necklaces, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, and music and song.
Verse: Through prostrating and making offerings to the wondrous stupa of the seven jewels, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship;
immeasurable sentient beings realized Pratyekabuddhahood; and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the Bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

(Devadatta was capable of committing all manner of evils; thus he was called the most obstinate and foolish, a great sinner, and one possessed of an ugly appearance. The wise observe well and do not give rise to enmity or partiality based on slander. This is why the Buddha also bestowed upon him the prediction of attaining Buddhahood:

it was to reveal that while evil karma constitutes the "traces," Buddha-nature is the "root. Once the root exists, the traces can be eliminated; once sin is extinguished, Buddhahood can be realized. Therefore, he cites the case of the Dragon Girl’s sudden attainment of Buddhahood to substantiate this).

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In a future age, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, believe and revere it with a pure mind and do not give rise to doubt, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
They shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and in every place where they are born, they shall constantly hear this sūtra. If they are born among humans..."
In the heavens, they shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss; if they are before the Buddha, they shall be born by transformation within a lotus flower.

At that time, from below, the Bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa), who had accompanied the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying, "I should now return to my own land.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakūṭa, "Good son, wait but a moment. Here there is a bodhisattva named Wén..."
“Mañjuśrī, you may meet with him and discuss the sublime Dharma; you may then return to your own land.
At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel, and the bodhisattvas who had come together with him likewise sat upon precious lotus flowers.
From the great ocean, the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King, they spontaneously surged forth and remained suspended in mid-air, proceeding toward Vulture Peak Mountain.
Descending from the lotus flower, he went to where the Buddha was and prostrated himself at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Having completed his acts of reverence, he went to where Prajñākūṭa was, exchanged greetings with him, and withdrew to sit to one side.
(As Mañjuśrī did not rise to depart, that land likewise became defiled and then pure.
The Bodhisattva Jñatikauṇḍinya asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous One, how many sentient beings have been transformed by you during your visit to the Dragon Palace?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Their number is immeasurable; it cannot be calculated, nor can it be proclaimed by words, nor conceived by the mind."
"What you have measured, wait but a moment and you shall know for yourself through direct realization.
Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas, seated upon precious lotus flowers, emerged from the ocean and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain, where they remained suspended in the void.

All these bodhisattvas were those who had been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they were fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and were all together discussing the six pāramitās. Their original...

The śrāvakas, who were in the midst of the void expounding the practices of the śrāvakas, now all practice the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness (having now heard the teaching of reality, they all abide in the Dharma of the Great Vehicle).
Mañjuśrī said to Jñānakūṭa, "Such were the deeds performed in teaching and transforming beings within the ocean.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa praised him with these verses:
Possessing great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, you transform and deliver immeasurable multitudes. Now,
this entire great assembly and I have all witnessed you expound the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
revealing and elucidating the Dharma of the One Vehicle to widely guide all sentient beings, so that they may swiftly attain Bodhi.
Mañjuśrī said, "Within the ocean, I have always been preaching only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Jñānākara asked Mañjuśrī, "This sutra is profoundly deep and subtle, a jewel among all sutras, rare in the world.
Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor, practice this sutra and quickly attain Buddhahood? Mañjuśrī replied:
There was the daughter of the Naga King Sāgara, only eight years of age. She possessed sharp faculties and wisdom; she was well-versed in the faculties, karmas, and activities of sentient beings.
Having attained *dhāraṇī*, she was able to receive and uphold all the profound secret treasuries spoken by the Buddhas.

She had entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and thoroughly understood all phenomena. In the space of a single *kṣaṇa*, she gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained the stage of non-retrogression. Her eloquence...

He possesses unimpeded eloquence. He regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness as if they were his own infants. Fully endowed with merit, he expresses through speech what his mind contemplates—subtle, wondrous, vast, and great.
Compassionate, kind, and yielding, his will is harmonious and elegant; thus he is able to reach Bodhi.

(The dragon girl praised by Mañjuśrī does not go beyond her great vows, meditative concentration, wisdom, and various practices: wisdom is her insight; deep penetration is her concentration; and compassionate mindfulness is her vow.)

The Bodhisattva Jñānakoṣa said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult and painful practices, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to bodhi without ever ceasing.
He surveyed the trichiliocosm and found not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he had not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings. Then...
"Thus one attains the path of Bodhi. Before he had finished speaking, the daughter of the Dragon King suddenly appeared before him;
she prostrated herself in reverence and stood to one side, praising him with these verses:
Profoundly penetrating the nature of both sin and merit, he shines universally throughout the ten directions.
His subtle and wondrous Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics.
Honored and looked up to by devas and humans, revered by dragons and spirits, he is so for all classes of sentient beings.
There is none who does not revere her; furthermore, it is heard that she shall attain *bodhi*.
Only the Buddha should bear witness to my exposition of the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of delivering sentient beings from suffering.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: "That you will attain the unsurpassed path before long—this matter is difficult to believe."
Why is this? The female body is defiled and impure; it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could one attain unsurpassed bodhi?

The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the perfections (pāramitās) can one finally achieve it.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstacles: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, Śakra; third, a Māra King;
fourth, a Cakravartin Sage-King; and fifth, the body of a Buddha. How then can a woman’s body quickly attain Buddhahood?
At that time, the Dragon Girl had a precious jewel worth a trichiliocosm, which she took and—

She offered it to the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately accepted it. The Dragon Girl said to the Bodhisattva Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa) and the Venerable Śāriputra, "I offered this precious jewel and the World-Honored One accepted it;
was this matter not swift? They replied, "It was exceedingly swift. The girl said, "By means of your supernatural powers, observe my attainment of Buddhahood; it shall be even swifter than this."

(The perfect sphere symbolizes the cultivation of the perfect cause; offering it to the Buddha signifies bringing the cause to fruition. That the Buddha accepted it quickly symbolizes the Dragon Girl’s swift attainment of the fruit.)
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva.
She immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment, manifesting the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Possessing the eighty minor marks, he universally expounds the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

Even Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, and their consorts do not discard their current bodies nor receive new ones; they all attain Buddhahood in their very present forms. Therefore, the verse says: "The nature of phenomena is like a great ocean; ordinary beings, sages, and saints are equal, without high or low. It depends only on the defilement or purity of the mind; to realize this is as easy as turning over one's palm."

At that time, in this Sahā world, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others—both human and non-human—all saw from afar that the dragon girl had attained Buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the entire assembly of humans and devas. Their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.
Immeasurable sentient beings, having heard the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression; immeasurable sentient beings received [the precepts].
The Record of the Path: The stainless world shook in six ways. In the Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression;
three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.

[The passage concerning] "immeasurable sentient beings" and so forth refers to those who receive benefits in that land. [The passage concerning] "the Sahā world" and so forth refers to those who receive benefits in this land. Since the conditions were ripe in the south, it was appropriate for him to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment there; whereas the conditions in this land were thin, he merely used a dragon girl to provide instruction.
"This is the power of skillful means: the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body, by which one attains a single body as all bodies.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence with faith.

(At first, Zhijizhang did not believe or accept [the teaching], holding the Separate Teaching to be a source of doubt. Śāriputra likewise did not believe or accept it, raising objections based on the Tripiṭaka Teaching. Only now do they realize that the Dragon Girl, by practicing according to the Perfect Teaching, swiftly attains Buddhahood;
therefore, they all remain silent and accept it with faith).

Chapter Thirteen: On Upholding (The Two Myriad Bodhisattvas receive the command to propagate the sutra; hence it is named the Chapter on Upholding. The sutra is the lamp that illuminates the mind; the mind is the ground for upholding the sutra.)

"When upholding this sutra, let ten thousand concerns sink away; Encountering adversity or favor, do not groan. When one’s practice reaches the ground of utmost sincerity, The three periods and the ten directions are but one mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna, together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha: "We pray only that the World-Honored One..."

We resolve: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings in future evil ages—those whose roots of goodness have diminished, who abound in overweening pride, who crave gain and offerings, and whose unwholesome roots increase, thereby distancing themselves from liberation.
Although they are difficult to transform, we shall arouse the power of great patience to read, recite, uphold, and explain this sutra.
They shall copy it and perform various kinds of offerings, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.

At that time, five hundred arhats among the assembly who had received predictions of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, we too vow to extensively expound this sutra in other lands.
Furthermore, eight thousand persons, both those still in training and those beyond training, who had received predictions of enlightenment, rose from their seats and joined their palms.
Facing the Buddha, they made this vow: "World-Honored One, we too shall extensively proclaim this sutra in other lands. Why is this?

Because in this Sahā world, people are for the most part corrupt and evil; they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and their minds are turbid with anger, crooked with deceit, and lacking in sincerity."

(These śrāvakas, having received their predictions, have already ascended to the first stage [bhūmi], shattered the delusions of ignorance, attained the patience of non-arising, and initiated the state of a Tathāgata, reaching ultimate peace and bliss.)

In the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Buddha deeply praises those who uphold this sutra. In the "Chapter on Devadatta," he further exhorts seekers of the Dharma to exhaust their sincerity; thus, twenty thousand bodhisattvas, including Bhaiṣajyarāja, made vows to uphold the sutra.

Although five hundred śrāvakas and eight thousand learners had received predictions of enlightenment, their power of patience was not yet sufficient; therefore, they vowed to uphold the sutra in other lands. The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī despised her own female body, and though she heard that the śrāvakas had received predictions, she still doubted whether she possessed the capacity for it.
Only now, seeing the dragon girl attain Buddhahood, has she finally resolved to do so.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs— both those in training and those beyond training—
rose from their seats, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting her eyes for even a moment.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī:
(Kauṇḍinya, the leader of the community of nuns).
Why do you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful countenance?
Does it not occur to your mind that I have failed to mention your name when bestowing the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Kauṇḍinya, I previously spoke of all voices in general.

I have heard that they have all already received their predictions. Now, if you wish to know your own prediction: in a future age, amidst the teachings of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, you shall become a great Dharma Master;
furthermore, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training, you shall all be Dharma Masters.
In this manner, gradually perfecting the path of a bodhisattva, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Sarvasattva-... (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana).
“Gautamī, this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana,
as well as the six thousand bodhisattvas, shall successively receive the prediction of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, had this thought: "In the prophecy, the World-Honored One alone did not mention my name.

The Buddha said to Yaśodharā: "In the future, amidst the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices and become a great Dharma teacher; you will gradually fulfill the path to Buddhahood. In the [Sūtra on] Good...

Within this land, he shall attain Buddhahood, receiving the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Complete with Ten Million Marks of Radiance.
The lifespan of this Buddha shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī...
Together with the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā and her retinue, they were all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
They then spoke these verses in the presence of the Buddha:
The World-Honored One, the Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans—having heard this prediction, our hearts are fully satisfied.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too are able [to go] to other regions."
"The kingdom shall widely proclaim this sutra. At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These bodhisattvas were all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), turning the wheel of the non-retrogressive Dharma and having attained various *dhāraṇīs*.
They immediately rose from their seats, approached the Buddha, and with single-minded palms joined, formed this thought: "If..."
The World-Honored One commanded us: "Those who uphold and expound this sutra should widely proclaim this Dharma in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.
Furthermore, they thought: "The Buddha is now silent; we see no further command. What should we do?
Then, those bodhisattvas, out of reverence for the Buddha’s intention and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, let out a lion’s roar before the Buddha and made this vow:

They said, "World-Honored One, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness—all through the majestic power of the Buddha.
We pray only that the World-Honored One may behold us from afar in other lands and protect us. Thus they spoke.
Then all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
"We pray that you do not worry Regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; In the midst of that terrifying and evil age, We shall expound the teaching extensively."
(These bodhisattvas request protection for the wide propagation of the sutra; this is their own account of the method for propagating it.
There may be ignorant people who revile us with foul language, Or even attack us with swords and staves—all these we shall endure.
In this degenerate age, there will be bhikṣus Whose minds are crooked due to false wisdom.
Claiming to have attained what has not been attained, their minds are filled with the conceit of "I.
Some dwell in forest hermitages, wearing robes of rags in secluded places, claiming to practice the true path.
Out of greed for gain and offerings, they look down upon those in the world, preaching the Dharma to laypeople and receiving the world's veneration.
Like an arhat possessing the six supernormal powers, this man harbors an evil mind;
constantly preoccupied with worldly matters, he falsely claims to be a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*). He delights in exposing our faults and speaks thus:
"These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the doctrines of external paths."
They have composed this sūtra themselves to deceive and delude the people of the world;

for the sake of seeking fame and renown, they have analyzed this scripture. Constantly amidst the great assemblies, desiring to disparage us, they approach kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of bhikṣus.
Those who slander me and speak ill of me, calling me a person of wrong views, preach the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

[The term *āraṇya*—alternatively *ārañña*—is translated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as "a place of seclusion"; in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, it is translated as "a quiet and solitary place," or alternatively, "a place free from contention" (*araṇa*).]
Out of reverence for the Buddha, we shall endure all these evils. Because of this, they will speak words of contempt, saying, "You are all Buddhas. Such words of disdain must all be endured.
In the midst of the evil world of the turbid kalpa, there will be many terrors; Evil spirits will enter their bodies.

Though they revile and humiliate us, we who revere and trust in the Buddha shall don the armor of patience for the sake of preaching this sutra, enduring all such hardships. We cherish not our own bodies or lives, but only the unsurpassed Way;
in future ages, we shall uphold that which the Buddha has entrusted to us.

The World-Honored One himself should know that in this turbid age there are wicked bhikṣus who do not understand the Buddha’s skillful means and the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate; they speak with foul mouths and knit their brows in frowns.
Repeatedly they are expelled and kept at a distance from the stūpas and monasteries. Because of such manifold evils, I call to mind the Buddha’s admonitions.
I shall endure all these matters; to all those in villages and cities who seek the Dharma, I shall go to their abodes and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
As a messenger of the World-Honored One, I am fearless in the midst of the assembly;
I shall skillfully expound the Dharma, and I pray that the Buddha may dwell in peace and security.
Before the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I make this solemn vow:
"The Buddhas themselves shall know my heart.

(Śamala is the name of King Golden; Mahoraga is the great serpent deity; Gandharva is the music deity; Tuṣita is the name of the Heaven of Joy; Asura is the name of the Non-Gods; Garuḍa is the winged bird; Kinnara...)

...Rākṣasas, humans, non-humans, and those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). (Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm: the Four Heavenly Kings experience desire through physical union; the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven experiences desire through wind; the Yāma Heaven experiences desire through embracing; the Tuṣita Heaven experiences desire through holding hands; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven experiences desire through gazing and smiling;

and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven experiences desire through mere gazing. They are called "Heavens" (*deva*) because they are naturally so, their bliss is superior, and their bodies are superior; they are also called "Most Victorious" (*parama-jaya*) and "Radiant" (*prabhāsvara*). Because their desires differ, they are named the Six Heavens of Desire. As for the five desires, the first is...)

1. Desire for wealth; 2. desire for form (sensuality); 3. desire for food and drink; 4. desire for fame—that is, the pursuit of power and reputation; 5. desire for sleep (when people sleep, they become indolent and dissolute, delighting in it without satiety).

(The five supramundane desires are as follows: wealth is the dharma-wealth of merit; form is the thirty-two marks and the purple-golden hue; food is the food of dharma-joy and the food of meditative bliss; name is the full possession of the ten titles with one's renown heard everywhere;
sleep is the *Śūraṅgama* samādhi, the great concentration).

(Examine closely the intent of the sutra: hired labor was originally a skillful means; direct inheritance is the Buddha’s fundamental aspiration. If one can take responsibility for oneself right now, why seek the three chariots outside the gate? Why wait fifty years to meet a true son? The burning house is itself a land of cool serenity;
those who are deluded and impoverished are all children who have reached home.)

(When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, this Lotus Sūtra was hidden within heaven, earth, and all things. When the Buddha appeared in the world, he revealed it from his own mouth. Now that the Buddha has passed away, it is the Buddha’s own emanation.
If one does not encounter this Lotus Sūtra, where can one hear the Buddha’s words? Where can one behold the Buddha’s form?)

The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not transcend the common domain of both mundane and supramundane phenomena. Yet sentient beings do not awaken to these phenomena; failing to comprehend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they remain in a state of profound ignorance regarding this very realm, thereby creating various evil karmas and wandering through the cycle of birth and death.

Therefore, the Great Sage pointed to them as being like dreams and illusions, or like bubbles and shadows, leading people to seek within this realm of dharmas a truth that is signless, nameless, immovable, and unchanging. As for the śrāvakas and others, they have not yet penetrated the perfect subtlety of all phenomena.

Within this realm, one grows weary of suffering and seeks happiness, thereby shattering attachment to existence and realizing emptiness. For this reason, the Great Sage points out that these dharmas are themselves true emptiness and themselves wondrous existence, leading people to seek within this dharma-realm a state of perfect, harmonious, and wondrous realization of the enlightened nature.

Even when Bodhisattvas of the Mahayana undergo arduous cultivation through kalpa after kalpa and exert their strength life after life, striving to deliver all sentient beings and realize the ultimate fruit of the Way, they have not yet directly reached unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, the Great Sage further points out that these dharmas are themselves the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), themselves the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and themselves the Buddha-principle.
*An Outstanding Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Four;
*An Outstanding Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Five.
Originally translated by the Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Commentary by Xu Changzhi of Wuyuan, the Wayman Without Reliance, on the Zhou Family Edition.
Chapter Fourteen: The Practice of Peaceful Abiding (*Anle-xing-pin*).

(To have no other destination in the mind while remaining composed is called "peace" (*an*); for the nature to find its proper place and be perfectly compliant is called "bliss" (*le*); to remain unchanging over a long duration while achieving high merit is called "practice" (*xing*).)

(To be able to practice peaceful conduct without fail, With every thought the mind ceases its outward wandering; As days pass and merit deepens until it becomes one whole, The great trichiliocosm is like lapis lazuli.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these bodhisattvas are truly rare.
Out of reverence and obedience toward the Buddha, they have made great vows to protect [the Dharma] in the evil ages of the future."
To uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
(This praises the Bodhisattvas of profound practice mentioned in the preceding chapter, who are able to fulfill the command to propagate the sutra in this defiled and evil world.)
“World-Honored One, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva preach this sutra in the future evil age? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to preach this sutra in the future evil age, they should abide securely in four dharmas.”
(This indicates the vows of body, speech, and mind; it is the fourth [of the] four assurances.
First, a bodhisattva dwells securely in the sphere of practice and the sphere of association, and is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, what is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells...
The stage of patience is gentle, harmonious, and compliant, without sudden outbursts of violence, and the mind is not startled.

Furthermore, one does not engage in any activity regarding phenomena (*dharma*), yet observes all phenomena as they truly are; one neither acts nor discriminates. This is called the sphere of practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

(Explaining the spheres of practice by way of three dharmas: first, by way of one dharma; second, by way of two dharmas; third, by way of three dharmas—all of which constitute practices of peaceful dwelling.
What is called the sphere of association for a bodhisattva mahāsattva? A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials.
(Below this is the explanation of the "near" [proximate] places; by clarifying the ten afflictions that are distant, one speaks of the near through the distant).

One does not associate with various non-Buddhists, such as Brahmins and Nirgranthas, nor with those who compose worldly literary works, praise foreign scriptures, or follow the Lokāyatas and the Prāsaṅgika-Lokāyatas.
(This is the second [category]: those who distance themselves from the ways of heterodox persons.

[These include] Brahmin renunciants who are non-Buddhist outsiders, Nirgranthas who are lay non-Buddhist outsiders, and Ājīvikas who follow the Lokāyata; they are called "Ājīvikas" because they go against the *gāthā* and do not conform to the world.
Nor does one associate with those who engage in various violent games, such as boxing, wrestling, and the various acrobatic displays of the *nara* and others.

(This is the third [point] on distancing oneself from violent games. Boxing and wrestling are violent games; *nara* here means "strength," referring to the sport of wrestling or the display of physical prowess.)
Furthermore, one should not associate with caṇḍālas, nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, fishermen, or those who follow other such evil vocations.
If such persons should ever come to him, he should preach the Dharma for them without any expectation of reward.
(This is the fourth type of distant candāla. A candāla is called a butcher; if one associates with them, it causes people to have little compassion.
Furthermore, one does not associate with bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who seek śrāvaka-hood, nor does one inquire after their welfare.
Whether in a dwelling, on a walking path, or in a lecture hall, one does not dwell or stay together with them. Or...
When those who come arrive, he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, without seeking anything for himself.
(This is the fifth [category], distancing himself from the assembly of the Two Vehicles. Those of the Two Vehicles are mired in empty quiescence and are unable to give rise to the bodhicitta.)
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not take up the signs that give rise to thoughts of desire regarding the bodies of women when preaching the Dharma,
nor should he take pleasure in seeing them. If he enters the homes of others, he should not converse with young girls,
virgins, widows, and the like.
(This is the sixth distant thought regarding desire; the thought of desire can harm the bodhicitta).
Furthermore, one should not draw near to the five kinds of impotent persons and treat them as close friends.
(This is the seventh [case]: the distant eunuch).
One should not enter the homes of others alone. If there is a necessary cause or condition for which one must enter alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
(Eighth, Avoiding Harm):
When preaching the Dharma to women, one should not smile showing one’s teeth nor expose one’s chest. Even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become overly intimate;
how much less so for other matters.
(This is the ninth point regarding the avoidance of reproach.
He does not delight in keeping young disciples or novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*), nor does he delight in having them share the same preceptor as himself.
(Tenth: Distant Cultivation. He constantly delights in sitting meditation, dwelling in a secluded place to cultivate and collect his mind. Mañjuśrī, this is called the first stage of close proximity.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that all phenomena are empty.

(Previously, he distanced himself from the ten kinds of disturbances, which constitutes the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Now, he constantly delights in sitting meditation, which constitutes the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*). Next, he contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, which constitutes the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).)
It is according to reality and without inversion; it is unmoving, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving.
Like space, its nature is non-existent; all paths of language are cut off. It is unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated; it is nameless and signless. In truth, it is nothing whatsoever;
it is immeasurable, boundless, unobstructed, and unimpeded.

Regarding "not inverted" (*aviparyāsa*): ordinary beings take the two types of retribution—the primary and secondary—to be permanent when they are fundamentally impermanent; they take them to be pleasant when they are fundamentally suffering; they take them to be self when they are fundamentally non-self; and they take them to be pure when they are fundamentally impure. These are the four inversions of ordinary beings.

The followers of the Two Vehicles, conversely, take the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity to be suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity. These are the four inversions of the Two Vehicles. Because Bodhisattvas lack these eight inversions, it is said they are "not inverted. Regarding "immovable":

they are not moved by the two kinds of birth and death—those of fragmentation (*pariccheda*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*). Regarding "non-retrogressive": they accord with the principle of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). Regarding "non-revolving": they do not revolve through birth and death like ordinary beings, nor do they...
[This refers to] the two vehicles transforming from the state of ordinary beings into that of sages).
However, because [phenomena] exist through causes and conditions and arise from inversion, they are described as permanent and blissful.
To contemplate such characteristics of phenomena is called the second station of intimacy for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

(Above, it was explained that the wisdom of contemplation regarding the Middle Way is neither understanding nor delusion, transcending the characteristics of the two extremes. Now it is explained that [this wisdom] illuminates both extremes simultaneously: from the causal conditions of delusion, birth and death arise; from the causal conditions of understanding, nirvana arises.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: “If there be a bodhisattva who,
in the evil world of the future, desires to preach this sutra with a mind free from fear,
they should enter the proper sphere of conduct and the sphere of association.”
One should always keep far from kings and princes, from ministers and high officials,
and from those who engage in cruel and dangerous amusements; likewise, one should not associate with *caṇḍālas*,
non-Buddhist brahmins, those of overweening pride, or those who are greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle.
One should not associate with those who study the Tripiṭaka, precept-breaking bhikṣus,
those who are merely bhikṣus by name or arhats in name only, those who delight in frivolous laughter,
those who are deeply attached to the five desires while seeking parinirvāṇa in this present life, or any upāsikās. Do not draw near to them at all.
If such persons come with a sincere heart to the place of the Bodhisattva to hear the Buddha-way,
the Bodhisattva, with a mind free from fear and harboring no expectations,
shall preach the Dharma for them— whether they be widows or virgins.
And those who are impotent—do not associate with any of them. Do not even associate with those whom you might consider close friends.
Nor should you associate with butchers, executioners, or those who kill for profit by hunting, trapping, or fishing;
nor those who live by selling meat, or those who traffic in female beauty.
One should not associate with such people at all: those who engage in violent wrestling and various games, nor with courtesans;
one must never associate with them, nor preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place. However, when preaching the Dharma, [one may do so]...

One should not engage in frivolous laughter; when entering a village to beg for food, one should be accompanied by another bhikṣu, or if there is no other bhikṣu, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.
This is called the "place of practice" and the "near place. By means of these two places, one is able to dwell in peace and joy while preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas;
not discriminating between conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, or real and unreal dharmas;
and neither apprehending nor perceiving whether these are male or female—this is what is called [the practice].

The sphere of practice of a bodhisattva consists of all phenomena, which are empty and non-existent, lacking any permanence, and likewise devoid of arising or ceasing; this is called the sphere of intimacy for the wise.
It is free from the inverted conceptualizations of the existence or non-existence of phenomena.
Whether real or unreal, whether born or unborn, dwelling in a secluded place,
he disciplines his mind; abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru,
he contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, just like empty space.
Without solidity, neither arising nor emerging, unmoving and non-retrogressive,
eternally abiding in a single mark— this is called the "place of proximity.
If there are bhikṣus who, after my parinirvāṇa, enter this sphere of practice and draw near to this place of proximity.
When preaching this sutra, he was without any timidity or weakness. At times, the bodhisattva would enter a quiet chamber;
with right mindfulness, he contemplated the Dharma according to its meaning.
Rising from meditative concentration, he [preached] for the sake of kings, princes, ministers, and subjects.
The Brahmins and others, having been enlightened and instructed, expound this sutra;
their minds are at peace, free from any timidity.

(This explains the cause of peace and happiness. Because they cultivate wisdom through right mindfulness, they are detached from all grasping and attain the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Being free from internal inversion, their minds are not timid; this is called peace and happiness.)
Mañjuśrī, this is called the bodhisattva who dwells securely in the first dharma and is able,
in future ages, to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the period of the final dharma, those who wish to preach this sūtra should dwell in peace.

Regarding the practice of joy: whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of others or of the scriptures, nor should one treat other Dharma masters with contempt.

(When those who first practice the propagation of the sutras encounter seekers of the Dharma, they explain it solely by means of the Mahāyāna. Those who dwell deeply in the propagation of the sutras clarify the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] throughout its beginning and end by means of the three categories, such as the Tripiṭaka.)

One does not speak of the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others. Even regarding those who are śrāvakas, one does not mention their names to speak of their faults or evils, nor does one mention their names to praise their virtues.

(Do not speak of others' shortcomings; do not speak of one's own excellence. Regarding those such as the śrāvakas: the spiritual faculties of śrāvakas are indeterminate. If one praises the two vehicles, it may cause them to regress from the Mahāyāna and adopt the Hīnayāna.
If one disparages the two vehicles, it may cause them to lose both the Great and the Small Vehicles. Therefore, neither disparagement nor praise is appropriate.)
Furthermore, they do not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion. Because they have skillfully cultivated such a mind of peace and happiness, those who listen do not oppose their intentions.
When faced with difficult questions, they do not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explain them solely through the Mahāyāna, enabling others to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

(As one has already contemplated the emptiness of all phenomena, the mind dwells within the principle of emptiness and is free from grasping or attachment. One will certainly not cling to the "great" while disparaging the "small," but will instead act in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings, without contradicting the characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma with peace and security;
Upon a pure ground, he provides seats and couches; He anoints his body with oil and bathes away all dust and impurity.
Wearing new, clean robes, pure both within and without,
he sat upon the Dharma-seat and taught according to their inquiries.
If there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, or princes...
To the ministers, officials, and the people, he spoke with a serene countenance on the subtle and profound meaning.
If there were any who questioned him, he answered according to the principle of the matter, expounding and analyzing it through causes, conditions, and parables.
By these skillful means, he caused them all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.

Gradually increasing [in merit], they enter the Buddha-way; Eliminating slothful intent and thoughts of indolence, They depart from all sorrows and afflictions, And preach the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness.

(When a heart of resentment arises, there is laziness and sorrow; now, by preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness, resentment is utterly severed, and through diligence, there is no sorrow.)
Day and night they constantly preach the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha,
using various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables to reveal and instruct sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice;
and regarding clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicine, within these matters—
Without any expectation, one should simply focus the mind on the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma, vowing to attain the path of Buddhahood and causing all beings to do likewise;
this is the great benefit and peaceful offering. After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be any bhikṣu...
One who is able to expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* will have a mind free from envy,
anger, and all afflictive hindrances; they shall likewise be without sorrow or those who revile them,
nor shall they have fear of being struck with swords or staves, nor shall they be expelled.
Because they abide in patience, the wise person who thus skillfully cultivates their mind can dwell in peace and happiness.
As I have explained above, the merit of such a person could not be fully described even through calculation or analogy throughout thousands of millions of billions of eons.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish during the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who receive, uphold, read,
and recite this sutra shall harbor no thoughts of envy, flattery, or deceit.

(Those of the Two Vehicles seek to transcend birth and death; therefore, they first eliminate desire. Bodhisattvas seek to transform others; therefore, they first eliminate anger and [wrong] views. Jealousy contradicts compassion and is not the method for transforming others. Deceit and guile deviate from wisdom and are not the method for one's own practice.)
Furthermore, do not disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way, nor seek out their faults.

Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they seek the stage of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva path—you must not distress them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them: "You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain it."
"Omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this? You are a person of negligence, for you are indolent regarding the Path.

(The four assemblies, such as the bhikṣus, all possess the potential for the three vehicles; therefore, it says "seeking śrāvaka-hood," etc. This precept should not be interpreted according to the Perfect Teaching [of the Tiantai school], but rather as a general rebuke for those of the three vehicles in the Shared Teaching.)
Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding phenomena nor contend with others.
One should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, regard all Tathāgatas as loving fathers, and regard all Bodhisattvas as great teachers.
One should always, with a profound mind, pay homage and prostrate to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, maintaining equanimity toward all sentient beings.
He preaches the Dharma because he accords with the Dharma; it is neither too much nor too little. Even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively.

(This refers to the equal dismantling of the disputes of biased attachments. Since the Dharma is fundamentally equal, it is said to "accord with the Dharma. That it is "neither too much nor too little" means that he measures the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.)
Mañjuśrī, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in the final age at the time when the Dharma is about to perish,
have accomplished this third practice of peace and happiness, will be unable to be disturbed or distracted while they are preaching this Dharma.
(This refers to the practice of dwelling in peace and happiness.
One obtains good companions with whom to read and recite this sutra together; one also gains a great assembly that comes to listen and receive it.

Having heard it, they are able to retain it; having retained it, they are able to recite it; having recited it, they are able to explain it; having explained it, they are able to write it down, or cause others to write it, and thereby make offerings to the sutra.
[He] reverenced, honored, and praised [it]. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, One should abandon envy, anger, and pride;

With a mind free from flattery, deception, and falsehood, One should constantly cultivate straightforward conduct. Do not look down upon others, Nor engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma."
Do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood. These sons of the Buddha preach the Dharma with constant gentleness and patience;
they are compassionate toward all and do not give rise to a mind of indolence.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path out of pity for sentient beings; one should therefore give rise to a heart of reverence.
This is my Great Teacher; toward all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should conceive the thought of them as one's unsurpassed father.
Destroying the mind of pride, he preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
A wise person should protect this third dharma in this way, practicing with single-minded tranquility and joy, and being honored by immeasurable multitudes.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in the future final age, when the Dharma is about to perish,
there will be those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra.
(Below this is the fourth vow, the Practice for Peaceful Living. With body, speech, and mind, one joins with compassion and makes a vow to circulate this sutra.
One should give rise to great loving-kindness toward those among the laity and renunciants, and great compassion toward those who are not bodhisattvas.
One should reflect: "Such people suffer a great loss; the Tathāgata has taught through skillful means according to what is appropriate."
Regarding this Dharma, they have not heard it, do not know it, do not perceive it, do not inquire about it, do not believe it, and do not understand it.
Although such persons do not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, wherever they may be, [I shall bring them to maturity].
By means of the power of supernatural faculties and the power of wisdom, they lead them so that they may abide within this Dharma.
Mañjuśrī, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, accomplish this fourth dharma will be without fault when preaching this Dharma;
they will always [be honored] by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the state...
Kings, princes, ministers, and the populace—brahmins, householders, and others—made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised him.
Furthermore, the devas dwelling in the void constantly attended upon him in order to hear the Dharma.
Whether he was in villages, cities, or in secluded forests, whenever anyone came wishing to pose difficult questions, the devas constantly guarded him for the sake of the Dharma, day and night.
It protects them and enables all who hear it to attain joy. Why is this?
Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Mañjuśrī, this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
In immeasurable lands, even their names cannot be heard, let alone being seen, upheld, or recited.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King who, wishing to subdue various kingdoms by his majestic power, finds that the minor kings do not obey his commands;
at that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various armies and goes forth to punish them.
When the king sees that his troops have achieved merit in battle, he is immediately filled with great joy and bestows rewards according to their merit.
He may grant them fields and houses, villages, or cities; or he may grant them clothing and ornaments for the body;
or he may grant them various kinds of rare treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, chariots, and male and female slaves, as well as subjects.

The field is samādhi; the house is wisdom; the village is the three fruits; the city is the nirvāṇa of the fourth fruit. Clothing is the wholesome dharmas of shame and patience; the various ornaments for adorning the body are the seven factors of enlightenment and so forth.
Only the bright jewel from within his topknot he did not give to him. Why was this? Because this single jewel alone rested upon the king’s head;
had he given it away, the king’s entire retinue would have been greatly shocked and astonished.

(The topknot symbolizes the provisional; the jewel symbolizes the real. Its position atop the head signifies that it is the ultimate goal of all schools. "Startled and amazed" refers to sentient beings whose great capacity for awakening has not yet been stirred, as well as those of the Two Vehicles who harbor doubts and feel astonishment.)
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this. By the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the Dharma-realm and reigns as king over the three realms.
Yet, the various Māra kings refuse to submit. The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle;
those who achieve merit therein also bring joy to his heart. Within the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras for their sake, causing them to...

His heart was filled with joy. He bestowed upon them the wealth of all dharmas—the dhyānas, liberations, and the faculties and powers free from outflows—and further granted them the city of nirvāṇa, declaring that they had attained extinction. Thus he guided their minds, causing them all to rejoice;
yet he did not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them. Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing his troops, rewards those who have performed great service.
His heart was filled with great joy. "This pearl, so difficult to believe in, has long remained within my topknot; I have not given it to anyone recklessly, yet now I give it to you.
(Untying the topknot signifies the opening of the provisional; giving the pearl signifies the revelation of the real.)
The Tathāgata is also like this. Within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King who teaches and transforms all sentient beings through the Dharma.

Seeing the army of the noble ones battle against the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, and achieving great merit therein—extinguishing the three poisons, emerging from the triple world, and breaking the net of Māra—the Tathāgata likewise experiences great joy at this Dharma.
The Lotus Sūtra can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).

Though it is full of enmity and difficult to believe in throughout all worlds, that which was never previously taught is now being taught. Mañjuśrī, this Lotus Sūtra is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas;
among all teachings, it is the most profound. It is bestowed at the very end, like a powerful king.
I have long guarded this bright jewel and only now do I bestow it upon you. Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas;
among all sūtras, it stands supreme. I have guarded it through the long night and have not proclaimed it recklessly.
Beginning from this very day, I shall expound it for you all.

[He] can understand all internal phenomena and their internal names, and he can also understand all external phenomena and their external names; however, because he cannot, by means of every path, give rise to every aspect [of knowledge], he is therefore called "One of All-Knowledge" (Sarvajña).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all, One is then able to expound this sutra praised by the Buddha.
In the future, during the final age, Those who uphold this sutra..."
Those who remain in the household life, those who have left the household life, and those who are not bodhisattvas—toward such as these, one should give rise to compassion.
If they do not hear this sutra and do not believe it, it will be a great loss for them.
Once I have attained the Buddha-way, I shall, through various skillful means, preach this Dharma for their sake.
Causing them to dwell therein, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King who,
having achieved merit in battle, bestows various rewards: elephants, horses, chariots,
ornaments for the body, as well as fields, houses, villages, and cities.
Or he may joyfully bestow upon them garments, various kinds of rare jewels, slaves, servants, and wealth;
just as a king who possesses courage and can perform difficult feats unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and grants it to them, so too is the Tathāgata.
As a sovereign king of all dharmas, possessing the great power of patience and the treasure-store of wisdom,
he transforms the world according to the Dharma through great compassion.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and desiring liberation, he wages war against the māras.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he preaches various teachings; by means of great skillful expedients, he speaks these various sutras.
Having known that the sentient beings have gained sufficient strength, only at the very end does he preach this Lotus Sutra, like a king untying the hair-knot on his head.
I bestow this bright jewel upon you; this sutra is the most honored, the highest among all sutras.
I have always guarded it and have not revealed it in vain.
Now is the very time for me to speak it for your sake. After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way—
Desiring to attain peace and security, one who expounds this sutra should draw near to these four dharmas.
Those who read this sutra shall always be free from sorrow and affliction, as well as physical illness;
their complexions shall be bright and pure, and they shall never fall into poverty.
Though lowly, base, and ugly, all sentient beings delight in seeing him;
like noble sages or celestial youths, they serve as his attendants. Weapons do not strike him, and poisons cannot harm him.
If someone reviles him with evil words, that person’s mouth shall be closed.
Wandering fearlessly like a lion king, with the light of wisdom shining like the sun; even in dreams, one sees only auspicious things—
beholding all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones amidst assemblies of bhikṣus.
Surrounded by those preaching the Dharma, he further beheld nāgas, devas, asuras,
and others as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who, with palms joined in reverence,
saw his own body preaching the Dharma to them. He also beheld all the Buddhas, their bodies golden in color.
Emitting immeasurable light that illuminates all, he expounds all dharmas with a Brahma-voice.
For the fourfold assembly, the Buddha preaches the unsurpassed Dharma;
seeing his form standing amidst them, they join their palms in praise of the Buddha and rejoice upon hearing the Dharma.
And having made offerings, they obtain dhāraṇīs and realize non-retrogressive wisdom.

The Buddha, knowing their minds and seeing that they have entered deeply into the Buddha-way, immediately bestows upon them the prediction of attaining supreme perfect enlightenment: "O sons of good family, in a future age..."
Attaining immeasurable wisdom, the Great Way of the Buddhas; the land is adorned, pure, vast, and beyond compare.
There are also the fourfold assemblies, with palms joined, listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests, practicing wholesome dharmas.
Realizing all true realities, they enter deeply into meditative concentration.
They see the Buddhas of the ten directions, their bodies golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. Hearing the Dharma, they preach it for others;
such auspicious dreams they constantly have. Furthermore, they dream of becoming kings, yet renounce their palaces, retinues, and kin.
And having enjoyed the five supreme sensual pleasures, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree upon the lion throne, he sought the Way for seven days.
Having attained the wisdom of all Buddhas and realized the Unsurpassed Way, he arose and turned the wheel of Dharma, preaching the teaching to the fourfold assembly.
Having expounded the sublime Dharma free from outflows for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, and having delivered immeasurable sentient beings,
he shall subsequently enter nirvana, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended.
If, in a future evil age, one can preach this supreme Dharma, that person will obtain great benefit, equal to all the aforementioned merits.
Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth (The Dharma-body neither goes nor comes;
It is lamentable that people of this age vainly conjecture. The three periods of time and the ten directions are all severed; Heaven and earth are truly but specks of dust in the eye.
At that time, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from lands in other directions, numbering more than eight *gaṅgā*-sands. At that...
Rising from within the great assembly, they joined their palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if you would permit us, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, to diligently apply ourselves with vigor in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to this sutra, we shall extensively expound it here in this land. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
“O assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, stop! Sons of good family, there is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra.

Why is that? In my Sahā world, there are already sixty thousand Ganges-sands of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, each of whom has a retinue of sixty thousand Ganges-sands. These individuals will be able to protect [this sutra] after my parinirvāṇa.”

They shall uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra. At the time the Buddha spoke these words, the earth throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe quaked and split asunder; and within it, there were immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Simultaneously they emerged. The bodies of these bodhisattvas were all golden in color, possessed the thirty-two marks, and radiated immeasurable light.
Previously, they had all been beneath this Sahā world, dwelling in the space of this realm.

"The place of abiding" refers to the *dharmadhātu* of eternal quiescence and light. "Eternal" is the virtue of permanence; "quiescent" is the virtue of bliss; and "light" comprises the two virtues of purity and self. This secret treasury of the four virtues is that place of abiding.
These bodhisattvas, having heard the sound of the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, came ascending from below.
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas was a leader among the great assemblies, each bringing with them a retinue of sixty thousand Ganges-sands;
how much more so those who brought retinues of fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand Ganges-sands? How much more so, moreover...
Even down to one *gaṅgā-vāluka*, half a *gaṅgā-vāluka*, or a quarter of a *gaṅgā-vāluka*; even down to one part in ten million *koṭi-nayuta*.
How much more so for ten million *koṭi-nayuta* attendants? How much more so for hundreds of millions of attendants?
How much more so for ten million, one million, or even ten thousand? How much more so for one thousand, one hundred, or even one?
Tenth: How much more so for those who lead four, five, three, two, or one disciple; how much more so for those who dwell alone, delighting in the practice of seclusion.
Such examples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy. These are all bodhisattvas.
Having emerged from the earth, they each proceeded through the air to where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was in the wondrous stupa made of the seven treasures, and where Śākyamuni Buddha was.
Upon arrival, they bowed their heads at the feet of these two World-Honored Ones.

Then, going to the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees, they likewise paid homage to them all, circumambulated them three times to the right, and with palms joined in reverence, [honored] them with all the bodhisattvas.
They praised him with various methods of praise and stood to one side, joyfully gazing up at the two World-Honored Ones.

From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first emerged, they had praised the Buddha with various bodhisattva methods of praise for a duration of fifty intermediate kalpas. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha remained silent.

Yet they remained seated, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty minor kalpas; through the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great multitude to perceive this duration as being like half a day.

(Fifty minor kalpas are said to be like half a day. The fourfold assembly sees this everywhere. This is a case of concealing the long to manifest the short; by borrowing his supernatural power, he causes the narrow to appear as vast. Both are inconceivable.)
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the fourfold assembly also saw the bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.

Within this assembly of bodhisattvas were four leaders: the first was named Upward-Going (Urdhvaga), the second Boundless-Going (Anantagati), the third Pure-Going (Śuddhacaryā), and the fourth Established-Going (Pratiṣṭhitagati). These four bodhisattvas, within that assembly...
They were the foremost leaders and guides among them. Standing before the great assembly, they all joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after him, saying:
"World-Honored One, are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is it not difficult for those who are to be delivered to receive your teachings? Do we not cause the World-Honored One to grow weary? At that time, the four great bodhisattvas...
He spoke in verse:
"Is the World-Honored One at ease? Are you free from illness and affliction?
Do you teach and transform sentient beings without weariness? Furthermore, are these sentient beings easy to transform?"
"Does this not cause the World-Honored One weariness?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "So it is, so it is, noble sons.
The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction. These sentient beings are easy to transform and deliver; there is none [who cannot be saved]."
They are weary. Why is this? These sentient beings have, from lifetime to lifetime since the distant past, constantly received my transformation.
They have also revered and honored the Buddhas of the past, planting various roots of goodness. Yet these sentient beings have only now first beheld my body.
Upon hearing what I have said, they will all believe and accept it, entering into the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna;
even such persons as these, I shall now cause to hear this sutra and enter into the Buddha-wisdom.

Those whose faculties are dull and whose merit is meager have, from lifetime to lifetime, failed to receive the great transformation; therefore, it was necessary to open the way for the sudden teaching by expounding the gradual. Thus, even these individuals may now hear the Lotus Sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
“Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! All sentient beings can easily be transformed and delivered;
You are able to inquire of the Buddhas Regarding their most profound wisdom.”
Having heard this, they practiced with faith, and we rejoiced in it.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas, saying, "Excellent, excellent!

Sons of good family, you are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata. Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva and eight thousand [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...

The assembly of bodhisattvas all had this thought: "From the distant past until now, we have neither seen nor heard of such a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these, who have emerged from the earth, stand before the World-Honored One, join their palms in worship, and inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya knew of the eight thousand bodhisattvas, [as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges...
With minds filled with such thoughts, and desiring to resolve their own doubts, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and asked him in verse:

"O Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, please explain this: These immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great assemblies of bodhisattvas— whom we have never seen before— from where have they come? By what causes and conditions have they gathered?"
Possessing massive bodies and great supernormal powers, their wisdom is inconceivable;
their resolve is firm and they possess the power of great patience. They are a joy for all sentient beings to behold.
From where have these individual Bodhisattvas come? The number of the retinues they bring with them is immeasurable.
There may be great bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers,
who, together with such a great assembly, single-mindedly seek the path of the Buddha. These great masters,
numbering as many as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers, shall all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra.
Fifty thousand Ganges-sands, with numbers exceeding even these; forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand down to ten thousand;
one thousand, one hundred, and so forth; even down to one Ganges-sand, half of one, or a third or fourth part; a ten-millionth part, a hundred-millionth, or a nayuta.
Disciples numbering ten billion, down to fifty million; their number further exceeding a hundred thousand, reaching ten thousand, one thousand, and one hundred;
fifty, ten, and even three, two, or one—those who dwell alone without retinue and delight in solitary seclusion.
They have all come together to where the Buddha is, their number exceeding even that;
if one were to count this great assembly by using tally-sticks for kalpas more numerous than the sands of the Ganges,
one still could not fully know these bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor— whom did they hear the Dharma from?
Having been taught and brought to maturity, from whom did they first resolve their minds?
Whose Buddha-dharma did they praise, and whose sutras did they uphold and practice? Which Buddha-way did they cultivate?
Thus, these bodhisattvas, with their supernormal powers and great wisdom-force, caused the earth in the four directions to split open, and all emerged from within it.
World-Honored One, since my coming here, I have never before seen such a thing. I pray that you will tell us the names of the lands from which they come.
I have constantly traveled through various countries, yet I have never seen such a multitude;
among this assembly, I do not recognize a single person, who has suddenly emerged from the earth.
I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for this present great assembly;
these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas all desire to know this matter—the fundamental and derivative causes and conditions of this host of bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One of Immeasurable Virtue, we only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude.

At that time, the various emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha who had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath jeweled trees in the eight directions.
The attendants of those Buddhas each saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas coming from the four quarters of the trichiliocosm.

They emerged from the earth and stood in the air. Each addressed their respective Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, asankhyeya assemblies of bodhisattvas come? At that time, each of those Buddhas told their attendant:
"Good sons, wait but a moment. There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, [who was] Śākyamuni’s..."
This was the prediction bestowed by the Buddha Niyue (Nirvāṇa); he will become a Buddha next. Having already asked about this matter, the Buddha now answers it;
you yourselves shall hear it through this.
[This refers to the doubt of the bodhisattvas from other lands. The attendants of that Buddha are, in fact, the manifested bodies and retinues of bodhisattvas from other directions.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
You are indeed able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this. You all should now be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firmness."
"O Ānanda, the Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, the power of the sovereign spiritual transformations of all Buddhas,
the power of the lion’s majestic leaping of all Buddhas, and the power of the fierce and great might of all Buddhas."

"Masterful supernatural power" refers to benefiting sentient beings in the past. "The Lion’s Vigorous Dash" refers to the places where his emanations pervade throughout the ten directions; this refers to benefiting sentient beings in the present. "Great Power and Majestic Ferocity" refers to benefiting sentient beings in the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should practice with diligence and single-mindedness; I wish to speak of this matter, so do not harbor doubt or regret.
The wisdom of the Buddha is inconceivable; Now exert the power of faith and abide in the goodness of patience."
The Dharma never heard before, you shall now all hear. I now comfort you;
do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue.
His wisdom is immeasurable, and the supreme Dharma he has attained is so profound it is difficult to discern. Such as this, I shall now proclaim.
"Listen with one-pointed minds!
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: 'Ānanda, I now announce to you all within this great assembly:
Ājita, these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable, innumerable, and asaṃkhyeya...'"
"Ji, they have emerged from the earth—beings whom you have never seen before.
