Since I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this Sahā world, I have taught, guided, and instructed these bodhisattvas, taming their minds and causing them to resolve upon the Way. All these bodhisattvas dwell beneath this Sahā world."
They dwell in the empty space of the realms. Regarding the various sūtras, they read, recite, and master them;
they contemplate, analyze, and maintain right mindfulness. Ajita, these sons of good family do not delight in being among the crowds nor in speaking much;
they always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligent vigor without ever resting, and they do not rely upon or dwell among humans or devas, but always delight in the profound.
His wisdom was without obstruction, and he constantly delighted in the teachings of all Buddhas. With single-minded diligence, he sought supreme wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Ajita, you should know that these great bodhisattvas, who have practiced the Buddha’s wisdom for incalculable eons, are all those transformed by me; I have caused them to resolve upon the mind of the Great Way.
These are my sons, who dwell in this world and constantly practice the dhūta austerities.
Delighting in quietude, they have abandoned the clamor of the great assembly and take no pleasure in much speaking.
Such sons as these study my Way and Dharma, constantly exerting themselves day and night for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
For this purpose, they dwell in the space below within this Sahā world.
With the power of resolve and mindfulness firm and steadfast, always diligently seeking wisdom, you preach various sublime dharmas with a mind free from fear.
At the city of Gayā, seated beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; only then did I bring them to transformation and instruction.
Causing them to first resolve upon the mind of enlightenment, they now all abide in the stage of non-retrogression; they shall all surely attain Buddhahood.
I now speak these words of truth: you all, believe with one mind! From time immemorial, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly.
(Ānanda, "Ajita" means "Invincible"; Gayā is the name of a mountain).
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas felt doubt and wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence, and they thought to themselves:
"How is it that the World-Honored One, in such a short interval of time, has brought so many to transformation?"
He caused immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) great bodhisattvas to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. From [that time...]
Since that time, only slightly more than forty years have passed. World-Honored One, how is it that in such a short period you have performed such great Buddha-work?

By the power of the Buddha and by the merit of the Buddha, you have taught and transformed such a vast multitude of great bodhisattvas, so that they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. World-Honored One, even if this great assembly of bodhisattvas were to...
Even if one were to count them for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one could not exhaust their number nor reach their limit. Since time immemorial,
these beings have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, accomplished the path of the Bodhisattvas, and constantly cultivated pure conduct.
(Since those to be converted are so numerous, their stages of practice are profound and subtle, and they cling to what is distant while doubting what is near.

"World-Honored One, such a matter is difficult for the world to believe. It is like a person with a handsome appearance and black hair, twenty-five years of age, who points to a hundred-year-old man and says, 'This is my son,' while that hundred-year-old man likewise points to the youth and says, 'This is [my father].'"

"My father raised us; this matter is difficult to believe" (his complexion was beautiful and his hair black, entirely remaining in the prime of youth—this is like the Tathāgata being our father, analogous to the aforementioned proximity of attaining enlightenment. Pointing to a hundred-year-old man, he compares him to the bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth, analogous to the aforementioned vast number of those transformed).

The Buddha is also like this. Although it has not been long since he attained the Way, this great assembly of bodhisattvas has, for the sake of the Buddha-way, practiced with diligent vigor for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
They have skillfully entered, emerged from, and dwelt in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of samādhis;
they have attained great supernatural powers and have long cultivated pure conduct, being well-able to proceed through the stages in succession.
He has practiced all wholesome dharmas and is skillful in question and answer; he is a jewel among men, exceedingly rare in all the world.

(Regarding "skillfully entering, emerging, and abiding": the nine successive attainments are skillful entry; the *siṃhavijṛmbhita* samādhi is skillful emergence; the *vyutkrāntaka* samādhi is skillful abiding.)
Today, the World-Honored One has just said that when he first attained the Way of the Buddha, he first caused us to resolve our minds [for enlightenment],
teaching and guiding us to turn toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. That not long after the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, he was already able to perform such a deed of great merit—
though we have faith in the Buddha’s teachings according to his skillful means, the words spoken by the Buddha have never been false.

False. That which the Buddha knows he has fully penetrated. Yet, there may be bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds on awakening who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, upon hearing these words, might not believe or accept them, thereby giving rise to the causes and conditions for the karmic offense of destroying the Dharma.
(To explain by way of analysis, so that those who slander may give rise to faith, and those who already have faith may increase their progress on the Path).
"Indeed, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this for us, to remove our doubts and those of all good sons in future ages."
Having heard this matter, they likewise gave rise to no doubt. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Formerly, the Buddha left the Śākya clan And went forth near Gayā; He sat beneath the Bodhi tree."
Not long has it been since they came; these sons of the Buddhas are immeasurable in number.

Having long practiced the Buddha-way and abiding in the power of spiritual transformations, they have skillfully studied the bodhisattva path and remain unstained by worldly dharmas, like lotuses in the water. They have surged forth from the earth.
All have given rise to a heart of reverence and stand before the World-Honored One. This matter is inconceivable;
how can it be believed? The Buddha attained the Way so recently, yet that which he has accomplished is so vast.
We pray that you will dispel our doubts and explain it according to reality, distinguishing it clearly—just as one might describe a young man.
His age is only twenty-five, yet he shows himself as a father of a hundred years; with white hair and wrinkled face, such as these are those born from me.
The son also calls him "father," yet that the father is young while the son is old is something the whole world cannot believe.
The World-Honored One is likewise so: though he has attained the Way, it has been but a very short time.
These bodhisattvas are firm in resolve and free from timidity;
having practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable kalpas, they are skillful in answering difficult questions.
Their minds are fearless, their patience is resolute, and they are upright and majestic, praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
They are well able to analyze and explain [the Dharma], yet they do not delight in being among men.
Always dwelling in meditative concentration for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, they abide in the lower voids. We have heard this matter from the Buddha and have no doubt;
we pray that the Buddha, for the sake of those in the future, will expound it so that they may attain understanding.
If there are those who, regarding this sutra, give rise to doubt and do not believe, they shall immediately fall into the evil realms;
I pray that you will now explain for them how these immeasurable bodhisattvas, in a short time,
were taught and inspired to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], thereby abiding on the stage of non-retrogression.
Chapter Sixteen: On the Lifespan of the Tathāgata (The Great Way of Heaven and Earth is fundamentally perfected;

The waters are green by nature and the mountains are blue by nature. If one seeks further from others for the ultimate truth, One knows with certainty that the absence of rain is the very nature of heaven.
At that time, the Buddha addressed all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly: "O sons of good family, you should have faith."
He understood the Tathāgata’s words of truth and further addressed the great assembly: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
He addressed the great assembly once more: "You all should have faith and understanding in the Tathāgata’s words of truth."

The Buddha’s intent is to establish the treatise as a warning; the various capacities of beings receive it as faith. Furthermore, not doubting what is near and about to be accomplished is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); clearly understanding the distant origin is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*). Previously, for those on the seven stages of expedient means, whatever was taught was all speech according to the intentions of others.
Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the teaching of the pure, perfect, and revealed truth—shows them the essential; therefore, it is said to be "truthful and real."
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, with Maitreya at their head, joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of this;
we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words. Having requested thus three times, they spoke again: "We pray that you will speak of this; we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing that the bodhisattvas had made their request three times without ceasing, addressed them:

"Listen attentively to these words. Regarding the power of the Tathāgata’s secret spiritual penetrations, all the devas, humans, and asuras in the world say that the present Śākyamuni Buddha left the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. However, O sons of good family,"
In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
(The following clarifies the shattering of attachments and the dispelling of delusions.
For example, suppose there were five hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas of trichiliocosms. Provisionally...

Suppose there were a person who reduced [this world] to fine dust and, traveling eastward across five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asankhyeyas of worlds, dropped a single grain of dust.
Continuing in this manner toward the east until all such dust had been exhausted—O sons of good family, what do you think?
Could one conceive of, calculate, or know the number of these worlds? Maitreya Bodhisattva...
Śāriputra and the others all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these worlds are immeasurable and boundless;

they cannot be known by calculation, nor can they be reached by the power of the mind. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even with their untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), are unable to contemplate or know their limit.
We, who abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), likewise [are unable] regarding this matter..."
"I do not understand, World-Honored One. Such worlds as these are immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas: "Good sons, I shall now clearly declare to you:

if all these worlds—both those where atoms are placed and those where they are not—were entirely reduced to dust, and if one were to take one atom to represent one kalpa, the time since I attained Buddhahood would exceed even that."

In this regard, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, ever since that time, I have constantly remained in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
I have also guided and benefited living beings in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of other asaṃkhyeya lands. Sons of good family, during this interval, I spoke of Dīpaṃkara.
The Buddha and others further state that he entered nirvana; all such statements are made through skillful means and distinctions.

(Previously, seeing that the causes for practice described in various teachings were inconsistent was a cause for doubt regarding the cause. Furthermore, seeing that the predictions received at various times were inconsistent was a cause for doubt regarding the fruit. Now, to dispel these doubts, he points to the causal practices performed during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, thereby dispelling doubt regarding the cause.
He also points to the prediction received and the entry into nirvana during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, thereby dispelling doubt regarding the fruit.)
"O sons of good family, if there are sentient beings who come to me, I observe their faith and other faculties with my Buddha-eye—
whether they are sharp or dull— and deliver them according to what is appropriate for each."

"Those who come to me" refers to the gradual and sudden capacities of sentient beings of the past, who silently strike against the Dharma-body. "Observing with the Buddha-eye" means that having long since attained Buddhahood, one uses the Buddha-eye to reflect and illuminate all things without omission or error.

"The faculties such as faith" refers to the five faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The Tathāgata fully illuminates the wholesome capacities within the ten realms and manifests forms and sounds according to what is required for deliverance to benefit them.
In various places, he speaks of his own name differently and manifests different ages, both great and small; he also declares that he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
(For those who are to be saved through extinction, he manifests extinction, causing them to feel longing and veneration so that they may attain liberation.)

Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma, enabling sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy (although he initially employs gradual methods, he ultimately causes them to enter the Great Vehicle; therefore, it is said that he can cause them to rejoice).
"Good sons, when the Tathāgata sees that sentient beings delight in inferior teachings and possess meager virtue and heavy defilements, he speaks for their sake, saying:
'I left home at a young age and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Yet, in truth, it has been this long since I truly attained Buddhahood.
It is only through skillful means (*upāya*) that I teach and transform sentient beings, leading them to enter the Buddha-way."
He spoke thus: "O sons of good family, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of delivering sentient beings.
Sometimes he speaks of his own person, or speaks of another's person; sometimes he manifests his own person, or manifests another's person; or he reveals his own deeds."
Or he may manifest other matters; whatever he speaks is entirely true and not false. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are:
there is no birth-and-death, neither passing away nor emerging; there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa.
It is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor otherwise.
The sentient beings of the six realms perceive the three realms as distinct; those of the two vehicles perceive the three realms as suchness.
Yet, they do not perceive the three realms as they truly are. Such matters as these are clearly seen by the Tathāgata, without any error or delusion.
(Only the Buddha internally possesses the function of true wisdom; therefore, he exhaustively and accurately illuminates the reality of the triple world.
This is because sentient beings possess various natures, various desires, various conducts, and various memories, thoughts, and discriminations.

(The faculties of sentient beings vary in sharpness or dullness, and their progress differs as gradual or sudden. Desiring to cause their various roots of goodness to increase, he thus proclaims the teachings for himself and others.

To cause the arising of various roots of goodness, he performs the work of a Buddha without ever ceasing for a moment, preaching the Dharma through various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions.
(This is the bestowing of benefit according to the specific capacity of the audience, intending to cause those of gradual and sudden capacities to produce various roots of goodness.
Thus it is, that since I attained Buddhahood, an immensely long time has passed; my lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, eternally abiding and never perishing.
O sons of good family, the lifespan I achieved while originally practicing the bodhisattva path remains even now unexhausted.
[The number of kalpas] is exhausted; it is again double the aforementioned figure. However, this is not yet actual parinirvāṇa, yet one proclaims that one shall attain parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it does not perish, yet one proclaims its perishing: because the Dharma is fundamentally unborn, there is nothing that can perish. Regarding the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), it does not perish, yet one proclaims its perishing: who possesses wisdom? Who possesses afflictions? To say that "wisdom can destroy [afflictions]" implies a duality that does not exist.

Regarding the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya), it does not perish, yet one proclaims its perishing: the response is the function of the reward; since the essence has no cessation, how could its function ever come to an end?

The Tathāgata employs these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings. Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, those of meager virtue would fail to plant roots of goodness;
being poor, lowly, and base, they would become greedily attached to the five desires and fall into the net of discursive thoughts and false views.
If they were to see that the Tathāgata always remains and never perishes, they would give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, conceiving feelings of weariness and indolence.
One cannot give rise to the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, nor can one develop a heart of reverence.

(If one sees the Buddha as always remaining in the world, one will instead give rise to arrogance and indolence; unable to generate reverence, arrogance and self-indulgence increase, which augments the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Indolence gives rise to the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). If one does not conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, one cannot produce the understanding of the truths (*satya-abhisamaya*);
therefore, one cannot sever the delusions of views. If one lacks reverence, one cannot produce the path of contemplation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); therefore, one cannot sever the delusions of cultivation.)
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful expedients: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because those of meager merit may, after passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, perhaps see a Buddha."
Or, regarding those who do not see [the Tathāgata]: for this reason, I say, "O monks, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet;

with hearts full of longing and yearning for the Buddha, they will then plant roots of goodness. For this reason, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into extinction, he speaks of his extinction.
[The Buddha] said, "Furthermore, good son, the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is always thus. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false.
It is like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning, proficient in formulating medicines, and adept at curing all manner of illnesses."

(The skilled physician is a metaphor for the Buddha, who internally possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and the five eyes—these constitute the eight arts—and has perfectly mastered the nature of the medicine. Externally, he recognizes the root causes of the illnesses arising in all sentient beings. His "wisdom" refers to the two wisdoms of skillful means (*upāya*) and reality (*bhūta*), through which he profoundly understands the two truths.

His "erudition and penetration" refers to the five eyes discerning the capacities of beings, ensuring that the sudden and gradual teachings do not err. The twelve divisions of the teaching, with their profound principles and phrasing, are like clearly refined prescriptions and medicines.)
That man has many sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or even a hundred in number. On account of some business matter, he travels far away to another country. Later, his sons drink a poisonous drug;
the poison takes effect, causing them to become dazed and confused as they writhe upon the ground.
At that time, their father returns home. Among the sons who have drunk the poison, some have lost their original minds while others have not; from afar, he sees them.
His father was filled with great joy; he prostrated himself, knelt, and inquired after his well-being, saying, "You have returned safely and in peace. We were foolish and mistakenly took poison;
we pray that you will save us from it and grant us our lives once more."

(The analogy of the figure benefiting [the father] refers to the Buddha returning to be born in this land. To believe and accept the teachings of false teachers is called "drinking poison. "Losing one's mind" means being greedily attached to the five desires of the triple world and losing the roots of goodness of the three vehicles previously planted).

Seeing his sons suffering in such a manner, the father, following the prescriptions of various medical treatises, sought out excellent medicinal herbs that were fully endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.
He pounded and sifted them together to create a compound, which he gave to his sons to take.

Form (*rūpa*) is like ethical discipline (*śīla*); because it guards the body and speech, its characteristics are manifest and evident, and thus it is like form. Fragrance is like meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the wondrous fragrance of its virtues permeates all things. Taste is like wisdom (*prajñā*); it is able to attain the flavor of principle (*tattva*).
And he spoke these words: "This great, excellent medicine is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor. You should take it;
it will swiftly eliminate your suffering and affliction, so that you shall have no further ailments. Among his sons, those who had not lost their wits saw this excellent medicine.
The color and fragrance were both excellent, so he immediately took it; his illness was completely cured.

As for the others who had lost their minds, although they were joyful to see their father arrive and inquired after him while seeking treatment for their ailments, they would not take the medicine when it was offered to them.
Why was this? Because the toxic vapors had penetrated deeply and they had lost their original minds; thus, they found that medicine of excellent color and fragrance to be unpalatable.
The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable; he has been struck by poison and his mind is completely deranged.
Although he sees me and rejoices, seeking a cure, he refuses to take such excellent medicine as this."

(This analogy illustrates the reason for his passing into extinction: it is precisely because sentient beings have meager merit that they perceive the Buddha as eternally abiding; thus, they only increase their arrogance and negligence rather than practicing, which is equivalent to being unwilling to take medicine.)
I shall now employ skillful means to cause him to take this medicine.
(This is like the case where remaining in the world causes harm, while manifesting extinction brings benefit; thus, one must employ skillful means.)
He then spoke these words: "You should know that I am now old and infirm, and the time of my death has arrived.
This excellent medicine remains here; you may take it and drink it. Do not worry that you will not be cured. Having given this instruction, he departed once more for another country.
A messenger was sent back with the message: "Your father has already passed away.

Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, he has left the sūtras in the world as an excellent and wholesome medicine. As for the phrase "further proceeding to another land," this refers to manifesting extinction in this region while manifesting birth in another region. Regarding the dispatch of messengers and so forth, the treatise states: "I now proclaim and propagate this Dharma which he has left behind."
"You should receive and practice this.
At that time, when the sons heard that their father had passed away, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and distress, and they thought to themselves: "If our father were still alive..."

"Have compassion for us; you were able to protect and save us. Now you have abandoned us and perished far away in another land. Reflecting on my own solitary and exposed state, I find no one left to rely upon.
Constantly harboring grief and sorrow, my mind has finally awakened, and I now realize that this medicine possesses color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor."
Even if they take it, their toxic illnesses will all be cured.
(This is truly because after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings awaken; they take the medicine and practice cultivation, thereby creating the necessary conditions.)
When the father heard that his sons had all recovered, he immediately returned and allowed them all to see him.

(This illustrates the future benefit of sentient beings: when the father hears of their recovery, it constitutes the responsive capacity that can evoke the response; "allowing them all to see him" refers to the arising of the future response.)
"Sons of good family, what do you think? Could anyone say that this skilled physician has committed a falsehood? "No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "I am also like this. Since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas.
For the sake of sentient beings, by the power of skillful means, I have said that I shall enter extinction."
Furthermore, there is no one capable of rightfully accusing me of the fault of falsehood. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Throughout this time, I have constantly preached the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
From that time until now, for immeasurable kalpas, I have acted for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Through skillful means he manifests nirvana, yet in reality he does not pass into extinction; he eternally dwells here preaching the Dharma.
By the power of his various supernatural faculties, he causes deluded sentient beings not to see him even though they are near.
When the multitude perceives my passing into extinction, they extensively make offerings to my relics.
All of them harbored longing and affection, giving rise to hearts of thirsty adoration.

Once the sentient beings had gained faith and submission, their natures upright and their intentions supple, they desired with single-minded devotion to see the Buddha, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
At that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; I then spoke to the sentient beings:
I am always here and do not perish; yet, by the power of skillful means, I manifest death and non-death.
In other lands where there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight [in the Dharma], I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma among them.
You do not hear this, and thus you merely say that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
Seeing all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction, I do not manifest my body to them so as to inspire in them a longing for me;
because their hearts are filled with yearning, I then appear and preach the Dharma.
Such is the power of my supernormal faculties: throughout incalculable kalpas, I have always remained on Vulture Peak Mountain.
And in all other dwelling places, when sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and the great fires that consume them, my land remains peaceful and secure, forever filled with devas and humans.
Adorned with various jewels, its gardens, groves, halls, and pavilions are magnificent;
its jewel-trees abound with flowers and fruit, providing a place of joy and recreation for all beings.
The devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform various musical arts; they rain down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitude perceives it as being consumed by fire, filled with grief, fear, and all manner of suffering—all such beings who have committed transgressions.
Due to the causes and conditions of evil karma, for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem.
Yet, for all those who cultivate merit and are gentle, mild, and upright, they shall all see my body here preaching the Dharma;
or at times, for this assembly, I shall preach that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable.
To those who have seen a Buddha only after a long time, I speak of how difficult it is to encounter a Buddha.
My power of wisdom is such that its light shines immeasurably; my lifespan lasts for incalculable kalpas. This is what has been attained through long-cultivated practice.
You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this life; you should sever them and seek their total exhaustion.

The Buddha’s words are true and not false; like a physician skilled in expedient means, for the sake of curing his mad son, he says the son is dead though he is actually alive—no one can say this is a falsehood.
I too am the Father of the World who rescues those afflicted by suffering; for the sake of deluded ordinary beings, I say that I have entered extinction though I am actually present.
Because they constantly see me, they give rise to a mind of arrogance and self-indulgence; being heedless and attached to the five desires, they fall into the evil realms.

I always know the sentient beings—whether they practice the Path or do not—and according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various Dharmas for them, constantly forming this thought within myself:
By what means may sentient beings Attain entry into unsurpassed wisdom And swiftly accomplish the Buddha-body? Chapter Seventeen:

Discerning Merit (When the Buddha spoke of the lifespan, the past disciples who emerged from the earth and the present disciples on Vulture Peak obtained various benefits; hence it is called "merit. As these benefits vary in depth, it is called "discernment.")

"To have faith without doubt in even a single phrase of this sutra Is itself the moment of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm. The myriad kinds of conditioned phenomena all involve exertion; My mind’s sudden awakening is itself Bodhi.

At that time, having heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan and the vast duration of kalpas in this manner, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings attained great benefit. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:
Ajita, when I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty million *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore,
there were a thousand times more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining.
(1) The dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining: all languages and all phenomena that are heard by the ear are never forgotten; (2) the dhāraṇī of analytical knowledge; (3) the dhāraṇī of entering sounds).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system who attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).

Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system who attained the immeasurable *dhāraṇī* of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of revolutions. Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm.

They were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in two thousand intermediate world-systems who were able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas numbering as many as the atoms in one small thousand-world system who would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight births. Furthermore, there were [bodhisattvas] from four sets of four-continent worlds...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a single world-system shall, after four births, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in four world-systems who shall, after three births, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in two world-systems...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, in two lifetimes, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and furthermore,
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in four *cāturmahādvīpaka* worlds, who, in one lifetime, shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

(One lifetime. This refers to entering the Vajra-mind of Equal Enlightenment. From the first abode up to Equal Enlightenment, one destroys one grade of ignorance at each stage; then, by destroying one further grade of subtle ignorance, one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment.)
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When the Buddha spoke of how these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained the great benefit of the Dharma, in the midst of the void...
It rained *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, scattering them upon the Buddhas seated on lion-thrones beneath immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of jewel trees,
as well as scattering them within the stūpas made of the seven treasures. They were also scattered upon Śākyamuni Buddha seated on his lion-throne,
as well as upon the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who had long since passed into extinction, and likewise upon all the great bodhisattvas.
The fourfold assembly [gathered]. Furthermore, fine powders of *candana* sandalwood, aloeswood (*agaru*), and other incenses were suspended in the void.
Celestial drums resounded spontaneously with profound and wondrous sounds. Moreover, a thousand kinds of celestial garments rained down, along with hanging necklaces:
necklaces of pearls, necklaces of *maṇi* jewels, and necklaces of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), pervading the nine directions. Countless precious incense burners burned priceless [incense].
Incense naturally pervaded everywhere, making offerings to the great assembly.

Above each Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies, ascending in succession as far as the Brahma Heaven. These bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
(At that time, the assembly, having heard the profound and far-reaching Dharma, attained great benefit. Desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they prepared offerings.
Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
The Buddha has preached this rare Dharma, never heard before; the World-Honored One possesses great power, and his lifespan is immeasurable.

When the countless sons of the Buddhas hear the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition and obtain the benefit of the Dharma, joy suffuses their entire bodies, and some dwell on the stage of non-retrogression.
Some have attained dhāraṇīs, some possess unimpeded eloquence, and some hold the *koṭī-niyuta-parivarta* dhāraṇī.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a great trichiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma; there are also bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within a medium chiliocosm.
Each and every one is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, who have eight births remaining before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
Moreover, there are those with four, three, or two [births remaining], like the atoms of all the four continents. There are also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of these worlds.
Becoming Buddhas according to their number of births, or [becoming so] within a single four-continent world-system;
bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms remaining with only one birth left before they shall attain all-knowledge—
when such beings hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, they obtain immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure karmic fruition.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds who, upon hearing the Buddha speak of his lifespan,
all resolved their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way. The World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas that bring great benefit, like the boundlessness of space.

(Regarding those who attain Buddhahood according to their respective numbers: the verse refers to bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of the four continents attaining *bodhi*. "Attaining the wisdom of the Omniscient One" refers to the wisdom of the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) attained after one more lifetime following the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*).

"Attaining the fruit of untainted purity": this is said to be "immeasurable" to distinguish it from the limited [attainments] of the two vehicles; it is said to be "pure" because it is evoked by wondrous causes; and it is called "fruit of retribution" because it is the unobstructed realm.)
It rained *māndārava* flowers and great *mahāmāndārava* flowers.
From as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges, Śakra and Brahmā came, raining sandalwood and aloeswood that fell in profuse,
swirling showers like birds descending from the sky, making offerings to the Buddhas while celestial drums resounded in the void.
Naturally, wondrous sounds issued forth; ten million kinds of celestial garments descended, swirling down from above.
Miraculous incense burners made of various jewels produced priceless incense, which naturally pervaded everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.
The assembly of great bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures.
Exalted and sublime in ten trillion varieties, they ascend in succession to the Brahma-heaven;
before each and every Buddha, precious banners are suspended with superior pennants. Furthermore, with ten million verses, they sing praises to all the Tathāgatas.
Such various matters as these have never occurred before; now that we hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable.
All were filled with joy; the Buddha’s fame resounded throughout the ten directions.
Widely benefiting all sentient beings, they all came to possess roots of goodness, thereby assisting their unsurpassed resolve.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: “Ajita, there are sentient beings who hear of the Buddha...”
The lifespan is thus long-lasting, even to the point of being able to give rise to a single thought of faith and understanding (this clarifies the four types of faith in the present;

as for the four types of faith: first, the single thought of faith and understanding, though one is not yet able to expound it; second, a brief understanding of the course of words; third, explaining it extensively for others; fourth, the accomplishment of profound faith and contemplation).
The merit thus obtained is immeasurable. If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who,
for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practiced the five *pāramitās*— the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *śīla-pāramitā*,
the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, and the *vīrya-pāramitā*— for eighty million *nayuta* *koṭis* of eons...
Honey. The dhyāna-pāramitā, excluding the prajñā-pāramitā (prajñā being the correct wisdom that is now used to evaluate the five perfections; hence it says "excluding prajñā").
Compared to these merits, the former merits do not equal even one hundredth, one thousandth, or even one hundred-thousand-billionth part;

they are beyond the reach of calculation or analogy. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family possesses such merits, it is impossible for them to fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

(At the initial stage of the ten stages of faith in the Perfect Teaching, one hears of the merit of the lifespan, which provides external support; one’s perfect, compliant faith and understanding provide internal cultivation. Thus, one does not regress. [This applies to] śīla (precepts), kṣānti (patience), and vīrya (diligence).)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, For eighty quadrillion nayuta kalpas, They practice the five pāramitās;
Throughout all these kalpas, They give in charity and make offerings to the Buddhas."
To the Pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattvas,
[he offers] rare and extraordinary food and drink, superior garments, and bedding; he constructs monasteries of sandalwood and adorns them with gardens and groves—
making such offerings as these, all of which are exquisite, throughout the entirety of these kalpas.
By dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-way, and furthermore by upholding the prohibitive precepts, pure and without flaw, seeking the unsurpassed path—
this is what all Buddhas praise. Furthermore, if one practices patience and abides in the stage of gentleness,
even if various evils should be inflicted upon them, their mind shall not waver.
Those who have attained some dharma, harboring overweening pride, may treat one with such contempt and vexation;

yet one should endure this as well. Furthermore, if one applies oneself with diligent vigor, keeping the mind and mindfulness ever firm, for immeasurable billions of kalpas, with a single-minded resolve that never slackens, and likewise throughout countless kalpas—
Dwelling in a secluded place, whether sitting or walking in meditation, one should constantly restrain the mind by removing drowsiness.
For this reason, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Abiding with an undisturbed mind for eighty billion *koṭis* of kalpas, one takes the merit of this single-mindedness and vows to seek the Unsurpassed Way.
I have attained all-knowledge and exhausted all meditative concentrations; If such persons as these good men and women, as described above,
Should practice these various merits throughout hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas,
And upon hearing me speak of this lifespan, Should believe it for even a single thought-moment, [their merit would be far greater].
The merit of that person would surpass all others; if there were no one else at all, and one with a deeply sincere heart were to believe for even a moment, their merit would be just like this.
As for those bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas, upon hearing me speak of the lifespan, they will then be able to believe and accept it.
May these people who receive this sutra upon their heads, and I as well, in the future possess long life to deliver sentient beings,
just as the World-Honored One does today— the King among the Śākyas,
the Lion’s Roar at the site of enlightenment— who fearlessly preaches the Dharma. May we likewise do so in future ages.
When all those who are honored sit within the site of enlightenment, they likewise speak of their lifespan.
Those who possess a profound mind, who are pure and upright, who have heard much and are able to maintain it in memory,
and who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning— such persons as these have no doubt regarding this.

"One who has practiced the Path for immeasurable kalpas" refers to having long cultivated the various perfections (*pāramitās*). "May I, in the future... and so forth expresses the arising of the vow of compassion. Having heard of [the Buddha's] long life and having heard this sutra, one gains the merit of faith and understanding.

Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear of the Buddha’s lifespan being so long and far-reaching, and understand the meaning of these words, the merit obtained by such persons will be immeasurable;
they shall be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
(This is the second faith; a brief explanation of the meaning of the words).
How much more so for those who hear this sutra extensively, whether they cause others to hear it, uphold it themselves, cause others to uphold it, or write it down themselves.
If one teaches others to write it, or makes offerings to the sutra scrolls with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps,
this person’s merit will be immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
(This third faith [should be] widely taught to others).
Ajita, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, should believe and understand it with a profound mind,
they shall see the Buddha as always dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, surrounded by great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
He circumambulated and preached the Dharma. Furthermore, he saw that in this Sahā world, the ground was made of lapis lazuli, level and even.
Jāmbūnada gold delineated the eight paths, and rows of jewel trees stood in order. All the terraces and towers were composed entirely of jewels.
The assembly of bodhisattvas was everywhere amidst them. One who is able to contemplate in this manner should be known as one who possesses deep faith and understanding.
Characteristics.

(This is the fourth faith. It is the faith of deep conviction in the accomplishment of contemplation; that is to say, possessing the three aforementioned types of faith, one further cultivates contemplative practice, enters meditative absorption, and employs wisdom.)
Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy,
you should know that this is already a sign of profound faith and understanding.

(Explaining the five grades after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa: 1. Rejoicing; 2. Personal upholding; 3. Encouraging others to uphold; 4. Practicing the six pāramitās concurrently; 5. Properly practicing the six pāramitās.)
How much more so for those who read, recite, and uphold it! Such persons shall be as if they were bearing the Tathāgata upon their heads.
Ajita, these sons and daughters of good family need not further erect stūpas or temples for my sake, nor build monasteries, nor provide the four requisites to the Saṃgha.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family have received, upheld, and recited [this teaching].
This sutra is equivalent to having already erected a stupa, constructed monasteries, and made offerings to the Sangha;
it is as if one has used the Buddha’s relics to erect a stupa of the seven precious gems, vast and high, gradually tapering upward to the Brahma-heaven, adorned with hanging banners,
canopies, and various jeweled bells, and provided with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, burning incense, various drums, music, flutes, pipes, and lutes.
Performing various dances and plays, they offered praise and hymns with exquisite voices; having thus made such offerings for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.

(This is the second section on the merits of this calculation. Fearing that those with novice resolve might be distracted by worldly circumstances and hindered in cultivating their primary practice, it is taught that if one simply recites and upholds this sutra with single-minded devotion, one thereby bears the Tathāgata upon one's crown and makes offerings to the Saṃgha.)

Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there should be those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it— whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it (previously they had only recited and upheld it themselves,
but now they can further teach others)— [they shall attain great merit].
He then erected monasteries and constructed thirty-two halls out of red sandalwood, each eight *tāla* trees in height, magnificent and exquisitely adorned.

Within them dwelt hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus. Parks, groves, bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves were provided, along with clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; all manner of requisites for comfort filled these places. Just as...

These monasteries and halls are numerous—hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions, their number immeasurable. By means of these, they presently make offerings to me and the community of bhikṣus.
Therefore, I say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain [this sutra] for others;
or if they write it themselves, or teach others to write it, and make offerings to the scripture scrolls, they need not rise again.

To build stūpas and temples, as well as to construct monasteries for the sake of making offerings to the Saṃgha—this constitutes the third grade of merit. (The *tāla* tree resembles a *tāli*; its fruit is red when ripe.)

How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom. (From the beginning of this chapter to this point:
if the contemplation of principle becomes mature, external involvement will not hinder the internal; mundane affairs will assist the Way, like raising sails while going with the current.)

Their virtue is most supreme, immeasurable and boundless, like space. Just as the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir are immeasurable and boundless, so too are the merits of these people immeasurable and boundless; they shall swiftly attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
(Regarding the fourth category of merit from this calculation):
If a person reads, recites, receives, and upholds this sutra; explains it to others; writes it themselves or instructs others to write it;
and further erects stupas and constructs monasteries, making offerings and praises to the assembly of śrāvakas, even with hundreds of thousands of millions...

They praise the Dharma with billions of eulogies, extolling the merits of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, for the sake of others, they explain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through various causes and conditions according to its meaning.

Moreover, they are able to maintain the precepts purely, dwell together with those who are gentle and mild, practice patience without anger, remain firm in their resolve and mindfulness, always value seated meditation, attain profound concentrations, and exert themselves with vigor.
Vigorously gathering all wholesome dharmas, with sharp faculties and wisdom, one skillfully answers difficult questions and challenges.

(Reaching the fifth stage, the comprehensive contemplation becomes somewhat mature; principle and phenomena begin to merge. Engaging in phenomena does not obstruct principle, and abiding in principle does not separate from phenomena; thus, one fully practices the six perfections.)

Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that these persons have already proceeded toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they are seated beneath the tree of enlightenment. Ajita, these sons of good family and...
O woman, whether sitting, standing, or walking, one should erect a stūpa at that very spot;
all devas and humans should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha.
(This is the fifth chapter on the merits of this calculation).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold this sutra, the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable."
As has been explained above, this constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings:
by erecting stupas for the śarīra, adorned with the seven treasures, their spires exceedingly high and wide,
extending gradually upward to the Brahma-heaven, with billions of precious bells that emit wondrous sounds when stirred by the wind.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable kalpas, one has made offerings to this stūpa with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold music;
by lighting lamps of fragrant oil and ghee, it is constantly illuminated on all sides.
In the final age of the Dharma during evil times, one who is able to uphold this sutra is already as described above.
If one can uphold this sutra, they will be fully endowed with all offerings; it would be as if the Buddha were present in person,
and one were to construct a monastic dwelling out of gośīrṣa-candana, thirty-two cubits in height and eight tāla trees in depth,
providing it with exquisite food, fine clothing, and every necessary bed and bedding.
The dwellings of hundreds of thousands of beings, the gardens, and the various bathing pools, the walking paths and meditation caves—all are exquisitely adorned.
(On Mount Malaya grows sandalwood known as "ox-head"; if one anoints the body with it, even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn.)
If there are those with a mind of faith and understanding who receive, uphold, read, recite, or copy [this sutra],
or further teach others to copy it and make offerings to the scripture scrolls— scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense,
and constantly burning lamps with perfumed oil made of sumana, campaka, and atimuktaka— those who make such offerings:
One attains immeasurable merit, as boundless as space; such is the nature of that merit.

How much more so for one who upholds this sutra, while also practicing generosity, observing the precepts, enduring with patience, delighting in meditative concentration, and remaining free from anger and harsh speech!
(Sumanā—here translated as "Well-Guided Mind. Its flowers are yellowish-white and extremely fragrant. Campaka, also called "Yellow Flower," is small but fragrant. Atimuktaka is a fragrant herb.)
Revering the stūpas and temples, Humble toward all bhikṣus, Far removed from a haughty mind, constantly contemplating wisdom,
Not becoming angry when questioned or challenged, Explaining the teachings in accordance with the truth—
If one can practice such conduct, Their merit will be immeasurable. If one sees such a Dharma-preacher,
Having accomplished such virtues, one should scatter celestial flowers upon him, cover his body with celestial robes, and pay homage by joining the palms and touching the feet.
One should give rise to a mind that regards him as a Buddha, and further reflect:
"Before long he will go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state, bringing vast benefit to all humans and devas."

Wherever they dwell—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—even if it is but a single verse they preach therein, a stūpa should be erected and made magnificent and beautiful, adorned with all manner of offerings.
Sons of the Buddha who dwell in this stage are the very objects of the Buddhas' enjoyment; they are always present within it.

An Exquisite Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Five;
