Chapter Eighteen: The Merit of Rejoicing.

(Regarding "rejoicing": it means to accord with both principle and phenomena, being non-dual and without distinction. "Rejoicing" refers to celebrating for oneself and for others. The merit of hearing this wondrous sutra is so boundless that it cannot be measured; therefore, the merit of rejoicing is praised by extending it through the fiftieth person who hears the teaching).
(The great highway is fundamentally without detours; It is simply that one’s own insight is slow. If today one can truly attain realization, What dharma before one’s eyes would not be suchness?

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain? And he spoke in verse:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, after the Tathāgata has passed away, if one were to compare..."
Whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or other wise persons— whether old or young— who, having heard this sutra and rejoiced in it,
depart from the Dharma assembly and go to another place, whether to a monastery or to a secluded spot.

Whether in cities, streets, villages, or fields, they shall expound [the Dharma] according to their hearing for their parents, kinsmen, good friends, and spiritual teachers to the best of their ability.
When these people have heard it, they shall rejoice and further teach it to others; when those others have heard it, they too shall rejoice and teach it to others.
In this manner, it shall be transmitted in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person, O Ajita. As for that fiftieth...
"O fifty sons of good family and daughters of good family, I shall now speak of the merit of sympathetic joy; you should listen well.
Suppose there were four hundred million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and within them all sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth—whether born from eggs, born from a womb,"
Moisture-born beings, transformation-born beings; those with form or without form; those with perception or without perception; those who are neither with nor without perception;

those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet—whosoever is thus reckoned among the class of sentient beings, if there is someone seeking merit who provides them with whatever articles of enjoyment they desire, giving to each and every being as much as would fill the continent of Jambudvīpa.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various other exquisite treasures;
as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems—this great donor gave such gifts.
After eighty years had passed, he thought to himself: "I have already bestowed upon sentient beings all manner of objects for their enjoyment, according to their every desire."
However, these sentient beings were all already aged; they were over eighty years old, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death would soon come for them.

"I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma," he thought, and immediately gathered these sentient beings together to proclaim the transformative teaching of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
In a single moment, they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the stage of *anāgāmin*, and the stage of *arhat*.

The Way of Han [the Buddha] exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Within profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he attained mastery over all things and was endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

(The six destinies refer to the six paths of existence; the four modes of birth refer to viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformational births. A *srotāpanna* has entered the stream of the noble ones; a *sakṛdāgāmin* returns to the desire realm to undergo rebirth only once; an *anāgāmin* does not return to undergo rebirth.)

"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much or not? Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the merit of this person is exceedingly great—immeasurable and boundless.

If this donor were merely to bestow all instruments of happiness upon sentient beings, his merit would be immeasurable; how much more so when he causes them to attain the fruit of Arhatship? The Buddha told him:

Maitreya, I now speak to you clearly: suppose a person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the sentient beings of the six realms throughout four million *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* worlds, and furthermore cause them to attain the fruit of arhatship;
the merit thereby acquired would not equal even a hundredth part of the merit of rejoicing in a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by the fiftieth person.
A thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part—none of these would equal even one part of it; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Ānanda, such is the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices in it.

It is already immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya); how much more so for those who, at the very beginning within this assembly, hear [this teaching] and rejoice in it with sympathetic joy?
Their merit is even more supreme, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, such that no comparison can be made.

(Regarding the comparison: first, one bestows worldly happiness and extracts the suffering of the fruits [of karma]; later, one bestows nirvāṇa and extracts the suffering of saṃsāra. This is a brief enumeration of Brahma-merit used for the purpose of comparison.)
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastic dwelling and listens to or receives it for even a brief moment,
whether sitting or standing, by virtue of this merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephant and horse carriages,

precious palanquins and litters, and even ride in celestial palaces. Furthermore, if there is a person sitting at a place where the Dharma is being preached, and another person comes and exhorts them...
He causes them to sit and listen, or he shares his seat and invites them to sit.

The merit of such a person is that, upon changing bodies, they will obtain the seat of Śakra, the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King. Ajita, if there should be another person...
He says to others, "There is a sutra named the Lotus Sutra; we should go together to hear it. They then accept his instruction and listen for even a brief moment.
The merit of such a person is that, upon changing bodies, they will be reborn in the same place as bodhisattvas who possess dhāraṇīs.

Possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they shall never be mute or speech-impaired; their breath shall not be foul, and their tongues shall always be free from disease.
Their mouths likewise shall be free from ailment; their teeth shall not be stained or black, nor yellow or sparse, nor shall they be missing, crooked, or uneven.
His lips do not hang down, nor are they drawn back or shriveled; they are neither coarse nor rough, nor are they scarred or cracked;

they are neither missing nor crooked, neither thick nor large, and neither dark nor discolored. They are free from all that is loathsome. His nose is not flat or collapsed, nor is it curved or twisted;
his facial complexion is not black, nor is it narrow or long, nor is it sunken or distorted. There is nothing whatsoever that is unseemly.
He possesses the marks of joy: his lips, tongue, teeth, and gums are all perfectly adorned; his nose is long, high, and straight; his countenance is full and round; his eyebrows are high and long;
and his forehead is broad and level. Endowed with these human characteristics, in every birth he shall behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and faithfully accept their instructions.

These six sense-faculties possess specific merits: sharp faculties and wisdom are the merit of the mind; not being mute or speech-impaired is the merit of the tongue; a well-developed and prominent nose is the merit of the nose; seeing the Buddha is the merit of the eyes; hearing the Dharma is the merit of the ears;
and the remainder are the merits of the body. (Note: *zhěn* refers to sores in the mouth; *kuò* refers to a distorted mouth; *piǎn-xī* refers to thinness; *wā* refers to unevenness.)

Ajita, observe this: if the merit of merely exhorting a single person to go and listen to the Dharma is such as this, how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, recites it, explains it in detail for the sake of the great assembly, and practices according to what has been taught?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If a person at a Dharma assembly hears this sutra, even if they merely rejoice in a single verse and speak it for others,
and thus teach it in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person,
the merit obtained by that final person shall now be analyzed: suppose there were a great donor.
I have provided for immeasurable multitudes for eighty full years;
yet now I see the signs of their old age—their hair has turned white, their faces are wrinkled, their teeth are sparse, and their forms are withered.
Thinking that their death will not be long delayed, I must now instruct them so that they may attain the fruits of the Path.
He then, as an expedient means, preached the true Dharma of Nirvāṇa:
"The world is entirely insubstantial, like foam, bubbles, and flames. You all should quickly give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
When the people heard this Dharma, they all attained arhatship, fully endowed with the six supernormal powers.
Those who possess the three knowledges and the eight liberations—this is the final [case], the fiftieth.
If one hears even a single verse and rejoices with sympathetic joy, the merit of that person surpasses theirs; it cannot be compared by any analogy.

If such is the case for those who hear it through successive transmission, their merit is already immeasurable; how much more so for those who hear it for the first time at the assembly of the Dharma and rejoice with sympathetic joy?
If there is one who exhorts another person, leading them to listen to the Lotus Sutra, saying, "This sutra is profound and wondrous,
difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas," and that person follows the instruction and goes to listen— even if they hear it for only a brief moment—
the karmic reward of such a person shall now be explained in detail: in every successive life, they shall have no afflictions of the mouth.
The teeth are neither sparse, nor yellow, nor black; The lips are neither thick, nor upturned, nor deficient. There are no loathsome features;
the tongue is neither dry, nor black, nor short. The nose is high, long, and straight; The forehead is broad and even.
The countenance is entirely dignified and majestic, Delightful for all people to behold, And the breath is free from foul odors.
The fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issues from his mouth.
If he intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling wishing to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he shall hear it with joy in an instant. Now I shall describe his merit:
in future lives he will be born among gods and humans, obtaining exquisite elephant-drawn chariots, horse-drawn carriages, and precious jeweled litters.

And those who, riding celestial palaces, or at places where the Dharma is preached, encourage others to sit and listen to the sutras—by the causal conditions of this merit, they shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin King.
How much more so for those who listen with a single mind, explain its meaning and intent, and practice according to what is taught; their merit is beyond measure.
Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma Master (*Dharmabhāṇaka-guṇa-parivarta*).

[The merits of the Dharma Master refer to the merits of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) attained above the five stages [of the Five Receptivities], which correspond to the stage of semblance within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).*]

(One’s own mind believes and one’s own self knows; / Why need the Tathāgata exert his power to uplift? / Once he has exerted his power and awakened them, / Where in the great trichiliocosm would there not be radiance?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāparigṛhīta:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—whether by reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing—that person shall obtain eight [qualities]."
The merit of a hundred eyes; the merit of twelve hundred ears; the merit of eight hundred noses; the merit of twelve hundred tongues;
the merit of eight hundred bodies; and the merit of twelve hundred minds. By means of these merits, one adorns the six sense faculties.
All are rendered pure.
(Because form is pure, Prajñā is pure; because Prajñā is pure, the five faculties are pure; because the five faculties are pure, the faculty of mind is pure.
These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, see the three thousand great...

Within a thousandfold world system—encompassing all mountains, forests, rivers, and oceans from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above—he likewise sees all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions, their retributions, and the places where they are born; he sees them all and knows them all.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If, amidst a great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sūtra with a heart free from fear, listen now to its merits:
such a person shall obtain eight hundred eyes of supreme excellence;
because they are adorned by these, their eyes—those born of their parents—are exceedingly pure.
They see the entire trichiliocosm: the inner and outer Mount Merus, Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, as well as all other mountain ranges and forests; the great oceans, rivers, and streams;
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above; and all the sentient beings therein—they see them all.
Although he has not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the power of his physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is such as this.

(The "physical eye" refers to that born of one's parents; it is able to see both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm, which should properly be the divine eye. The Brahma King obtains the divine eye as a karmic retribution; within his own realm, he sees the great trichiliocosm everywhere. However, beyond the great trichiliocosm there is a wind-wheel that acts as an obstruction to his vision, so he cannot see what is outside.

That he can now see the large and small, the interior and exterior, yet is still called the "physical eye," indicates that within the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), through the power of the sūtras, there is the function of superior faculties; though termed the "physical eye," it possesses the functions of all five eyes).
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the ear. With these purified ears, they will hear everything within and without the trichiliocosm,
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above, including all the various seeds therein.

Various kinds of linguistic sounds: the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots; the sounds of weeping and lamentation; the sounds of conch shells, drums, bells, and gongs; the sounds of laughter and speech;
the voices of men and women; the voices of boys and girls; the sound of the Dharma and the sound of what is not the Dharma;
the sounds of suffering and the sounds of joy; the voices of ordinary worldlings and the voices of noble ones; the sound of delight and the sound of lack of delight.
The sounds of devas; the sounds of nāgas; the sounds of yakṣas; the sounds of gandharvas; the sounds of asuras; the sounds of garuḍas;
the sounds of kiṃnaras; the sounds of mahoragas; the sounds of fire; the sounds of water; the sounds of wind; the sounds of hell-beings;
the sounds of animals; the sounds of pretas; the sounds of bhikṣus; the sounds of bhikṣuṇīs; the sounds of śrāvakas; the sounds of pratyekabuddhas; and the sounds of bodhisattvas.

Sounds. As for the voice of the Buddha—to speak briefly—within this trichiliocosm, all sounds, whether internal or external, he hears and knows entirely with his naturally born, pure, and ordinary ears, even though he has not yet attained the divine ear.
Thus he discriminates various sounds without impairing his faculty of hearing. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The ears born of one’s parents are pure and free from defilement; with these constant ears, one hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system:
the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums;
the sounds of lutes, harps, and *konghou* zithers; the sounds of flutes and pipes; and the sounds of pure, beautiful songs.
Listening to them without attachment, they can fully understand and comprehend the voices of countless kinds of people;
they also hear the sounds of the devas and their subtle, wondrous songs, as well as the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls;
they hear the calls of the kalaviṅka birds amidst the mountains, rivers, and steep valleys.
The jīvaṃjīvaka and other various birds all hear their sounds; the cries of manifold agonies and bitter torments from the denizens of hell;
the voices of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, as they seek food and drink;
and when the asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean speak among themselves.
From great sounds, such as those who preach the Dharma, dwelling here they hear these various voices from afar, yet their faculty of hearing remains unimpaired.
The cries and calls of birds and beasts throughout the worlds of the ten directions— the person preaching the Dharma hears them all here.
The sounds of speech from all the Brahma heavens— the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna,
and even up to the Bhavāgra— hear them all while the Dharma Master remains here;
likewise, the entire assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as they recite and chant the sūtras.
If one explains it to others, while the Dharma Master dwells here, they shall hear it all.
Furthermore, there are various bodhisattvas who read and recite the sūtras and the Dharma;
whether they explain them to others or compose and collect commentaries on their meaning—all such sounds shall be heard in their entirety.
The Buddhas, the Great Holy Honored Ones, who transform and guide sentient beings, expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma amidst great assemblies; those who uphold this Lotus Sutra shall hear it all.
Within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, all sounds from within and without, down even to the Avīci Hell, [shall be heard].
Up to the Peak of Existence, all hear their voice; yet their faculty of hearing remains unimpaired.
Because their ears are keen and sharp, they discern and know everything.
Those who uphold this Lotus Sutra, though they have not yet attained the divine ear, do so using only their natural ears; such is the merit already possessed by them.
(The faculty of hearing also possesses the five functions of the ear; therefore, it is able to hear universally the sounds of the ten dharma realms, both within and without the trichiliocosm).
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a good man or a good woman receives and upholds this sutra, whether reading or reciting it,
If one explains this or writes it down, one will achieve eight hundred merits of the nose.
With this purified faculty of the nose, one will perceive all kinds of fragrances throughout the great trichiliocosm—above, below, within, and without—such as the fragrance of the sumanā flower.
The fragrance of *jāti* flowers, the fragrance of *mallikā* flowers, the fragrance of *campaka* flowers, the fragrance of *pāṭala* flowers,

the fragrance of red lotuses, the fragrance of blue lotuses, the fragrance of white lotuses; the fragrance of flowering trees, the fragrance of fruit-bearing trees, the fragrance of *candana*, the fragrance of *agaru*,
the fragrance of *tamarapada*, the fragrance of *tagara*, and ten million kinds of blended incenses— whether in powder or in pills.
If one who upholds this sutra remains here, they will be able to distinguish all types of scented ointments. Furthermore, they will specifically know the scents of sentient beings:
the scent of elephants, the scent of horses, the scent of oxen and sheep, the scent of men, the scent of women, the scent of boys, and the scent of girls;
as well as the scents of grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—whether near or far—they shall perceive all such fragrances in their entirety.
It is not otherwise. Those who uphold this sutra, though dwelling here on earth, shall likewise smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens:
the fragrance of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, as well as the fragrance of māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, sandalwood, and aloeswood.
He perceives all varieties of powdered incense, various blended floral fragrances, and such celestial perfumes produced from the blending of diverse ingredients, none of which he fails to perceive.
Furthermore, he perceives the bodily fragrances of the devas: the fragrance when Śakra-devānām-indra is sporting and enjoying the five desires upon his magnificent palace;
the fragrance when he is in the Sudharmā Hall preaching the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa devas; or...
While playing in the various gardens, they smell the fragrances of themselves and other gods and goddesses from afar.

In this manner, it extends successively even to the Brahma-world; they likewise smell the bodily fragrances of all the gods up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the incense burned by the gods, and the fragrances of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
The fragrance of their bodies is likewise smelled from afar, and they know where it originates. Although they smell this fragrance, their faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded;
if they wish to discern it or explain it to others, their recollection is unerring. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The nose of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul, they perceive all various scents.
They know the scents of sumana, jasmine, tamāla, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon;
they know the scents of various flowers and fruits, as well as the scents of sentient beings.
Whether it be men or women, or the incense of those who preach the Dharma dwelling afar—one knows their location by smelling the fragrance.
The powerful universal monarchs, the minor wheel-turning kings, and their sons, as well as the ministers and palace ladies—one knows their location by smelling the fragrance.
One also perceives the precious jewels worn upon the body and the treasures hidden within the earth.
The precious daughter of the Wheel-Turning King knows her location by smelling her scent;
likewise, the various ornaments and garments that people wear, as well as the diverse perfumes they apply to their bodies—one who upholds this Lotus Sutra knows these things by smelling their scents.
Furthermore, whether the gods are walking or sitting, playing or manifesting supernatural transformations, one who upholds this Lotus Sutra knows them all by smelling their scents.
By smelling their fragrance, one can fully know all the trees, flowers, and fruits;
likewise, those who uphold this sutra, while dwelling here, can know the locations of all things.
Even in deep and perilous mountain places where sandalwood trees are in bloom, they can fully know by scent all sentient beings dwelling therein.
The Iron Ring Mountains and the great ocean, the sentient beings within the earth— all who hold this sutra shall perceive them by their fragrance,
exactly where they are. When the male and female asuras, along with their retinues, are engaged in strife or play,
those who hold this sutra shall be able to know it all by their fragrance, even in remote wildernesses and perilous defiles.
Lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like—by smelling their scent, he knows their locations.
If there are those who are pregnant, even before the sex of the child can be distinguished, he knows them all by scent;
even for those without roots or who are non-human, by the power of smelling their scent, he knows they have recently conceived.
Accomplishing both success and failure, bringing peace and giving birth to virtuous sons; by the power of smelling fragrances, one knows the thoughts of men and women—
their minds of lust, delusion, and anger— and likewise knows those who practice virtue,
as well as the various treasures hidden in the earth, such as gold, silver, and precious gems contained within bronze vessels.
By smelling their fragrance, they can know all kinds of necklaces and ornaments, such that no one else can recognize their value;
by smelling the fragrance, they know their worth, their origin, and where they are located.
They can likewise smell all the celestial flowers, such as the Māndārava and Mañjūṣaka, and the Pārijātaka tree, knowing them all through their fragrance.
The various celestial palaces, distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior, adorned with myriad precious flowers—one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
The celestial gardens, groves, magnificent halls, and sublime Dharma-assembly chambers where they take delight—one can know them all by smelling their fragrance.
If the devas are listening to the Dharma, one can know it all by smelling their fragrance.

Whether enjoying the five desires, or coming and going, walking, sitting, or lying down, he can perceive by scent the garments worn by the celestial maidens and their adornment with exquisite flowers and perfumes;
while they move about and sport, he can perceive them all by scent. Thus progressing upward, even unto the Brahma world.
Whether entering or emerging from meditative absorption, he can know it all by scent;
from the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence, he can know by scent all those who are newly born or passing away.
O bhikṣus, he knows all sentient beings who are ever diligent in the Dharma, whether they are sitting or walking in meditation.
Whether reading and reciting the scriptures, or staying beneath trees in the forest,

those who sit in meditative concentration with single-minded devotion and uphold the sūtras shall have their locations known by the scent. Whether the Bodhisattva’s resolve is firm as they sit in meditation,
recite the scriptures, or preach the Dharma for others, they are able to know [all this] by means of the scent.
Wherever the World-Honored One may be, He is honored and revered by all. Out of compassion for the multitudes, he preaches the Dharma;
By smelling the fragrance, [the Bodhisattva] knows them all. Sentient beings standing before the Buddha, Hearing the sutras, all rejoice;
Practicing according to the Dharma, By smelling the fragrance, [the Bodhisattva] knows them all. Though they have not yet attained the state of a Bodhisattva.
The nose of one who gives rise to untainted dharmas and who upholds this sutra first attains these characteristics of the nose;
furthermore, they shall always be diligent. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds this sutra, whether reading it or reciting it.
If one explains [the Dharma] or writes it down, one will obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue.

Whether things be good or ugly, delicious or not delicious, or even bitter and astringent substances, when they come into contact with the faculty of the tongue, they all transform into a supreme flavor, like the nectar of the gods, such that there is nothing that is not delicious.
If, with this faculty of the tongue, one delivers a discourse within a great assembly, one emits a profound and wondrous voice, capable of...

They enter their hearts and cause them all to be joyful and happy. Furthermore, when the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas hear this profound and wondrous sound as it expounds the Dharma, they all come to listen to the sequence of its discourse.
Likewise, the nāgas and nāga-daughters, yakṣas and yakṣa-daughters, gandharvas and gandharva-daughters, asuras and asura-... [daughters] all come to listen.
Daughters, garuḍas and garuḍa daughters, kiṃnaras and kiṃnara daughters, mahoragas and mahoraga daughters—
all came to attend upon him for the sake of hearing the Dharma, approaching him with reverence and making offerings. This included bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
upāsakas and upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers and their retinues, and minor universal monarchs (cakravartins).
The great universal monarch, with his seven treasures and a thousand sons, along with his inner and outer retinues, shall all board their palaces and come together to hear the Dharma.
Because this bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, the brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom will attend upon and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas will always delight in seeing him.
In whichever direction this person may be, all Buddhas shall turn toward that place to preach the Dharma;
they will be able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, and furthermore, they will be able to produce profound and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.
(The nose and tongue faculties both fully possess the five functions of the nose and tongue).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The tongue-faculty of this person is pure, And he shall never experience foul flavors; Whatever he may eat or drink..."
All have become nectar through his profound, pure, and wondrous voice as he preaches the Dharma to the great assembly.
Using various causes, conditions, and parables, he guides the minds of sentient beings; all who hear him rejoice.
They present various supreme offerings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras alike.
All have come together with a mind of reverence to listen to the Dharma.
If this teacher of the Dharma wishes to fill the three thousandfold world-system with his wondrous voice, he can, according to his will,
reach as far as the great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their thousand sons and retinues, who join their palms with a mind of reverence.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas shall always come to listen to and receive the Dharma;
with hearts full of joy, they shall always delight in coming to offer worship.
Brahmā, Māra, Īśvara, Maheśvara, and all such hosts of devas shall always come to where he dwells.
When the Buddhas and their disciples hear the sound of their preaching the Dharma, they constantly keep them in mind and protect them, and at times manifest themselves before them.

(The Sovereign Lord refers to Paranirmita-vaśavartin, who dwells at the summit of the Desire Realm and is also the Māra King; the Great Sovereign Lord refers to Maheśvara, the deity at the summit of the Form Realm.)
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains,
or transcribes this sutra, they will obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli.
Because the body of the sentient being Joy-to-See is pure, all sentient beings of the trichiliocosm—
at the time of birth and death, whether high or low, beautiful or ugly, born in good or evil realms— all appear within it; as do the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains,
Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other mountains, as well as the sentient beings dwelling therein, all appearing within it.
He manifests [himself] everywhere, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above; all things and all sentient beings appear within him.
Furthermore, the preaching of the Dharma by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas—all their physical forms and appearances are manifested within his body.

(The body-faculty [possesses] the five functions of the body. At one time they manifest simultaneously; at one time they function interchangeably; at one time they are without error; at one time they are without attachment.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, Their body shall be exceedingly pure, Like that clear lapis lazuli, which all beings joyfully behold;
Furthermore, like a clean and bright mirror, In which all forms and images are clearly seen."
Within their purified bodies, Bodhisattvas perceive everything that exists in the world; they alone clearly understand it, while others do not see it.
Within the trichiliocosm—all the various classes of beings, including devas, humans, asuras, those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—such are the forms and images they behold.
Within his very body appear the palaces of all the devas, and so forth, up to the Peak of Existence;
the Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Meru, and Mahāmeru, as well as the waters of all the great oceans—all appear within his body.
Therein also appear all the Buddhas, the śrāvakas, and the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas.
Whether alone or in the midst of a multitude, the teaching of the Dharma is manifested in all its forms.
Although they have not yet attained the wondrous body of the dharma-nature that is free from outflows, through their pure and eternal essence, everything is manifested therein.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, receive and uphold this sutra.
Whether reading, reciting, explaining, or transcribing it, one attains twelve hundred mental merits.
By means of this purified faculty of mind, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings.
Having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for as long as one month, four months, or even a year. All...
The teachings he expounds accord with their underlying meaning and do not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Whether he speaks of secular scriptures, worldly discourse, or the means of livelihood, all are in accordance with the True Dharma.
He fully knows the mental activities, the movements of the mind, and the conceptual proliferations of the minds of sentient beings throughout the six realms within this trichiliocosm; although...
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), their faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is thus purified.
Whatever this person contemplates, deliberates, or speaks is entirely the Buddha-dharma; it is all true and nothing but what was taught in the sūtras of the Buddhas of the past.
(The faculty of mind also possesses the five functions of the mind. The twelve months are the twelve links of dependent origination; the one month is the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
This person’s mind is pure, clear, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement. With this sublime faculty of intention, they discern phenomena as superior, middling, or inferior.
Even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and explain them in sequence according to the Dharma.
Whether for a month, four months, or a year, throughout the interior and exterior of this world-system, [they teach].
All sentient beings— whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, and those within the six realms of existence—
the various kinds of thoughts they harbor, [the Bodhisattva] knows them all at once as the fruit of upholding the Lotus Sutra.
The countless Buddhas of the ten directions, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, [are likewise known].
They preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and all who hear it are able to receive and uphold it.
They contemplate immeasurable meanings and their preaching of the Dharma is likewise immeasurable; from beginning to end, they never forget or err.
Because they uphold the Lotus Sutra, they fully know the characteristics of all dharmas; they recognize the sequence according to their meaning and master names and language.
Whatever this person speaks in accordance with what they know, all that is the teaching of the former Buddhas;

because they expound this Dharma, they possess no fear therein. One who upholds the Lotus Sutra has such purity of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that, although they have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), they already manifest such signs.
This person who upholds this sutra dwells securely in a rare and marvelous state;

they are a source of joy for all sentient beings and are loved and respected by them. Because they uphold the Lotus Sutra, they are able to analyze and expound the Dharma through thousands of myriads of skillful modes of speech.

(Meru means "light. It is one of the seven golden mountains. Kalaviṅka is a bird with a beautiful voice. Jīvajīvaka is the long-lived or double-named bird. Jāti is the "gold coin" flower. Mallikā is the jasmine. Punnāga is the "excellent fruit" tree.

Pāṭala is the trumpet-flower. Dhūpāgandha is the incense flower. Tamālapatra is the "noble and stainless" tree. Tagara is the wood-fragrance. Kovidāra is the tree of the great sporting ground. Pārijātaka is the tree in front of Śakra’s palace.)
Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging (Within his heart he harbors the understanding of "never disparaging";

outwardly he honors the objects of "never disparaging"; in person he establishes the practice of "never disparaging"; in speech he proclaims the teaching of "never disparaging"; and people give him the title of "Never Disparaging").

"By pure maintenance and sudden awakening, the six sense faculties are permeated; Through the merit of wondrous deeds, all capacities are universally benefited. The Buddha-nature pervasively supports those within the realm of ignorance; The conditions for enlightenment are widely recorded within the mind.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "You should now know this:
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold the Lotus Sūtra, and if someone should speak to them with harsh words, revile, or slander them..."
To slander [this] results in a retribution of great sin, as previously described. The merit one thereby attains is as described above:
the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind become pure, and one attains great power.

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Voice (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Vidyācaraṇasampanna.
One who is perfected in conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed being, a charioteer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One.
The eon was named Free from Decay, and the land was named Great Achievement. In that world, the Buddha King of Majestic Sound preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras;
for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, delivering them from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

For those seeking ultimate nirvana, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination. For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, based on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās*.

Having reached the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha and attained great power, this was the Buddha King of Awesome Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), whose lifespan lasted for four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of Ganges sands.
For as many kalpas as there are atoms in one Jambudvīpa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world;

for as many kalpas as there are atoms in the four continents, the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world. After that Buddha has extensively benefited sentient beings, he will then enter parinirvāṇa.
Following the complete extinction of both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, another Buddha will appear in this land, also named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśravaṇarāja). Just as...

Come! One Worthy of Offerings, One Perfectly and Fully Enlightened, One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, One Gone to Bliss, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—there were twenty trillion Buddhas in succession, all bearing this same title.

After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had first entered parinirvāṇa, and following the extinction of the True Dharma during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were bhikṣus of overweening pride who possessed great power. At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Constantly Not Disparaging.
He attained great power. For what reason was this bhikṣu named "Never-Disparaging"?
Whenever he saw anyone—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—he would prostrate to them all, praise them, and speak these words:
I deeply respect you all and do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this? Because you are all practicing the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Yet this bhikṣu does not devote himself exclusively to reading and reciting the sūtras, but merely practices prostrations.
Even when he sees the fourfold assembly from afar, he still intentionally goes to them to prostrate, praise, and say these words: "I do not dare to treat you with contempt."

"Regarding you all: you shall all become Buddhas. Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to a mind of anger and impurity, speaking with harsh words and insults, saying: "This is an ignorant bhikṣu! From where has he come?
He says of himself, 'I do not slight you,' yet he bestows upon us the prediction that we shall attain Buddhahood. We have no need for such false predictions!"
[Commentary: Thus he passed many years, constantly subjected to insults and abuse, yet he never gave rise to anger.
He always spoke these words: "You shall all become Buddhas. When he said these words, the people sometimes struck him with sticks, water, tiles, or stones;
though he retreated and stayed at a distance, he still cried out in a loud voice: "I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas."
Because the Buddha constantly spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of overweening pride called him "Never-Disparaging.

When that bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the void all twenty thousand koṭis of verses of the Lotus Sūtra previously taught by the Buddha King of Majestic Voice, and he was able to receive them all.
Upon upholding it, he immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye; likewise, he attained the purity of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having attained this purity of the six faculties, his lifespan was further increased by two hundred trillion nayutas of years.
He extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for others. At that time, there were members of the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and [laywomen]—who possessed overweening pride.

Vaiśī, as for that person whom you held in contempt and gave the name "Not-Disregarded" (Adhimātra), you saw that he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great, sublime tranquility. Upon hearing what he taught, all believed, submitted, and followed him.
That Bodhisattva further transformed thousands of millions of billions of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. After his life came to an end...
He encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp). Within their teachings, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
By these causes and conditions, he further encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Meghasvaradīparāja (Cloud-Sovereign-Lamp-King).
Because he received, upheld, read, recited, and explained this sūtra for the fourfold assembly within the teachings of these various Buddhas, he attained this permanence.
His eyes were pure; his faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind were all pure.
He preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a heart free from fear, having attained great power. This was the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Not Disparaging.
He made offerings to as many Buddhas as these, honoring, respecting, and praising them, thereby planting various roots of goodness. Thereafter, he again encountered ten million billion Buddhas.
Furthermore, within the teachings of all Buddhas, he preached this sutra; through the accomplishment of its merit, he shall attain Buddhahood.

(This bhikṣu, this bodhisattva—all refer to Not-Disparaging—proclaimed and practiced the wondrous conduct of this sublime sutra. His mind was equal to the realm of empty space; he manifested dharmas equal to empty space; when he realized the time of empty space, there was neither "is" nor "non-is").
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? Was the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging at that time someone other than myself? It was indeed I.

Had I not in past lives upheld, recited, and explained this sutra to others, I would not have been able to so swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It was because I upheld and recited it under previous Buddhas..."
Because they have recited this sutra and explained it for others, they shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and obtain great power.

At that time, because the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—treated me with contempt out of a mind of anger, they shall for two hundred billion kalpas never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṅgha; and for a thousand kalpas...

They underwent great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell. Once these karmic retributions were exhausted, they again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who taught them the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and they attained Great Power (*mahāsthāmaprāpta*). What do you think?
Were those four assemblies who formerly habitually disparaged this bodhisattva anyone else? They are none other than the Bhadrapāla and others present in this assembly now.
These were the five hundred bodhisattvas headed by Rāṣṭrapāla, the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs headed by Siṃhacandrā,
and the five hundred upāsakas headed by Cinti, all of whom were non-retrogressive in their progress toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

(Bhadrapāla is translated as "Good Protector. If sentient beings hear his name, they will ultimately attain *samyaksambodhi*; therefore, he is called "Good Protector. Alternatively, he is called "Worthy Head" [Bhadramukha], as he dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment.)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
In the past there was a Buddha Named King of Majestic Sound. His divine wisdom was immeasurable;
He led all beings— Gods, humans, dragons, and spirits— Who all made offerings to him together.
After the extinction of this Buddha, when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was attached to the Dharma—those who are attached to the Dharma [are so called because] this Dharma cannot be demonstrated;

if one definitively asserts it to be existent, one is then said to be attached to the Dharma; even if one definitively asserts it to be neither existent nor non-existent, one is likewise said to be attached to the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging went to where they were and spoke to them, saying:
"I do not disparage you; all of you who practice the Way shall become Buddhas.
When those people heard this, they treated him with contempt, reviled, and abused the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging.
If one can endure [this], their transgressions will be exhausted;
at the time of death, they shall hear this sutra, and their six sense faculties will become pure.
By the power of their supernormal faculties, their lifespan will be increased, and they will further expound this sutra extensively for all people.
The multitude of those attached to dharmas were all brought to maturity through the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation,
and were established in the Buddha-way. Because Not-Disparaging (Adhimātra) met countless Buddhas at the end of his life and preached this sutra,
he attained immeasurable merit and gradually perfected his virtues.
He quickly attained the Buddha-way; at that time, "Not-Disparaging" was none other than my own self.
At that time, the fourfold assembly who were attached to the Dharma heard the words of Not-Disparaging:
"You shall become Buddhas. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they encountered countless Buddhas.
The assembly of five hundred bodhisattvas in this gathering,
as well as the fourfold assembly of faithful laymen and laywomen who are now listening to the Dharma before me—
these were all people whom I exhorted in previous lives to hear and receive this sutra.
The foremost Dharma, revealed and taught to others, Causing them to abide in *nirvāṇa* and to uphold it through successive lifetimes— Such a sutra as this, after billions upon billions of eons,
even beyond the inconceivable, Is heard only at such a time: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Throughout billions upon billions of kalpas, until they reach the inconceivable, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have at times preached this sutra.
Therefore, practitioners who hear such a sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa should not give rise to doubt or confusion; they should maintain a single-minded focus.
By extensively expounding this sutra, one shall encounter Buddhas in every lifetime and swiftly attain the Buddha-way.

(The preceding section clarified that the merit of a single instance of sympathetic joy surpasses that of the two vehicles; yet, regarding the purification of the six sense faculties through reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding [the sutra], it remains uncertain who has ever attained such a state. Therefore, the example of Sadāparibhūta is cited as proof: "I deeply revere you all.")
"Do not dare to treat [this] with contempt. You all practice the Bodhisattva path; you shall surely attain Buddhahood. Chapter Twenty-one:
The Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers (*Rulai Shenli Pin*). Regarding "supernatural powers" (*shenli*):

"Supernatural" (*shen*) refers to a spiritual intelligence that is unfathomable; "power" (*li*) refers to efficacious function (*gan-yong*). Because it is unfathomable, the essence of its natural spontaneity is profound; because it is efficacious function, the power of its transformations is great. Within this chapter, in order to entrust the profound Dharma, ten kinds of great functions are manifested.

[Chapter on Supernatural Power] (Carrying water and hauling firewood is a wondrous spiritual power; those who do not awaken within themselves are pitiable people. Once they suddenly awaken from this day forward, clods of earth and lumps of mud are the Dharmakāya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms of a thousand worlds, who had emerged from the earth, all [became...]
Before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion, they joined their palms, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in whatever lands and places where the World-Honored One’s emanations have entered parinirvāṇa, we shall extensively proclaim this sutra.
Why is this? It is because we ourselves also desire to obtain this truly pure Great Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and disseminate it."
One should transcribe it and make offerings to it.

(This is not merely to fulfill the command of benefiting others, but also because one personally aspires to attain this truly pure Great Dharma. "Distributing the body" refers to the various scriptural teachings, which are the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s spoken word.)

At that time, the World-Honored One [addressed] Mañjuśrī and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had long resided in the Sahā world, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Before all the assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.

(Regarding Mañjuśrī and others: these are the assemblies converted within the traces [of his past lives]. As for those who have long resided [there]: these are the assemblies originally converted throughout the ten directions).
He manifested great supernormal powers and extended his broad and long tongue upward as far as the Brahma-world.

(This is the first supernatural power. Regarding the manifestation of the tongue: the teaching expounded in this sutra opens the three to reveal the one, and opens the near to reveal the far. The Brahma-world is precisely the Peak of Existence, which is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—what is called vertically exhausting the three periods of time.)
From every pore, they emitted immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors, which completely illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees likewise extended their broad and long tongues and emitted immeasurable light.
When Śākyamuni Buddha and the Buddhas beneath the jewel trees manifested these supernatural powers, [the light] filled hundreds of thousands [of worlds].
The Year.

(This is the second supernatural power. Light is emitted from his entire body, pervading the ten directions so that there is nowhere it does not illuminate. This symbolizes the identity of the principle of the two gates.)
Thereupon, he withdrew his tongue-phenomenon and coughed once (this is the third supernatural power; "coughing" refers to the manner of being about to speak).
Together they snapped their fingers.
(This is the fourth supernatural power. As for snapping the fingers: it signifies rejoicing in the seven stages of expedient means and entering together into the perfect path.
These two sounds reached all the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and the earth shook in six ways.
(This is the fifth supernatural power. As for the two sounds, they are the clearing of the throat and the snapping of fingers.
Among them were sentient beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras.

The mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, all beheld this Sahā world with its immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas beneath trees of various jewels and upon lion thrones;
they also saw Śākyamuni Buddha together with the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, seated upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa. Furthermore, they saw...
Immeasurable and boundless—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly, reverently surrounded Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having seen this, they were all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
(This is the sixth supernatural power. That he universally beholds the great assembly signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is the same.
At that moment, the various devas, from within the void of space, cried out in a loud voice:
"Beyond these immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a land named Sahā. Therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni."

“Nī, I shall now, for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, preach the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
You all should rejoice with profound hearts; you should also pay homage to and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.”
(This is the seventh supernatural power.

(This demonstrates that the Buddha possesses such wondrous applications of supernormal powers. Yet, viewed with the eyes of the world, such things as the Yellow Emperor riding a dragon, Luan Ba spitting wine, Pang Ba entering a stone, and Zhang Fang shrinking the earth are all rare and difficult feats.)

When viewed with the eye of the Way, Vimalakīrti’s single chamber can accommodate hundreds of thousands of seats; Śākyamuni Buddha, in a single moment, traverses hundreds of thousands of long years; with a single tongue, he reaches the heights of ten million miles in the First Dhyāna;
and with a single sound, he pervades the vastness of ten million worlds throughout the ten directions—all of which are but minor matters for the Great Sage.
Having heard the voice from the midst of space, those sentient beings joined their palms toward the Sahā world and spoke these words:
"Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha! Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha!"
(This is the eighth supernatural power.

With various flowers, incenses, necklaces, banners, canopies, and all manner of ornaments for the body, as well as rare jewels and exquisite objects, they all together scattered them from afar toward the Sahā world.
The various Buddhas who were thus honored had come from the ten directions, gathering like clouds. They transformed—
It formed a jeweled canopy that completely covered all the Buddhas within this realm (this is the ninth supernatural power). At that time,
the worlds of the ten directions were pervaded without obstruction, as if they were a single Buddha-field.
(This is the tenth supernatural power.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Upward-Going and the others: "The supernatural powers of all Buddhas are thus immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
If, by means of such supernatural power, I were to [act] throughout immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions..."
Even if one were to spend incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to proclaim the merits of this sutra for the sake of entrustment, they could not be fully exhausted.

To state the essentials: all the teachings of the Tathāgata, all the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgata, all the secret and essential treasuries of the Tathāgata, and all the most profound matters of the Tathāgata are all proclaimed and revealed within this sutra.
[It is] said:

"All dharmas" means that all are Buddha-dharmas; this concludes the sublime names. "The power of penetrating all things without obstruction and possessing the eight masteries" concludes the sublime functions. "The secret treasury of all things" pervades all places.
All these are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This concludes the subtle essence. As for the "profound matter," cause and effect constitute this profound matter. This concludes the subtle thesis.
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you should all receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe them in their entirety.
As it has been taught, wherever in any land one may uphold, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the teaching—
whether at the place where the sutra scrolls reside, or in a garden, or in a grove, or beneath a tree, or in a monastery,
or in a layperson’s house, or in a hall, or in a mountain valley or wilderness— in that very place...
One should erect stupas to make offerings to all of them. Why is this? You should know that such places are indeed bodhimaṇḍas;
it is here that all Buddhas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and it is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma.
It was here that all Buddhas entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, saviors of the world, Abiding in great supernormal powers, For the sake of gladdening sentient beings..."
Manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers, with tongues reaching as far as the Brahma-heaven, and bodies emitting countless rays of light—
for those seeking the Buddha-way, he manifests these rare wonders.
The sound of the Buddhas’ coughing and the snap of their fingers is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions, and the earth trembles in six ways.
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
all Buddhas rejoice and manifest immeasurable supernatural powers (the verse mentions ten powers; here only five appear, as the latter five are missing).
Because of entrusting this sutra and praising those who receive and uphold it,
even throughout immeasurable kalpas one could not exhaust the merit of such a person; it is immeasurable and without end,
like the empty space of the ten directions, its limit cannot be found.
(These four dharmas are summarized in a single verse. It simply says "entrustment. To receive and uphold [this teaching] is to uphold the Buddha’s own body.
Whoever is able to uphold this sutra Has already seen me, And has also seen the Buddha Prabhūtaratna As well as all his emanations;
Furthermore, they see me today Teaching and transforming the bodhisattvas.
Those who can uphold this sutra shall cause me and my emanations,

as well as the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who has entered parinirvāṇa, and all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, to be filled with joy. (To uphold the Dharma is to uphold the body of the Buddha.)
Furthermore, those who have passed away and those yet to come— I see them all and also make offerings to them;

May I cause all Buddhas seated at the site of enlightenment to rejoice. The secret and essential Dharma they have attained, one who can uphold this sutra shall also obtain it before long. One who can uphold this sutra, regarding the meaning of all dharmas...
With names and phrases, their eloquence is inexhaustible; Like the wind in the sky, they are entirely without obstruction.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, They will know the causes, conditions, and sequence of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha;
Explaining them according to their meaning as it truly is, Like the radiance of the sun and moon.
Able to dispel all darkness, such a person walks through the world; Able to extinguish the gloom of sentient beings, they teach immeasurable bodhisattvas To ultimately abide in the One Vehicle.
(Preaching the Dharma to shatter darkness and enter the One Vehicle—this is the profound matter of the Buddha.)
Therefore, those who possess wisdom, having heard these benefits and merits, should uphold this sutra after my parinirvāṇa;
such persons will have no doubt whatsoever regarding the Buddha-way.
(This summarizes the four dharmas, stating that if one can uphold them, one upholds the four dharmas.)
Chapter Twenty-Two: Entrustment (The term "entrust" [嘱] refers to what the Buddha has committed to others;
"to burden" [累] means to trouble you with the propagation [of this teaching]. It intends that you shall transmit and recite the wondrous Dharma, so that its benefit may reach infinity.)

"The Way flourishes when propagated by people; its subsequent flow Transmits the life of wisdom, benefiting all without ceasing. The Dharma of Bodhi accumulated through many lifetimes Is once received in person and cultivated through direct realization.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha rose from his Dharma-seat and manifested great supernormal powers.

With his right hand, he stroked the crowns of the heads of immeasurable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and spoke these words: "I, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas..."
"Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you have cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to attain.
I now entrust it to you. You should, with a single mind, propagate this Dharma and cause it to increase and flourish extensively.
Having thus placed his hand upon the heads of all these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he spoke these words: "For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads..."
Having cultivated this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to attain, over billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I now entrust it to you all.
You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and widely proclaim this Dharma, so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know it.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion and is free from all stinginess.
Furthermore, they possess no fear. They are able to bestow upon sentient beings the wisdom of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and self-arisen wisdom.
The Tathāgata is the great donor to all sentient beings; you also should follow and learn the Dharma of the Tathāgata, and do not give rise to stinginess.

(Regarding "Samama": This is a repeated entrustment, manifesting that this Dharma is exhaustive and leaves nothing remaining. For those of great capacity, it speaks directly of the Six Perfections: through stinginess and greed, it speaks of giving; through the violation of precepts, it speaks of ethical discipline;

through anger, it speaks of patience; through indolence, it speaks of diligence; through distraction, it speaks of meditative concentration; and through ignorance, it speaks of wisdom. This is called "arising from conditions. If stinginess and greed and the like are once destroyed, then indolence, distraction, and the rest are all extinguished simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said: "each according to where it finds its ease.")

In future ages, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom, you should expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them so that they may hear and know it, in order to enable those people to attain the Buddha-wisdom.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe or accept it, you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them within other profound teachings of the Tathāgata. You all...
If one can act in this way, then one has already repaid the kindness of all Buddhas. (If the roots are deep and the wisdom sharp, one explains the Buddha’s wisdom directly.

If the recipient is not yet capable, one instructs, benefits, and gladdens them through other profound teachings. The Buddha’s wisdom is profound but not otherwise; the six provisional means are "otherwise" but not profound;

the sequential teaching of the Separate Vehicle is both "otherwise" and profound. If you can assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s wisdom through these other profound teachings, that is skillful repayment of the Buddha’s kindness. This is called the admonition and entrustment.)
At that time, when the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas heard the Buddha speak these words, they were all filled with great joy that pervaded their entire bodies.
Increasing their reverence, they bowed their heads with bodies bent forward and joined their palms toward the Buddha.

Together they raised their voices and said, "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall fully carry it out. So be it, World-Honored One; may you have no further concern. Thus spoke the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Thus they repeated this three times, all speaking with one voice: "As the World-Honored One has commanded, we shall carry it out in full. So be it, World-Honored One;
may you have no further concern."

(The Buddha spoke of entrusting the three karmas; the Bodhisattvas also received them through the three karmas with joy. To receive them with the mind, they bowed their bodies and lowered their heads; to receive them with the body, they did as they were instructed; to receive them with the mouth, they all uttered these words together).
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha commanded all the emanated Buddhas who had come from the ten directions to each return to their own lands, saying:
"May the various Buddhas each abide as they please; the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna may return to its former state.
When these words were spoken, the immeasurable emanated Buddhas from the ten directions who were seated upon lion thrones beneath the jeweled trees, as well as [the Buddha Prabhūtaratna]...
The Buddha Ratna and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas such as Uttaramantriṇ, along with the boundless asaṃkhyeya assembly of bodhisattvas,
Śāriputra and the other fourfold assembly of śrāvakas, and all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
were all greatly rejoiced.
(The Buddhas rejoice because they have accomplished the task of transforming others; the Bodhisattvas rejoice because they have attained the Dharma for their own practice).

Bodhisattva Rājanirghoṣa, in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,

Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. That Buddha remained for eighty-two thousand koṭis of kalpas.
The lifespan of the Bodhisattvas is also equal [to that of the Buddha]. That land has no women, nor are there hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, or any of the eight difficulties.

At that time, that Buddha [was teaching] for the sake of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and...

After twelve thousand years had passed, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. Having attained this samādhi, he...

Immediately he entered this samādhi. In the midst of the void, there rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, along with finely ground, solid black sandalwood, filling the void and descending like clouds. Furthermore, there rained down the fragrance of *sāgara-cīrṇa* sandalwood;
six *zhu* of this incense was worth as much as the entire Sahā world, which he offered to the Buddha. Having done this, he—

In the sand-grain worlds, the Buddhas therein simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is true diligence;

this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. It cannot be equaled by offerings made to the Buddha. Even if one were to give away kingdoms, cities, wives, and children as alms, it still would not equal it.
"Good son, this is called the foremost gift; among all gifts, it is the most honored and supreme, because it is the offering of the Dharma to all Tathāgatas.
Having spoken these words, they each remained silent, and their bodies burned with fire for twelve hundred years.
After this period had passed and his physical body was exhausted, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having performed such a Dharma-offering,
at the end of his life was reborn in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. Within the house of King Vimalaśrī,
he suddenly manifested by transformation, sitting cross-legged, and immediately spoke these verses to his father:

(Internally employing the contemplation of wisdom, one contemplates the causes and effects of afflictions; because all are washed away by the contemplation of emptiness, it is called the True Dharma).
Great King, you should now know: "I am now traveling to that place; immediately I attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Bodies.

Having spoken these verses, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness Virtue still currently exists.

"Great King, I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha. Having said this, he immediately sat upon a terrace of the seven precious gems and ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having spoken these verses, addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, ...”
“World-Honored One, you still remain in the world. At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana:
“Good son, the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; the moment of my final extinction has come.
