"Son of good family, I entrust to you the Buddha-dharma, as well as the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and the dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

I also entrust to you the great trichiliocosm world made of the seven treasures, its jeweled trees and jeweled terraces, along with all the attendant devas. After my parinirvāṇa, all my relics shall likewise be entrusted to you."
"I also entrust this to you; you must cause it to circulate and establish extensive offerings. You should erect several thousand stupas.
After the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had thus instructed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, he entered parinirvāṇa during the final watch of the night.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha’s passing, was moved by profound grief.
Filled with grief and longing for the Buddha, he immediately used sandalwood from this side of the ocean to construct a pyre and offered it as an oblation to the Buddha’s body, cremating him.
After the fire was extinguished, he collected the relics and fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars, constructing eighty-four thousand stupas.
These were three worlds high, adorned with ornate spires and banners, draped with various canopies, and hung with many jewels.
[The sound of] the bell. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana thought to himself again:
"Although I have made these offerings, my mind is still not satisfied. I shall now further offer to the śarīra.
He then addressed the assembly of all bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others: "You all should maintain single-minded mindfulness as I now make this offering."

He venerated the relics of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. Having spoken these words, he immediately before the eighty-four thousand stupas set ablaze his arms—adorned with a hundred merits—for seventy-two thousand years as an act of offering.
By doing so, he caused countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya persons to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They all caused him to dwell in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and others, seeing that he was without arms, were filled with grief and sorrow, and spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher and the one who has instructed us; yet now his arms have been burned, and his body is incomplete."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made this vow amidst the great assembly: "I shall sacrifice both my arms;
I must surely attain the golden-hued body of a Buddha. If this is true and not false, may my two arms be restored as they were before.
Having made this vow, his arms were naturally restored, due to the profound depth of this bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down precious flowers;
all humans and devas attained what they had never experienced before.

[Regarding] the one with a golden-colored body: he had previously attained the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms—that is, the golden-colored body [attained through] the eightfold manifestation of the path to enlightenment.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña: "What do you think? As for the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana..."
Could this have been anyone else? It was none other than the present Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The number of times he sacrificed his body as an act of giving was thus immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there are those who resolve their minds to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should be able to burn a finger, or even a single toe, as an offering to the Buddha.
A stūpa is superior to one who makes offerings of their kingdom, city, wife, children, as well as the great trichiliocosm with its mountains, forests, rivers, ponds,
and various precious treasures.
(One’s own body is the "inner self"; wife and children are the "outer self"; the kingdom, cities, and so forth are "outer wealth.

Furthermore, if there were someone who filled the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and offered them as alms to the Buddhas, the great Bodhisattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of one who upholds this Dharma.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is stated that even a single four-line verse yields the greatest merit.

(When King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his body and offered his arm as an offering to this sūtra, he burned his body to empty the notion of self and offered his arm to forget the grasping at self. Burning the body and offering the arm is like clouds dispersing and clouds gathering—the sky is fundamentally pure;
whether in this realm or other worlds, if flowers bloom and fall, what mind does the tree possess?)
Sudhana, it is like this: among all the streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is the foremost.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise; among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast.
Furthermore, it is like the earth mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and the Ten Jewel Mountains—among all such mountains...
Among mountains, Mount Sumeru is the foremost; this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise so, being the most supreme among all sūtras.

Furthermore, just as among the many stars the Moon Deity is the foremost, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise so, being the most illuminating among the hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of sūtra teachings. Furthermore, it is like the sun...
"O Son of Heaven, just as one is able to dispel all darkness, so too is this sutra; it can shatter the darkness of all that is unwholesome.
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost, so too is this sutra."
Among all the sūtras, this is the most honored. Just as Śakra is the king among the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, so too is this sūtra the king among all sūtras.

Furthermore, just as the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings, so too is this sūtra the father of all noble ones—those in training and those beyond training—as well as those who have resolved to attain the bodhicitta.

Just as among all ordinary persons, the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha* are the foremost, so too is this sutra; it is that which has been spoken by all Tathāgatas.
Whether spoken by a bodhisattva or spoken by a śrāvaka, among all the sūtras and dharmas, this is the foremost.
Any who are able to receive and uphold this sūtra shall likewise be the foremost among all sentient beings.
Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost; this sutra is likewise so, being the most supreme among all sūtras and dharmas.
Just as the Buddha is the king of all dharmas, this sutra is likewise the king among all sūtras.
O宿王華 (Dṛḍhadhvajaprabhāsa), this sutra is able to save all sentient beings. This sutra...
It can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction.
This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations, like a cool pond that satisfies all who are parched with thirst;
like one who is cold finding fire; like a naked person finding clothing; like a merchant finding his master; like a child finding its mother; like a traveler finding a boat. Like...
It is like a sick person finding a physician; like one in darkness finding a lamp; like a poor person finding treasure; like a subject finding a king; like a merchant finding the sea;
like a torch dispelling the darkness.

(Because the Dharma is sublime, it is the foremost; those who propagate the sublime Dharma are likewise foremost. The twelve matters, including the cool pond and so forth, all praise the function of the sutra in bringing about happiness.)
This Lotus Sūtra is also like this. It can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all illness;

it can untie all the bonds of birth and death. If a person hears this Lotus Sūtra, whether copying it themselves or causing others to copy it, the amount of merit they obtain—if measured by the wisdom of a Buddha—its limits cannot be reached. If...
One should make offerings with these volumes of sutras, flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, and unguents; with banners, canopies, and robes;

and with various kinds of lamps: lamps of ghee, oil lamps, lamps of various fragrant oils, lamps of *campaka* oil, lamps of *sumanā* oil, lamps of *pāṭala* oil, lamps of *bhalliśaka* oil, and lamps of *nāgamallī* oil. Such is the merit of this offering.
Virtue is also like this.

(The flower that blooms in summer is called *puspaka* [the sound "pu" is pronounced as "feng"]; it is also called *varṣapuṣpa*. There is the *nāgapuṣpa* flower; *mālya* refers to garland flowers; *kunduruka* is resinous incense; *tūlaparvaka* is grass incense; and *pippalī* is clove.)
Rājapadmavṛṣabha, if there are those who hear this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.

to the place where Amitābha Buddha dwells surrounded by a multitude of great bodhisattvas, and sit upon a precious throne within a lotus flower.

Having attained this patience, their faculty of the eye becomes pure. With this purified faculty of the eye, they see seven million two thousand *koṭis* of...

"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, to receive, uphold, read, recite, and contemplate this sutra, and to explain it for others—such merit as you obtain is immeasurable and boundless; fire cannot burn it, nor can water [wash it away]."

You have now been able to defeat the mara-enemies, destroy the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other adversaries.
Son of good family, hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, protect you together. Among all the devas and humans in every world, there is none—

If anyone hears this 'Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja' and is able to rejoice in it and praise it..."

As for the virtuous person: in this present life, their mouth constantly emits the fragrance of blue lotuses, and the pores of their body constantly emit the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood. The merits they obtain are as described above.

King Aśoka invited the Saṃgha into the palace to provide offerings. There was a bhikṣu named Utpala whose mouth emitted the fragrance of an utpala lotus flower. Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, I entrust this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" to you.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must widely proclaim and disseminate it throughout Jambudvīpa so that it does not come to an end.
Let not evil Māras, the followers of Māra, or the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others find an opportunity to cause harm. Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, you—
You should, by the power of your supernormal faculties, protect this sutra. Why is this? This sutra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa.

Suvarṇaprabhāsa, if you see anyone who receives and upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses and fill [a vessel] with them...

People should give rise to such a mind of reverence. While this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being preached, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings.
From within the jeweled stupa, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised the Bodhisattva Rājādhiṣṭhānavaśavartin, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Rājādhiṣṭhānavaśavartin, you have accomplished..."
Regarding these inconceivable merits, you are able to inquire of Śākyamuni Buddha about such matters,

Chapter Twenty-Four: The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
(This chapter clarifies that the Bodhisattva, through his wondrous voice, proclaims this sutra by adapting to the various types of beings.)

(Fundamentally there is neither birth-and-death nor rising and sinking; vast, profound, empty, and wondrously deep. From this day forth, I shall no longer be deceived by people; for ten thousand ages, throughout heaven and earth, I am named Wondrous Sound.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the radiance from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the mark of a great man—and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shone everywhere upon as many Buddhas in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in one hundred and eight million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.

(Because the merit of the hairs on his entire body, the merit of his secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), the merit of his primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and the merit of his *ūrṇā-kośa* do not equal the merit of his *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance), it is therefore called a mark of a Great Man.)
At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara.

He attained the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Mark, the Lotus Samādhi, the Samādhi of Pure Virtue, the Samādhi of the Play of the Constellations King, the Samādhi of No-Conditioning, the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom, the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings, and the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
The Samādhi of Virtue, the Samādhi of Purity, the Samādhi of Playful Supernatural Powers, the Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom,
the Samādhi of the Adorned King, the Samādhi of Pure Radiance, the Samādhi of the Pure Treasury, the Unshared Samādhi, and the Sun-Turning Samādhi.
He attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of such great samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
(The sixteenth samādhi is the adornment of merit.
Śākyamuni Buddha’s light shone upon his body, and he addressed the Buddha Pure White Flower Constellation King Wisdom, saying:
"World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world to pay homage, draw near to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and [the assembly]."

He saw the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the Bodhisattva Sūradatta, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, the Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritramati, the Bodhisattva Vyūharāja, and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara: "Do not disparage that land, nor give rise to thoughts of it being inferior. Good [son]..."
"Good man, that Sahā world is uneven, with high and low ground; it is filled with earth, stones, mountains, and impurities.
The Buddha’s body is short and small, and the forms of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small, whereas your body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height."

My body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height. Your body is foremost in its beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of blessings, and its radiance is exceptionally sublime.

Therefore, you should go; do not hold that land in contempt. If one conceives thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their lands, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall now proceed to the Sahā world. All...

This is the power of the Tathāgata; it is the Tathāgata’s playful mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*); it is the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom. (The power of the Tathāgata is the power of the seat;

the power of supernormal faculties is the power of the chamber; the power of adornment is the power of the robe. This conveys the great purport of receiving and upholding the vast sūtra, and the essential core for benefiting sentient beings.)
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body, entered into samādhi. By the power of this samādhi,
not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak Mountain, he manifested eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels,
with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and *kiṃśuka* gems.
He used it to construct his terrace.
(As for Jāmbūnada gold: there is a river in the Western Regions near the Jambu tree; this gold is produced from within that river. *Kiṃśuka* is a red-colored gem.)
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotuses, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this omen appeared first? There are many tens of millions of lotuses, with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and pericarps made of karketana gems. At that time, Śākyamuni...

The Muni Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara wishes to come from the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharāja to this Sahā world, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, in order to make offerings to, attend upon, and pay homage to me;
he also wishes to make offerings to and hear the Lotus Sūtra. Mañjuśrī...

Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what roots of goodness have these bodhisattvas planted in the stream of existence, and what merits have they cultivated, that they are able to possess such great supernormal powers?
What samādhi do they practice? We pray that you will tell us the name of this samādhi.”
"We, too, wish to diligently practice this samādhi; only by practicing it can we behold the physical form, stature, and deportment of this bodhisattva.
We pray that the World-Honored One, through your supernatural power, will cause that bodhisattva to come so that we may see him.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa..."
"The Tathāgata shall manifest his form for you. Then, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas: "Come, noble sons!

The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī wishes to see your forms. At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas. As they passed through various countries, [the earth shook] in six ways.
The earth shook, and everywhere there rained down seven-jeweled lotus flowers. Hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

This bodhisattva’s eyes were like the broad petals of a great blue lotus; even if one were to combine the light of hundreds of thousands of millions of moons, his countenance would still be more upright and beautiful than that.
His body was of true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits and majestic power.
Blazing with brilliance and radiating light, his various marks were perfectly complete, like the firm body of Nārāyaṇa.

He entered a pavilion of the seven treasures and ascended into the void, remaining at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him reverent homage.
He has come to this Sahā world, to Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).

(In India there is a blue lotus whose petals are long and broad, with distinct blue and white colors and the appearance of eyes; thus it is said that his eyes are "like those of the vast [lotus]," etc.). The celestial *malla* is named Prabhāsa; he is handsome and possesses courageous strength.
Having arrived, he descended from the seven-jeweled terrace and, taking a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to where Śākyamuni Buddha was.

Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he presented the necklace and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom inquires after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness? Are the four great elements in harmony?"
Are you at peace? Can you endure the affairs of the world? Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Do they lack excessive greed, anger, ignorance, jealousy, stinginess, and pride?
Do they lack filial piety toward their parents, disrespect for śramaṇas, wrong views, or unwholesome minds?
Do they fail to restrain the five senses? World-Honored One, can sentient beings subdue all Māras and enemies? Has the long-extinguished Prabhūtaratna [Tathāgata] [attained parinirvāṇa]?
"Has the Tathāgata come from within the stupa of the seven treasures to listen to the Dharma? Furthermore, may you inquire after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna:
Is he at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure dwelling here for a long time? "World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will show it to me so that I may behold it."

(Now, the fact that the sutra inquires after his illness and distress in three places is because it accords with the fundamental principle of dwelling together within the realm of transformation; secondly, because it is so by the natural law of ritual propriety; and thirdly, because it relates to the three bodies which encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Since the emanated bodies have already dispersed, the stupa remains closed as before. Because Prabhūtaratna resides within the stupa, he makes this vow to manifest himself so that [the Buddha] may see him).
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to Prabhūtaratna Buddha, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to see you.
Then Prabhūtaratna Buddha addressed Gadgadasvara, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
You have come here for the sake of making offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, for hearing the Lotus Sutra, and to behold Mañjuśrī and the others. At that time...
The Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara planted?
(Since Prabhūtaratna had already complied with the Buddha’s request, he answered Gadgadasvara from within the stupa; he was then asked what roots of goodness Gadgadasvara had planted in past lives.)
"What merit did you cultivate to possess such supernormal power?
(This question addressed to Gadgadasvara asks: "What merit did you cultivate in the interim that you now possess such supernormal power?")
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King (*Meghadundubhisvararāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
His land was named Manifesting All Worlds (*Sarvalokadarśana*), and his eon was named Joyful Sight (*Priyadarśana*).
The Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) for twelve thousand years made offerings to the Cloud Thunder Sound King with a hundred thousand kinds of musical performances."
The Buddha, together with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven treasures, was offered as a gift.

By the karmic fruit and retribution of these causes and conditions, he has now been born in the land of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Śubhavyūha) and possesses such supernatural powers. Flower Virtue, what do you think?

Is the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound (Gandhahastin), who at that time in the presence of the Buddha Cloud Thunder Sound King (Meghadundubhisvararāja) performed offerings of music and presented those precious vessels, anyone other than this?

"O Manuṣya! It is this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara. Puṣpadatta, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and attended upon immeasurable Buddhas, having long planted the roots of virtue.
Furthermore, Puṣpadatta, he has encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Puṣpadatta, you see only that the body of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is here."
This Bodhisattva manifests various bodies and, in all places, preaches this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
He may manifest as the body of Brahmā, or the body of Śakra, or the body of Īśvara,
or the body of Maheśvara, or the body of a celestial general, or the body of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, or as a Cakravartin king.
The body of a holy king; or manifesting as the body of various minor kings; or manifesting as the body of an elder; or manifesting as the body of a householder;
or manifesting as the body of a government official; or manifesting as the body of a brahmin; or manifesting as the body of a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā;
or manifesting as the body of an elder’s or householder’s wife; or manifesting as the body of a government official’s wife.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of a Brahmin woman; sometimes they manifest in the body of a boy or a girl;
or they manifest in the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, and preach this sutra.
They are able to [save] all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and all places of great hardship.
He provides relief, even to the point of transforming into a female body within the royal harem to preach this sutra.
Flower Virtue, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is one who can protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifests such various transformations of his body here in the land of Sahā to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.
He is a master of supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom, never suffering any diminution thereof.
This bodhisattva, with various forms of wisdom, illuminates the Sahā world, causing all sentient beings to each attain what they need to know.

It is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions. If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests as a śrāvaka.
He manifests various forms to preach the Dharma. To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma.
To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a Bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma.
To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a Buddha, he immediately manifests the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma. In this way, according to their respective needs...
He manifests forms according to what is necessary for deliverance; even for those who are to be delivered through parinirvāṇa, he manifests parinirvāṇa.
Flower Virtue, such are the deeds of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, who has accomplished the power of great supernormal knowledges and wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has deeply planted [roots of merit]..."

"World-Honored One, in which samādhi does this bodhisattva abide, such that he is able to manifest himself in these various ways to deliver sentient beings—displaying the bodies of thirty-four ordinary beings and four noble ones (which, when summarized, constitute the ten dharma-realms and the six paths)? [This question asks: 'In what state does he now abide, yet remain thus sovereignly capable of benefiting others?']"
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue: "Good son, the name of that samādhi is 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is while dwelling in this samādhi that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound is able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

When this chapter on the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound was being spoken, eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound all attained [the vision of] manifestation.
The Samādhi of the Universal Form Body. In this Sahā world, immeasurable bodhisattvas have also attained this samādhi and dhāraṇī.

(Samādhi and dhāraṇī are identical in essence but differ in function: quiescence is samādhi; retention is dhāraṇī. Furthermore, the manifestation of the form body is samādhi; the eloquent discourse of voice is called dhāraṇī. Moreover, the tongue...)

The purification of the faculties is called *dhāraṇī*, while the purification of the remaining faculties is called *samādhi*; these are all but gateways to the Dharma of the purification of the six faculties.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara had made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, he returned to his own land.
As he passed through various kingdoms, the earth shook in six ways, and precious lotus flowers rained down, performing a hundred [miracles].

Accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of various kinds of musical instruments, having arrived in his own land, he was surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas as he went to the presence of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I went to the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings;
there I saw Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, where I paid homage and made offerings. Furthermore—
He beheld the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja, Vīryadatta,
and Śūradatta; he also caused these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.

(Guṇasvara returns to his native land; as for the shaking of the earth and the raining of flowers, it signifies that the Bodhisattva, having traveled through various lands, is able to bring benefit to all sentient beings.)
When this chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s coming and going was being preached, forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
and the Bodhisattva Puṣpadatta attained the Lotus Samādhi (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi).

When the Buddha emits light from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the mark of the Great Man—it signifies that this mind is the supreme, crown-like dharma. When he emits light from the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) between his eyebrows, it signifies that this mind surges forth from the Middle Way.

As for the light illuminating one hundred and eight million *koṭis* of Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction: when the minds of sentient beings stir, they are possessed of the one hundred and eight afflictions; yet the Sage thoroughly understands that such movement is non-movement, transcending affliction to realize the pure *dharmatā*.

Thus, by the power of *samādhi*, he manifests eighty-four thousand lotuses, which represents the transformation of the eighty-four thousand dust-like defilements into the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Universal Door of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva [Regarding the title, "Avalokiteśvara":

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the entry into the Way is described as relying solely on the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Here, however, the text primarily describes his meritorious virtues; therefore, it also incorporates the aspect of compassion. It is precisely this faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) that fully encompasses the merits of all six faculties, whereby he attains two kinds of supreme excellence from the Tathāgata:
first, above, he merges with the same power of compassion as all Buddhas of the ten directions; second, below, he merges with the same sorrowful longing of all sentient beings in the six realms.]

(A single mirror, vast and majestic, reflects all myriad forms; throughout the great trichiliocosm, where is there that does not shine? Transcending entirely the realm of sense organs and objects—yet who is it whose hands and eyes pervade the entire body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him thus:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named 'Avalokiteśvara'? The Buddha said:
"Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions,
and they hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly invoke his name."
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately perceives their cries and all obtain liberation.
If there are those who hold the name of this Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them, by virtue of this Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual power.
If they are being swept away by a great flood, by invoking his name, they will immediately find shallow ground. If there are hundreds of thousands...
There were ten trillion sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, and pearls, entered the great ocean;
suppose a black wind should blow their ship and cast it adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons.

If among them there is even a single person who calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, all such people shall attain liberation from the peril of the rākṣasas. For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who is about to be harmed and calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces.

They shall be destroyed and attain liberation. Even if the three-thousandfold world system were filled with yakṣas and rākṣasas wishing to come and harass people, upon hearing the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara being invoked, these evil spirits would not even dare to look at them with malevolent eyes, let alone inflict harm.
Furthermore, suppose there were a person—whether guilty or innocent—who was bound in shackles and manacles...

Should their bodies be bound by shackles and fetters, if they invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all such bonds shall be severed and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.

Suppose there were a great multitude of hostile bandits filling the three-thousandfold world system, and a merchant leader leading a caravan of merchants carrying precious treasures were to travel along a perilous road; among them, one person would cry out: "O virtuous sons..."
Sons, do not be afraid. You should with one mind invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings; if you invoke his name, [you shall be saved] from these hostile bandits.
They shall attain liberation. When the merchants heard this, they all raised their voices and said, "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
By invoking his name, they immediately attained liberation. Ajita, such is the majestic and sublime power of the spiritual authority of the Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Since the power of Avalokiteśvara is so great and his protective guardianship so vast, it extends far beyond merely the seven calamities; he is able to rescue and protect throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, he is described as "lofty and majestic."
If there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, and they constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately become free from desire.
If they have much anger and resentment, and they constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately become free from anger.

If they have much ignorance and delusion, and they constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will immediately become free from delusion. Akṣayamati, Avalokiteśvara...
O Bodhisattva Sound, you possess such great majestic spiritual power and bring benefit to many. Therefore, sentient beings should always keep you in mind with devotion.
If there is a woman who wishes to conceive a son, she should pay homage and make offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
They shall give birth to sons endowed with merit and wisdom. If they wish for a daughter, they shall give birth to a girl who is upright and possesses auspicious marks;
she will have planted the roots of virtue in past lives and will be loved and respected by all. Ajita, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such power.
If there are sentient beings who respectfully pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
their merit shall not be in vain (where "táng" means "in vain" and "juān" means "to discard").
Therefore, all sentient beings should receive and uphold the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

Ajita, suppose there were someone who received and upheld the names of sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and furthermore provided them with offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for the rest of their lives. What do you think? Would the merit of these good sons and good daughters...

“Is it not much, Akṣayamati? Akṣayamati replied, “It is very much so, Bhagavān. The Buddha said, “If there were another person who, for even a single moment, were to receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and were to pay homage and make offerings to him, the merit of these two persons would be exactly equal and without difference;
it could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas. Akṣayamati, [this is the power of] receiving and upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara.”
The Bodhisattva’s name is such that he attains the benefits of immeasurable and boundless merit.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara travel through this Sahā world?”

"Sixty-two *koṭis* [of beings]" refers to the abundance of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). "For as long as life lasts" refers to the abundance of time. "Endowed with the four requisites" refers to the abundance of seeds. "How does he wander? asks about bodily action (*kāyakarman*). "How does he speak? asks about verbal action (*vākkarman*). "Skillful means" asks about mental action (*manaskarman*).
"How does he preach the Dharma for sentient beings? What is the power of his skillful means, and what are its manifestations?

The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who are to be liberated by the body of a Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests in the body of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them. If they are to be liberated by the body of a Pratyekabuddha..."
To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a Pratyekabuddha, he appears in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma to them.

To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a Śrāvaka, he appears in the body of a Śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who should be liberated by appearing in the body of a Brahmā King, he appears in the body of a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma to them.
(As for the Brahma King— namely, the Lord of the Form Realm, named Śikhin, which here means "Crest"—
) to those who are to be liberated by the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma to them;
to those who are to be liberated by the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma to them.
(Śakra, who is the Heavenly King).
To those who should be liberated by means of the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who should be liberated by means of the body of a Heavenly General, he manifests the body of a Heavenly General and [preaches the Dharma for them].
He preaches the Dharma.

(8) To those who are to be delivered by the body of Vaiśravaṇa—such as the *kṣatriyas* (also called *kumbhāṇḍas*), the celestial *mallas*, and others—he manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be... [he manifests that form and] preaches the Dharma.
For those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, he manifests in the form of a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them.

(Vaiśravaṇa is translated here as "Much-Hearing. Among the celestial kings, he is the great one; among human kings, he is the minor one. Within the category of human kings, there are four types of wheel-turning monarchs [cakravartin]: those of gold, silver, copper, and iron.)
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a householder, he manifests the body of a householder and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a lay devotee, he manifests the body of a lay devotee and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a government official, he manifests the body of a government official and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a Brahmin...

He immediately manifests in the body of a brahmin and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be liberated through the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he immediately manifests in the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be liberated through the bodies of elders, lay devotees, officials, brahmins, or women...
For those to be delivered by the form of a woman, he manifests in the body of a woman and preaches the Dharma for them.
For those who should be delivered by the bodies of boys or girls, he manifests in the bodies of boys or girls and preaches the Dharma for them.

For those who should be delivered by the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—[he manifests in those forms and preaches the Dharma].

As for those to be delivered, he manifests himself before them all and preaches the Dharma to them. To those who are to be delivered by means of the Vajrapāṇi deity, he manifests as the Vajrapāṇi deity and preaches the Dharma to them.

In the past, there was a king whose queen gave birth to a thousand sons. Desiring to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, Kāśyapa Buddha drew the first lot, continuing down to Ruci, who drew the thousandth. A second queen gave birth to two sons.
One made the vow to become a Brahmā King and request his thousand brothers to preach the Dharma; another vowed to become a Vajra-wielder and protect the teachings of his thousand brothers.
Ajita, it is this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara who has accomplished such meritorious virtues, assuming various forms to travel through all lands and deliver sentient beings.
